If another element, namely the husks and the scrapings, were also enjoined, then there would be a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*)—[the sentence would have to enjoin both]: "They go to the *avabhṛtha*..."

“They go with the removal of the husks”—thus [it is said]. Now, for what purpose is the mention of the removal of the husks? It is purposeless, because there is no connection [between it and the preceding].

This being the case, we reply: "In the case of a substitute for a substance, it should consist of that substance. Regarding this substitute for a substance—namely, the rule "they go to the *avabhṛtha* with the husks of the grain"—it should consist of that substance; that is, it should consist of the husks of the grain. Why? Because of the connection with the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). The husks of the grain are directly heard in the text, whereas the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is inferential, being obtained through extended application (*atideśa*). [Objection: "But the sacrificial cake is also directly heard by its name. [Reply: Even if it is directly heard, it is obtained only in a general sense, whereas the husks of the grain are obtained in a specific sense; thus, [the general] is sublated [by the specific].

And [the word "puroḍāśa"] is a general term [restricted] by the specific [context]. Furthermore, while the *puroḍāśa* is understood through indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*), the "husks and scrapings" (*tuṣaniṣkāsa*) are understood through direct denotation (*śruti*); and between direct denotation and indirect indication, direct denotation is more authoritative. Therefore, [the sacrifice] has husks and scrapings as its substance. Now, as for what was said—that it is not connected with the *vabhṛtha*—[that is incorrect].

Regarding the objection that "it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) because of the mention of the removal of the husks," we reply: if the removal of the husks were enjoined independently of the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), then indeed there would be a syntactical split. However, the original *avabhṛtha*, characterized by the substance consisting of the removal of the husks, is what is being enjoined; thus, the injunction of an action accompanied by its quality is not contradictory. Furthermore, if the removal of the husks were not itself being enjoined, the mention of it [in the text] would be entirely purposeless.
It may be so. Therefore, the husked grain is a substance. "But the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) [is used] when there is no specific instruction," according to the Mīmāṃsā-darśana. [Page 48]

[The Bhāṣya states: "Because it has that as its material cause. What is logical?
That the apprehender is observed in a ritual action characterized by prescribed duties. Why?

It has been stated that "a word, when not prescribed [elsewhere], being heard, is a grasper [of properties]"—namely, "the naming of the action already mentioned" (7.3.1). In that context, even though this [word *siṃha*] possesses prescribed properties as seen in the *ātithya* rite, it is now seen joined with *siṃha* in a case where no properties are prescribed. This being the position reached, we reply: "But it is an injunction of a subordinate element (*guṇavidhi*), for it would not grasp [the properties], because of their equality. (17)

This is an injunction of an accessory (*guṇavidhi*); it enjoins the connection with Viṣṇu as the deity as an accessory of the *ātithya* [offering]. This [injunction] is unable to take up the ritual details (*dharma*). Why? Because of "equality" (*samatvāt*).

For this [injunction] is equal in regard to both the *ātithya* and that which is connected with the three [offerings]; just as it enjoins Viṣṇu as the deity there, so it does here as well. Furthermore, because the primary sense (*atyartha*) is impossible, the ritual details are [taken] through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*).

An appropriator is postulated; however, in this case, it is possible for the injunction regarding the deity to be the very meaning of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Therefore, this is not an appropriator—thus [it is concluded]. (7.3.9)

And it is the same with *nirmanthya* and so forth, as in the case of the word *vaiṣṇava*; here too, this word *nirmanthya* is etymological (*yaugika*), and it denotes fire that has been freshly churned.

"One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer cooked rice (caru)"—thus [it is said]. And how is that?

When there is an expectancy for a concluding injunction (vidhyanta), and when several types of concluding injunctions are present, [the choice is determined] by the specific mark (liṅga) consisting of the word "nirvapati" (he offers), which is not common [to other sacrifices] and is connected with the concluding injunction of the Darśapūrṇamāsa.

Its own *vidhyanta* (procedural details) would thus follow; nevertheless, when there is a possibility of the *vidhyanta* of multiple *apūrva*s—such as that of the *Āgneya* sacrifice and others—being applied, the *vidhyanta* of the *Āgneya* is restricted by a common characteristic, whether it be the fact of having a single deity or the material being an herb. This is understood as follows: "One should offer the *Sāṃnāyya* last, like the *Āgneya*; one should offer the *Āgnāvaiṣṇava* on eleven potsherds."

As in the case of the *agnīṣomīya* [sacrifice], it is thus everywhere; however, in order to avoid prolixity in the detailed exposition, the commentators have adopted the general term "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*). Thus, wherever there is even the slightest similarity—whether in terms of word, [form, or function]—[the rule applies].
The reading "tastha" in the Pā0 Pu0 manuscript is correct;
the reading "''" in the Kaṃ0 Saṃ0 Pu0 manuscript is [incorrect].
Chapter 8, Section 1.

Commentary (bhā.): If the object sought—such as the oblation, the deity, and so forth—or its qualities, such as color and the like, were perceived, then the procedural details (*vidhyanta*) pertaining to that [object] would be applicable. All of this has been stated here in brief.
The subsequent detailed exposition has been stated for the benefit of the disciples. As they also cite: "Having indeed spread out the great net and then condensed it, the Seer spoke;
for in this world, the learned desire both the concise and the detailed presentation."
Thus [ends the section]. (8.11.2a0)
Bhāṣya:
Section on the extended application (*atideśa*) of the *aiṣṭika* [rites] to the *kṣauma* [cloth].
Since the activity [of the procedure] is desired, the activity should apply to the Soma sacrifice. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 3 ||

It is heard in scripture: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. Regarding this, there arises a consideration: from which [source] should the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) for this [sacrifice] be derived? To that it is replied:

"Because of the commencement, the procedure of the iṣṭi should apply to the Soma [sacrifice]. The ritual procedure belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa should apply to the Soma. Why? "Because of the commencement": the Darśapūrṇamāsa procedure has commenced in the iṣṭis such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā; [it is seen] in the Dīkṣaṇīyā, the Ātithyā, the Prāyaṇīyā, and the animal sacrifice, after which the Soma [sacrifice] follows.

Even there, it is understood through its application (*pravṛtti*), just as in the case of "Devadatta is to be fed," "Viṣṇumitra is to be fed," and "Māṭhara, Kauṇḍinya, Bhāradvāja"— wherein even in the subsequent instances, the term "is to be fed" is connected by way of its application. Therefore,
the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the iṣṭi belongs to the Soma sacrifice.
Sūtra-bhāṣya: And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (Yukti 1)

"His one hundred *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s"—thus the ritual rules (*dharma*) pertaining to the *iṣṭi* are seen in the *soma* sacrifice; therefore, the *vidhyanta* (procedural framework) of the *iṣṭi* applies to this [sacrifice].
The reading in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā manuscript is "paṭharaḥ.
The reading in the Kaṭha Saṃhitā and likewise in the Kāṭhaka Saṃhitā is "ekaśataṃ prayājāḥ."
Puṇya-pāṭhaḥ | [Page 80]
Or rather, because it is prescribed as a complete injunction, it is something not previously established. (Siddhānta) || 5 ||
Commentary: Indeed, the Soma sacrifice is *apūrva* (unprecedented); it does not adopt any ritual details (*dharma*) from elsewhere.

Why? Because its procedure is prescribed [independently]. As it has been stated in the sūtra: "The *yajati* (sacrifice) is *pūrva* (preceded by a known model) because there is a prescription of the procedure" (7.4.1).
And this [Soma] has its procedure prescribed. Therefore, it is *pūrva*.
And because the absence of sprinkling with clarified butter for the *sva.* [the Soma] is a permanent restatement. (Yukti) || 6 ||
Bhāgavata-darśana-bhāṣya (Commentary on the Philosophy of the Bhāgavata)
Furthermore, there is a restatement of the absence of sprinkling with ghee (*abhighāraṇa*) in the context of the Soma sacrifice:

"The gods, having made ghee their weapon, slew Soma; therefore, the Soma-oblation is placed in the ladles (*srucau*), but they do not sprinkle the Soma with ghee. This is logical only if the Soma is an independent rite (*apūrva*); for if it were based on the *darśapūrṇamāsa* as its archetype, it would have been sprinkled with ghee and then offered with the two ladles. In that case, this scriptural observation would not be tenable.
Therefore, it is incomplete.
If it is argued that it is an injunction (vidhi), [we reply: No. (Ābhāsya) || 7 ||

If you think thus— because of the observation of the restatement of the absence of the holding of the *soma* as "the *soma* is full"— then why [is it] by virtue of being the archetype (*prakṛti*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices?
When the proposition stands that "this rule is not a prohibitor of the elision (*luk*) of *abhicāraṇa* which has already occurred," he challenges it with the following Sūtra.
[Sūtra 8: No, because it is a supplementary statement [of the context]. (Śrāddha-nirṇaya)
Bhāṣya:

This is not an injunction. Why? Because it is a supplementary part of another sentence (*vākyaśeṣatvāt*), and another injunction has been declared: "O divine Soma, may your immortal portion swell"—this [latter] is the supplement to that [former]. How is this known? By that...

"In this regard, both the statement of the Vṛtti and the Bhāṣya are improper; it is not known by what degree of *itikartavyatā* (procedural requirement) the expectancy is satisfied," and so forth—with these words, the author of the Vārttika has refuted the position of the Bhāṣya as being faulty.
[Page 81]
And because it is desired [as a supplement], as in: "They have indeed cut this Soma when they press it;

they have made it bitter for themselves when they pour it into the ladles; and because they have done something else nearby, when he says, 'O divine Soma, may thy stalk by stalk swell,' they cause that very stalk of his which was bitter for the one who took it to swell. If this were also an injunction, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); therefore, it is not an injunction.
And he suspects [the opposite] because of the lack of fasting; this is the prima facie argument (yukti). || 8 || (yu0) ||

Some [cite]: "If one were to depart without having fasted, they would not lead him to that world"—this being the case, since the procedure for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) exists, fasting would be mandatory; therefore, the rejection of fasting is not tenable.
Therefore, it is the unprecedented (apūrva).
a. The viewing [of the fire] should pertain to those sacrifices performed with oblations. (Śrāddha-niścaya) || 10 ||

As for the mention of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings that was taught as an indicative mark (*liṅga*)—namely, "For that [sacrifice], there are one hundred and one *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s"—that is a statement of the combination of those *prayāja*s and *anuyāja*s which belong to the rites such as the *dīkṣaṇīyā* that are constituent parts of the Soma sacrifice.
What is the reason? Because the Soma sacrifice is incomplete [without them], and because of the necessity of those [offerings] being so many.

Furthermore, because it exists [as a constituent], one can say that it is even a subsidiary part of that—just as the broth is a subsidiary part of the Vājapeya sacrifice. Therefore, the Soma comes first. (8.1.3.50)
The section concerning the gift of land for the pleasure of Indrāgnī and others.
In the case of the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there should be performance according to the [general] injunctions. 11.
Let this not be considered an example;

for there are others such as, "One desiring offspring should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni. Regarding that, there is a doubt: is the *viṣṭi* (the ritual sequence) that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa or that of the Soma sacrifice, or is it specifically that of the Darśapūrṇamāsa?

[Page 82] Bhāṣya: What is the conclusion? There is no fixed rule. The *vidhyanta* (procedural details) belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices exists also in the Soma sacrifice; and these *iṣṭis* require a *vidhyanta*, and by one *vidhyanta* alone—
It has been stated that [the result] must come to pass; however, no distinction is perceived in the restriction to either one [of the two alternatives].
Therefore, there is no fixed rule (aniyama). Sūtra.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "In the *iṣṭis*, there is the application (*pravṛtti*) of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* [rites]; this has been stated as the reason and is well-known. But what is that? It is the connection with the indicative marks (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*) in the injunction (*codanā*). But what, then, is that indicative mark of the archetype? It is the instruction regarding the deity by means of a *taddhita* suffix, the possession of potsherds (*kapāla*), and the word "he offers" (*nirvapati*)—as in: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Indra and Agni"; and likewise in the other case: "A cake on twelve potsherds to Indra and Agni."

Thus, the act of pouring out (*nirvapati*) is also mentioned in the text: "He pours out the oblations with the *agnihotrahavaṇī*. Furthermore, a specific rule for the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) is stated by means of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) from the archetype (*prakṛti*), according to the principle: "That which has an indicative mark [is applied] because of its connection with the purpose" (8.1.2). Therefore, the ritual procedure of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*) applies here. This is shown by the text: "At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* berry. Even in cases where there is no explicit indicative mark, an inference is made as in the case of the "pot-cooking rice" (*sthālīpulaka*). (8.1.4)
The section concerning the extension of the rules of the New and Full Moon sacrifices to the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma.
And because a sign is seen in the case of the animal sacrifice. || 12 ||

In the *Bhāṣya-pattrī*, the following is considered regarding the animal sacrifice (*agnīṣomīya*): Is the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*), or is it that of the Soma sacrifice (*saumika*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It is exactly as before. To this, the reply is stated: "And in the case of the animal sacrifice, because of the observation of indicative marks (*liṅga*). In the animal sacrifice, the ritual procedure is indeed that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. Why? Because of the observation of indicative marks—namely, "eleven... [etc.].

"Eleven fore-offerings (prayāja) and eleven after-offerings (anuyāja)," and likewise, "Having poured the clarified butter with the *laukī* ladle, he anoints the animal with the *juhū*. [Objection: "But you have cited an indicative mark (*liṅga*); from what [source] is the actual application obtained? [Response:
"From the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānyāt*). What is this commonality? It is the nature of being an explicit injunction (*vyakta-codanatva*)."
What is the manifest form? It is the possession of substance and deity, as in "the animal for Agni-Soma" (Agnīṣomīyaṃ paśum);
whereas the other is "the milk for Indra" (Aindraṃ payaḥ). But Soma is characterized by an unmanifest injunction. (8.1.1)
The section concerning the extension of the ritual characteristics of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice to the Savanīya and other animal sacrifices.
And [the rule] for the consecrated person applies to the others as well. || 13 ||

In this context, animal sacrifices (paśubandhas) serve as the examples—the Savanīya, the Nirūḍha-paśu, and those beginning with the Soma-related [sacrifices]. Regarding these, is the procedural rule (vidhyanta) that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (dārśapaurṇamāsika), or is it that of the Dikṣā [initiatory rite]? The term "Dikṣā" refers here to the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice, because of its connection with the Dikṣā. What is the prima facie position? That, according to the aforementioned reasoning, it is the rule of the New and Full Moon sacrifices.

— Thus [the objection stands]. To this, it is replied: "And in the case of the other animals, such as the *savanīya* and others, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *agnīṣomīya* applies, because of the commonality of the injunction to immolate (*ālambhati-codanā-sāmānya*), and because of the commonality of the injunction regarding the omentum and the skin (*vasā-tvac-codanā-sāmānya*). And this [text] demonstrates it: 'He proceeds with the omentum at the morning pressing, with the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) at midday, and with the meat (*jāghani*) at the third pressing'—thus it shows the performance of the subsidiary parts consisting of the omentum and the cake. And in some cases, there is a distinction, such as [the rule]: 'The post is made of *udumbara* wood...'"
"The sacrificial post becomes a broth"—thus [the text] indicates the sacrificial post. Therefore, the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma is the archetype for all animal sacrifices. (8.1.6)
The section concerning the extension of the rules for the evening [offering] to the *aikādaśina* animal sacrifice.
Because, among the animals of the set of eleven, there is the observation of the two-harnessing of the animal sacrificed on the day of Soma-pressing. || 14 ||

The animals of the *aikādaśina* group serve as the illustration—those recited beginning with "The ram-headed one is for Agni," and so forth, up to: "With the one for Agni he obtains offspring; with the one for Sarasvatī he creates a pair; with the one for Soma he procreates. Regarding these, there is a doubt: [to which specific ritual do they belong?]

—Is it the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, or rather that of the *savanīya*? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? By the reasoning previously stated, it belongs to the *agnīṣomīya*.

This being the position reached, it is said in reply: "In the case of the *aikādaśina* [animals], it is that of the *sautya*"; "the *sautya*" [refers to the sacrifice performed on the day of the Soma pressing].

[Page 84] Bhāṣya: Because they are characterized by the *sutyā* (Soma-pressing), the *savanīya* animals are included; therefore, their ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) applies to the *aikādaśina* (group of eleven) animals. Why? Because of the observation of the *hairaśanya* (the rule regarding the ropes): "Having taken two ropes for each of the two posts, he encircles each sacrificial post with two ropes. If the *āgnīṣomīya* were the archetype (*prakṛti*), there would be only one rope for each post.

"Now, why is this not a scriptural injunction? [The answer is: "In this context, the statement 'having taken two reddish-brown ones at each end' is what is being enjoined. If the duality of the reddish-brown ones were also enjoined, then there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*); therefore, that is merely restated as a reference (*anūdyate*). [Objection: But surely an indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been cited."
Whence is the attainment? It is said: since the nature of the body is the same, the lack of temporal distinction is a specific indicative mark; from that, there is attainment. (8.1.70)
The section concerning the extension of the rules for the set of eleven [animals] to the five sacrificial animals.
Its performance should take place with respect to the groups [of animals], because a sacrificial post is seen for each individual animal. || 15 ||
Bhāṣya:

Here, the following examples are cited: "In spring, one should sacrifice bulls with variegated marks," as well as, "One should sacrifice a white animal to Mitra, a black one to Varuṇa, and at the junction of waters and plants, one who is free from desire. Regarding this, it is now deliberated: [The discussion follows.]
Is the displacement (vidhvanta) that of the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, or rather that of the eleven animals (aikādaśina)?
According to the reasoning already stated, it belongs to the Agniṣomīya.

This being the prima facie view, the following is stated: "The application of that [displacement] should occur among the groups; the application of those eleven animals should occur in the groups of animals. Why? Because [it is prescribed] for each individual animal."

From the observation of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), [the text states]: "If one were to slaughter [animals] at three posts, he would diminish his own power and vigor and produce an enemy; therefore, one should slaughter at a single post"—thus, having prohibited the multiplicity of posts, it prescribes a single post for the *saucāmaṇī* sacrifice. This is logical if [the animal sacrifice] is divided into sets of eleven, for in that case there are multiple posts for each performance.
If the Agniṣomīya were the archetype, there would be only a single sacrificial post; however, this is not the case here.
Therefore, in groups of animals, there are eleven sacrificial posts for the Aikādaśinas. (8.1.80)
[Saṃbhāṣā] p. 85.
bhā. (Commentary)
Sabhāṣya, Section on the Extended Application of the Ritual Characteristics of the Soma Sacrifice to the Unmanifest Sacrifice.
But in the case of the unmanifested [plants], it belongs to Soma. || 16 ||

33. This is heard: "One should sacrifice with the Abhijit"—sacrifices of this kind. Regarding them, there is an inquiry into the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*): Is the procedure for these that of the Soma sacrifice, or that of the New and Full Moon sacrifices? Since there is no specific distinction, and thus an absence of restriction might be presumed, it is said: "But [the procedure] of the Soma [is applied], because of its being unmanifest (*avyakta*). What is this "unmanifest" nature? It is the absence of a specific material substance and deity.

For a sacrifice is manifested by means of its material and deity; however, these injunctions—such as "one should sacrifice with the Abhijit"—are without material or deity. In these cases, the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) of the Soma sacrifice should apply because of the commonality of being unmanifest (avyakta). Why? Because of the similarity of being unmanifest: the Soma sacrifice is also an unmanifest injunction, as in "one should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. But [one might object that] this [injunction], "one should sacrifice with Soma," is...
The injunction is explicit; nevertheless, because of the absence of a deity, it is unmanifest.

Thus, when it is enjoined as unmanifest in the text, "One should sacrifice with the Dūlāśa," it indicates the constituent parts of the Soma sacrifice, such as the Dīkṣaṇīyā and others, stating: "At the Dīkṣaṇīyā, twelve mānas of gold is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā);
at the Prāyaṇīyā, twenty-four mānas. Therefore, those [rites] belong to the Soma sacrifice.
The end of the section. (Adhyāya 1, Pāda 9, Sūtra).
The section concerning the extension of the dharma of the twelve-syllable [formula] to the *carmaleṣas*.
Among the groups [of sacrifices], [the rule] of the Dvādaśāha [applies]. || 17 ||
Here, the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) are the examples—those beginning with the *dīrātra* and ending with the *śatarātra*.

Regarding these, there is a doubt: is the procedure (*vidhyanta*) that of the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, or rather that of the *Dvādaśāha*? Since the former principle would suggest the *Saumika* [procedure] applies, it is replied: "In the case of groups (*gaṇeṣu*), the procedure is that of the *Dvādaśāha*. Why? "Because of the commonality of the injunction (*codanā-sāmānyāt*)."

"One should sacrifice with a twelve-day rite," "One should sacrifice with a two-night rite"—here the word *ahaḥ* (day) also denotes a day-and-night period, and the word *rātriḥ* (night) likewise provides a linguistic indicator (*liṅga*) contained within this term. Furthermore, there is the quality of being a group (*gaṇatva*) inherent in the meaning; for it is a group itself that is favored by the properties of a collection.
[Page 86]

In the case of a capable [sacrifice], it is not a single day. Starting from the statements "He cuts off hair with two [blades]" and "He cuts off flesh with two," [the text] shows that twelve *upasads*—a feature exceeding [the norm by] twelve—are present in the *Gavām ayana*. Therefore, among the multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*), the *Dvādaśāha* is the archetype (*prakṛti*).
In the subsequent sacrifices of the Rūpa-saṃvatsara series, there is the extension of the *mavā* and *abhyanīka* [rites]; and for the *gavya* sacrifice, it applies to those beginning with that. 18.

Bhāṣya: Here, the examples are the year-long sacrificial sessions (*saṃvatsarasatra*), such as the *Ādityānām ayana* and others. Regarding them, there is this inquiry: "Is the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) that of the *Dvādaśāha*, or is it that of the *Gavāmayana*? By the previously stated principle, the *Dvādaśāha* procedure being the prima facie view, it is replied: "And of the *Gavya* in those beginning with that. "Gavya" refers to the *Gavāmayana*, because of its connection with cows, as in the text: "The cows indeed performed this sacrificial session. Of that—

[The rule] "viśvantaḥ" would apply to those multi-year sacrificial sessions (*saṃvatsarasatra*) beginning with that [Mahāvrata]. Why? Because of the commonality of being a year-long session; for the text "the attendants (*upagātṛ*) sing along" indicates that the duty pertaining to the Mahāvrata applies to the *saṃvatsarasatra*, and "the priests (*ṛtvij*) sing along" applies to the thousand-year session. (8.1.11)
The section concerning the extension of the principles of a preceding school to subsequent schools.
And there would be the occurrence of [dharmas] belonging to one's own category within subsequent moments of the preceding [moment]. || 18 ||
Commentary:

"Nikāya" refers to a collection (saṅghāta) existing in a state of vertical succession; those who possess such a collection are called "nikāyins," just as, for example, the Sāhalas and the Sādyaskas. Of these, [the rule applies] to the former.
Certain dharmas have been prescribed, while those that follow are non-dharmic (adharmaka). Regarding this, one considers:
"Is the *vidhvansana* (disruption) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, or of the first group (*nikāyin*)?
Because the injunction for the Jyotiṣṭoma is unmanifest (*avyakta*).
This being the position reached, it is replied: "And for those belonging to a group, there is the performance of the *pūrṇāhuti* in the subsequent [rites].
(Jaimini Sūtra 8.1.8).
Page 87, Chapter 8, Pāda 1.

[It] should remain [there]. Why? Because of the commonality of being a *nikāyin* (belonging to a group), because of the commonality of being a *sāhasra* (thousand-fold) among the *sāhasras*, and because of the commonality of the *sādyaska* characteristics among the *sādyaskas*.

Thus, in every case, having prescribed a thousand-cow herd (*sāhasra*) as the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for the preceding *sāhasra*, the text shows it for the subsequent one: "As many as the northern cow of this *sāhasra* has been brought together..."
"There is indeed this world from that world"—thus [it is said].

Likewise, while in the earlier *Sādyaskra* sacrifice the tradition (*āmnāya*) states, "The three-year-old bull with testicles is the means for purchasing Soma for those who are contending," the subsequent [text] also shows that very same thing:
"A cow is the means for purchasing Soma; for among these, the one with testicles is excluded for those who are contending. Therefore...
The rules for the *pūrva* [fire] apply to those that follow. (8.1.12 Śrauta Sūtra)
Section on the Non-extension of the Fruit and Other Factors:

Kha. But because the ritual act does not proceed [in the case of the fruit], there is no connection of the fruit, the restriction, the agent, or the group, since they are dependent upon it. (Siddhānta Sūtra 20)

Bhāṣya: Here, the combination of the fruit, the restriction, the agent, and the aggregate serves as the illustration; the fruit is heaven, the restriction is lifelong repetition, the agent is one desiring heaven, and the aggregate is the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice. Regarding this, the inquiry arises: does the application of the fruit, the restriction, the agent, and the aggregate extend to the Sautrāmaṇī and other such rites, or not? What is the prima facie view? By the principle stated in [Sūtra] 8.1.11, "In the iṣṭis, there should be the application of the Darśapūrṇamāsa," it follows that there is application. This being the position reached, it is said in reply:
The activity belongs to the aggregate of the fruit, the rule, and the agent. Why?

Because of the non-activity of the action, and because the fruit and so forth are bound to it; first of all, the action does not proceed. What is the reason? Because dharmas proceed through fear, and the action [does not proceed].
That which is prescribed at the end of an injunction is [also] prescribed at its beginning;

therefore, it does not proceed, because of its non-proceeding. The meaning is that there is "non-connection" (ananvaya)—that is, non-proceeding—of the "aggregate of fruit, restriction, and agent. Why? Because, first of all, the fruit is bound to that.
"One should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices"— this is what is heard as being connected with the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
[Page 88]

Bhāṣya: Where there are the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there [the rule] ought to apply; however, those two do not exist in the Sautrāmaṇī and other such rites, and therefore heaven also does not exist there. Thus, the restriction "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa as long as one lives" pertains specifically to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices.
Bhāṣya on the Epitome (ET).

How could it exist in the case of a [single] constituent? Likewise, how could there be one who is bound by the ritual action, as in "one desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with the Darśapūrṇamāsa"—for how could that [bondage] exist when those two [sacrifices] are absent? Furthermore, the collection of the Āgneya and other [rites] does not exist in the Saurya and other [subsidiary rites]; therefore, how could their collection be present there?
Consequently, they do not function [as a whole] in those cases.
And also because the activity is for that purpose. (Yukti 21)
Moreover, the application of ritual elements (*dharma*) is for the sake of the ritual act, that is, to assist the ritual act;

yet the fruit and other such factors do not assist the ritual act. Rather, the fruit assists the person, not the ritual act, for it has been stated: "And the fruit [is for the person], because it serves the purpose of the person" (3.1.5). Furthermore, it has been stated that this restriction (*niyama*) is not a property of the ritual act, but is a property of the agent (*kartṛdharma*), as in: "Or rather, [it belongs] to the agent..."

"Because of the connection with the Vedic text" (2.4.20). Likewise, the one who desires heaven (*svargakāma*) is not for the sake of the ritual action; rather, the ritual action is for the sake of the one who desires heaven. For the one who desires heaven is not enjoined to the ritual action; rather, it is the ritual action that is enjoined for the one who desires heaven—namely, "One who desires heaven should sacrifice," meaning "He should sacrifice and perform no other [action]. Thus...

The collection [of subsidiaries] does not have ritual action as its purpose, but rather has the fruit as its purpose—as in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. Thus, because these [subsidiaries] would not contribute to the ritual action, their performance would be purposeless; therefore, they would not be undertaken.
And because there is no scriptural statement [to that effect]. (Sūtra 22, Ābhāsaniyama)

Bhāṣya: Objection: "If, due to their connection with the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, the results and so forth do not apply [to other rites], then it follows that the Prayājas and other such subsidiaries also do not apply, for they too are connected to those sacrifices. Response:
Although they belong to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices...

The details of the procedure (*vidhyanta*) are indeed extended by implication to the *saurya* and other such sacrifices; however, the results and so forth are not extended by the details of the procedure, because for them there exists a direct scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that prompts their performance.
It might be so; then they would proceed [to perform it], but that [condition] does not exist. Therefore, because of the nature of the Vedic revelation (śruti), they do not proceed. (8.1.13)
The section concerning the extension [of rules] to the *modohana* and other [vessels] for those desiring a beautiful face:
In the case of [rites performed] for the sake of a desired quality (*guṇakāma*), there should be application because of being dependent [on the primary rite]. (23) (50)

The desire for secondary results (*guṇakāma*) provides the examples: "One should bring water in a *godohana* vessel for one desiring cattle," "O men, sing unto him," and "One should employ the *pratipad* verse for one desiring a village," and so forth. In this regard, an inquiry is made: do the desires for secondary results apply to the modified (*vaikṛta*) rites, or not? Therefore, the commencement begins with the ladle (*sruk*): "In the case of desires for secondary results, there should be application because they are dependent [on the primary act]"; that is, there is an "application" (*pravṛtti*) of the desires for secondary results.

Why? Because it is dependent. The *godohana* vessel is dependent upon the act of carrying water (*praṇayana*), as expressed in the injunction: "One should carry water with the *godohana*. Now, that act of carrying water proceeds, and when the substratum proceeds, that which depends upon it also proceeds; just as when a cloth is being pulled, that which is dependent upon it [the cloth] is also pulled along.

The extraordinary [result] is also drawn forth; and just as the *camasa* vessel is employed, and just as it is said, "One should make a sacrificial post of *khadira* wood for one desiring vigor," so too would the *godohana* vessel be employed.
And when the *godohana* is employed, the desire dependent upon it must also be fulfilled.
Therefore, those who desire specific qualities engage [in ritual action].
Or rather, there is cessation [of the ritual], because of the difference in the agent. (Siddhānta 24)

Bhāṣya: "The cessation [of the use] of those things desired for their qualities" means their non-employment. Why? "Because of the difference in action," that is to say, because of the difference in purpose.
The purpose of the *godohana* vessel is one thing, while that of the *camasa* cup is another;
the *camasa* serves the purpose of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), whereas the *godohana* serves the purpose of the person (*puruṣārtha*). Thus it has been said:
"In that which a person finds pleasure, there is a desire for its acquisition, because it is distinct [from the sacrifice]" (JS 4.1.2)—this is stated here.

That which is not for the sake of the ritual (*akratvartha*)—for what purpose would one engage in it? For its engagement is indeed for the sake of assisting the ritual; such is the case with the *pratipad* verses. Therefore, those who desire subsidiary results (*guṇakāma*) should not engage in them.

[Page 90] As for what was proposed— that "just as there is an engagement [to act] in the case of the injunction, 'One desiring vigor should make a sacrificial post of khadira wood,' so too is it here"— to that we reply: "Or rather, because it is not a subordinate part of that [specific desire], and because it serves the purpose of the sacrifice, there would be engagement [in the ritual]."

25 || (Pūrvapakṣayukti-nirṇaya) Bhāṣya: "Or rather," in such cases, there should be an application [of the rule]. Why? Because it is a modification of that; the *khadira* wood is not a modification for the sake of the sacrifice, but this [other wood] is also indeed for the sake of the sacrifice.
As it has been said: “But when one thing serves two purposes, there is the principle of ‘separateness of conjunction’” (4.3.50).

If [the act] were for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), it would proceed like the *palāśa* leaf; and while that [act] proceeds, the desire (*kāma*) dependent upon it also proceeds, for he accomplishes that [desire] by means of the *khadira* wood, and that...
The Khadira wood exists; therefore, it will accomplish the desired result. (8.1.14a)
The section concerning the optional alternative for the touching of the two [cakes] in the *saurya* cooked rice offering.
Sūtra: In a single ritual act there is an option, because the injunction is one and there is no division. (26)
Bhāṣya:

"One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a cooked oblation to Sūrya"—thus it is heard in scripture. However, in the archetype (prakṛti), there exists this pair of touchings: "He should touch the full moon [offering] with the Caturhotṛ formula, and the new moon [offering] with the Pañcahotṛ formula. That [pair] is extended here by the rule of transfer (codaka). In that regard—

Saṃjaya asks: When the Sautrāmaṇī is performed on the full moon day, should it then be concluded with the *catuhhotṛ* formula? Or when it is on the new moon day, then with the *pañcahotṛ* formula? Or is there an option for both—either the *catuhhotṛ* or the *pañcahotṛ*—on either occasion? What is the prima facie view? That there is a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*). Why? Because of the favoring of the extended injunction (*codaka*) from the archetype (*prakṛti*).
A fixed rule has been established; here too, the injunction brings about that fixed rule.
This being the case, it is replied: in this single ritual act, there is a modification of the *saurya* offering.
Why? Because there is no separation, since the injunction is one. This is a single injunction: "One desiring spiritual luster should offer this rice-pap (caru). In that case, there is no separation.
[Page 91]
Chapter 8, Section 1.

[Objection: Let it be so; both [options] are obtained through direct injunction (*abhimaśena*). Since they have a single purpose, a combination (*samuccaya*) is not possible; therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*). As for the argument that "there is a fixed rule (*vyavasthā*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*)," that is not a matter of time (*kāla*), but rather a matter of the collection (*samudāya*). Nor...
Those two [offerings] constitute the two groups for the Saurya sacrifice. [Objection:

"If this is so, then the touching (*abhimarśana*) would not apply at all, because those two groups do not exist. To this it is replied: It does not apply, if the touching were intended for the two groups; however, since those two groups are not to be touched, [the touching applies] to the individual members of the groups.
That is stated by way of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*): the modification belongs to the constituent parts; therefore, the rule of transfer (*codaka*) extends it there as well. (8.1.15)
Section on the Extended Application of the Āgneya [Rite] at Evening:
Sūtra 27—There should be an option because of the commonality of the characteristic mark. (Pūrvapakṣa)

In the *Bhāṣya*, it was stated that in the *Saurya* rite, the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* applies—according to the rule, "The application of the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* is [extended] to the *Iṣṭis*" (Sūtra 8.1.11).

However, there are indeed constituent rites therein, such as the *Āgneya* and others. Regarding this, the inquiry is: does the procedure of any particular *Darśapūrṇamāsa* rite apply to the *Saurya*, or...

Regarding the Āgneya [sacrifice]: what is the prima facie view? It is that there is an option (*vikalpa*). Why? Because of the commonality of the indicative mark (*liṅga*). When the procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Full-Moon sacrifice is extended to the Saurya sacrifice, the indicative mark that is taught—namely, "At each *prayāja* offering, he offers a *kṛṣṇala* grain"—is applicable to the procedure of all [the sacrifices]. Furthermore, there is no combination (*samuccaya*); therefore, there is an option.
Bhāṣya: Or rather, it should be restricted because of the identity of purpose; for, as in the previous case, it is a modification. (Siddhānta) 28.

"The procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Āgneya [offering] should be restricted [to the Sāṃnāyya]. Why? Because of "identity," that is to say, because they have the same deity—the Āgneya has a single deity, and the Sāṃnāyya does as well; therefore, by this mark (*liṅga*) of having a single deity, the procedure of the Āgneya should be restricted, "because it is like the previous case" (Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 8.1.2).
[Page 92] Mīmāṃsā-darśana.

This [sacrifice] of the Saurī belongs to the full [model]. It requires the entire procedure previously mentioned, for "it is a modification" (vikāra)—this is the sense; all modifications are based on the original, because the injunctive sentences are incomplete. In that regard, it was stated that the determination of the specific procedure occurs through an indicative mark (liṅga); and the state of having a single deity is such a mark. Therefore, the procedure of the Āgneya sacrifice applies.
Sūtra: "If it is argued that it is not so, because it is not heard [in the scripture]. (Ābhāsya)

To this, [the opponent] replies: "This might be so if multiplicity were heard [in the text], but it is not heard. How so? This designation is made by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*), namely, 'sauryam' and likewise 'āgneyam'. In that case, the precise mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) is not known: is it [that the sun is the deity]?"
"The deity of this [offering] is also to be heard from the *svayamātṛṇṇā* bricks," and likewise in the case of the *āgneyī* bricks as well.
It may be so, because of the existence of an indicative mark. || 30 ||
Bhāṣyasūtra (Āvaśyakaniryukti) ||

"There may be a fixed rule regarding singularity. Why? Because of the existence of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). What is that mark? Singularity is heard in the supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) of the *saurya* [offering]:
'He approaches that very Āditya with his own share;
he (Āditya) leads him to union with Brahman and glory. And in the case of the *āgneya* [offering], [it says] 'The Aṅgirases, indeed, from here...'"
The best [of them] went toward heaven; they approached the sacrificial site and saw the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) crawling about like a tortoise.
They said to it: "Be intent upon Indra! Be dear to Bṛhaspati!
Be dear to the Viśve Devas! It said to them: "Not for the sake of intent. They said to it: [Continue as before].

"Be strengthened for the beloved," he said; "O beloved one, when the cake on eight potsherds for Agni is offered unswervingly at the new moon and the full moon, one indeed prospers Agni with his own share.
And likewise there is the observation of another purpose [in this regard]. (Sūtra 31) (Nirṇaya).

In the *anuvākyā* verses there is a unity of purpose: "Agni is the head of heaven" in the verse dedicated to Agni, and "Upwards that Jātavedas" in the verse dedicated to Sūrya. [Objection: "But is this not a redundant presentation of these two indicative marks? [Response: It is not redundant; for here, one [mark]... [Page 93]

The view is that there are two types of injunction (*codanā*): one pertaining to the impulsion (*madyagata*) and one pertaining to the direction (*codanāgata*). That which pertains to the impulsion is that which causes one to reach [the action], while that which pertains to the direction is that which illuminates what has already been reached. (8.1.16)
The section concerning the greater strength of the commonality of the oblation when there is a conflict between the deity of the formula and the deity of the sacrifice.
Or rather, in case of conflicting injunctions, it should be regulated by the oblation, because the ritual act is designated by that [oblation]. (Siddhānta 32)

Bhāṣya: This is heard [in the scriptures]: "One should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Indra," and "Milk belongs to Agni. In this regard, there is a doubt: on account of the commonality of the deity, does the procedure (vidhyanta) of the Aindra cake apply to the Sānnāyya, and that of the grain-offering (auṣadha) apply to the milk belonging to Agni?

The commonality of the deity is more powerful; however, due to the commonality of the oblation (*havis*), is the commonality of the oblation stronger in the latter case of the *sānnāyya* and in the former case of the *śrīṣadha*? What is the conclusion? It is said: the commonality of the deity is stronger.

Why? Because of primacy. The deity is governed by primacy—as in "belonging to Indra" or "belonging to Agni"—whereas the oblation is governed by subordination. When there is a conflict between these two, preference must be given to the primary, because the primary functions without contradiction, whereas the subordinate is [governed] by the primary.

There is a conflict in the application [of the rule]. Therefore, the commonality of the deity (*devatāsāmānya*) is stronger. This being the position reached, we reply: "In case of conflict, it should be determined by the oblation (*havir*); in this conflict between the oblation and the deity, one should be determined by the oblation.
Why? Because the ritual act is dependent upon that; the ritual act [consists of] the substance [being offered] toward the deity."
"Utsarga" (the act of relinquishing) is perceived—that is, it is apprehended—in relation to the sacrificial oblations (*havis*).

The oblation is seen being relinquished. What follows from this? From this, [it follows that] the oblation is proximate to the ritual action, and proximity is an indicative mark (*liṅga*). "But is not the deity also connected with the sacrifice? No.

"Without it, the sacrifice takes place. It is replied: True, they are connected; however, that [connection] is one of remote assistance (*ārādupakāriṇī*), and thus it is not abandoned; therefore, it is extrinsic (*bahiraṅga*). Consequently, the commonality of the oblation (*havis-sāmānya*) is stronger.
And because of the connection with that action. (Yukti) [Page 94] Sūtra 33.
Bhāṣya:

"And by being conjoined with that oblation (haviḥ), the ritual act is enjoined—as in 'the offering for Indra' (aindram) or 'the offering for Agni' (āgneyam)—where the word denoting the oblation is the primary term. What follows from this? From this, [the connection] appears in the intellect."
That mark is "proximate" (sannihita); for example, smoke that has entered the domain of cognition is the mark of fire, but its mere existence is not.

"But surely, a deity is also heard here, as in the expressions 'belonging to Indra' and 'belonging to Agni'. It is replied: "The mention of the deity is subordinate [to the substance]. (Sūtra 34, Ābhāsaniścaya).

In this case, the deity is heard as the qualifier and the oblation as the qualified; and that which is qualified is present in the intellect, not the qualifier. Therefore, that qualified [deity] is excluded from the qualified [oblation].

How is this known? From the connection with the adjunct of the qualified object (*viśe�ṣya*). Just as when it is said, "The king’s man is to be honored," it is understood that the man is to be honored, not the king; so too here, when it is said, "The milk for Indra (*aindraṃ payaḥ*)," the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥ*) is present in the mind, not the deity. And furthermore...

It has been stated that the indicative mark (liṅga) is present in the cognition [of the mantra]. Therefore, the commonality of the oblation (havis-sāmānya) is more powerful; consequently, the procedure of the cake for Agni (āgneya-vidhyanta) applies to the cake for Indra (aindra-puroḍāśa), and the procedure of the milk-oblation (sānnāyya-vidhyanta) applies to the milk for Agni.

“*Guṇatvena devatāśrutiḥ*”—this is another interpretation of this sūtra. This is the subsequent sūtra: "As for what was said—that the similarity of the oblation (*havis*) is stronger—this is not correct; rather, the similarity of the deity (*devatā*) is stronger. Why? Because of the *sarvavedyatva* [the quality of being known across all Vedas]."

Effort is solely for the purpose of propitiating the deity, for a pleased essence bestows the fruit. Thus it is heard in scripture: "Indra, being satisfied, satisfies him with offspring and cattle"—referring to that which is known as the means of propitiating Indra. Furthermore, when Indra is to be propitiated, that very same [means] must be employed; therefore, the commonality of the deity is more powerful.
— thus [it is said].
To this we reply: this would indeed be so if the fruit were to arise from the deity.
[Page 95]
Chapter 8, Section 9.

2. [The Bhāṣya states: "But the fruit [arises] from the sacrifice," for it is heard in scripture: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice. As for the statement, "Indra, being satisfied, [grants him this]," to that it is replied: "The mention of the deity is as a subordinate factor" (*guṇatvena*); the deity is a subordinate element in the sacrifice, and its status as a giver is expressed by way of praise.
For example: "The village was given to me by the minister," or "The village was given to me by the commander-in-chief.
Yet neither the minister nor the commander-in-chief has power over the village; the king alone has such power.
When the other is subordinate, the statement regarding his being the giver is merely for the sake of praise. Therefore...
By the very same reasoning already stated, the generality of the oblation (*havis*) alone is more powerful—thus [ends the section]. (8) 1.17 (Śrauta-sūtra).

The section concerning the extension of the application of medicinal herbs to the hundred-wool blanket and the footwear.
Gold possesses the properties of clarified butter because of its luminosity. (Purvapaksha)

It is heard in scripture: "One desiring long life should offer a caru-oblation of gold weighing one hundred *kṛṣṇalas* in clarified butter (*ghṛta*) to Prajāpati. In that case, it should follow the ritual procedure (*dharma*) of the *upāṃśuyāja*. Why? Because of the commonality of being luminous (*tejas*). Luminosity is the common property; gold is the essence of stones, and clarified butter is the essence of cows—this is the meaning. Alternatively, gold is radiant because of its brilliance, and clarified butter is likewise radiant because of its clarity. Therefore, due to this commonality, the oblation of one hundred *kṛṣṇalas* follows the ritual procedure of the *upāṃśuyāja*.
And because of the favor toward the Dharma. (Yukti 36)
Furthermore, many properties of the clarified butter (ājya), such as pouring and so forth, are observed in gold;
however, the properties of the plant-offering (oṣadha), such as threshing and so forth, would be excluded. Therefore, the properties of the clarified butter [apply] even to the gold.
The reading in the Pāṭha of the Soḍhala-puṭa is "ghṛtena."

Or rather, it is medicine, because of its clarity. (Siddhānta) || 37 ||
Alternatively, there is a piercing [of the skin] for the vegetable medicine (śrauṣadha) upon gold. Why? Because of its clarity;
gold is clear, and the vegetable medicine is also clear. What, then, is the distinction between these two commonalities? Indeed, there is none at all, except for that of clarity.
The twofold cause is the corroborative factor; of these, the first is the favor shown toward your majesty.
And because of the word "caru. (Yukti 1)

And here the word *caru* occurs: "The *caṣma* belongs to Prajāpati. And the word *cara* is a designator of vegetable food (*auṣadha*); therefore, it is a powerful indicative mark (*liṅga*) for vegetable food.
And in that case, it is not heard [in the scripture]. (YU 2) || 38 ||

And regarding that clarified butter (*ājya*), cooking is heard [in the scripture]: "He cooks in ghee. What follows from this? From this it follows that, since the cooking is obtained through the procedure of the vegetable-oblation (*auṣadha*), only the clarified butter will be enjoined there; whereas in the case of the clarified-butter procedure, the cooking is already established.
If both [the cooking of rice and the cooking of grain] were to be enjoined, the sentence would be split.
Regarding the statement, "And because of the mention of cooking in that [other sacrifice]," there is another interpretation:

here it is said, "Since this very [cooking] is heard here, therefore its ritual procedure (vidhyanta) applies. To this, the following reply is given: "And because of the mention of cooking in that"; the cooking belonging to the Darśapūrṇamāsa is heard "in that" other sacrifice as a subordinate quality; that commonality [of the act of cooking] exists there.
But the group of oblations (*havirgaṇa*) possesses clarity, as does the word *cara*; therefore, those two are stronger. (8.1.18–20) [Page 97]
In the Madhyandina recension,
the properties of the Upāṃśuyāja are applicable to the subsequent offerings, as they fall within the scope of the same injunction.
ba. Honey and water, due to their common property of being liquid, would be a modification of milk. || 40 ||
(Pūrvapakṣa)

In the *Bhāṣya* on [Jaimini-sūtra] 8.8.8, it is stated regarding the constellation Citrā: "Curd, honey, ghee, parched grain, water, and rice—this mixture belongs to Prajāpati. And therein, [it is said]: "Honey and water..."
"It should be a modification of milk. Why? "Because of the commonality of the suffix -iva; for both honey and water are liquids, and milk is also liquid."
Or rather, clarified butter [should be used], because of the similarity of color. (Siddhānta) || 41 ||
Bhāṣya:
Or rather, these two [the curd and the honey] might undergo modification; the procedure (vidhyanta) of the Upāṃśuyāja would apply to them.
Why? Because of the similarity of color; for honey and water are of the same color as clarified butter (ājya).
And because of the favor toward the Dharma. (Yukti 42)

Furthermore, many properties belonging to other substances—such as honey and water—can be applied [to milk], such as straining and so forth; however, properties belonging to milk itself, such as milking and so forth, cannot.
And because the preceding [reason] is not distinguished [from the present one]. (43)

As for the reason previously stated— that the general property of fluidity is common [to both], and clarified butter (*ājya*) also becomes liquid through contact with fire— therefore, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the *upāṃśuyāja* applies to honey and water. (8.1.19)

The section concerning the extension of the rules for the *iṣṭakā* (bricks) to the *socāma-thūri* [type of altar] by means of the *iṣṭakā-dhātu*.
The status of being Soma belongs to the *vājina* because of its connection with the *saucāmaṇī*, and to the cups (*graha*) because of the application of that same designation. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 1 ||

Regarding the *vājina* offerings heard in the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices—namely, "to the Vājins, the *vājina*"—and the *surā* cups in the *Sautrāmaṇī* sacrifice—namely, "he draws the cup for the Aśvins, for Sarasvatī, and for Indra"—there arises a doubt: does the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of both belong to the Soma sacrifice, or to the New and Full Moon sacrifices? To this it is replied: "In the case of the *vājina*..."
And in the *Saucāmaṇī* and the *Mahā* sacrifices, there is "fullness with Soma," which is the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) belonging to the Soma sacrifice. Why?
Because of "the designation" (*tācchandyāt*), that is, because of the word "Soma. For the word "Soma" is heard here:
"Soma indeed is the swift *vājina*, Soma [is the *vājina*]," and it is not the case that the *vājina* is Soma.

Nor is there any similarity between those two [the *turāṣāḍ* and the *indramādana*] and the *soma*; and it is through similarity that a word for one thing is applied to another. Therefore, similarity is what is prescribed here.
And in this context, only the properties of the *soma* can be prescribed as the basis for that similarity, and nothing else. Sa...
This is a transfer of properties by name, not by the end of the procedure, as in the case of the Agnihotra in the Kauṇḍapāyina sacrifice.
And [the rule applies] also to the secondary *vaṣaṭ*-calls. (Yukti 1)

The Bhāṣya shows that the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* also possesses the characteristics of Soma: "He performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* with 'Oṣṭhī for the Vājina'; he performs the *anuvaṣaṭkāra* with 'Oṣṭhī for the Surā'."

two silken garments are tied [to it]; young sprouts of grain are present"—if this were a single injunction, there would be sentences with multiple meanings, such as [the injunctions regarding] the *kayā* and the lead (*sīsaka*), and so forth.
They perform [the rites]. Therefore, the ritual procedure (vidhyanta) of the Soma sacrifice applies to both.
kha. Or rather, it should be restricted by the oblation, because that is its purpose. (Siddhānta) || 5 ||

Or rather, by virtue of the commonality of the oblation (*havis*), the procedural details (*vidhyanta*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*dārśapaurṇamāsika*) should be applied here. Why? Because it is a modification (*vikāra*) of that;
for *surā* and *vājina* are modifications of the sacrificial food-oblation (*auṣadha*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and *surā* is a modification of the *sānnāyya*.
The swift steed.
i. Praśaṃsā: The word "Soma" [is used] as a praise. (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti-nirṇaya)
No, no. Now, as for what was said—"on account of its being so designated"—to that we reply: it is for the purpose of praise.

The word "Soma" does not have the sense of an injunction, because there is no injunctive element present. —this is the meaning; here, the offering to Śuci is second, while in the archetype (prakṛti) the offering to Agni-Soma is second; elsewhere, the offering to Agni-Viṣṇu is first, while in the archetype the offering to Agni is first;
by the mark of commonality of place, the latter [belongs] to the former [offering], and the former to the latter.
A transformation.
[The time] would be restricted by its own deity, because it possesses a [specific] word, whereas for the other there is no such scriptural statement.

(Siddhānta) Or rather, there should be no restriction of place; what then? [It is restricted] "by the deity," on account of the commonality of the deity. Why? Because the deity is denoted by a word, as in "this is the Āgnivaiṣṇava" and "to Agni."

Regarding the phrase "for the sake of purity": because another deity is not heard of—that is, no other deity is mentioned in the scripture—but rather [the deity] is understood through the context (prakarana). What is heard? This follows from it: in an injunction for ritual action, the cognition of the deity arises because it is immediately proximate.
The other, however, arises in dependence upon what precedes and follows; therefore, it is secondary.
[End of] the eighth section of the first quarter.

And it is logical that [the procedure] should be repeated. Therefore, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the cake for Agni applies to the one for Śuci-Agni, and that of the cake for Agni-Soma applies to the one for Agnāvaiṣṇava. (8.3.1)
In the Janaka-saptarātra sacrifice, because of the presence of the *cit* bricks, there is an extended application (*atideśa*) of the twelve-day rite; [this is] the section concerning that.
[Sūtra 3: "In an injunction for a group (*gaṇa*), the repetition of that which possesses the indicative mark (*liṅga*) should be understood, as in the case of the *Āgneya*. (Pūrvapakṣa)

In the *Janakasaptarātra*, it is heard: "There are four *cintya* days," and elsewhere it is heard: "There are nine *cintya* days. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is this a repetition of the first [day] of the *pārṣṭika* [section], or is it an injunction for various stomas for twelve additional [days]? What [is the conclusion]?

Is it obtained? — "In the case of an injunction for repetition (*āvṛtti*), that which has the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) should be understood as the object of repetition, just like the *Āgneya* [offering]. In such an injunction for repetition, that which possesses the characteristic mark—namely, the threefold nature (*tritva*) of the first day of the side-period (*pārśvika*)—that alone should be understood as the object of repetition, because of the commonality of the injunction (*codanāsāmānyāt*), "just like the *Āgneya*. For example, in the case of "to Agni Pāvaka" and "to Agni Śuci," because of the identity of the deity and the commonality of the injunction, there is a repeated performance (*abhyāsa*) of the *Āgneya* sacrifice with all its parts; so it is here as well.
Or rather, it is for various days, because it is a composite whole and because of the injunction indicated by the sign of commencement. (Siddhānta)

Bhāṣya: Or rather, the [twelve-day] days (*dvādaśāhika*) should proceed, not the first day alone. Why? Because of its being a composite whole (*saṅghātatvāt*); this is declared to be a composite whole, namely, "four thirty-day periods"; for it is established as consisting of distinct parts.
"Four"— thus [are] the agreements; "it exists"—
thus there are the various days, twelve and also those well-established ones.
But it is not possible to effect the connection of *tu* and *ṭi*.
It is prescribed.
[Page 119] The verbal root *bhaj* is heard; therein, the activity belongs to that which has become subordinate, by way of elimination (*pāriśeṣyāt*); and where...
And there is the injunction to sit upon the sacrificial seat (*āsana-upāvicodanā*) for that which has become the *sattra*. Why? Because it is equal to the archetype (*prakṛti*) by its very nature;
for the root *vid* (to sacrifice) becomes synonymous with the word "equal" (*tulya*) by its very nature.

Therefore, due to the commonality of the injunction, there is a restriction to the archetype; and the injunction to sacrifice (*yajati-codanā*) is of the nature of a *ahīna*, as in: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*). [This applies] to that which has become the *sattra*.

And there is the injunction regarding the practice of sitting: "Those desiring supernatural power (*ṛddhi*) should approach [the fire] for twelve days; those desiring supernatural power should sit near [the fire] for twelve days."
The *hirācā* and other sacrifices up to the *ekādaśarātra* are *ahīna* sacrifices because they are enjoined by the term *yajati*. (Sūtra 26; Ābhāsa-nirṇaya 1)

"Now, which are those multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) enjoined for procreation, in which he proceeds as one who is deficient? Or which are those enjoined for sitting and approaching, in which he is complete? To this it is replied: "From the *dvirātra* up to the *ekādaśarātra*..."

Regarding "non-deficiency": therein, one proceeds as one who is non-deficient, because they are enjoined by the word "sacrifice" in the injunction, "One should sacrifice with the Hiraṇyakeśin [rite]."
[Objection: In the case of the thirteen-night sacrifice and others, [the rule does not apply] because there is an injunction for both the seat and the means of approach. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya 2)

"Those desiring non-duality should undertake the thirteen-night sacrifice; those desiring stability should perform the fourteen-night sacrifice"—thus it is stated in the *Bahvṛca* [Brāhmaṇa]. Likewise, because the injunction for the *yajati* (sacrificial offering) is absent, the thirteen-night sacrifice and others are not considered "deficient" (*ahīna*), for they indeed consist of *yajati*-injunctions. Furthermore, because the injunction for the *āsana* (seating/chanting) is the *sūkta*, therefore the thirteen-night sacrifice and the others are *satras*.
And those [words] are injunctive—thus [it is said].
And because of an indicative mark. (28) (Yukti)
Prajāpati is indeed the Adhidaiva; he begot the subsequent days and nights. He said to them:
"Do not abandon me," and so it was for them.

Sūtra Bhāṣya:
Both the Pañcadaśarātra and the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana are indeed *satras*.

Why? Because they have an *atirātra* on either side; both of these are *ahīna*s because they have an *atirātra* on one side or the other. First, there is the fifteen-night sacrifice (*pañcadaśarātra*), which begins with "The *agniṣṭut* is an *agniṣṭoma*, an *atirātra*," and continues through the ten-night sacrifice (*daśarātra*) and ends with the concluding *atirātra* (*udayanīya*). Likewise, the *kuṇḍapāyinām ayana* also begins with "They offer the *agnihotra* for a month" and extends up to "The ten-night sacrifice, the *mahāvrata*, and the concluding *atirātra*."
And that which is an *atirātra* on one side is an *ahīna*. How is this known?

Because the state of being an *ahīna* is seen in those cases where it occurs; that is, "in those cases where it occurs"—meaning in those instances where there is an *atirātra* on one side—the state of being an *ahīna* is heard [in scripture]: "That which is an *atirātra* on one side, by that it is an *ahīna*."
And they possess unimpaired speech. (30) (0)
And this fifteen-night rite is explicitly stated to be an *ahīna*— namely,
that it is an *ahīna* because it has an *atirātra* on either side. Therefore,
it is indeed an *ahīna*.
Or rather, because there is an injunction regarding the means. (Siddhānta) || 31 ||

"These are either part of a Sattra, not Ahīnas. Why? Because of the injunction [beginning with] 'upāṃśu,' and because of the reading in the second Paṭala of the Kaṇva recension: 'udayanīyo 'tirātraḥ'.
[Page 121]
In the eighth chapter, second quarter,
the Bṛhadbhāṣya states: "Those very ones who desire prosperity as their goal should undertake this fifteen-night rite."

Also in the *Kuṇḍapāyināmayana*, [it is said]: "Those desiring prosperity should perform [the sacrifice]. What, then, is the distinction between these two indicative marks (*liṅga*)? One is contained within the injunction (*codanā*), while the other is contained within a separate sentence (*vākyāntara*).
That which is contained within the injunction is internal (*antaraṅga*), whereas the other is external (*bahiraṅga*).
And this is another distinction: by means of the constant indicative mark of the *Ahīna* sacrifice, [the status of] the *Ahīna* [is established].
The designation "Ahīna" (non-deficient) is not logically applicable; for if this were a logical justification— namely,

that "because it has a *tirātra* on either side, it is therefore an Ahīna"— then if that justification were valid, the status of being an Ahīna would be established even in other cases where such a statement exists.

If it were not authoritative, even the measurement [of the sacrificial post] would not be established. Therefore, this statement is not an injunction; rather, it is a restatement (anuvāda) for the purpose of praise. Such praise is not possible for the *ahīna* sacrifice on account of its being characterized by the permanent mark of having [the rite] performed on either side with the *atirātra*.

For this reason, it is indeed a *satra* that is deficient on one side (*anyataratas-tirātra*). However, it is appropriate for a *satra*, because insofar as it is deficient on one side, it is a *tirātra*, and yet by its very nature it is a *satra*; therefore, being of both natures, it is superior to others.
"To the bulls"—thus [it is said].
And the scripture shows it by means of a common characteristic. (32) (0)

Furthermore, the indicative mark of a *satra* is shown in the Kuṇḍapāyināmayana sacrifice: "The householder, the householder; the Subrahmaṇya, the Subrahmaṇya. For the householder is indeed prescribed in the *satra*: "They should enter the *satra* with the householder as the seventeenth. And in the *satra*, there is a need for that [householder] to perform the functions of the sacrificer (*yājamāna*) which belong to the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), because the other functions of the sacrificer have already been assigned [to others]. Therefore, these two [terms] refer to the *satra* alone. (8.2.6)
Thus ends the second quarter of the eighth chapter in the Mīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śabarasvāmin.
The third quarter of the eighth chapter.
In the case of the *śucidevatā* offering, the *pātnīvata* [offering], and the *agnīṣomīya*, there is an extension of the procedure from the *dharṣa* [offering].
In a group of oblations (*havirgaṇa*), the subsequent [procedure] applies because of the commonality of location. (Pūrvapakṣa)

Commentary: Here, the groups of oblations serve as examples: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agnāiṣoma, a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvatī, and a cake to Bṛhaspati; [and] to Pāvaka..."

"to Agni Mucya"—and so forth. Regarding this, a doubt arises: is the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of the Agniṣomīya applicable to that which has Śuci as its deity, and that of the Āgnāvaiṣṇava applicable to that which has Agni as its deity; or is it the reverse? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? "In the case of a conflict over the sacrificial material (*haviḥ*), the latter [takes precedence]. That which has Śuci as its deity...

The [offering] to Agni-Soma is a modification (*vikāra*) of the subsequent [Agni offering], while the [offering] to Brahma-Viṣṇu is likewise a modification of the preceding full [Agni] offering. Why? "Because of the commonality of place"—that is to say, because of the commonality of sequence;
for here, the second [offering] has Śuci as its deity, and in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the Agni-Soma offering is also second.

The second [alternative]: even elsewhere, the *śyāmāveṣṭi* is first, and in the archetype (*prakṛti*) as well, the *āgneya* is first; by the mark of similarity in deity, the latter is a modification (*vikāra*) of the former, and the former is a modification of the [original] first.

Ba. Or it may be restricted by the deity, because [the sacrifice] possesses the nature of being expressed by a word, whereas for the other [alternative], there is no scriptural statement. (Siddhānta) || 2 ||

Bhāṣya: Or rather, there should be no restriction regarding place; what then? [The rule applies] "by virtue of the deity," because of the commonality of the deity. Why? Because the deity is associated with the word "Agni," as in "O Agni, come hither" and "To Agni, the Pure. Since there is no scriptural mention of "the other" place, there is no [restriction of] place.
It is heard [in scripture], but rather it is understood through accumulation. What follows from this?
This results: in an injunction for ritual action, the cognition of the deity is primary because of its immediate proximity;
the other, however, arises in dependence upon the sequence of preceding and following elements; therefore, it is secondary. Primary—
These are the verses.

And favor is proper. Therefore, in the rite dedicated to Śuci, there is the displacement of the Agneya [offering], and in the rite dedicated to Āgnāvaiṣṇava, there is the displacement of the Āgnīṣomīya [offering]. (8.3.1)

In the Janaka-saptarātra sacrifice, because there is a threefold repetition, the rule of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is extended; [the view is that] when there is an injunction for a group (*gaṇa*), the repetition of that which possesses the indicative mark (*liṅga*) should be understood, as in the case of the Āgneya offering. (Pūrva-pakṣa) 3.

In the *Bhāṣya*, it is heard in the *Janakasaptarātra*: "There are four *cintis* days," and likewise elsewhere it is heard: "There are nine *cintis* days. Regarding this, there is a doubt: Is this a repetition of the first [day] of the subsequent [period], or is it an injunction for various twelve-day stomas? Which [is it]?

Is this not so? — "In the case of an injunction for a group, the repetition of that which possesses the characteristic mark should be understood, as in the case of the Āgneya. In such an injunction for a group, "the repetition of that alone" should be understood "which possesses the characteristic mark"—namely, the fatherhood of the first day among the side-days—because of the commonality of the injunction, "as in the case of the Āgneya.

For example, in the case of "to Agni Pāvaka, to Agni Suci," because of the identity of the deity and the commonality of the injunction, there is a repetition of the entire Āgneya rite; so it is here as well.
Not so; for it is multiple days because of its being a composite whole, as enjoined by the indicative mark of the performance. (Siddhānta) || 4 ||
"Or various days" (meaning twelve or more) might proceed, but not necessarily the first day. Why? Because of its being a collective whole; this is declared as a collective whole:
"four days are to be considered"—for it is indeed established separately.

"Four"—this is a number, which implies distinctness. And there exist therein, by virtue of the injunction, four great days of various types belonging to the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*); it is possible to refer to those and enjoin the drinking (*pitva*), but one cannot refer to the individual days and enjoin the number four therein.
