And likewise, there is the observation of another [scriptural] fact. (Yukti 5)

The Bhāṣya states: "There are four days having the Agniṣṭoma as their chief"—meaning those for whom the Agniṣṭoma is the first, while the others are not Agniṣṭomas; these are understood when this is said.
It does not mean that all [four] are Agniṣṭomas, just as when it is said, "The cutting of the clod of earth has iron as its chief."

It is not understood as being for all [the days]. And if there were a piling up (*citi*) [of the altar], then all [the days] would be Agniṣṭomas, for that [Agniṣṭoma] is indeed the Agniṣṭoma. Therefore, the piling up (*citti*) is prescribed for the twelve-day-period days obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction). Thus, nine piled days come into being—so it is said. (8.3.2)
The section concerning the extension of the rule to both [the *ṣaḍaha* and the *dvādaśāha*] consists of thirty-six [adhikaraṇas].
Bādari [holds that] even when there is repetition of time, [the rite is repeated], because of the difference in the acts. (Pūrva-pakṣa)

In a certain specific ritual action, it is heard in the scripture: "There are six days; there are four days; there are twelve days. Regarding this, a doubt arises: does the procedure of the twelve-day rite (*dvādaśāha*) apply here, or that of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*)? What is the prima facie view? "Even in the case of repetition of time, [the rule applies]—so says Bādari"; even when this repetition of the time of the six-day rite is heard, Bādari maintains [that the twelve-day procedure applies].
The Teacher considered that there is a commencement of the twelve-day rites. Why?
"Because of the division of the ritual acts" (karmabheda). By the term "six-day," six Soma-sacrifices are mentioned here;
and a division of those sets of six is understood—namely, "four... [etc.].

Regarding the term "ṣar̤ahāḥ" (six-day periods), because it is used in the plural, there is a sense of plurality. If one were to assume the repetition of only a single six-day period—whether it be the *pārṣṭika* or the *abhiplavika*—then the expression would have been "catuḥ-ṣar̤ahāḥ" (four six-day periods); however, [the text says] "catvāraḥ ṣar̤ahāḥ" (four six-day periods).
When this is stated, twenty-four days are understood;

that injunction regarding a collection of days, because it possesses the characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*), adopts the daily procedure (*pravr̥tti*) belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).
Therefore, there is a manifold adoption of the elements of the twelve-day sacrifice.

The reading in the Kaśmīra manuscript (Ka0 Saṃ0 Pu0) is "sayopupitacchedanam. [Page 125] But Jaimini [holds that there is] a repetition of that [mantra], because it is connected with the direct perception [of the action]. (Sūtra 7)
(Śi0) 103 Mā. "Its extraction"— the extraction of the well-known *ṣaḍaha* which follows as a subsequent part.
The teacher Jaimini held this view. Why? Because there is no contradiction with the direct statement. The number twenty-four is understood through inference from the direct statement;
and that inference is based precisely upon four sets of six. Therefore, one first perceives those four sets of six, and by combining them, one arrives at the number twenty-four.

Just as one first perceives smoke and afterwards fire, and one who has achieved his purpose through the cognition of smoke alone does not pay heed to the cognition of fire; so too here, since the engagement [with the sacrifice] is accomplished by the cognition of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) itself, what will he do with the comprehension of the group of twenty-four days, having already achieved his purpose through that? Therefore, [the term refers to] the six-day period.
[Commentary:

Repetition. Now, as for what was said—"In the case of the *bhā* [sacrifice], the *sani* [suffix] would be understood as residing separately"—to that we reply: "The six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*)"—thus is the six-day rite known from this *sani*.

In that case, there is a connection with the four-fold limbs (catuḥkhaṅga) for it; this either exists directly or will come to be, as in the case of the Upasads, the Prayājas, and the Anuyājas. Even for one for whom the twenty-four-night sacrifice is enjoined as "four six-day periods" (catvāraḥ ṣaḍahāḥ), for him also [it applies].

When the *dajarācī* [sacrificial session] is being performed, there is indeed a filling of the vessels by means of the *śrāddha* itself, because of the absence of separate six-day periods (*ṣar̤aha*). And that deity which belongs to both does not exclude one side.
(8 | 3 | 3 Śrauta Sūtra) | The section concerning the extension of the twelve [offering cups] to the *saṃsthā* sacrifices.
In the case of formal assemblies, that practice would be understood [as applicable], because of the inclusion of the defining characteristics. (Pūrvapakṣa 8)
In this context, the assemblies (*saṃsthāgaṇa*) serve as examples— such as: "The Agniṣṭoma has five Ukthyas," "There is a hundred Agniṣṭomas," "There is a hundred Atirātras," and so forth.

One reflects: Is this a repetition of the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, or is it a statement regarding days characterized by specific terminuses (saṃsthās) gathered in such a manner? What is the prima facie view? "In the case of groups of terminuses, a repetition of that [original] should be understood; this is a repetition of that very original Jyotiṣṭoma. Why? Because of the adoption of its established definition; this is its established definition: 'the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, the Ṣoḍaśī, and the Atirātra.'"

Thus, these *saṃsthās* (concluding rites) have arisen through conjunction with that; he conquers by means of them, and having conquered, he will establish the *saṅka*. However, in the debate, both the *saṃsthā* and the number are enjoined separately: "The *ukthya* is the *saṃsthā*," and "And those are five. In this way, the sentence would be split.
Therefore, there is a repetition of the Jyotiṣṭoma.
[Sūtra 8: Or rather, it is the archetype (prakṛti) as qualified by that [context], because of its authority; for the designation [of the rite] is caused by that. (Siddhānta)
Bhāṣya: This is not so—that there is a repetition of the Jyotiṣṭoma. How then? "The archetype (prakṛti) should remain as it is;
the days belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) should be those for which the rules of completion (saṃsthā-vidhi) are prescribed.
Why? Because of the qualification (adhikāra); those [elements] are extended here by the general rule (codaka), and thus there will be favor toward the general rule."
"But is it not the case that the Jyotiṣṭoma is directly enjoined by such terms as *agniṣṭoma* and so forth?"—No, he says.

How so? "Because the designation is based on that [cause]: the designation *agniṣṭoma* is caused by the *saṃsthā* (concluding rite); it does not denote the Jyotiṣṭoma itself, but is able to express the sacrifice (*kratu*) when it has that *saṃsthā*, not the Jyotiṣṭoma alone. As for the objection that there would be multiple meanings; it will not have multiple meanings, because [the term applies] to the days obtained through the injunction of the group (*gaṇacodanā*).

Only the fivefold nature will be prescribed; even in the compound "pañcāgnihotram," the word denotes a sacrifice qualified by both attributes, and thus it has but a single meaning. As it is read in the Nyāyamālā: "It becomes a Śataudana, it becomes a Śatātirātra, and the Pañcāgnihotra is to be performed with five animals."

For example, as in the case: "The priests, wearing red turbans, perform the ritual. In this way, the connection established by separate mention will be upheld. Therefore, there is a statement regarding the various days of the twelve-day sacrifice. (8.3.4)
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the increase of the *stoma* in the *śatokthya* and other sacrifices from the *jyotiṣṭoma*.
The increase [of the number] is from the group, because that is its source. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 10 ||

It is heard in the scripture: "There is the Śatokthya, there is the Śatātirātra. In that context, the days of the Dvādaśāha proceed; and since those are for the most part of the Ukthya configuration—as stated in the rule, "Two Agniṣṭomas, [then] the Śatokthya"—the increase of the Ukthya-stotra is obtained for the two Agniṣṭomas. From the statement, "There is the Śatātirātra," the increase of all the night-rounds (rātriparyāya) is obtained. Regarding this, a deliberation arises: should the increase be performed from the Dvādaśāha, or from the Jyotiṣṭoma? What is the prima facie view? "The increase is from the Gaṇa (the group, i.e., the Dvādaśāha). Why? Because...
"Because they have that as their archetype"—these multi-day sacrifices (*ahargaṇa*) have the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) as their archetype;

therefore, the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) belonging to the twelve-day sacrifice is obtained for them. If there is an extension from the twelve-day sacrifice, in this way the injunction (*codaka*) will be upheld.
Therefore, the extension is from the group.
Or rather, it should be for one day, because of their equality. (Siddhānta) || 11 ||
The addition [of days] is from the Jyotiṣṭoma, not from the Dvādaśāha.

Why? Because of their equality; for there is an equality between the Dvādaśāha elements and the other modified (vaikṛta) elements, in that they both require a concluding rite (saṃsthā) from elsewhere.

These also [are required]; and mendicants do not desire [them] from a mendicant when there is another mendicant capable of providing them. What is this that is being said? Because the *saṃsthā-stotras* (concluding stotras) of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) are not recited [in the archetype], they are desired from where they are recited; however, those [stotras] are not recited on the modified (*vaikṛta*) days.

[Page 128] Bhāṣya: Thus, therefore, even the modified (vaikṛta) days, where they are prescribed, ought to expect [their requirements] from that very source; and those [requirements] are recorded in the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Therefore, there is an addition from the Jyotiṣṭoma (8.3.5).
[This constitutes] the section concerning the introduction of the *māyatrī* in such passages as "This day becomes the *māyana*," which deals with the origin [of the rite].
In the case of the *gāyatrī* verses, there is an exclusion of the original [verses] because of the context of the archetype;
due to being a number, like the *agniṣṭoma*, it is designated by that name because of its non-difference [from the archetype].
12 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||
Enough. Accumulation has been considered; now, diminution is being considered. This is heard:
"Having sacrificed with the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava"; and therein this [is the case].

It is traditionally handed down: "This day becomes a Gāyatra. Here it is deliberated: should that verse be made into a Gāyatra by omitting syllables from the original Triṣṭubh and Jagatī verses, or should there be an addition from the Dāśatayī collection of Gāyatrīs produced at the beginning?

"Having done what?"—thus [is the question]. Here, the commencement is by means of the sūtra itself: "In the *gāyatrī* verses, there is the excision (*avaccheda*) of the *prakṛti* [verses]. When *gāyatrī* verses are being heard—[as in the injunction] "This day becomes *gāyatra*"—there must be an "excision" (*avaccheda*) [meaning the removal of syllables] of the *prakṛti* verses, namely the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* ones. Why? Because of the authority of the *praśasti*, and because of the *codaka* [the rule of transfer]. Here, the *prakṛti* *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* verses are obtained and exist in excess; if...
If the arrival of the *ṛc*s were to be performed through repetition (*abhyāsa*), the original injunction (*prākṛta-pratyaya*) would be sublated.

[Objection: "But surely the *gāyatrī* verses are directly heard in the scripture; therefore, those obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) should be sublated by them. [Reply: No, he says. Why? "Because of the number (*saṅkhyātva*). This word *gāyatrī* denotes a number. How is this known? "Because there is no deviation (*avyatirekāt*)."

This does not deviate from the number twenty-four; it is never seen without the group of twenty-four, because of the governing context of the twenty-four—this is the reading in the Kāśmīra manuscript (Kā0 krī0 pu0).
[Page 129] It is observed in the *bhā.* that it is devoid of the group of twenty-four in the *ciṭuṅ* and *jagatī* meters.

It never occurs. Therefore, if this word *saṅkhyā* is the same as the word *saṅkhā*, the elision of syllables must be applied. It is like the case of *agniṣṭoma*; for instance, when it is said, "There is a *śatāgniṣṭoma*," there is an elision of syllables from the twelve-day (*dvādaśāhika*) rites.
It is done; so it is here as well.
And that statement [of the Sūtra] applies even when those [subsidiaries] exist separately, as it is eternal. (Yukti)

Thinking that the word "gāyatrī" expresses merely a number—just as the word "bhā" [is used] in the sense of "that which is eternal"—the statement regarding them occurs even with respect to *jagatī* verses that are distinct from (i.e., different from) the *gāyatrīs*, such that they are not actually *gāyatrīs*: namely, "for those two are *gāyatrīs*, and that one is a *jagatī*. If the word "gāyatrī" refers to the number, then this statement—"in the *jagatī*, there are two [of twenty-four syllables]"—is appropriate; but if...
If there were only three *ṛc*s, then the statement "therefore, two *ṛc*s do not exist in the *jagatī*" would be untenable; for this reason as well, the word *gāyatrī* refers to the number four.
Likewise, there is this other observation: "He makes three *anuṣṭubh*s and four *gāyatrī*s."
— thus.
[Objection: If it is argued that there are not ten in twenty. (Ābhāsya)

Now, someone might say: "The number twenty does not exist; nor does a number reside within another number, for number is a quality (guṇa), and qualities do not reside in other qualities; likewise, the number twenty-four does not exist within the number forty-eight."

Therefore, even if the word *gāyatrī* refers to the collection [of verses], the statement "one *jagatī* is equal to two *gāyatrīs*" is simply untenable. Furthermore, a defect that applies to both cannot belong to one alone.
The reciter.
It should be a single Saṃgha alone. (Ācārya-nirṇaya 15)

To this it is replied: we do not say that the number resides in the collection (*saṅgha*); rather, within the forty-eight recitations delimited by the number forty-eight, there are two constituent parts consisting of the number twenty-four, but not two *ṛc*-verses. Nor is it the case that...
It does not exclude another *saṅga*.

If it were to exclude it, then there would be only one *saṅga*, and this statement—"He who has ten cows has two groups of five"—would not exist! Yet it does exist; therefore, it does not exclude another *saṅga*.
Or thus: "If it is argued that 'ten' is not [contained] in 'twenty'" (1.2.39).
Even though the word *gāyatrī* refers to a number, nevertheless, one must not disregard the syllables. Why? Because ten are contained within twenty.
What follows from this? First, it follows from this that by whom twenty are taken up, by him ten are taken up;
likewise, by whom *triṣṭubh*s and *jagatī*s are employed, by him those *gāyatrī*s contained within them are also employed.

[They] exist. Therefore, the performance should be without modification; in this way, there is compliance with the injunction (*codaka*), and the *gāyatra* day is accomplished. [Objection: "It should be of a single number," he says;
for when the *jagatī* and *triṣṭubh* have been taken up, there are no *gāyatrīs*.

They become appropriated. How so? That [meter], while delimiting the means of accomplishment (*sādhana*), becomes subordinate to the action; it is not a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the *jagatī* or the *triṣṭubh*, but rather the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* [themselves] are the means of accomplishment.

Now, if it should be argued that—on account of the statement, "This day becomes *gāyatra*," the constituent part itself is the means here—then in that case, the omission of syllables would necessarily follow, because the subsequent constituent part would not be a subordinate element (*anaṅga*). And when a non-subordinate element is not being employed, the *coraka* [the rule regarding the syllable count] is not sublated. Therefore, as for what was said, even though...

"The word *gāyatrī* refers to a number; even so, its application remains without modification"—this is incorrect. For it shows that when a subsequent number is employed, the preceding numbers are not thereby included—as is seen in the expression "one and ten."
"One hundred and one thousand and a hundred thousand"— thus it enumerates all numbers; and if, when a higher number is employed, the preceding numbers are also included,
"it would be merely a single number," meaning there would be only one final unit, which is that [highest] number.
[Page 131] Chapter 8, Section 3.

108 mā. tri. This is superior to all [the others]. Since even single-syllable [names] have been enumerated, it is therefore understood that when a subsequent aggregate is employed, the preceding aggregates are not included.
They become appropriated.
Or rather, the word for a substance may [be applied] on account of a quality, because it does not apply to all [substances]. (16)
(Si0) Bhā.
Su. (Bhāṣya-sūtra)

This is not so; the word *gāyatrī* does not denote a number. How then? It is "on account of a quality" (*guṇāt*) that it is "a word for a substance" (*dravyaśabdaḥ*), meaning it denotes a substance consisting of twenty-four syllables. Why? Because "it would have too broad an application" (*atiprasaṅgaviṣayatvāt*). If it were a word for a number, it would apply to everything possessing the number twenty-four, such as a herd of cows and the like. But this is not the case.
And since it functions [in this way], it is therefore not a word denoting number.
And the state of being a cow is the possession [of that genus]. (Yukti 1) || 17 ||

Commentary (Bhāṣya): Just as, for example, in the case of the word "cow" (*go*), although the common property of "going" (*gamana*) is the basis for its application and it denotes a substance in general, the word "cow" is understood to apply specifically to that which possesses a dewlap and so forth, and not to anything else; in the same way, this [word] too is to be understood as denoting specifically the *ṛc*. Sūtra.
Bhāṣyasudhā: It is logical.
And because number is denoted by a word, [it is not a substance]. (Yuktidīpikā 2)

There is no word that denotes the number twenty-four— namely, "twenty-four"— which has the same meaning as this other word "gāyatrī," because a name exists for the purpose of conventional usage, and since conventional usage is established by one [term] alone.
And because the other is not mentioned in the scripture. (Sūtra 18) (Yukti 3)
Commentary: "Of the other" means of the Ṛg-verse substance; "because it is not heard" means because it is not mentioned by word.

Even for that, there is a purpose for the name-word for the sake of conventional usage; and in that case, this word "Gāyatrī" possesses its own meaning, whereas in the Saṅgāna [chanting], it would be purposeless. Therefore, also... [Page 132]
The word "ṛk" is the correct term; therefore, an addition of ṛg-verses in the gāyatrī meter must be made.
Thus it is said.
Because it is introduced as a distinct substance, it would be characterized by the omission of the Ukthya cups. || 20 ||
Bhāgavata Purāṇa, 10th Canto,
87th Chapter.
(Pūrvamīmāṃsā-sūtra 1.2.1)

As for what was described—that [the sacrifice] is "like the Agniṣṭoma"—to that we reply: there is no application of the term *agniṣṭoma* to any other substance, just as the word *gāyatrī* applies to the substance of a *ṛc* verse. For this term denotes the state of ending with the *agniṣṭoma* alone;

and since the state of ending with the *agniṣṭoma* for the twelve-day (*dvādaśāha*) rites does not occur without the omission of the *ukthya*, the omission of the *ukthya* must necessarily be performed. Furthermore, it has been stated that this word *gāyatrī* is the designator of the substance of the *ṛc* verse; and it is not [applied] by the omission of syllables.
Therefore, that object of the Ṛgveda is attained; hence, this comparison is unequal.
Thus it is said.
And because it does not possess the characteristics of the Śāstra. (21) (Yukti)

Furthermore, the *uktha* hymns characterized by the *aśāstra* [recitation] in the *śatāgniṣṭoma* are set aside by those characterized by the *śāstra*, because the *agniṣṭoma* concludes with the *śāstra*. Here, however, the situation is reversed: the *gāyatrī* verses characterized by the *śāstra* are based on inference, whereas the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* verses are not.
They are able to obstruct the Gāyatra.
Because it is their own origin and their name, [the term "sacrifice"] may be applied figuratively to those [acts] that exist separately.
22 || (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti-nirṇaya 2) ||
[Commentary]: Now, as for what was said—"The word *gāyatrī* is seen in the *saṅgara* [hymn], where it says, 'These two *gāyatrīs*, that is one *jagatī*'—what is the resolution of that? It is replied:
it has already been stated that this is the original name of the *ṛc*. Therefore...

"Because it is a name based on its origin," the usage of the term 'yogya' for a collection of twenty-four syllables forming a word-part in the world is to be understood as being "figurative" (bhaktyā), for there is no [other] meaning for a single word [in this context]. (Chapter 1, Section 1).

No; it is not right to assume multiple meanings when a single meaning is possible. By what figurative sense [is this meant]? By the commonality of measure—that which is the measure of the two, *ḍi* and *āyoga*, is the same for the one, *ru*.
(RvBh)
[It means] "of the Jagatī. Therefore this has been said: "That which is Gāyatrī is indeed one Jagatī"—just as when it is said, "Those two Kauravas are one Vāhīka."

And this statement is for the purpose of praising the rising of the *gāyatrī*. How so? This is heard: "For a Vaiśya, [the offering] is with two *gāyatrīs*. That which is stated here seems inappropriate, because the duty of a Vaiśya is with the *jagatī*; for a Vaiśya is indeed *jāgata* (of the *jagatī* nature). Therefore, this...
"It is performed with two *gāyatrī*s; that becomes a hundred *jagatī*s—'for those two *gāyatrī*s are one *jagatī*. Therefore, this is not a reason for the word *gāyatrī* to signify the *saṅga*."
If it is argued that this is merely a statement, [we reply: No. (Śrā0) || 23 ||
This much may indeed be possible there where the word *gāyatrī* is a mere restatement (*anuvāda*);

but where it is an injunction (*vidhi*), how can that be? As in the case of: "He makes three *anuṣṭubhs*, four *gāyatrīs*. What, then, is the distinction in the case of an injunction? [The answer is: In an injunction, it is by the primary meaning of the word (*śabdārthena*).
In common usage, it is impossible to make four *gāyatrīs* out of three *anuṣṭubhs*,
but it is possible to make four [sets] of twenty-four syllables. Therefore, in that context,
the word "gāyatrī" refers to a collection [of syllables].
To this we reply:
"As much as has been stated" (sūtra 24). (Ābhāsara-nirṇaya)

"No; it occurs here alone for the sake of the meaning of number, and not elsewhere, because it is seen [only] in this context. [Objection: "If that is so, and it does not express number, how has it come to have the meaning of number here? [Reply: It is said: A designation can also occur through secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). For example, in common usage, one says, "Let these balls of flour be made into lions," and in the Veda, "They stand near with the *pṛṣṭha* [stotras]. And yet, in those cases, the word "lion" does not denote a physical likeness.

The word *dṛṣṭaḥ*— as well as the word *pṛṣṭha* elsewhere— is understood to denote a representation (*pratikṛti*), or it may denote the state (*bhāva*) of being a back; and when a word is used figuratively (*lakṣaṇayā*), its primary meaning is not thereby determined.

For this reason, it is only while remaining in its own primary sense that a word indicates another meaning; if it were to abandon its own sense, it could not indicate at all. Therefore, this too is not a valid reason.
Śrī Bhagavadgītā-bhāṣya-vivaraṇa.
And there would be an option regarding the previously unestablished [number], if it were a prescription of number. (Yukti) 25.

"In the case of the *apū* [offering] in the *darśapūrṇamāsa* ritual, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) if the word *gāyatrī* were used in the *saṃgraha*; for it is heard there: 'One should conclude with a *gāyatrī*.
Such being the scriptural injunction, [this applies] to the collection of twenty-four syllables of the *ājuhotā* verse."

And there would have to be an option; in the case of an option, there would be a sublation of the injunction "śrā juhotā," and that is improper when an alternative course is available. Therefore, for this reason as well, this is not an injunction of a number.
If it is argued that [the *ṛc*] is not [the primary object] because it possesses the quality of being a *ṛc*, [we reply: No. (Sūtra 26)
To this it is replied: there shall be no option regarding the archetype (prakṛti).
Why?
Because of its being a quality of the *ṛc*. For in that case, the performance is accepted as having the *ṛc* as its quality; [it is] of the *ṛc* that it [is a quality].

The *sāmidhenī* verses are prescribed [in the context of the *āghāra* offerings]. If one were to conclude with a verse recited as a subsequent formula (*anuvāka*), the quality of being a *ṛc* would be sublated. Therefore, in that case, one shall conclude with the *ājyāhuti* itself; thus, it will be concluded with a *gāyatrī*, and the quality of being a *ṛc* will be maintained.
Likewise, it would be as in the previous case. (Ā0 Ni0) || 27 ||
Commentary: "In the *Apūrva* [Dṛhaspatisava] as well," it would be thus;

just as in the *Apūrva*, here too the performance characterized by the *ṛc* is accepted by the *codaka* (the rule of extension). There also, when the *ṛks* are being employed in the sacrifice, the day becomes made of the *Gāyatrī* [meter]; for the *ṛc* is the primary element.
And it is not contradicted; therefore, there is no elision of syllables.
Sūtra:
And there is the penetration of the qualities everywhere. (Yukti 28)
In the Bhāṣya, however, the word "ca" (and) is used in place of the word "tu" (but); and where the word "tu" is seen, the word "ca" is used in the sense of "api" (also).
[Page 135]

Commentary: For example, [it is asked], "And what do you say, sir? The number twenty-four, which is a quality (*guṇa*), applies to the whole *ājyāhuti* and not to its individual parts; therefore, when that [verse] is employed, both its status as a quality of the *ṛc* and its numerical value are accepted.
Furthermore, regarding the verses belonging to Bṛhaspati which are accepted by the *codaka* (archetypal injunction),

their constituent parts are established in the number twenty-four; if that [number] were adopted, the quality of being a *ṛc* would remain unadopted, whereas it is indeed adopted in the case of the original *gāyatrīs*.
Therefore, when the word "gāyatrī" denotes a number, there is no requirement for the addition of the original gāyatrīs.
Sri Bhagavad Gita Sutra (or Verse) 18.45.

Furthermore, this proponent of the *saṅkha* [number] should first be asked: "Why do you restrict yourself only to the number residing in the syllables (*akṣara*), and not also to numbers residing in other things—such as those residing in the cups (*graha*) or the goblets (*camasa*)? For there is no distinction between them.
It has been heard: "This day becomes gāyatra"; this being the case, it follows that the introduction of the quality [of the gāyatrī] would apply everywhere.
If it is argued that [the term] "accomplished" implies that it is not [so], [we reply: no. (28) (0)

If he should say: "The word *gāyatrī* is well-known where this [meter] is established"—that is the meaning—then its inclusion would be logical; however, this word is well-known only in reference to the collection of syllables, not everywhere; therefore, it is not taken as referring to every kind of collection.
—thus; he should be told: "In this case as well, it would be so. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya) || 30 ||
Just as it is seen only in the arrangement of syllables and not elsewhere,

so too it is seen only in the season and not in anything else, whether in prose consisting of twenty-four syllables or otherwise; and just as it is seen only in syllables— thus it is not understood in that which is without syllables— so it is here.
"It is seen [to apply] to the *ṛc*—thus it is not right to understand it as applying to non-*ṛc* verses.

To this he says: "Even though this word *gāyatrī* refers to the *ṛc*, nevertheless the elision of syllables must be performed. What is the reason? Because of its connection with the archetype (*prakṛti*), and because of the injunction..."

[Page 136] Bhāṣya: By what means have the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* meters been brought here? These will be the ones designated as such. And the word *gāyatrī*, on account of its commonality of dwelling, is capable of denoting its constituent parts; thus, both injunctions—the archetypal (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*)—will be upheld. Therefore, he recites the answer: "Or rather, in the absence of doubt, there is a restriction because of the connection with the archetype, even in the case of the *śloka*s."
It would be established. (0 Ni. || 31 ||

Bhāṣya: "If," even in the absence of doubt (*aviśaye*), the word *gāyatrī* is applied to non-*gāyatrī* verses because of the connection with the term *mala*, then the word *śara* must likewise be applied to *kuśa* grass in the case of the statement, "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara*"; for the function of the sacrificial grass must be performed by *kuśa* alone, or else some specific distinction must be stated.
If it is argued that the application has been observed [in the case of the word *sra*]. || 32 || (0) ||

This specific point has not been observed: that the word *gāyatrī* is applied to the number twenty-four when it resides in the syllables—as in the statement, "The two *gāyatrīs* are one *jagatī*. Therefore, it is possible to infer [this].
Likewise, it is so even in the case of the arrows. (Śrauta-nirṇaya 33)
Bhāgavata Purāṇa,
Book 10, Chapter 87.
The word *śara* is also seen used for *kuśa* grass, as in: "This desert forest is indeed a forest of *kuśa*."
If it is argued that [it is so] because of devotion, (Ābhāsasūtra 34).

To this it is replied: that word "reeds" (*śara*) is used there figuratively; because of their length and broad leaves, it is a metaphorical expression. [The opponent argues: "This grove of reeds is indeed a grove of *kuśa* grass"—thus, while functioning in its own primary sense, it implies a similarity. It has been stated that the term *darvihoma* is a name for a ritual action (*karmanāmadheya*). Regarding this, it is now considered: Are the *darvihomas* something entirely new (*apūrva*), or are they distinct from some other set of ritual properties (*dharma*)? [The reading in the Kāṭhaka-Kalpa-Purāṇa is: "With the words *bhūtebhyas tvā*, he digs up the earth upwards. This discussion begins from the second section of the Mīmāṃsā-sūtra commentary (numbered 33) of the Kaśmīra Saṃskṛta Vidyālaya.

If you think thus—that this is a mere statement (darśana)—then why is it not an injunction (vidhi)? Because it has the *nāriṣṭa* oblations as its archetype (*prakṛti*), it would be an injunction prohibiting the already established fuel-sticks (*idhma*) and so forth, thereby enjoining a new purpose (*apūrva*). A restatement (*anuvāda*) that does not produce a specific activity would be useless; therefore, while the counter-position remains, he challenges it with the Sūtra.
Not so, because it is a supplementary statement; and a reconciliation for the sake of a subordinate quality is possible only through diversity [of the acts]. (Sūtra 23, Ābhāsaniyama)

Bhāṣya: This injunction is not appropriate. What is the reason? Because another injunction is heard: "One should offer a pap of rice in clarified butter to Āditya, having returned home"—this is the remainder of that [other] sentence. How is this known? Because it is required by that [injunction]. Having proclaimed the defect, "The Cāmbaka offerings are indeed unstable," [the text continues].

This is heard [in scripture]: "One should offer a pap of rice in clarified butter to Āditya, having returned to one's home"; and, "Āditi is indeed this earth; she is the foundation; in her alone he finds firm support. This is understood to be for the purpose of removing that defect; therefore, it forms a single syntactical unit with that [preceding injunction], and occurs in its midst.
Those statements regarding the absence of fuel and so forth are also rightly considered to be supplementary to that [primary injunction], because they are recited together;

if they were assumed to be independent injunctions, they would constitute separate sentences, and in that case, the form of a single sentence (*ekavākya*) would be sublated, and there would be the assumption of a disconnected construction (*vyavahita-kalpanā*). Nor is this [the case for these].
[The opponent says: "They possess injunctive force, because they have the nature of restatements; therefore, they are not injunctions.

Now, what is the distinction here, such that—while the injunctive suffix (liṅ) is common to both—the observation of the *antaḥparidhi* is non-probative, whereas the other is probative? [The author replies: The distinction will be explained later.
We shall explain.
Or rather, it would belong to those for whom there is no other [prescribed] oblation, because there is no contradiction. || 24 ||
(Second Pūrva-pakṣa)

Bhāṣya: "Or rather, for those sacrifices" in which there is an "offering" in the "two latter" [pressings], "for them" there would be the performance—meaning the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. Why? "Because there is no contradiction. There is no contradiction there that was mentioned regarding the performance of the *nāriṣṭa-homas*, because in that case, non-existence is the cause; for their fuel is the *barhis*.

And the *sāmidhenī* verses are not an auxiliary part [of the *patnīsaṃyāja*]; therefore, the observation of their absence there is not contradictory. Furthermore, those [verses] possess the characteristic of being "great" (*mahat*), as indicated by the injunction "he offers" (*juhoti*) and the specific rule "he offers together with the wife" (*saha patnyā juhoti*). Therefore, they are to be employed.
Those medicinal herbs that are prescribed should be understood [as required] by their location. || 25 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not tenable. What is the reason? Because, "In that [context], medicinal herbs are enjoined" in the Darvīhoma, such as "in the Āmbakas there is a sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa), bowls of groats (karambhapātra), rice grains," and so forth; "these would be understood through their position" by virtue of the displacement of the clarified butter (ājya).

If *yajyādharmas* (the ritual properties of the *yajyā*) were to be obtained, they could not be performed there; or, even if they were performed, they would remain unaccomplished, and thus the *codaka* (the rule of extension) would be sublated. Therefore, there is no purpose for their application. Furthermore, the *yajyā* and *anuvāka* are set aside by the *mayi*, and the *vaṣaṭkāra* is replaced by the *svāhākāra*.

Or rather, [the rule applies] to the remaining two oblations because of the indicative mark. (Third Pūrvapakṣa)

There should be the application of the flour-oblation (*piṣṭaja*) and the husk-oblation (*phalīkaraṇa-homa*) by way of option (*vā*). Why? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*), namely the commonality of the vegetable substance (*auṣadha*). Furthermore, the defect that was stated regarding the application of the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings—namely, the futility of the ritual properties (*dharma*)—does not apply here. In that case, the vegetable-substance properties such as pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*) and so forth can be performed. Therefore, there is the application of those two.
— thus [it is said].
But those two [the *rū* and *pratipatti*] occur [in the case of the *ṛk*]; therefore, it does not undergo modification. || 27 ||
Bhāṣya 1:
But this is not so. Why? Because these two oblations are acts of dedication (*pratipattikarma*).

The ladle-offerings (*darvihoma*) are primary rites; their distinction [from other rites] is remote, yet the general application of ritual properties (*dharma*) is intended for them. As for what was stated—that the properties of the medicinal herbs (*auṣadha-dharma*) can be performed there—it is not at all a motive (*aprayojaka*) for the pouring-out (*nivapana*) and so forth, because they are acts of disposal (*pratipatti*).

Since they are *dhagmāṇām*, their status as having that [the *darvihoma*] as their archetype is not established by that very same reasoning; nor is it purposeful. Therefore, this too is incorrect. Thus, the acquisition of ritual properties (*dharma*) for the *darvihomas* does not result from any source whatsoever. Consequently, the former [view] is correct.

In a case of conflict among contradictory [rules], the non-application [of one] would be understood because of the established nature of the originative injunctions and because the purpose cannot be determined [otherwise]; however, there should be an extension [of the rule] by virtue of the explicit statement. (Sūtra 28, Śrāddha-nirṇaya)

[The objection: "Now, why is it that when there is the presence of indicative marks (liṅga) that establish both sides, only non-activity (apravṛtti) is perceived, and not activity (pravṛtti)? [The reply: It is said:
"In the case of a collision of opposing factors," the activity of these indicative marks cannot be perceived.

It is not logical. Why? Because of the established distinction between the originative injunction (*vidhi*) and the applicatory injunction (*utpatti-vidhi*); for the applicatory injunctions are those [beginning with] "the wife's consecrations" (*patnīsaṃyājānām*).
[Page 150]

The origin is the textual recitation (*pāṭha*), and that is fixed: some [mantras] are recited in the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, while others are in the Soma sacrifice. Regarding those [mantras], the "non-transferability of the purpose" applies to what has been recited; when they are transferred elsewhere, the *prakaraṇa* (context) is overridden. Therefore...

"The eating [of the remnant] would be extended. Regarding this, it is asked: "Is this the general rule that there is no application [of the details] everywhere? This being the position reached, it is replied: "There would be extension by virtue of a specific scriptural statement, as in the case of the *rāṣṭrabhṛt* offerings during the *udghāta* rites; in the absence of such a statement, however, the previous [rule applies]. Now, as for those cases where an indicative mark (*liṅga*) is cited, such as: "If an insect should fall [into the offering], one should pour it out within the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), standing within the altar (*vedi*), he offers the *sāvitra* oblations"—[in such cases, the details are extended].

"What is the meditative concentration (samādhi) for those two? It is replied: because it is preceded by an improper [literal] application, that statement is understood figuratively (lākṣaṇika) as "in the interior of the enclosing-sticks" (paridhi) and "in the interior of the sacrificial altar" (antarvedi), since the enclosing-sticks and the altar do not exist there; just as when one says, "The night itches my leg."
"‘My mole is throbbing’—thus, even in the absence of passion and in the absence of a mole, speakers make such statements by means of the characteristic of that location. (8.4.4a)
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the eighth chapter in the Mīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śrī Bhartṛśvarasvāmin. And this eighth chapter is completed.

The section concerning whether the colors mentioned in connection with the Agnihotra and other rites are employed for the sake of the apūrva (the transcendental result). (Compiled from two versions.)
B.

Sacrificial ritual is the primary factor, for it is that which is enjoined; its purification regarding substances is prompted by that [ritual], because those substances are for the sake of that [ritual]. (Sūtra 1)

In the eighth chapter, the definition of specific extended application (*viśeṣātideśa*) has been completed; now we shall discuss the definition of modification (*ūha*). And modification is threefold, pertaining to the subject matter of mantras, *sāmans*, and ritual preparations (*saṃskāra*).

Here, the primary subject is being discussed, while other matters will be addressed by way of introduction (*upodghāta*) and incidental discussion (*prasaṅga*). However, this specific point is considered first for the sake of establishing the definition (*lakṣaṇa*). The *agnihotra*, the *darśapūrṇamāsa*, and the *jyotiṣṭoma* serve as examples; in these cases, distinct ritual properties (*dharma*) have been traditionally taught. Regarding them, there arises a doubt: are they prompted by the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), or are they prompted by the sacrifice itself (*yajati*)? If they are prompted by the *apūrva*, the exclusion (*jaha*) is established; if they are prompted by the sacrifice...
But there would be a confusion of the ritual properties (dharma). How so? For those sacrifices are indeed sacrifices;

when properties are enjoined for the general category of sacrifice denoted by the word "yajati," they ought to apply everywhere. However, if they were enjoined for its specific instance based on the application of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), [they would not apply elsewhere].
There will also be specific details regarding that [substitute] in another section; therefore, the carrying [of the fire] is established there.
[Objection: "But surely all of this was already examined and decided upon in the seventh [book] (10)."

It is stated again, that very point being recalled for the purpose of introducing the subsequent deliberation. Alternatively, this is stated to clarify that which was not mentioned there regarding the purpose. And what is that? "The refinement of the substances belongs to that [sacrifice], as it is employed for its sake"—and by this, there is a purpose here.

"I am speaking of what is intended; for it is in this way that it succeeds. In that regard, this was not stated, nor is there any need for it there. Such is the extent of the consideration therein: whether the ritual properties (*dharma*) are restricted to each specific section, or whether they all apply everywhere? That [discussion] remains incomplete.

This is established both in the case of being prompted by the [general] sacrifice and in the case of being prompted by the *yajati* (the act of sacrificing); it is not established, however, if the refinement of the substance were for the sake of a transcendental result (*apūrva*). But that [prompting by the sacrifice] is established here; and for the sake of conventional usage, the term "promoted" (*prayukta*) is employed once its establishment as being prompted by the *apūrva* has been achieved. Therefore, there is no tautology.
The second section.

Alternatively, we shall here state another consideration: are the dharmas prompted by the sacrifice (*yajinimitta*) and applied by the *apūrva*, or are they prompted by the *apūrva* and applied by the *apūrva*? Now, however, it is considered whether they are applied by the sacrifice or applied by the *apūrva*. What, then, is the prima facie view? That they are applied by the sacrifice.

Why? Because the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is connected with the word "sacrifice" (*yajati*), as in: "one should perform the sacrifice in this manner," or "one should act by means of the sacrifice in this manner.
Now...
This being the case, we reply: that which is the effect of the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is the primary element;
it is enjoined as the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance). Where there is a duty to be performed, there alone does the *itikartavyatā* apply.
As for what was said—that the ritual details (*dharmas*) are connected with the word *yajati*—that is now addressed:

"The purification (*saṃskāra*) which occurs in relation to the substances and in the act of sacrificing (*yajati*) is prompted by that [sacrifice] (*tatprayukta*), meaning it is prompted by the *apūrva* [the transcendental result], because the sacrifice is for the sake of that [result].

Furthermore, the connection of the substances with the ritual duties (*dharma*) is established through their belonging to that [sacrifice], not by their own nature; for there is no [direct] connection between the meaning of the verbal root (*dhātvartha*) and the ritual duties."

Furthermore, there exists a mutual requirement; for it is by means of the purpose (the *pratyayārtha*) that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is required—namely, "How is it to be done?"—and not "Of what nature is the sacrifice (*yajati*)? Therefore, only that which is to be accomplished has a connection with the procedure, and that is the *apūrva*.
Consequently, [the subsidiaries] are employed for the sake of the *apūrva*.
The third section.

Or rather, regarding these very examples, one considers this: "Is the sacrifice (*yajña*) the cause (*nimitta*) and the *apūrva* the motivator (*prayojaka*), or is the *apūrva* the motivator and the cause? What is the prima facie view? The sacrifice is the cause and the *apūrva* is the motivator. Why? Because it is not possible for a single thing to possess both the status of being a motivator and the status of being a cause.

For that for whose sake the ritual acts (dharmas) are performed is their *prayojaka* (the motivator); that in the presence of which they are performed is their *nimitta* (the occasion). And since no unseen potency (*apūrva*) is produced in a single word, yet these [acts] exist in relation to the unseen potency (*apūrva*).
[Page 153]
But one cannot say "iti" (thus) at 131 bhā., for the mode of expression is indeed different in the case of apūrva matters.

And there is another [reason]: the term *apūrva* exists [only] when the sacrifice is present; however, the word is appropriately construed as being caused by the sacrifice—namely, "one should effect [the result] by means of the sacrifice. Thus, when the sacrifice is present, the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) are conducive to the *apūrva*, but when it is absent, they are not conducive.
Therefore, the sacrifice is the cause (*nimitta*), while the *apūrva* is the motivator (*prayojaka*).

This being the case, we reply: "The sacrificial act is primary; it is the effect of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice). It is enjoined as possessing a fruit. Therefore, whatever refinement (*saṃskāra*) pertains to its materials and to the act of sacrificing itself [is for the sake of that primary act]."

Since they are employed for the sake of the *apūrva*, they are performed with that as their purpose; they have no connection with the meaning of the root (*yajati*). These [subsidiaries] are connected with the meaning of the suffix by means of the *prayogavacana* (the injunction of performance), for it is that which possesses expectancy, not the meaning of the verbal root. Therefore, they are prompted by the *apūrva* and have the *apūrva* as their cause. As it has been stated: "The *apūrva* is the prompter and the cause."

"It is not tenable because of the difference in the mode of expression"—to this it is replied: "The status of being the motivator (*prayojakatva*) is based on the scriptural statement, while the state of being the cause (*nimittabhāva*) will indeed arise from the statement itself;

for when something is employed by another, that [latter] becomes the cause of the former, just as for a gardener, the garden is both the motivator and the cause in the payment of wages regarding the garden."
When he exists, the wage is given to him; there is a connection with the wage for the purpose of protecting the forest.
The section concerning the non-primacy of what has been previously employed, together with an alternative interpretation.
For those engaged in the formative acts (saṃskāra), [the ritual] should be prompted by them, because it is for their sake. (Pūrva-pakṣa) || 2 ||

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they recite: "They thresh with the mortar and pestle that have been sprinkled; he grinds with the grinding stones that have been sprinkled. Regarding this, there is a point of doubt: is the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) subservient to the acts of threshing and grinding, or is it subservient to the transcendental result (apūrva)? What is the prima facie view? [Page 154] That it is for the sake of the preparatory rite (saṃskāra).

In the case of *piṇyāka* (oil-cake) being employed, the threshing (*prokṣaṇa*) performed upon it would be "prompted by that" (*tatprayuktatā*), meaning prompted by the *saṃskāra* (consecration). For threshing and grinding are indeed *saṃskāras*. Why is there this state of being prompted? Because of its being for that purpose (*tādarthyāt*). That by which something is to be accomplished is the prompter of that thing.

If the *apūrva* is produced by this [action], then the *apūrva* is the prompter of it. If it is threshing and grinding, then those two are the prompters. And from the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is the *apūrva* that is to be accomplished.
"It is understood from the sentence that *hanti* and *piṣati* [are to be performed]; moreover, the sentence is stronger than the context (*prakaraṇa*).
[Objection: But surely, if *hanti* and *piṣati* are performed [as part of the sacrifice], they will have an incomplete purpose;
thus both the context and the sentence will be respected. [Reply: No."

It is possible for both to be favored; however, it is not understood that something is recited for the sake of the meaning of the two things belonging to the context merely by being recited within that context. Rather, from the recitation within the context, there arises syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the subject matter at hand, and from that, its subservience to that purpose (*tādarthya*) is understood.
But here, the syntactic unity of the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is established through the two verbal roots *han* and *piṣ*.
That [proximity] would sublate the indirect syntactic unity with the primary context; nor could there be syntactic unity with both simultaneously.
When there is syntactic unity with one, then for that which has its requirement satisfied by it, no further syntactic unity with another through hearing is to be assumed.
Therefore, because there is no syntactic unity with the primary context, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) does not serve a new purpose (*apūrvārtha*).

Objection: "But surely the cooking and grinding are for the sake of the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), and therefore the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is an auxiliary that assists the *apūrva*. Reply: It is indeed an auxiliary by way of a sequence (*praṇāḍyā*), but it is not prompted by the *apūrva*. For there are two ways in which one auxiliary assists another:

some are connected to the auxiliary because they are specified as belonging to the *apūrva* through the phrase "this is a specific part of this [main act]"; others, however, are connected by their very nature, without even requiring a connection to the *apūrva*.

It is connected with a cause in such a way that, having taken a previously established connection as the cause, a class of dharma is connected with a specific subsidiary; that [dharma] becomes employed by something not previously [established].
And such [a dharma], when its function is transferred to another purpose in a modified ritual (vikṛti), must be abandoned. However, where again—
The essential nature (*svarūpa*) of a constituent part (*aṅga*) becomes the cause for its connection with a property (*dharma*); that [nature] is prompted by its own essence.

In that case, although an unprecedented result (*apūrva*) is accomplished by means of that [part] which possesses the property, the *apūrva* being accomplished there does not become the cause for the employment of the property; thus, that *apūrva* is not the prompter (*prayojaka*) of its essential nature.
[Page 155] "It does not exist"— thus the term *dharma* is not applied. Ru.
In that case, since the modified form lacks that specific character within the interval, modification (*ūha*) is not possible. This being so, there is no definitive determination of the sentence.

If the sentence declares that the *apūrva* (the transcendental result) is the cause [of the action], then it is prompted by the *apūrva*; if, however, it is the subsidiary (*aṅga*) that is the cause, then it is prompted by the subsidiary. And this has been stated because of the absence of a specific rule: "It would be prompted by the *apūrva*, but from the sentence, it is prompted by the subsidiary. Therefore, it is prompted by the act of killing.
Regarding the sprinkling— wherever the roots *hanti* and *piṣi* are employed, in each such case they possess these same ritual properties.

Because of that purpose, there is a connection with the sacrifice; therefore, there is a relation to dharma, and thus it should be prompted by the sacrifice, since the purificatory rite is for the sake of that [sacrifice]. (Siddhānta) || 3 ||

The word "mā" (not) sets aside the previous position; it is not the case that "sprinkling is enjoined by the act of killing. Rather, it is "by means of that purpose," namely, by the act of killing, [the sprinkling is performed]. Since there is a connection with the *apūrva* (the transcendental result), therefore its connection with the sprinkling belongs to that [result]; that is, the connection with the purificatory rite of sprinkling is caused by the specific *apūrva* as the means, not caused by the acts of killing and grinding. Why? Because the acts of killing and grinding would be purposeless if they were merely for their own sake.

Sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) is likewise purposeless; therefore, it is not prompted by that [sacrificial act]. An objection is raised: "The acts of striking and grinding are not purposeless, as they assist the *apūrva*. It is replied: There is no connection whatsoever between sprinkling and the *apūrva*;
if sprinkling were not performed, the acts of striking and grinding would not attain the status of being means for the *apūrva*.

They do not go [to the sacrifice]; therefore, although the acts of striking and grinding are auxiliaries to the *apūrva*, nevertheless, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) connected with them is indeed purposeless.

Now it is said: "The purpose for which the pounding and grinding are undertaken is to perform them as connected with the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) within the context (prakṛta), and not otherwise. To this it is replied: there is no such word [to that effect]. To that he says: "This very word expresses this meaning. How so? Because they recite regarding the two sprinkled [grains]: "The grain (anna) [is obtained] from the context" (ka0 saṃ0 pu0 reading). [Page 156]

The Bhāṣya says: "He grinds with the two consecrated [grains]"—this means that what is performed by the acts of striking (*hanti*) and grinding (*piṣi*) is done with those two things connected to the consecration (*prokṣaṇa*). Thus, the consecration is connected to the purpose of striking and grinding, not to those two acts themselves. It is replied: This is not so; if that which is performed by striking and grinding were connected with the consecration, then there would indeed be a connection.

There would be no [need for] sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), for that [apūrva] is brought about by those two; what else could that sprinkling bring about? "Now, an *apūrva* is produced by means of the two [stones] that have been sprinkled"—this is the connection. In that case, it is not [connected] with the verb *hanti* (he strikes) or *piṣati* (he grinds).

Or: "Now, if it is argued that its connection [to the Apūrva] is also stated"—in which case, the sentence would be split due to multiple connections! Therefore, the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*), being connected to *hanti* and *piṣati*, would be purposeless; thus, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it is connected with the *Apūrva*.
"Objection: In this way, the relationship between the act of striking and the act of grinding would not be possible. Reply: It will indeed be possible, we say. How so?

Here, for one who is exerting effort toward threshing, two results are accomplished: the form of the act of threshing itself, and the production of rice grains; and [this occurs] through the causal sequence (*praṇāḍyā*).

A specific *bhāvanā* (productive operation) not previously established, namely the production of rice grains, is that which is intended to be accomplished by the act of threshing; with that [production], the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) is connected. Although, when connected in its form as threshing, the connection would be through direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), nevertheless, because it would be purposeless there, only indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to. This is indirect indication.

For that [visible effect] is directly perceived; it is more logical to assume that than to postulate an unseen [effect]. Furthermore, it is understood that the *śravaṇa-homa* does not produce an *apūrva* (transcendental result) as a remote auxiliary (*ārādupakāraka*); rather, while performing a visible benefit, it makes [the sacrifice] perfect through an unseen capacity—even though [this may be the case].

Even so, sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) would be entirely purposeless if it were not connected to a benefit through its relation solely to the *avahanti* (threshing). Therefore, its connection is with a specific benefit indicated by the *avahanti*. Consequently, even that which does not perform the *avahanti*, provided it takes over its function, there indeed occurs the sprinkling—just as when the feet are pierced by nails, [the act] applies to the nails. Therefore, a duty (*dharma*) of this kind is indeed prompted by the *apūrva* (transcendental result).
— thus.
"sambadhyamānam" is the reading found in the Kaśmīra manuscript (ka0 saṃ0 pu0).
