The first quarter.
Bhāṣya.
Another section: (The section concerning whether the sound *cāvacat* is prompted by the supreme *apūrva*).
Or thus:

There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein this is recited: "One should recite at the Dīkṣaṇīyā with as much voice as one desires; softly at the Prāyaṇīyā, more softly at the Ātithyā, and in a whisper at the Upasads. Regarding that—

This matter is doubtful: are these ritual duties (dharmas) prompted by the ultimate transcendental result (paramāpūrva), or are they prompted by the intermediate transcendental results (apūrva) such as those of the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? Since this duty is connected to the "refinement" (saṃskāra) which is the ultimate apūrva, and because it serves the purpose of that ultimate apūrva, the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites themselves must also serve the purpose of the ultimate apūrva.

For it is the supreme apūrva that possesses the fruit; that which is connected with the state of being "to be performed" (kartavyatā) is alone connected with the dharmas, not the subsidiary apūrvas, for those are purposeless.

Because of that purpose, due to the connection with the sacrifice, there is a relationship with the *ha* [the vessel]; therefore, it should be employed for the sake of the sacrifice, since the refinement (*saṃskāra*) is for that purpose. (Siddhānta 3)

Bhāṣya: "By that purpose," namely the Dīkṣaṇīyā and other rites, because they are connected with the ultimate transcendental result (*paramāpūrva*), therefore the *paramāpūrva* itself possesses such qualities through these types of ritual elements (*dharma*).
Consequently, this collection of ritual elements is prompted by the performance of the subsidiary sacrifices; thus says the Śruti.

The word [denotes the primary meaning]; otherwise, there would be figurative indication (lakṣaṇā). Furthermore, the *apūrva* of the Prāyaṇīya and other rites is not purposeless, for it is beneficial to the Jyotiṣṭoma.
Nor is the *apūrva* of the Prāyaṇīya and others established by such a quality (*dharma*) in its absence, as is the case with the acts of threshing and drinking.

As for what was said—that "that *apūrva* will exist even without a ritual act (*dharma*)"—that is not so. Why? Because that *apūrva* is understood from the Vedic word itself as being "existent"; it is not established by any other means of knowledge prior to the word. And in matters of this kind where the word is the authority, whatever the word declares is our authority. And the word [declares] that this ritual act (*dharma*) is an auxiliary to the *apūrva* of the *Prāyaṇīya* sacrifice and others.
[Objection: No, it is not the supreme apūrva, because of the authority of the scriptural statement.
[Page 158] Bhāṣya:
And thus, since the non-supreme apūrva is produced and is undecaying and imperishable, it is here the dharma.
Once established, it will not transition to another *apūrva*; even so, it is capable of fulfilling its purpose.
Therefore, such a class of ritual elements (*dharma*) is indeed employed solely for the sake of the subsidiary *apūrva*. Sūtra.

"What is the purpose [of this discussion] regarding one case or the other? It is said in reply: In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is recited, "The Traidhātavīyā is the consecration of the sacrificial ladles. If a duty (*dharma*) of this kind is prompted solely by the *apūrva* (transcendental result) of the supreme [sacrifice], then—being bound to a specific benefit—it will apply to the Traidhātavīyā which has entered into that [result]. On the other hand, if it is prompted by the *apūrva* of the Āgnāvaiṣṇava [offering], then since this is not the *apūrva* of the Āgnāvaiṣṇava, it would not apply there in the case of the Traidhātavīyā-*apūrva*.
"He shall not be united with that dharma"—thus [it is stated]. (9.1.2 Śrauta-sūtra)
The modification [of the mantra] is also due to its being employed for a new purpose, even though it is connected with the fruit and the deity;
and this applies to both the fruit and the deity. (Pūrvapakṣa)

The *Bhāṣya* states: There are the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsau*), as in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices. In that context, duties connected to the fruit and duties connected to the deities are heard. First, those connected to the fruit: "We have gone to heaven; we have become united with light," and so on. Also, those connected to the deities: "May I conquer following the victory of Agni; may I conquer following the victory of Soma," and so forth. In this regard, there is a doubt: Is heaven alone the motivator for the rite connected to heaven, and are Agni and the others alone the motivators for the rite connected to Agni and the others? Or...

In both cases, is the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) the motivator? If the connection is made thus—"We have gone to heaven, and may I follow the praise of Agni and the others"—then it is motivated by heaven and so forth. But if it is made thus—"We have come... [the connection is otherwise].

"The fruit of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the deities of the Darśapūrṇamāsa are [the objects] for which the *ujjiti* (recitations) are uttered. Therefore, what is established first? That it is prompted by heaven, fire, and so forth. Why? Because of the power of the scriptural injunction; it is understood from the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) that "that which is the designator of a purpose must be mentioned here," and thus heaven, fire, and so forth are [established].
The word *bhā* (in *bhāgārhau*) is a direct denotative term (*vācaka*) for the two deities of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifice by means of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore,
that which is understood as being connected to the fruit and the deity— namely, the *svagā* and other such elements— is the ritual duty (*dharma*) prompted by that [connection].
It may be so—thus.
No, for its quality [is known] from the injunction. (Uddyota)

Bhāṣya: This is not so—that [the injunction] is prompted by heaven, fire, and so forth. Rather, from the *codanā* (Vedic injunction), there would be that specific quality (*tādguṇyam*): whatever is enjoined as possessing a fruit is connected with a procedure (*itikartavyatā*). And it is the *apūrva* (the unseen potency) that possesses the fruit, not heaven, fire, and so forth; for if the statement were intended for their sake, it would have to be assumed to have an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).

Furthermore, if the word were taken figuratively (lakṣaṇā) to mean the unseen potency (*apūrva*) that yields the fruit, then the visible purpose [of the sacrifice] would be set aside due to the encouragement [provided by the text]. When this alternative is seen, it is not logical to assume an unseen *apūrva* for the words "khādira" and so forth, because the meaning of the word is already established as being the deity who yields the fruit; thus, the figurative sense would be unobserved. Therefore, a duty (*dharma*) of this kind is employed solely for the sake of the *apūrva*.

"What is the purpose of this deliberation? [The answer is: Just as in the previous case, the mantra should be employed without modification in the *saurya* rite; so too, according to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), it is recited by the sacrificer:
"We have gone to the splendor of sacred knowledge (*brahmavarcasa*); may I win the victory following the victory of Sūrya."
It culminates in the fruit; the subsequent deliberation will concern the deity. (9.1.3)
The section concerning being impelled by the deity Dharmālāma.
Or rather, the deity should prompt [the performance], because the feeding of guests is for that purpose. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 6 ||

Bhāṣya: This is not so—that Agni and the others are the instigators; rather, the deities as a collective must be the instigators of all the ritual duties. Why? Because "the eating is for that purpose"—for this sacrifice, which is called a rite, is the food of the deity, and the substance is what is to be eaten.
[Page 160]

[The Bhāṣya says: It is given to the deity, thinking "she shall eat it. For this sacrifice is heard in scripture as having the deity as its recipient (*sampradāna*), and a recipient is indeed more intended than even that which is most desired by the action. Therefore, the deity is not subordinate;
rather, the substance and the action are subordinate with respect to the deity. Furthermore, what is called "sacrifice" (*yāga*) is the worship of the deity, and worship...
In this world, no one is seen to be subordinate to the object of worship; therefore, this should be viewed "like a guest" (*atithivat*).

Just as whatever service is rendered to a guest is entirely for the sake of the guest, so too is this case. Objection: "But by speaking thus, you must be accepting that the deity possesses a physical body (*vigrahavatī*) and eats. Reply: Certainly, we do accept that the deity possesses a physical body and eats.

And why? Because of tradition (smṛti), because of figurative usage (upacāra), and because of the observation of other purposes. For thus they remember: "The deity possesses a body"; and tradition is an authority for us.

Likewise, they treat the deity as possessing a body—they depict Yama with a staff in his hand and speak of him so; similarly, Varuṇa with a noose in his hand, and Indra with a thunderbolt in his hand.

We infer the firmness of the memory even from figurative usage (*upacāra*). Likewise, there is a statement for another purpose which shows the deity as having a physical body: "O Indra, we have grasped your right hand.
For a human body indeed has both a right and a left hand.

It is so; likewise, [in the verse] "O Indra, these two vast and boundless worlds are yours; O Maghavan, when we grasp them together, they are but a handful for you"—the term "handful" (kāśi) refers to a fist, and that too is appropriate only for one possessing a human form.
Similarly, [in the phrase] "tūvigrovaḥ vayodaraḥ subāhuḥ randhaso... [it is likewise appropriate].

"Indra slays the Vṛtras"—thus there is the perception of a human form, such as "the neck, the belly, the arms. Therefore, the deity possesses a body; and it acts as well. How is this understood? From Smṛti and from figurative usage.
Furthermore, because they perceive another purpose, they remember it thus: "The deity eats.
And accordingly, they treat her as if she were eating, in that they offer various services to her. Thus, there is a statement regarding another purpose concerning one who is [in fact] not eating.
The reading is exactly the same everywhere; however, in the Kāśmīra manuscript it is *jagṛmbhā*, while in the Kāśmīra-Saṃvat manuscript it is *baṣṭamā*.
The Puṣpasūtra recension [Page 161] states that it causes one to understand the deity: "O Indra, drink of the *prasthita*," and likewise...
And [it is said]: "He holds all trusts within his belly"—and, "With one [sip], he drank thirty lakes at once. Also:
"The deity does not eat; and if the deity were to eat, [there would be no need for] an oblation for the deity."
It might be argued that [the deity] would consume what has been offered. To this it is replied: the deity is understood to be a consumer of the essence of food, like a honey-bee.
How so? When the oblation is offered to the deity, it becomes sapless; therefore, it is inferred that the deity consumes the essence, just as a bee does.
And because of the lordship over wealth. (Yukti 7)
Bhāṣya: If a deity were the mistress of some object and, when propitiated, would grant it, then this worship of the deity would be undertaken for the sake of attaining that object;
however, neither of these two conditions exists—thus it is said: "The deity is the mistress of the object."

— thus [it is said]. How is this understood? From Smṛti, from figurative usage (upacāra), and from the observation of other passages. For they remember thus: "The deity rules over things. Likewise, the figurative usage of terms such as "village of the gods" (devagrāma) and "field of the gods" (devakṣetra) confirms that very Smṛti.
Similarly, a statement for another purpose shows the deity to be the ruler: "Indra of heaven... [and so forth].
"Indra is the lord of the earth, Indra is the lord of the waters, Indra indeed is the lord of the mountains; Indra is the lord of the established, Indra is the lord of the wise;
Indra is the lord in peace, Indra is the lord in exertion. Likewise: "O Indra, the ruler of this moving world, the lord of heaven, the ruler of all that stands still."
Likewise, we accept that [the deity] becomes gracious through both remembrance and ritual application; for thus they remember: "The deity becomes gracious. Likewise, they apply such terms:
"Paśupati has become gracious to him; a son has been born to him"; "Vaiśravaṇa has become gracious to him."
"By this, wealth has been obtained"—thus there is a perception of another purpose, as in: "With the *prātis*, Tādo gratifies the gods," and "To him, being pleased, they bestow food and vigor."
Sūtra:
And therefore, there is a connection with that. (Yukti 2)
Bhāṣya: "Therefore," there is a "connection" with the deity "by means of" that fruit for the one who performs the service;
she connects him who serves the deity through sacrifice with the fruit.
How is this understood? From both scripture and conventional usage; for they remember it thus: [smṛti].
The statement that "the deity bestows the fruit" serves to reinforce that very recollection through figurative usage, as in:
"Paśupati was propitiated by him; a son was obtained by him.
Likewise, another scriptural observation (anyārthadarśana) demonstrates this same point: "He, indeed, with his people..."

"He, with his people, with his offspring, with his sons, and with his men, brings forth wealth—he who strives to win over Brahmaṇaspati, the father of the gods, with faith, a seat, and an oblation. Likewise: "Indra, being satisfied, satisfies him with progeny and cattle. Therefore, the deity is propitiated by means of the oblation and by words expressing qualities;
being pleased, she bestows the fruit. Of that action by which Agni has been propitiated, [he receives the result].
One has mastery over the fruit; one bestows it upon the agent; it is not for one's own sake that one ought to give it.
This is understood from the scriptural statement—namely, "Who gives what?"—just as there is a scriptural statement regarding the boat, but not regarding the sun.
Or rather, because it is preceded by the word [of the Veda], the sacrificial act should be primary; the mention of the deity is subordinate. (Siddhānta) || 8 ||
Bhāṣya:

"Or rather"—this turns back the previous position. It is not the case that what was stated—that the deity is the motivator—is correct; rather, the sacrificial act (*yajñakarman*) should be the primary factor, as it is the object of the root *yaji* (to sacrifice).
It is unprecedented. Why? Because it is preceded by the word (*śabdapūrvatvāt*). For that which bestows a fruit is the motivator;

this knowledge that "it bestows a fruit" is preceded by the word and is not apprehended through perception or other means of knowledge. And the word, through the verbal root *yajati* (to sacrifice), declares the fruit.

Not of the deity. How is this understood? Because the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are designated as the instrument (*karaṇa*), as in: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *darśapūrṇamāsa*s" (Bhāṣya);
likewise, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *jyotiṣṭoma*"—for it is the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) that is intended.
The mention of the deity is not co-ordinated with the desire for heaven. [Objection:

But surely the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) consists of substance, deity, and action. [Reply: This is true; however, the scriptural mention of the deity is subordinate. For substance and deity are already established entities (*bhūta*), whereas the meaning of *yaj* is that which is to be brought into being (*bhāvayitavya*). And when an established entity and that which is to be brought into being are mentioned together, the established entity is taught for the sake of that which is to be brought into being. Therefore, the deity is not [the primary object].
[She is] the motivator (*prayojikā*).

Now, as for what was said— that "the object of action is more intended than that which is merely desired"— we do not deny its status as being intended, whether it is connected with a word ending in a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) or with the dative case.

From the sentence, it is understood that the deity is intended for the sake of the sacrifice; however, the connection with the fruit belongs to the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) by virtue of the sentence itself, and its status as an instrument is understood through direct denotation (*śruti*), not that of the deity. In that case, although the sacrifice is understood to be for the sake of the deity, its being for the sake of the fruit is not thereby precluded; and the fruit is for the sake of the person, and the person is [the ultimate beneficiary].

Our activity is not [prompted] by that deity; therefore, we shall not proceed impelled by the deity. However, the fact that the recipient is intended [as the goal] is possible only when it serves as a means for the fruit-bearing sacrifice.

And as for the claim that "in the world, sacrifice to a deity is observed to have the worshipped deity as its primary element," it need not be so here; in this context, the sacrifice itself is the primary element.
For that which possesses a fruit is the motivator (prayojaka); therefore, the sacrificial act is the motivator. Moreover, on this view, the deity possesses a body and partakes [of the offering].
It must be understood that [the deity] possesses a body and eats, for neither giving nor eating is possible for one who lacks a body and does not eat.

As for what was said—that she possesses a body and eats on the basis of Smṛti, conventional usage, and the observation of other purposes—that is not so; because Smṛti is rooted in Arthavādas. It is directly perceived that the knowledge which forms the root of Smṛti arises from both the Mantras and the Arthavādas; and we shall explain later that those Mantras and Arthavādas do not have such [a literal] purpose.

The opponent objects: "If it is not of such a nature, then that cognition is not rooted in the mantras and arthavādas. It is replied: Those who perceive the mantras and arthavādas merely through superficial observation—[Page 164]—mu.
And therefore, there is a connection with that. (Yukti 2)
"Then there is a 'connection' with the deity through that 'fruit' for the one who serves;
she connects him who serves the deity with sacrifice with the fruit.
How is this understood? From both scripture and usage they remember it."
The statement that "the deity bestows the fruit" serves to strengthen that very same figurative convention (upacāra), as in: "Paśupati was propitiated by him," or "A son was obtained by him.
Likewise, the observation of another purpose (*anyārthadarśana*) demonstrates this very point: "He, indeed, with his people..."

"He, with his people, with his offspring, with his sons, and with his men, wins wealth—he who clothes the Father of the Gods with faith, with the seat [of sacrifice], and with the oblation, O Brahmanaspati. Likewise: "Indra, being satisfied, satisfies him with progeny and cattle. Therefore, the deity is propitiated by means of knowledge and words expressive of qualities;
being pleased, she bestows the fruit. Of that ritual action by which Agni has been propitiated, [he is the recipient].
He rules over the fruit and bestows it upon the cultivator; he ought not to give it for his own sake.
This is understood from the scriptural statement as to who bestows what—just as there is a specific statement regarding fire, but not regarding the sun.
Or rather, because it is preceded by the word, that which is the primary element would be [the deity]; the mention of the deity is subordinate. (Siddhānta 8)
Bhāṣya:

The alternative view introduced by "api vā" (or rather) is set aside. It is not the case that what was stated—that the deity is the motivator—is correct; rather, the sacrificial act itself should be primary, for one performs the sacrifice when [the substance] has been produced.

It is unprecedented. Why? Because it is preceded by the word (*śabdapūrvatvāt*). For that which bestows a fruit is the motivator; this knowledge that "this [act] bestows a fruit" is preceded by the word and is not apprehended through perception or other means of knowledge. And the word declares the fruit from the verbal root *yajati* (to sacrifice).

Not of the deity. How is this understood? Because the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa) are designated as the instrument (karaṇa), as in: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (darśapūrṇamāsābhyāṃ svargakāmo yajeta); and likewise, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma. For it is the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) that... [Page 165] Bhāṣya. Thus, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma"—it is indeed the meaning of the root *yaj* that...
The mention of the deity is not in grammatical coordination with the one who desires heaven. [Objection:

But surely the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) consists of substance, deity, and action. [Response: That is indeed true; however, "the scriptural mention of the deity is subordinate" (*guṇatve devatāśrutiḥ*). For substance and deity are already accomplished entities (*bhūta*), whereas the meaning of the root *yaj* is that which is to be brought into being (*bhāvayitavya*). And when an accomplished entity and that which is to be brought into being are mentioned together, the accomplished entity is taught for the sake of that which is to be brought into being. Therefore, the deity is not [the primary object].
[She is] the motivator.

Now, as for what was said— that [the object] is "more desired than that which is intended by the action"— we do not tolerate its being intended in that way, whether it be connected with a secondary derivative suffix (*taddhita*) or with the dative case.

From the sentence, it is understood that the deity is intended as the object; however, the connection with the fruit belongs to the meaning of the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) itself through the sentence alone, and its status as the instrument is understood from direct Vedic statement (*śruti*), not that of the deity. In that case, although the sacrifice is understood to be for the sake of the deity, its being for the sake of the fruit is not thereby precluded; and the fruit is the purpose of the person, and the purpose of the person is...

Our activity does not originate from the deity, nor does it belong to the deity; therefore, we shall not proceed impelled by the deity. However, that which is the intendedness of the recipient is possible only when it exists as a means for the fruit-bearing sacrifice.

And as for the claim that "in the world, the worship of a deity with form is observed to have the worshipped object as its primary focus"—it should not be here as it is in the world; here, the act of worship is the primary factor, and whatever is productive of fruit is the motivator. Therefore, the sacrificial ritual is the motivator.
Furthermore, according to this view, the deity possesses a physical body and partakes [of the offering].
It must be admitted that she possesses a body; for it is not possible for one who is bodiless and does not eat to receive gifts or consume food—
as it has been stated, she possesses a body and eats, based on the evidence of traditional texts (smṛti), conventional usage (upacāra), and the observation of other purposes (anyārthadarśana).

This is not so, because the Smṛti is rooted in the Mantras and Arthavādas. It is directly perceived that the knowledge which constitutes the root of the Smṛti arises from both the Mantras and the Arthavādas; and we shall explain that those Mantras and Arthavādas do not have any other purpose [than what they explicitly state]. Objection: "If they do not have any other purpose, then that knowledge cannot be rooted in the Mantras and Arthavādas. Reply: This is true for those who perceive the Mantras and Arthavādas merely as superficial observations. [Page 166]
Bhāṣya: For those who see [the matter] superficially, that [Smṛti] has its basis in Smṛti; however, for those who examine it with precision, that [Smṛti] is sublated.
Furthermore, it may serve as the basis for someone else's Smṛti;
therefore, the Smṛti arises from that very [source], and even figurative usage (upacāra) has its basis solely in Smṛti. As for the observation of another purpose, [it is as follows:]...
It has been said: "O Indra, [I grasp] your right hand. This is not so;
it does not mean that Indra possesses a hand, but rather that which is his right [hand].
"We have grasped his hand"—from this statement, the existence of Indra's hand is not established.
He says: "If he does not exist, [how could we have said] 'we have grasped his hand'?"—thus...
It is not tenable [to say]: "The existence of the hand is determined [by the thought], 'This is my hand;
we have grasped it. That is untenable, for even if he were to have a hand, it is a matter of direct perception that they did not grasp it.
Nevertheless, this is not at all tenable; in that case, it must be understood either as irrelevant or as a mere eulogy, and that is equally true for my position as well.
Now, if it is argued: "This statement belongs to him who has accepted [the view]."

"Desired"—this is what is recited. This is not to be accepted, for the fault of having a beginning would attach to the Veda; nor can it be said that he "had grasped it [before]," because there is a lack of evidence. If it is argued, "From this very statement, it is inferred by implication that there was one who grasped the desired [text]," that is not so, because even an utterance that does not correspond to reality is possible, as in the case of: "Ten pomegranates, six figs. This is also the case for whom...
And as for this position—that Indra is possessed of a body—even in that case, the mention by the word "Indra" is for the purpose of addressing him;
the address is for the sake of recitation, and since it is understood that he is connected therein, recitation is logical. Yet, he [is not so connected] in any manner whatsoever.

It is understood that [the person] is connected [to the action]; for if this were not understood, the address would be purposeless. If it is argued that "it is understood that he becomes aware [of the command] through the authority of the word," it has already been stated that in the postulation of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*), the postulation of hands and so forth is untenable. Nor is this...
The reading in the Kaśmīra manuscript is "arthaḥ."
[Page 167] Bhāṣya:

It is understood that he is "the Fully Awakened One" (sambuddhaḥ) because there is no evidence [to the contrary]. Therefore, the vocative expression is not for the purpose of addressing him, but solely for the purpose of designation. Even in the view that [the deity] has no physical form (avigraha-pakṣa), it will likewise be for the purpose of designation alone. In that case, the use of the non-singular case-ending is for the sake of praise.

Thus, this deity is the most effective means of accomplishment; having awakened [the practitioner], just as one who possesses consciousness, it brings about accomplishment. Being treated as if possessing consciousness, it is addressed with the word "awakened" (*sambuddha*); likewise, being designated by the word of address (*sambodhana*), it is spoken to—meaning: "We have grasped your hand; we have you as our refuge. By us...
The statement "Indra’s deed must be performed" is what is being established by this [text].

Likewise, in the passage, "These two, heaven and earth, are far and boundless; yet when you grasp them, O Maghavan, your fist is honored," he speaks of the fist as if it were actually present for the sake of praise; there is no authority for its existence, nor is this a literal statement.
"The Kāśī is great; however, that which is your Kāśī is great"—this means "your Kāśī has another purpose," or "another [region] of yours is greater than Kāśī.
If it is argued, "For praise is appropriate only for what exists," this is not so.

Even for that [sacrifice] which necessarily possesses a connection with the constituent parts of the human ritual procedure (*pauruṣavidhika*), there is praise by means of those very constituent parts of the human ritual procedure, as follows: "These speak like a hundred, like a thousand; they cry out with their green mouths. O stones, pierce through with your strength;
even before the Hotṛ, you have attained the eating of the oblation."

Likewise, [the text says]: "Sindhuravinā yoked the comfortable chariot. Therefore, the figurative representation of the deity as having the form of a person does not arise from scriptural statement through presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*). Similarly, the statement "Indra has a thick neck" is not intended to mean that he literally possesses a neck.

"Indra"—[one might argue]—but rather, that which is his neck is large; there is no authoritative basis for [interpreting] the mention of the neck as a literal fact. Nor is this praise of the neck a case of *arthāpatti* (presumption), because praise is possible even in the case of what is not anthropomorphic.
Furthermore, by these two words, "Indra slays the Vṛtras,"...
The reading "svam eva sarvam" is the one; it would be more appropriate for it to be "upacaryamāṇam. [Page 168] Bhāṣya:
The word "Indra," being already connected, cannot enter into a connection with "tuvigrīva" and the other epithets.

Otherwise, the separate recitation of this [text] would follow: "Indra is to be known as having a thick neck," and "Indra kills with his thunderbolt"—for if it were so, there would be a syntactical split;

yet a single, unified sentence is perceived. Therefore, it is understood that if qualities such as "having a thick neck" were not being taught here, then these qualities like "having a thick neck" are mentioned for the purpose of praise.
"In the exhilaration of the soma, such a one slays the enemies"—this is the grammatical construction;
however, this statement is intended to teach the killing of the *ṭac* [the suffix]. As for the statement, "the arms..."

"O Indra, those two [arms] are hairy; O Indra, those two eyes are tawny"—thus, even there, it mentions the hairiness of the arms and the tawniness of the eyes, not the existence of arms or the possession of eyes. Even when it speaks of the possession of eyes, it is understood as "to one who possesses eyes."
"I say this to you who hear"—this statement also does not serve the purpose of establishing a connection with the eyes;

rather, "I say this to you who possess sight" serves the purpose of establishing a connection with the speech. It utters the possession of sight as if it were actually present for the sake of praise. How is this understood? From the use of the dative case; for if one were to determine it as the mere meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), then the sentence would be split.
It might be addressed as "O you who possess eyes," and one might say, "I speak to you, O possessor of eyes.
Therefore, no such perception of another object indicates that the deity possesses a human form; nor is this [the term] a food offering, for the deity is not [a consumer].
"He eats"; therefore, the statement that "he eats because eating has that [sacrifice] as its purpose" is a false assertion.

As for the claim that he eats based on Smṛti, figurative usage, and the observation of other purposes, that has already been refuted by the fact that [the deity] lacks a physical body. Furthermore, the sacrificial oblation offered to a deity who eats would simply perish!

Furthermore, there is no authoritative evidence that the deities consume the essence of food like honey-bees; while this is directly perceived in the case of honey-bees, it is not so in the case of the deity. Therefore, the deity does not eat. As for what was said—that the oblation offered to the deity does not become sapless—this is not a fault, for it may become sapless when struck by the wind.
And [the body] has become cold; furthermore, she does not have mastery over anything. Being without mastery, how could she give?—thus [it is said].

As for what was stated—that the deity is the master by virtue of traditional authority (*smṛti*), conventional usage (*upacāra*), and the observation of other purposes (*anyārthadarśana*)—[that is refuted here].
[Page 169] Chapter 8, Section 1.
"It is understood"— this is not so, because it has been stated that the Smṛti is based on Arthavāda (explanatory passages).

Even regarding the metaphorical usage—such as "the village of the gods" or "the field of the gods"—this is merely figurative. For whatever one is capable of employing according to one's own intention, that belongs to oneself; however, the deity does not employ the village or the field according to its own will.
