he draws [the line] around the fire-altar with *malhūka* grass. In this regard, there is a point of doubt concerning the meaning: is it for each individual brick (*iṣṭakā*)?
Should it be performed by drawing [the thread] and pronouncing [the mantra] repeatedly, or should it be performed only once?
Thus [it is asked] in the Mīmāṃsā-darśana. [Page 180]

In this regard, first it is deliberated: does the word "fire" (agni) refer to the collection of bricks, or to a different substance distinct from that? If it refers to the collection, then, since no distinction among them is perceived, all the bricks must undergo sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and drawing away (vikarṣaṇa).

But when it refers to a different substance, then [the rite] is performed only once. What is the prima facie view?—"For each individual brick. Why? Because the word "fire" applies to the collection. How is this known? Because there is no other substance; indeed, there exists no other substance whatsoever.

What could be designated by the word "fire"? In what could fire be deposited? How, then, is it understood that [the whole] does not exist? Because of its distinctness from other substances; for it is understood that in that case there exists another substance, wherein, having grasped one part, the whole is dragged along. What is the intention? If one part, being conjoined with the hand, is dragged, [then the whole must exist].

It is not a separate substance. What is the consequence [of this]? That a second part would also be pulled out from there. Now, if a separate substance is also pulled out from there, then the pulling out is logical because the parts that are the inherent causes (*samavāyin*) of that separate substance are themselves without parts. Nor is it a case of conjunction with what is conjoined (*saṃyuktasaṃyoga*).

These [bricks] are distinct substances; this property is thus accounted for. For in this case, when one piece of wood in a bundle of wood is being pulled, the other pieces of wood are not pulled along. Indeed, where a single cognition arises from mutual contact and no cognition of individual parts is perceived, nor can it be inferred by any means of inference, there it is said that a distinct substance has come into existence. But here, when a particular brick is grasped and pulled, that very brick alone comes, and not the other bricks; moreover, the joints are visible, whereby it is understood that there is no configuration of a composite whole.
Therefore, there is no separate substance [other than the bricks].

In that regard, regarding the injunction "one piles the fire-altar with bricks," the act of piling itself must be performed with bricks; however, no visible purpose is served by the mere act of piling alone. Consequently, since no specific distinction is perceived among all the bricks intended for the placement of the fire—which are characterized by the collective process of piling—the *prokṣaṇa* (sprinkling) applies to all of them.
And a drawing out (vikarṣa) must be performed, "as in the case of the Full Moon sacrifice" (paurṇamāsīvat); just as it is said, "He who, knowing thus,
sacrifices at the Full Moon, and he who, knowing thus, sacrifices at the New Moon," [referring to] the Āgneya and other offerings.
These are merely performed; there is no separate entity whatsoever. It is the same here as well.

kha. Or it may belong to the fire, because of the unity of the substance, since the others are for its sake. (Siddhānta 27) The word "or" (vā) reverses the previous position. It is not the case that it should be performed with each brick; rather, how then? Only once. Therefore, this is explained: a different substance is constructed by means of the bricks, and the fire is to be deposited therein; and the word "fire" (agni) applies to that [construction]. How so? Because the bricks are designated for the sake of another, as in: "One should build the fire-altar with bricks. (TS 5.6.4.3)
By the instrumental case in the word "cinute," it is understood that the bricks are for the sake of another;
if only the act of piling were expressed here, then it would be understood as being for the purpose of consecrating the bricks,
in which case there would be a connection with the accusative case, and the connection with the instrumental case would be sublated.

Therefore, something else is performed with the bricks; in that [something else], the fire is to be deposited, and for that purpose there is the piling of the bricks—or rather, it is the piling itself.
He says: "But has this not already been stated? Since that [fire] is absent, this other alternative is adopted."
To this it is replied: the cognition of oneness there is not due to non-existence;
that [cognition] is not observed in the case of separate bricks. Nor is a junction of parts seen in the case of those covered by earth.
Therefore, because the cognition of oneness arises even when there is a connection between the baked and the unbaked, there is one [entity] distinct from the bricks.

The substance exists for the purpose of being deposited in fire; or rather, it is understood through a single cognition as the refinement of the bricks. As for the statement, "By the pulling of one, there is the pulling of the parts," that is true, for in that case a separation is made within what is conjoined; indeed, substances are of two kinds.
● *Sampatiriti* is the reading in the Kāśmīra Jīva-puṇya manuscript; likewise elsewhere.
[Page 182] Both stationary (*sthāvara*) and moving (*jaṅgama*) [beings exist]; therein, among the stationary, there is a cutting off (*vicchoda*).

Just as when a tree is pulled after being grasped by its branches, it is not said to be "crooked" because of its immobility; so too is this case, for this sacrificial substance (agnidravya) is indeed immobile. Therefore, the sprinkling (prokṣaṇa) and the dragging (vikarṣaṇa) should be performed only once.
And that [name] would apply to the Full Moon sacrifice as a whole, because of the collection of injunctions. (0ni0)

Bhāṣya: Now, as for the statement, "He who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the full moon day; he who, knowing thus, sacrifices on the new moon day"—here there is no distinct entity other than the Āgneya and the other constituent rites. So it might be argued here as well. To this it is replied: It is appropriate that such is the case regarding the Paurṇamāsī (Full Moon sacrifice), because there the ritual act consists of a collection of injunctions (*codanā-samudāya*), and there is nothing to be accomplished by the ritual act itself [other than the result of the sacrifice]. But here, it has been stated, there exists a different substance (*dravya*). Therefore, there is a dissimilarity with the Paurṇamāsī. (8/1/70)
Sūtra:
The section concerning the *saṃvāja* [chanting] at the end of the *patnīsaṃyāja* for the great sacrifices of the highest class.
The conclusion with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings applies to all [the Soma sacrifices], because there is no distinction. (Pūrvapakṣa 29)

There is a multi-day sacrificial session (*ahargaṇa*), [as stated]: "One desiring progeny should cause [him] to sacrifice with the twelve-day rite. In that context, it is heard: "The days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. Regarding this, there is a point of doubt: does the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* apply to all the constituent parts (*aṅga*) of the days, or only up to the penultimate day? The doubt is raised excluding the tenth day, for its [conclusion] is...

The conclusion at the *mānasa* [cup] has been stated by the scriptural text. What, then, is established? That it applies to "all" days. Why? Because there is no distinction; it is stated without qualification that "the days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. And no specific distinction is adopted;
therefore, it applies to all.
Sūtra:
Or rather, [the conclusion follows] from the indicative mark, prior to the final [verse]. (Siddhānta) 30.
The word *vā* [in the sūtra] serves to exclude the previous position. From the words "prior to the last," the sequence would end with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.
Why? Because of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). There is an indicative mark: "[The rites] end with the *patnīsaṃyāja*s."
"The days conclude; one does not throw the *barhis* grass onto the fire, for at that time the sacrifice is not yet completed.

By this, it is shown that on whichever day the sacrifice is not yet completed, it ends with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. How so? The non-completion is indicated by way of a reason (*hetu*), because these [days]...

The great [sacrifices] are not concluded; therefore, among these, the conclusion consists in ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. "Conclusion" (*saṃsthiti*) occurs on the final day. Furthermore, in those days where the conclusion consists in ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja*, "non-conclusion" (*asaṃsthā*) is observed to be mentioned; therefore, there is a grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between non-conclusion and ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja*. And having observed non-conclusion prior to the last [day], [it applies] precisely prior to the last.

We conclude that the conclusion [of the sacrifice] occurs at the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings; for this is a restatement, just as the concluding of the rite at night is a restatement of the Hotṛ’s duty. (31) (0)
Bhāṣya 1:

The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. This is not the case—that there should be a conclusion [of the sacrifice] prior to the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. What then? [The conclusion applies] to all [the sacrifices], because there is no distinction. As for what was said—that in those cases where the conclusion is seen to end with the *patnīsaṃyāja*, therefore [it applies only] to those that do not conclude otherwise—[that is incorrect].
"Before the final [offering], we determine that the conclusion of the Patnīsaṃyāja [should occur]. This is not so;

for this observation is not rooted in an injunction, nor is it based on any other means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*); therefore, this observation is merely like the appearance of a deer or blackness [which is deceptive].
As for the claim that "the non-conclusion is the cause," that too would not be the case, for it has been said: "But the praise... [is merely commendatory].

"Because it is preceded by the word" (1.2.230). Nor is there grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the ending with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings and the state of being the end for all sacrifices; for the *patnīsaṃyāja*-ending applies to all sacrifices by virtue of the scriptural statement: "For where the sacrifice has been completed... (as read in the Kaśmīra manuscript).
[Page 184]

It is understood that, according to the logical principle, the sacrifice remains incomplete until the day before the final day. As for this statement, "For then the sacrifice is indeed incomplete," this is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) intended to extol the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings;
for it is considered that the sacrifice, though incomplete, will be completed after a long time, because—

"It will conclude after a long time; therefore, let it be cut short. Let the days end with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings. This statement regarding the conclusion while the days are still in progress is for the purpose of praising the ending with the Patnīsaṃyājas, for those days do indeed have a formal conclusion; the remaining ritual elements, such as the Avasthāna, will be performed for them. Just as the mention of the release from the *dīkṣā* is an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) of the non-conclusion [of the sacrifice], so too should this be understood. "By the two Varuṇa-nooses, indeed, he..."

"He who is initiated is placed under the Varuṇa-nooses for a day and a night; if he were to conclude [the sacrifice] by day, he would be released from the two Varuṇa-nooses; it should be concluded at night, for thus he is released from the two Varuṇa-nooses to avoid injury to himself. Thus, as long as he is not released from the two Varuṇa-nooses, he is not yet released from the initiation, for the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) is for the purpose of releasing one from the initiation. Alternatively, it is said that "he is released as if from the two Varuṇa-nooses" because many restrictions are then relinquished; having considered these, this statement was made.
It occurs; likewise here too, having perceived that it will persist for a long time, there is the expression "not persisting."

Or rather, it should apply [to the end], because of its being prescribed as an independent injunction (anāramya-vidhāna) and because of the contradiction with the indicative mark (liṅga) at the conclusion.
(Ācārya-nirṇaya)

The word "or" (vā) implies an alternative. Or rather, the conclusion with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings would apply prior to the last day; for this rule is not prescribed starting from the last day. How then? It is established generally that the days conclude with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings.
[Page 185] "By means of the avadāna and the śāsa alone"—this is the reading in the Ka0 Sa0 manuscript.
Chapter 9, Pāda 1.
In your view, there is a contradiction with the indicative mark (*liṅga*). What, then, is the attainment [of the conclusion] through reasoning?

It is this: "The days conclude with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings. By this, it is stated that "the remainder is omitted," meaning they "conclude" rather than being performed; thus, the agent's activity [ceases].

In these [days], one ceases; that is to say, while those days are being performed together, one must necessarily stop at some point or other, and then another set of constituent elements (padārtha) must necessarily be performed.
Since there would otherwise be no fixed rule regarding when to stop, it is prescribed that the ritual should be concluded at the end of the Patnīsaṃyājas.

The purpose of this suspension is as follows: how may the simultaneity [of the rites] be maintained through the performance of the ritual acts during the interval? For that which is seen [as a visible result] is the reason for the suspension; and when something is seen in one place, it is not possible to assume that the unseen [result] exists there as well. In that case, there is no rule regarding the conclusion with the *patnīsaṃyāja* offerings.

And no other purpose for that exists; therefore, by the principle that "before this [rite], it ends with the Patnīsaṃyājas," there is the observation of an indicative mark: "For then the sacrifice is not yet completed. (2.80)
"He recites the first [verse] thrice": this is the section concerning the location-based property in the case of messengers and the like.
The repetition of the *sāmidhenī* verses is a property of the location because of its occurrence at the beginning.
It may be so. (Siddhānta) || 33 ||

I am performing the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices; therein, with reference to the *sāmidhenī* verses, it is stated: "He recites the first verse three times; he recites the last verse three times. Regarding this, the following point is subject to doubt: Is this a property of the *ṛc* (verse) itself—that wherever the verse "pra vo vājā" occurs, it must be repeated thrice?

Or is it a property of the position—that whatever else is first mentioned must be practiced for a long time? Why is there this doubt? Because it is tenable in both ways, provided that the connection is made thus:
"That which among the *māṇavaka-sāman*s is first uttered..."
[Page 186] "That [verse] which is known by the Mīmāṃsakas must be recited"; therefore, the rule is that the verse beginning with *pra vo vājāya* [is to be used]; and thus it is.
It is understood that "one should recite three times" is connected with the first [recitation]; therefore, this is a property of the position.

What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is a property of the *ṛc*. Why? Because the firstness is connected with the individual instance (*vyakti*), and the repetition is with the individual instance.
How is this known?

Because of the mention of the feminine gender—since "woman" (strī) indeed refers to a specific individual—if priority were its qualifier, then the mention of a specific gender would be appropriate; that woman too would be connected with the repetition. Alternatively, it might mean that by one who recites for the first time, it must be repeated three times.

Consequently, no specific individual would be intended to be expressed, and in that case, the specification of the feminine gender would be untenable. Furthermore, a split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*) would result: first it would be stated that "the first [verse] is to be repeated thrice," and then that "the verse spoken first is to be repeated thrice. In my position, however, [this applies] to that which is characterized by its being first.

The *ṛc* is said to be the locus of the rule (*dharma*); therefore, when a single purpose is enjoined, there would be no syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Furthermore, by direct statement (*śruti*), the feminine gender is connected with primacy, whereas repetition is not [connected] by syntactical connection (*vākya*); therefore, the rule of the *ṛc* applies wherever it occurs: "The verse beginning with ‘pra vo vājāḥ’ is to be repeated thrice."
This being the case, we reply: this triple repetition of the first *sāmidhenī* verse that is prescribed is a property caused by its position as the first, not a property of any particular *ṛc*.
It is based on the characteristic of being first. Why? Because even throughout the entire *Ṛgveda*, there is no verse whatsoever named "first" (*prathamā*) that could be repeated;

in that case, "being first" would have to be taken as a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In the other view, however, it is direct denotation (*śruti*), not figurative indication; and direct denotation [is stronger].
It is more difficult [to justify] through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, our position is the correct one.

Now, as for what was said—that because of the connection with the feminine gender, the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) belongs only to our side, and the sentence is not split because the feminine gender is appropriate—here it is replied: for words expressing qualities (*guṇavacana*)...
The reading in the Ka0 Saṃ0 Pu0 is *mlacaṇam*.

[Page 187] Since the gender and number of words arise from their substratum (*āśraya*), even when the substance (*dravya*) is not being specifically qualified, whatever gender is necessarily obtained there belongs to the quality by virtue of its being the substratum.
Even when the gender is not explicitly prescribed, the mention of a specific gender indeed serves as a restatement (anuvāda);

for example: "white" [is used for] a male, "white" for a female, and "white" for a neuter; likewise, "white" [is used for] one, "white" for two, and "white" for many; or as in the command, "bring a white garment. Even though...

If the bringing [of the substance] itself is not enjoined, there is merely an injunction regarding its connection with the quality "white"; in that case, no qualification by gender is made. Nevertheless, the reference to the feminine gender still occurs as a restatement (*anuvāda*), as in "bring the white [cow]" (*śuklām ānaya*). And because it is a restatement, there will be no syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).
This being so, even if the firstness is connected with the feminine gender...

Nevertheless, the connection through repetition belongs to the *prāthamya* (primacy) alone, not to the *liṅga* (mark); for if the connection of the *liṅga* with this were expressed, the *prāthamya* would have to be considered a mere restatement (*anuvāda*).
Furthermore, even if the *prāthamya* were being expressed, the sentence would suffer from syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) if everything were expressed simultaneously.
Moreover, there should be no dispute here: the word *strī* (female) is indeed a qualifier of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*).

The rule "the suffixes *ṭāp* and so forth are added after that nominal stem which denotes a female" means that a qualifier does not enter into a syntactic connection with another word, just as in the expression "the king’s servant goes.
When, however, the state of being first (*prāthamya*) is connected with repetition (*abhyāsa*), then the femininity (*strītva*) is merely restated as something already established.

Regarding those words in the *sāmidhenī* verses which are *ṛc*s, they possess the feminine gender because of the word *ṛk*. In that context, the substratum (*āśraya*) of the first word is the *ṛk*; and since for words expressing qualities the gender and number follow those of their substratum, the feminine gender will apply even to the *ṛk* when it is not specifically qualified. That which is the first word is "virāṭ," which is feminine.

And that *ṛc* is a *sāmidhenī*; therefore, the statement "he recites the first one thrice" is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of a characteristic already established, for the purpose of achieving the fifteen *sāmidhenīs*, as expressed in: "He recites the first one thrice and the last one thrice; they thus amount to fifteen."
In the Mīmāṃsā system, a repetition being uttered refers to a complete Ṛk verse, not to a portion of a Ṛk;
and since it is the complete [verse] that possesses the power of kindling, it is not a mere part of a Ṛk. Therefore, this is a restatement of what is already established.
The property of "being first" belongs to the *liṅga* (the indicative mark), not to the *ṛc* (verse). (8.1.12.0)

As long as one lives, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are to be commenced; this is the section concerning their performance. Sūtra: Upon the repetition of the sacrifice, the commencement should be repeated, just like the Prayāja offerings. (Pūrvapakṣa) 34.

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are established [by the injunction]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. In that context, the Ārambhaṇīyā offering is prescribed: "One should offer a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Viṣṇu, a pap to Sarasvatī, and a cake on twelve potsherds to Sarasvat and Agni."

"One who desires, 'May I be an eater [of food],' should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Bhaga. Some authorities state that this offering to Bhaga is obligatory (*nitya*). Regarding the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, a repetition is heard in the scripture: "One should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* as long as one lives.
There arises a doubt: does the *Ārambhaṇīyā* (inaugural offering) also repeat, or not?
What is the prima facie view? It repeats, because it must be performed every time the main action recurs.

In this way, the statement regarding the performance will be supported; "like the *prayāja*s. Just as the *prayāja* offerings, which are constituent parts (*aṅga*), are repeated, so too the *ārambhaṇīyā*, being a constituent part, should also be repeated.
(Śabara Bhāṣya).
In that regard, what is meant by "speaking falsely"?
Why? Because of the connection with a single commencement; there is only one commencement, since the performance lasts for as long as one lives. (Siddhānta 35)

The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. This is not the case—that what was stated, that the *ārambha-līyā* (the sacrifice at the commencement) should be repeated; rather, it should be performed only once. Why? Because of its connection with the commencement (*ārambha-saṃyogāt*). It is connected with the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, serving as a common [rite] for all the performances.
[Page 189]
It has begun. How so? Having established the sacred fires, one forms a resolution (*saṅkalpa*):

“At every lunar festival (*parvan*), the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) must be performed by me. Having thus determined that the New and Full Moon sacrifices are to be performed, the *ārambhaṇīyā* (inauguratory rite) is performed; for this very determination is what constitutes its commencement (*prārambha*).

And that [determination] is common to all performances (*prayoga*), because they are to be performed as long as one lives. Even if, on the other hand, commencement means the first engagement [in the ritual], even so, by one who has first engaged...
All preparatory rites have been performed; therefore, the Sakkadārambhaṇīyā offering must be performed.
(1.1.10) Or rather: Sūtra.
[The section concerning] the consecration of the person by the *cārabhakṣa* and *auḍa*.
In the repetition of the sacrifice, the *ārti* and *ārambhaṇīyā* [rites] are performed like the *prayāja*s. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 34 ||

Regarding the first point—that "commencement" (*ārambha*) is the primary ritual act—there arises this doubt: does the *Ārambhaṇīyā* sacrifice, when performed at the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, make that first ritual act perfect;
or does it, for the person who is about to commence, make the performer fit for the commencement of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices? Which is it?

Is it obtained? — Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), it would apply at the commencement of those two; otherwise, if there were a connection with the person, one would have to assume a fruit [for the act]. Therefore, it applies at the commencement of the New and Full Moon sacrifices. If this is so, then due to the difference in commencement, it would be repeated at each commencement, just as the *prayāja* offerings are repeated at each performance (*prayoga*).
Bhāṣya:
Because of the connection with a single commencement, there is one [performance]; but there is a repeated commencement because of the lifelong application. (Siddhānta) || 35 ||
It must indeed be performed once. Why? Because of its connection with the human undertaking;
for it is enjoined when a person is about to undertake the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Why? Because of the word "he should offer" (*nirvapet*).

For in this way, a connection with the agent is established; therein, the expression of human effort has its own intended meaning. Otherwise, if only the substance of the act were intended to be enjoined, the mention of the agent's effort would be unintended, as it would merely be restating what is already obtained through the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*). As for the necessity of postulating a result in connection with the agent, that shall indeed be postulated; moreover, the person who has commenced the *Ārambhaṇīyā* will be grasped by the injunction of performance. And thus, if [this applies] to a single commencement alone...

When the *ārambhaṇīyā* has been performed for a person, because of its application therein, that person remains one for whom the *ārambhaṇīyā* has been performed throughout his life; for when he first begins the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, he becomes one who has performed the *ārambhaṇīyā*, and even in subsequent performances, when he begins the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, he becomes one who has performed the *ārambhaṇīyā*— thus it will be appropriate.

Now it is argued: "The rule 'on the same day [the Ārambhaṇīyā is performed] for those who have not yet commenced' applies; however, in the second and subsequent performances, that person has already performed the Ārambhaṇīyā on the same day.

To this it is replied: Even in the second and subsequent performances, since the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices have been commenced on that very same day, he is one for whom the Ārambhaṇīyā has been performed, and thus it is appropriate.
Thus it will be. (9.1.10)
The section concerning the collection [of mantras] beginning with *samit* for the *nirvāpa* mantra:

"In the case of mantras, there should be the status of being subsidiary because of their connection with the expression of meaning; that which is not enjoined and has not been obtained [is used], because it expresses what is enjoined. (Sūtra 36, Siddhānta)

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are indeed [the subject]; therein is the mantra for the pouring out [of the grain]: "At the impulse of the god Savitṛ, with the arms of the Aśvins, with the hands of Pūṣan, I pour you out, acceptable to Agni."

[Page 191] Thus, in this regard, the following point is subject to doubt: is there modification (*ūha*) of the words *savitṛ*, *vipuṣ*, and *pūṣan* in the ritual variation (*vikṛti*), or is there no modification (*anūha*)? Therefore, this must first be considered: do these words denote a meaning that is inherent (*samaveta*) to the ritual action, or one that is not inherent (*asamaveta*)? If...
If it is connected [to the ritual], they will be modified; if it is not connected, they will be employed without modification.
Both of these cases shall be examined together. What, then, appears to us?

That they declare what is connected [to the ritual]. Why? Because this is the observed purpose of these mantra-words: that they illuminate a meaning that is connected [to the ritual]; and that does not occur in the illumination of a meaning that is not connected.

No visible purpose is seen [in merely naming the deities]; however, there is a visible purpose in the manifestation of those [deities] as being connected [to the sacrifice]. Therefore, these words are purposeful because they denote what is connected [to the ritual]. But how do they denote what is connected? If indeed words such as *Savitṛ* were denoters of Agni and the others, or if Savitṛ and the others were specific deities in the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices—then, lest the words of the mantras have a non-visible (transcendental) purpose, one of two things must be concluded: either there is a prescription of a deity based on the wording of the mantra (*māntravarṇika*), or words such as *Savitṛ* and the rest [are themselves the deities].

Or rather, they would be denotators of Agni and the others; therefore, because they possess meaning, one or the other must be determined as the primary referent. Here [the opponent] says: "But surely, in the case of 'to Agni, what is pleasing,' even though the constituent parts such as Savitṛ and so forth are indeed denotators of Agni and the others, they would not effect anything additional for the deity manifested by Agni and the others; nor, indeed, are they merely denotators of Savitṛ and the rest."
Those who hold the view that they are separate mantras are unable to establish the connection. To this it is replied:

these shall be distinct sentences, with the common *anuṣaṅga* (supplementation) "juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi" attached to them; these sentences are subordinate elements (*guṇabhūta*) within the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, provided they are limited to this much.

Since the oblations exist, they are thereby rendered possible; thus, by the principle of presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*), deities mentioned in the mantras are enjoined. Furthermore, the mention of Agni and others applies to Savitṛ and the rest, or else these are separate sentences that are optional alternatives (*vaikalpika*) to the sentence concerning Agni.
[Page 192]
In the Mīmāṃsā system, this being the position reached, we say: such [mantras] as these are not to be modified (*ūhitavya*).
Since modification does not apply to what is not enjoined, because a mantra expresses that which has been enjoined. From this, it follows:

"The Savitṛ and others denote things that are not combined [in the sacrifice]. How so? Because no ritual action dedicated to deities such as Savitṛ is enjoined here. Furthermore, the words 'Savitṛ' and so forth are not well-known in the sense of Agni and the other [deities]. To this, he says: "But surely it was stated that one or the other must be determined through presumptive implication (arthāpatti). For these sentences concerning Savitṛ and the others are only logically consistent if there is a ritual action dedicated to those deities, or if [the word] denotes Agni."

Since there must be a deity for the oblation, that deity is to be made manifest by means of the words of the mantra; and since the words in the *nirvāpa-vākya* (the formula for pouring out) are intended for the purpose of manifestation, they are appropriate only when they manifest the deity of the oblation and not otherwise— and thus Agni and the others are the deities of the oblation.
Therefore, it is determined that [the mantra] is not [to be used]. To this it is said:

if, when not being applied, these [mantras] were to become purposeless (*ānarthakya*), then one or the other might indeed be applied, on the basis of the principle: "In the case of mantras, there is the status of being subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) because of their connection with the expression of meaning" (Sūtra 3.2.1). However, such purposelessness does not occur even when they are not applied. Therefore, there is no reason for the application of either one.

This is the authoritative proof. Furthermore, these deities are not enjoined by this [text]. In that regard, "that which is not enjoined is not obtained"; however, because they are denoted by what is enjoined, [they are indeed obtained].

Now, as for what was said—that the deities are manifested here by a word that makes them known—and that there is no purpose whatsoever in manifesting those who are not heard [in the injunction], to that [we reply]:
It must be refuted; to this, it is said:
8. bhā.
Consequently, their non-utterance is employed for the sake of another purpose. (37)
(Ācāra-nirṇaya)
Therefore, for that reason, the statement of those who have not heard it is not made; "savi* tadacanam" is the reading in the Ka0 Saṃ0 Pu0 manuscript.
[Page 193] Chapter 8, Section 9.

[The word] *śabda* is used by the disputants. For what reason, then, is it employed? It is used for the sake of the other part, for the purpose of praising the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), [as in]: "In the impulse of the god Savitṛ," [meaning] by the god Savitṛ.

When impelled by the sacrificer, or when the sun has risen, [the Adhvaryu acts] "with the arms of the Aśvins," intending this as a purchase with the arms of the husband and wife, the two sacrificers; for they have indeed eaten at the establishment of the sacred fires (*agnyādheya*) through the gift of horses, or they have obtained the fruit of that sacrifice.
He designates their arms with the word "vau" (or "vāh"). Or rather, the Adhvaryu is the deity of the Aśvins.

Regarding the word *bāhrai*: one considers Pūṣan to be the sacrificer himself; thus, all [these words] are for the purpose of indicating specific details of the offering (*nirvāpa*). Here it is asked: "Why are the words *Savitṛ* and so forth, which are elevated [in status], not understood to denote Savitṛ, the two Aśvins, and Pūṣan in another context? Because of the indicative mark (*liṅga*)."

"Being drawn out [from their context], they ought to set aside the general topic. To this it is replied: "The words *sahavivāda* and so forth are formed with feminine suffixes as qualifiers of another [noun]; however, it is understood that 'the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is not distinct [from its gender]. In that case, the gender is set aside by direct statement (*śruti*), for gender..."

Considering that the manifestation of the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is for the sake of the deity, since there is no deity here [in the case of the *saṃyukta* formulas], it would be displaced (*utkarṣati*) wherever a deity exists. However, the direct hearing of the case-ending (*vibhakti-śruti*) indicates that the meaning of the nominal stem is a qualifier of another word-meaning, and such another word-meaning exists here. Since direct hearing (*śruti*) is stronger than indicative mark (*liṅga*), therefore there is no displacement.

He asks: "When [the terms] such as *savitr* refer to the sacrificer (*yajamāna*), then how can there be no modification (*anūha*) in the *sana*? It is replied: This sentence is for the purpose of pleasing (*joṣaṇa*), not for the purpose of requesting permission (*anujñāpana*). That which has not been pleased must be made to be pleased; in this regard, the visible purpose (*dṛṣṭa-artha*) is that the act of pleasing is performed, whereas requesting permission would be rendered superfluous by the preceding [formula], and thus it would result in an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭa-artha*). Furthermore, in the phrase "I offer what is pleasing" (*juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*), the act of pleasing is expressed by the verbal noun (*bhāva-śabda*) "I offer" (*nirvapāmi*), [as in] "of Savitṛ... [and so forth].

When the word "prasava" (impulse) is uttered by the Kautsa to signify the specific impulse that brings about permission, even if permission has not been granted, one must indeed perform the pouring out (*nirvapaṇa*), which is the literal meaning of the word; for the sacrifice is heard in scripture as being performed with the approval of the mind.
Therefore, because their purpose is to indicate the time [of the sacrifice], words such as "Savitṛ" and so forth are not intended to denote [the deities] themselves.
Sūtra-bhāṣya:
The mantra "agnaye juhuḥ" serves as the basis for the modification of the word *agni* in the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice).
If it is argued that the word "quality" (guṇa) is likewise [applicable], (Pūrvapakṣa 38).

In that very same passage regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recited: "I offer what is pleasing to Agni. In this regard, there arises a doubt concerning the meaning: is the word *agni* also not uttered in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), and is it therefore not expressive of something present [in the modification]? Or should it be omitted, since it is indeed expressive of something present? What is the prima facie view? If such is the doubt therein—

That word "quality" (*guṇa*) likewise denotes that which is not inherent (*asamaveta*). Why? Because in this sentence, words such as "with salt" (*saindhava*) denote that which is inherent; if the word "fire" (*agni*) were also to denote that which is not inherent, then there would be a lack of distinction (*availakṣaṇya*), and a lack of distinction is logical. If the cause is the same, then by that principle a lack of distinction is stated; and here the cause is indeed the same, since—

The meaning of these words is not present here in this application. Even the meaning of "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (*agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi*) is not present here; by the phrase "I offer what is pleasing to Agni," the offering of that which is already pleasing is expressed, but here there is no offering of what is already pleasing. Rather, what is not yet pleasing (*ajuṣṭa*) is to be offered here, and it becomes pleasing only through the act of offering itself. Therefore, [the word *juṣṭam*] does not denote something currently inherent in the rite. Furthermore, even though its literal meaning is absent, the statement would be employed for the sake of what follows—the offering (*nirvāpa*).
Regarding the phrase "for the purpose of praise": therefore, this too is not to be modified in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti).
Not so, because of the inherence [of the quality]. (Siddhānta 38)
Bhāṣya: This is not so, for the expression "I offer what is pleasing to Agni" (agnaye juṣṭaṃ nirvapāmi) refers to that which is already combined [with the deity].
[Page 195] But was it not said: "The offering of what is already pleasing is being enjoined, and yet that which is already pleasing is not to be offered"?

To this it is replied: by this sentence, the making [of the offering] agreeable (*juṣṭa*) is not expressed; rather, it is the making of the offering agreeable *by means of* the pouring out (*nirvāpa*), as in "I make it agreeable to Agni.
For in this way, it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārtha*). Therefore, because the causes are not identical, there is indeed a distinction.
This is logical; therefore, the word "fire" (agni) denotes that which is combined [with the ritual], and it is to be employed in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti). (8.1.12)
Or rather, in this way,
the word *dhānya* (grain) in the mantra for obtaining that [grain] constitutes the subject matter of the section.
If it is argued that the word "quality" (guṇa) is used in that same sense [as a figurative designation], (Pūrvapakṣa 38).
Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they prescribe: "He pours [the grain] into the mortar with the formula, 'Thou art grain; prosper the gods!
In this regard, there is a doubt concerning the word *dhānya* (grain): does it denote something actually present in the ritual context, or not?

What is established? This word "grain" (dhānya), which appears like a word denoting a quality, cannot be a word denoting that which is inherent [in the substance]. For the word "grain" denotes grain, yet grain is not being cooked; the word "grain" applies to the grain while it is still with its husk, whereas the manifestation of "grain" occurs only when the rice-grains are being cooked. Thus, the manifestation of that which is not inherent [in the cooking] results in an unseen effect (adṛṣṭa).
"Let it be as it is"; therefore, it need not be modified in the modified sacrifices (vikṛtis).
Sūtra: It is not [the case] because of inherence. (Siddhānta) 38.

This is not so; for the meaning of the word "grain" (dhānya) is inherently connected [to its constituents], and it applies to rice-grains because they are its products, just as [the term] "rice-porridge" applies to the Kāśikas, or "cows" [apply to their calves]. [Page 196]
Since the Vedic text states "they are drunk," one must postulate an unseen result (adṛṣṭa); thus, the word is assumed to be used figuratively (lākṣaṇika).
Therefore, it denotes that which is inherent [in the substance], and it must be modified when there is a modification [of the substance].
There is a purpose: the Śākya-sacrifice lasts thirty-six years;
this is recited in the sacred tradition (samāmnāyate): "On each day that has concluded, the householder goes out hunting;
the flesh of the wild animals he kills there serves as the sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) for the Soma-pressings."

Regarding this, according to the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), the formula should be used without modification as: "Thou art grain; satisfy the gods. According to the established conclusion (*siddhānta*), however, a substitution (*jah*) must be made:
"Thou art meat; satisfy the gods. (8.2.12)
Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the modification of the word *yajñapati* in the mantra for the offering of the *iṅga* fuel-sticks.
Sūtra 40: But when [the rite] is enjoined for another purpose, there should be no modification, as in the case of the injunction.

There are the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, [enjoined] by the text: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. In that context, there is the *ir̤ā*-recitation, beginning with: "The *ir̤ā* is invoked," and so forth; and this is further recited: "The divine officiating priests are invoked, as well as those of the human race who have protected this sacrifice and who have protected the lord of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*). In this regard, the meaning is subject to doubt: should the word *yajñapati* be omitted when there are many sacrificers, or should it be employed without modification?
First, this must be examined: does the word *yajñapati* denote one who is actually present [in the ritual], or not?

Or rather, does it denote that which is not present? How is it that it denotes that which is present? If the mention of the *yajñapati* (lord of the sacrifice) is for the sake of assisting the sacrifice, then it denotes that which is present; but if this is for the sake of praise, then it does not denote that which is present. What is the conclusion? That which denotes the present must be abandoned. How so? [Because of] the sacrifice—
[Page 197] Chapter 9, Section 1.

173. From the words addressed to the husband (*patikṛt*), the masters of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*) are encouraged; the praise of the masters of the sacrifice is expressed by means of the words independently of the offering of the *iḍā*. Therefore, the primary cognition [refers to the masters of the sacrifice], while the *iḍā* is secondary. Consequently, due to this remoteness of meaning, it is not a praise of the *iḍā*; thus, the word "master of the sacrifice" must be abandoned [in that context]. Only for whom prosperity (*vṛddhi*) is spoken of is he consecrated by the refinement of encouragement (*utsāha-saṃskāra*).
It would not be so. Therefore, all [the names] should be uttered for the purpose of consecrating the sacrificial post (*dṛṣi*); since all are to be uttered, the plural number should be used.
This being the position reached, we reply: "But when [a word] has been enjoined, because it serves another's purpose, there is a modification, as in the case of an injunction."

"Even that which, though enjoined, is connected [to another] and intended for the sake of another, not for its own refinement, should also be employed without modification; it must not be omitted because it is for the sake of another. For here, the mention of the *yajñapati* (the master of the sacrifice) is for the purpose of qualifying the increase (*vṛddhi*), and the mention of the increase is for the purpose of praising the *ir̥ḍā*. How is this understood? From the invocation of the *ir̥ḍā*."
Because of syntactical unity and because of the context of the *iḍā* offering.

Now, as for what was said: "It is understood that the statement regarding the increase of the sacrificer (*yajñapati*), independent of the word *iḍā*, serves to encourage them—namely, 'May those men who partake of the *iḍā* cause the sacrificer to prosper.'"

It is said: having stated, "He who, knowing thus, proceeds with the *iḍā*," it then says, "Now he begins: 'The *iḍā* is struck; the *iḍā* is struck; [I am] in the *iḍā*; the *iḍā* is struck. From this it is understood that the mantra beginning with this introduction belongs to the *iḍā*. That which falls within its course, such as "Men are invited" (*upahatā manuṣyāḥ*) and so forth, [belongs to the *iḍā*], as does [the portion] "the lord of the sacrifice" (*yajñapatiṃ*).

"...the rains," thus ends [the passage]. From the sentence, "Therefore, the *iḍā* offering should be recited," it is understood that the *iḍā* is to be recited. While there is the capacity for the recitation of the *iḍā*, there is no sentence stating that it should be recited in order to encourage the sacrificer; there is merely the capacity to recite it. Furthermore, applications do not occur by mere capacity alone without a scriptural statement (*vākya*).
And in this way, the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *iḍā* will be upheld, as there will be syntactic unity (*ekavākyatā*) with the *iḍā*. Therefore, this [is the case]. [Page 198]
The explicit statement is: "Those men who have been brought [as priests] are capable of causing the lord of the sacrifice to prosper.

In that case, prosperity qualified by the lord of the sacrifice must be expressed; thus, even when only a single sacrificer is mentioned, the function of the qualifier is fulfilled. Therefore, there should be no modification [of the plural form].

"According to rule" (*vidhivat*): where the sacrificer is prescribed as a subordinate factor (*guṇabhūta*), that rule is accomplished by any sacrificer whatsoever; for example: "The *udumbara* post is of the same height as the sacrificer," and "The sacrificer touches the *śukra* vessel. (ŚB 1.1.12)
Sūtra Bhāṣya:
The section concerning the word "sacrificer" (*yajamāna*) in the context of the weapon, the protector, and the crow.
The modification would belong to that which is predominant therein. || 41 ||

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is the *sūktavāka*: "With the *sūktavāka*, he throws the grass-bundle (*prastara*) into the fire. In this regard, the following is recited: "This sacrificer desires long life. Here, a doubt arises as to the meaning: does this apply in a modified sacrifice (*vikāra*) involving many performers?

Should the word "yajamāna" (sacrificer) be modified, or not? What is the prima facie view? It should be employed without modification; thus its functional capacity is maintained. Furthermore, this word does not denote something currently present [in the ritual action], for in the phrase "the sacrificer invokes long life," no visible purpose is served for the sacrificer by the invocation of long life. Therefore, the invocation of long life serves an invisible (transcendental) purpose. Thus, the blessing qualified by the "sacrificer" is fulfilled exactly as heard in the scripture, provided that even a single sacrificer is mentioned. Just as...
"The *udumbara* post is of a size commensurate with the sacrificer (*yajamāna*). This is the case here as well. Therefore, it should be employed without modification.

This being the position reached, we reply: there should be a modification (*vikāra*), that is, an omission (*jahat*), because that [the sacrificer] is the primary factor (*tat-pradhāne*). How is the sacrificer the primary factor? It is heard in scripture as follows:

Regarding the injunction, "One casts the prastara-bundle with the *sūktavāka*": if the *sūktavāka* reveals either the means or the result for the casting of the prastara-bundle, then the prastara-bundle [is connected] by means of the *sūktavāka*.

The *prastara* is thrown down; the fruit of the throwing is intended as a prayer for long life: "O Sacrificer, he prays for long life through this rite. Thus, the *prastara* is thrown down by the Sacrificer.
In that case, the Sacrificer, who is the primary agent with respect to the fruit, is not explicitly mentioned [as the one throwing it]. Therefore—

It would not be struck [as a plural]. Therefore, all who have assembled together must be addressed collectively; and when they are being addressed by all, the plural number is used. Hence, it belongs to many sacrificers.
From the *Sūtrakṛṣṇa*, the section concerning the word *harivat* in the *Subrahmaṇyā-nigada*:
*Sūtra 42:* "Because there is no connection [with the primary meaning], that which is qualified by it should be understood as intended for those purposes.
(Siddhānta) There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice; therein the *Subrahmaṇyā-nigada* is recited: "O Indra, come! O Harivan, come! O Medhātithi’s ram," and so forth.

In the *Amniṣṭut* sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "The *Subrahmaṇyā* formula belongs to Agni. In that case, the word *jahaḥ* is substituted in place of the word *indra*. Now, regarding the passages beginning with "O possessor of bay horses (*Hariva*), come hither," there arises a doubt: should [the substitution] be made, or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? "That which is qualified by it should be understood"—that is, it is qualified by that; therefore, the substitution of *jahaḥ* occurs in place of the word *indra*.

By this distinction, the word itself would be understood as qualified and yet unmodified. Why? Because "there is no connection with those meanings" (asaṃyogāt tadartheṣu). There is no connection of these words with those meanings in cases such as *harivanta* and so forth; qualities such as having bay horses (*harivat*) do not exist as inherent properties in Indra, because there is a lack of evidence. Since they do not exist [in him], they are spoken of [as belonging] to him. Thus is the meaning according to the direct statement (*śruti*).
Śeṣa states in the *Nyāyamālā* that for one who has drunk the poison of the *śāpa*, there is the notion of "Jārā" at the onset of the seizure of the *gaura-avaskanda*.
[Page 200] *Mīmāṃsā-damana* (The Subduing of Mīmāṃsā).

It becomes a formal proposition (*pratijñāta*); otherwise, there would be an indication (*lakṣaṇā*), and terms such as *harivattā* would not be uttered. By means of *harivattā* and the like, that quality of his is indicated. Now, if it were argued: "The words, though denoting things not inherent [in the subject], will have their primary meaning (*mukhyārtha*) alone and will not indicate its own quality," then that is precisely our position; therefore, the quality is uttered for an unseen purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*).
Thus, the application [of the mantra] would be without modification. In that case, the syntactical expression (vacanavyakti) becomes:
"O Indra, come; O Harivant, come," [thereby applying] the epithets such as "Harivant" to him.
One superimposes the qualities; for Indra, when connected with [epithets] such as "Harivat," becomes the cause of prosperity.
And it is possible to connect Agni as well with those [qualities]; therefore, the qualities are to be employed without modification.

It is argued: "From this very statement of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it follows that these qualities exist in Indra. To this we reply: even when [the qualities] do not actually exist, a statement of coreferentiality can still be justified on the basis of praise (*stuti*), just as one might say, "Indra is Bṛhaspati is Devadatta."
Sūtra Bhāṣya: If it is argued that this is so because of the absence of karma. (Objection) || 43 ||

If you should view it thus—that the mention of "having bay horses" (*harivat*) and so forth is by way of non-modification—this would be so only in the absence of [these] qualities; for these qualities indeed exist in Indra. [As it is said: "O possessor of bay horses, come! (*hariva āgaccha*).

"The two bay horses of Indra, the one of the waxing fortnight and the one of the waning fortnight; with them he carries away all that remains. "The ram of Medhātithi": for it was Medhātithi Kāṇvāyana whom the ram carried off.
Vṛṣaṇaśva had a daughter named Menakā; Indra desired her. "Gaurāvaskandan": having become a white deer, he roams about and drinks King Soma.
● Regarding the reading "ṭamavaśvasya" in the *Nyāyamālā*,
[Page 201],
these qualities are declared to belong to Indra by these statements; therefore, they are words denoting what is inherent [in him].

Words such as *harivat* and others are uttered for the purpose of producing the cognition of Indra; thus, there will be no assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭakalpanā*). In that case, the syntactical form is: "O Indra, come!

O Harivat, come!"—meaning, "He who possesses the quality of having bay horses (*harivattā*) and so forth, let him come. And metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is superior to the assumption of an unseen result. Therefore, words such as *harivat* and others should be supplied.
Not so, because it is for the sake of another. (Sūtra 44; Ābhāsa-nirṇaya)

Commentary: This is not so; for words such as "harivat" and others are for the sake of another—namely, for the purpose of praising Indra—and thus a connection with "harivat" and so forth is made for his praise; this has already been explained previously.

Furthermore, for the purpose of praise, it is possible to establish a connection between these [qualities] and Agni as well. As for what was said—that qualities inherent in Indra exist, as understood from such scriptural statements as "The two horses, Pūrvapakṣa and Aparapakṣa, belong to Indra"—in that case, these statements do not actually enjoin two horses belonging to Indra; nor is the connection made in that manner.
"As for these two, the prior and the posterior fortnights, they are Indra's two bay horses (harī);

for there a reason is taught: 'For by means of them he carries everything. Indeed, it is not a well-known fact that Indra carries everything by means of those two; for a reason must be something already established, not something yet to be proven."

However, just as these two are well-known as "seizers" (hartṛ) in the sense that "everything is diminished by time," so too there is no distinction whatsoever between Indra and Agni; in that case, the designation [of the mantra] applies to Agni itself.

Now, if it is argued that "Indra's possession of the two bay horses (harī) is being enjoined," then the sentence would be split; for this too—"these two are Indra's bay horses"—would have to be enjoined.
If that is what is enjoined, then the same fault remains: there is no distinction between Agni and Indra.

In the Mīmāṃsā system, it is further argued: "The two prior and subsequent positions belong to Indra; those two are his bay horses (harī), therefore Indra is called 'the possessor of bay horses' (harivān). However, that same defect remains, such as the non-establishment of the reason (hetvaprasiddhi) and so forth; it is not [resolved].

Furthermore, when [the mantra] is being prescribed, the word "vai" occurs; this word is seen in the remainder [of Vedic usage] as having the sense of what is already well-known, as for example: "There are indeed no friendships with women.

Likewise, passages such as "The ram of Medhātithi" appear like the statements of historical tradition (itihāsa). And if there were an injunction (vidhi) within such historical tradition, the defect of having a beginning (ādimattā-doṣa) would attach to the Veda.

If it is argued that "let it be so," then because that [text] would lack authority, there would be the non-establishment of the well-known expression "the ram of Medhātithi Kāṇāyana. Furthermore, there is an injunction regarding the *nigada* everywhere;
in that case, if another [quality] were enjoined, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākya-bheda*). Therefore, these qualities do not belong to Indra.

"Since they exist," [it is argued] that because the word does not denote something inherent [to the specific context], it should be used without modification. However, the ritualists do not approve of this;
they perform the substitution, saying: "O Agni, come, O Rohitāśva, Bṛhadbhāno, Dhūmaketo, Jātavedas, Vicarṣaṇi!"
Thus [ends the section]. (1.1.150)
Regarding that, the mantra "tasyai śṛtam" is the subject of the discussion.
Now, this [following] point is raised:
Sūtra: Because there is no connection with those [other] purposes, it should be understood as qualified by that [specific purpose]. (Siddhānta) 42.
[Commentary:

There is the Sādyaska sacrifice; regarding it, they recite this: "A one-year-old bull is the means for purchasing the Soma. However, in the archetype (prakṛti), there is a one-year-old cow intended for the purchase. In that case—

This is handed down in tradition: "This is a cow; with her I purchase from you; for her there is boiled milk, for her curd, for her whey, for her cream, for her the morning-milk, for her fresh butter, for her clarified butter.
[Page 203]
"Of her [is] the sacrificial fee; for her [is] the horse"—this is obtained here by the force of the extended injunction (*codaka*).

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the word *go* (cow) be replaced and the remaining words left unchanged, or should there be a modification (*ūha*) of all the words? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? The expression *jaha* (sacrificial fee) should be qualified by the meaning of the word *go* alone; there should be no modification of the words "of her [is] the dead [animal]" and so forth, because they have no connection with the meanings such as "dead" and the rest in relation to the *ekahāyanī* (one-year-old cow).

in this way, the word "Ṛk" will have a single meaning. They apply the term "Ṛk" figuratively by relying on some particular commonality; this has been stated thus because a specific number applies to a certain particular case, for otherwise, all numbers would apply everywhere.
For in that case, there would be an absence of conventional linguistic usage. Therefore, in the Mīmāṃsā system, those who possess the same intention [are considered identical].
And in cases where the deities are identical, because of the metaphorical application of the term *ṭac*, only those [verses] recited in the sequence of the *uttarāgraṇī* should be taken. (Ṭāśa 5)
While the *atijagatī* meter is being practiced, there is no grief; this concerns the locus of pride. (The second section.)
Or rather, the repetition of that [practice] should take place during the equal [days]. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 21 ||

Commentary: There is the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice, [instituted] with the injunction: "One desiring progeny should cause him to sacrifice with the *dvādaśāha*. On its fourth day, there is the *sāman* named *vaiśoka*, which has an *ati-jagatī* as its *udgītha* and a *pratijagatī* as its [stotra]: "The *viśvāḥ pṛtanā abhibhūtaram naram sajūstatathur indram ajanuṣo rājase | kratvā variṣṭham varāmurīm utogram ojiṣṭham tavasam tarasvinam*" (All the armies have united and brought forth Indra, the most victorious hero, for sovereignty—the most excellent in wisdom, the most beautiful, the fierce, the strongest, the most powerful, and the most swift). The two following [verses] are *bṛhatīs*; of these, the first is: "memim... [etc.]

"The inspired poets, shining brightly and swift as steeds, bow with their speech toward the ram, even at the ear, with their eager voices. (Rigveda 1.51.1) The subsequent verse says: "The singers have sung together to Indra for the drinking of Soma, so that he may increase the rain-giver; he who is firm in his vows, through his power and his aids. In this regard, the meaning is doubtful: are these other *pratijagatī* verses?

"Should one sing on the basis of the even [verses], using those very same *bṛhatī* verses that are the subsequent ones? Or should one sing on the basis of the uneven [verses]? "Lest there be a deficiency in the *saṃbhara* [hymn], one should practice this sāman on the even [verses] by taking those two *jagatī* verses which are produced [in the context]."

And thus, in the case of the Vaiśoka hymn which has the same deity, the metaphorical application of the term ‘ṛca’—as in the expression ‘aṣṭarca’—will be appropriate; for this reason as well, other [verses] should not be taken up. [The opponent] objects:

The source-verse (*yoni*) of the *rathantara* is: "We cry out to you, O Hero, like milch-cows lowing for milk; to you, the lord of this moving world, the beholder of heaven, the lord, O Indra, of all that stands still."
In the Mīmāṃsā system, the subsequent verse states: "But there is no other like you—neither celestial nor terrestrial; none has been born, nor shall be."
"He shall be born. O Indra, Maghavan, we, the singers seeking booty and desiring cattle, call upon you.

"O Indra, lord of the virtuous, men call upon you in battles against the Vṛtras; they call upon you in the races for the sun.
This is the fifth line [of the hymn]: "Thus, O wondrous one, wielder of the thunderbolt in your hand, being boldly praised as the great one, O Lord of the Stone."

"O Indra, bestow a village-horse, a chariot-steed, and a hall upon the victorious one. Regarding these two [sāmans], a Vedic-style singing is prescribed: "The Bṛhat and Rathantara do not indeed belong to a single meter;
of these two, the former is a Bṛhatī and the latter two are Kakubhs."

In this regard, the matter is one of doubt: should the other two *kakub* verses be brought in from elsewhere and sung, or should the *ṣaḍaha* rite be performed by interweaving (*pragrathana*) that which is the preceding [verse] and the *paṅkti* verse, thereby performing the singing in the form of the subsequent *kakub*?

What is established? That the *kakup* meters should be brought forward [from elsewhere]. Why? Because in this way, the origin of the other *kakups* will be meaningful through the *Atharvans*, provided they are employed for the purpose of the *kakup*. An objection is raised: "But surely they will have their purpose in the *Vācastoma*. It is replied: [No, that is not so.]
"It is true that there will be purposefulness in that case; however, the fact that it serves as the purpose for the *kakubh* [verse] is also understood, and that [purpose] must not be discarded.

This being the position reached, we reply: "But it is the *pragātha* [chanting]. The word "but" (*tu*) sets aside the previous view. The *sāman*-chanting should be performed as a *pragātha*; that which was the preceding *bṛhatī* and the following [verse]...

There is a *paṅkti* [verse] and a [verse] of those two; their composition (*pragranthana*) must be performed. For thus they remember: "The *pragātha* is *kākubha*. He says: "But surely, if the *kakubh* is not the first [verse], the designation *kākubha* would not apply. It is replied: [It applies] by the rule "this belongs to that" (*tasyedam*) or "that which occurs therein" (*tatra bhavaḥ*).
Or there is no fault.

Commentary: Furthermore, the term *pragātha* is appropriately applied here, for the prefix *pra-* indicates excellence (*prakarṣa*). That in which there is singing with excellence is a *pragātha*. And the commentary (bhāṣya) shows that the indicative mark (liṅga) exists everywhere without exception. How is it "without exception"? What is the indicative mark? It says this: "This is indeed the established *bṛhatī* which has a repeated foot; therefore, because one begins a foot again, it is a *vallī*."

"For he utters 'hiṅ' toward the mother"—this repetition of the commencement of the quarter-verse is appropriate in the case of interlacing (*pragrathana*), and not otherwise. There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Jyotiṣṭoma" (Mīmāṃsā, Tenth Book).

Thus it is said. "You flow forth, O god, the golden one, pouring out the treasure-bearing womb of Truth.

The next [verse] is a *viṣṭārapaṅkti*: "Milking the sweet, beloved honey from the lower [world], he has sat upon his common dwelling-place. He flows toward the invincible support; cleansed by the *ṛbhus*, he is far-seeing."

Therefore, there is this doubt: should the singing be performed upon the *samā* verses by taking the arrival (*āgama*) of the other two, namely the *bṛhatī* and the *bṛhatī*; or rather, should the singing be performed in the form of a *bṛhatī* by performing the *ṣaṭka*-work through the interweaving (*pragrathana*) of that preceding *bṛhatī* and the following *viṣṭārapaṅkti*?
What is obtained here? That even in the case of the blind, the two [mantras] must be brought forward. Why?
Because in this way, the origin of the ṛcs will be meaningful.

This being the case, we reply: "But it is a *pragātha*; however, the word 'but' (*tu*) sets aside the previous position. The *sāman* chant should be performed as a *pragātha*, and it should not be brought in from the original [verses] by means of the *utpatti-hṛti* [method];

rather, the interweaving (*pragrathana*) should be performed upon the two verses already present in the archetype. For thus they remember: 'The *bārhadgira* is a *pragātha*'; if the *utpatti-hṛti* were brought in, there would be no *pragātha*."
In that case, the traditional rule (smṛti) would be contradicted! Therefore, the interweaving (pragrathana) of the two original [verses] must be performed.
And [the rule applies] to the letter *kha*. (Yukti 1) || 26 ||

And because of the Vedic rule "khe," the singing will take place according to the original form; thus there is neither the abandonment of the original nor the introduction of something non-original. Therefore, for this reason as well, other *bṛhatī* verses are not to be brought in.

And for this reason also, the word *pragātha* will be appropriate; for that [term] occurs in the sense of excellence of singing (*prakarṣe gānasya*), and here, such excellence occurs when a verse-quarter (*pāda*) is repeated. Therefore, for this reason as well—
The other two Bṛhatī verses are not to be taken up.
And because of the observation of indicative marks and because of non-deviation [from the rule]. (Sūtra 28) (Yukti)
Furthermore, the commentary (*bhāṣya*) shows the indicative mark (*liṅga*) by way of non-exclusion. What is the indicative mark?
It says this: "The midday pressing consists of thirty *triṣṭubh* verses. How so?

[The] Indicative Mark (liṅga) 1: If the Bṛhatī-metres are produced by means of *pragrathana* (interweaving), then all the verses (*ṛc*) prescribed for every pressing (*savana*) amount to sixty; otherwise, there would be more than the Bṛhatīs required by their original production when they are being brought in. This very point is indicated: "The Gāyatrāmahīyava [stotra] occurs in two Gāyatrī verses; those are six Gāyatrīs. The Raurava-Yaudhājaya [stotra] occurs in two Bṛhatī verses; those also are six Bṛhatīs. The Ośanasa-Antya..."

Regarding the *viṣṭups*, those too are three *triṣṭubh*s. Now, when the *pṛṣṭha* chant is performed for the Hotṛ priest on either the *bṛhatī* or the *rathantara* with the seventeen-fold (*saptadaśa*) *stoma*, there are five *bṛhatīs* and twelve *kakups*.

How so? For this is the *viṣṭuti* (method of chanting) in each case: he utters *hiṃ* over five [verses]—three times with three [verses], once with one, once with one; he utters *hiṃ* over five [verses]...
"He [sings] with one, he with three, he with one; he utters the *hiṅ* for seven verses:
he with one, he with three, he with three"—in this regard, there are three *bṛhatī*s first and one *kakubh*, then again one *kakubh*, and then again one.
With three *hahatī*s and one *kakubh*; thus there are four *hahatī*s and six *kakubh*s. Then again, with one *hahatī*, and again with three [on the next page].

Furthermore, with the three *kakubh* verses of the *Mīmāṃsā-darśana*, there are likewise three *kakubh*s; thus, there are five *bṛhatī*s and twelve *kakubh*s. Together with those three *bṛhatī*s, there are eleven *bṛhatī*s in total.
Then, from six *gāyatrī*s, four *gāyatrī*s become twelve *kakubh*s, which result in twelve *bṛhatī*s. Thus, there are twenty-three *bṛhatī*s. Then, in the *Vāmadevya*...

There are seventeen *gāyatrī* verses; when combined with the two remaining *gāyatrī* verses from the *pāvamānī* hymns, they become nineteen *gāyatrīs*. Then, the seventeen *bṛhatīs* of the *nodhasa* and *kāleya* hymns are brought together with fifty-seven quarters of *gāyatrīs*, resulting in fifty-seven *bṛhatīs* and fifty-seven *triṣṭubhs*; when these are added to the *triṣṭubh* verses from the *pāvamānī* hymns, it is established that there are sixty *triṣṭubhs*. Next, the introduction of the *kakup* meters arising from the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* [sāmans] is performed; therein, those which...
Those [verses] recited in the *savana*s amount to sixty; as for those two *kakubh* verses not recited in the *savana*s, they are employed twelve times, and by that means those sixty are completed.
Those *ṛc*s which are recited in the *savana*s are referred to here by the term "savana."

It is said that the term *savana* is not used in the sense of an action; for in that context, it would mean "in the three *savanas* there should be *triṣṭubh*s," rather than "the midday *savana* consists of sixty *triṣṭubh*s.
Therefore, regarding those two *bṛhatī*s which precede and the subsequent *viṣṭārapaṅkti*, [one should form] a *pragātha* therein.

in the *kakubh*, the *poṣkala*; and the *kāva* in other *jagatī* [verses]. This which...

"The pressed juice flows forth with purifying power; Indu is like a well-fashioned steed. Toward that Soma, which is difficult to attain, men with every prayer urge the sacrifice with stones.

In this regard, there is a doubt concerning the meaning: should the chanting be performed on the verses made equal by introducing two other *anuṣṭubh* verses, or rather, [should it be done] with that very *anuṣṭubh* which precedes?
Regarding the two subsequent *gāyatrī* verses, having performed the *ṣaṭkarma* by means of their *pragātha*, should the singing be performed using the *anuṣṭubh*-mode?
What is the prima facie view?—that other *anuṣṭubh*s should be introduced. Why?

What is this? [The opponent says: "In this way, the originative injunctions for those [verses] will become purposeful. This being the position reached, we reply: "But it is *prāgāthika*"; that is, the singing should be performed according to the *pragātha* [meter]. For thus...
Regarding the statement "the *pragātha* consists of *anuṣṭubh*s," the status of being a *pragātha* is what is being enjoined;
for they record in their tradition: "The *anuṣṭubh*s are not to be displaced."

And the indicative mark (*liṅga*) occurs without exception; thus it says: "The twenty-four *jagatī*s are the third pressing (*tṛtīyasavana*); one *kakubh*. Therein it is indicated that the *ārbhava-pavamāna* has five meters and seven *sāmans*: "The two *gāyatra-saṃhita*s occur in the *gāyatra* *ṛc*s"; those six *gāyatrī*s become three *jagatī*s. In that case, when performed by means of *pradyathana* (transposition), there are six *anuṣṭubh*s for the two *sāman*s; those [six] become four *jagatī*s, which together with the previous ones make seven. The *yajñāyajñīya* chant consists of twenty-one verses; among these, the preceding are *bṛhatīs* and the subsequent are *viṣṭārapaṅktis*. Then, having made the two subsequent [verses] into *kakubs*, the *pragātha* is formed. And when the twenty-one-fold (*ekaviṃśa*) *stoma* is being performed, seven...
There are fourteen *bṛhatī*s and [four] *kakubh*s; those which are seven *bṛhatī*s become *paṅkti*s.

Together with the preceding ones, there are sixteen; one quarter of a *jagatī* consists of a single mora. Together with the preceding *gāyatrī* quarter, there are twenty syllables. Now, regarding the fourteen *kakubh*s:

The twelve *kakubh* verses become seven *jagatī*s; together with the preceding ones, they total twenty-three. Those two *kakubh*s that are left over constitute one *jagatī*, which, along with the feet of the *gāyatrī*s and the preceding ones, makes twenty-four syllables; thus, the foot of the *gāyatrī* is joined with the preceding twenty-two syllables.
The *kākubha* occurs. Thus, while being chanted (*pragāyamāne*), there is a fourfold division (*catuṣṭutiḥ*) of the *agastya*; [Page 241] in the ninth chapter, the first section.

And there is one *kakup*. Now, if the *pragātha* is not performed, then—following the case of the *śvāna*, *athāmbha*, and *gavaya* stanzas which are *anuṣṭubh*s later on, and the case of the *triṣṭubh* and *jagatī* stanzas where the *utpatti-kakup*s are merely added—the total number is accomplished simply by the addition [of verses]. Therefore, the chanting should be performed by means of interlacing (*pragrathana*). In the *Gavām ayana*, with reference to the *Brahmasāman*, they recite: "Four hundred *Indra*-verses in the *Bṛhatī* meter as *pragāthas*, and thirty-three *matī*-verses in the *Bṛhatī* meter as triplets."

In this regard, there is a doubt: should one sing by forming a *pragātha* from these two verses, or should one sing over three verses? What is the prima facie view? That it should be sung over three verses.

Why is this so? Because it is heard thus in the archetype (prakṛti): "Therefore, one *sāman* is performed over a triplet. That [rule] is extended here by the *codaka* [transfer rule], and thus it follows that it should be sung over three verses. This being the position reached, we reply: "But it is a *pragātha*," and "in the *ṛk*s," and "in the *pragātha*. (Sūtras 25–27).

The singing should be performed on two successive verses; thus, the *ve-gāna* will constitute the vow (*vrata*).
In what [context] is it? In the *pragātha*. How is the *pragātha* the context?
For it is prescribed in the *Gavāmayana* with reference to the *Brahmasāman*; therefore, the *pragātha* is the context for the *Brahmasāman*.
And by the word "negligent" (pramādya), one's own state is expressed as being "deep."

For there is indeed an indicative mark (liṅga) seen: "Five *subārhata* *pragāthas* are recited.

For there are one hundred and four *pragāthas* for you; in the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, there is a pair of *pragāthas* for the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara*;
likewise, in that same [sacrifice], there is a pair of *pragāthas* for the *Naudhasa* and *Kāleya*; and the *Indrakratu* *pragātha* occurs in the latter *yacas*.
These [together] constitute ninety-nine *pragāthas*.

The remaining [verses] are to be performed during the *abhiplava* periods. Regarding the *pṛṣṭha* days, the *satoḍahatya* verses are prescribed; for the *abhiplavas*, the *satoḍahatya* occurs on the third day. Thus, there are one hundred *abhiplava* days for the *abhiplavas*, and among them, some are *satoḍahatya* days, while on the other eighty-nine days there are eighty-nine *pragāthas*. The indicative mark (*liṅga*) "they are completed" is thus appropriately established.
If, however, while the chanting (*gāna*) is being performed, the sixty-six triplets (*ṛcas*) were to be completed in three months plus seven days, then—
on account of observing this indicative mark— it is considered that the chanting must be performed upon the *pragātha*.

He asks: "Why, then, after performing the chanting on the first *ṛc*, is the chanting performed by taking one *ṛc* from that same [verse] and taking two other *ṛcs* to form a *ṛc*-trio (*ṛca*)? It is replied: "The indicative mark shows that there is no deviation; the *ṛcs* are different, yet the *sāman* remains the very same."

In the Sāmaveda, there are a thousand methods of chanting (*gotyupāya*). It is asked: "What are these so-called methods of chanting? It is replied: Chanting (*gīti*) is a specific action; it consists of internal effort—

That which manifests the specific qualities of the *vanita* (the sung verse) is designated by the term *sāman*; it is chanted upon a *ṛc* of fixed meter. For the purpose of accomplishing that [chanting], there are modifications of syllables in the *ṛcs*, such as separation (*viśleṣa*), protraction (*vikarṣaṇa*), repetition (*abhyāsa*), pause (*virāma*), and musical interjections (*stobha*).

All [the methods] have been attained and are traditionally handed down. Regarding them, there is a doubt: are they to be combined (*samuccīyante*) or are they to be treated as alternatives (*vikalpante*)? What first appears to us is that they should be combined, because all are handed down and because the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*) encompasses all of them. This being the position reached, we reply: "But because the purpose is one, there should be an option. For they serve a single purpose.

The means for producing [the result]—namely, the songs—are employed with the thought, "How may the song be brought to completion? In that case, once the song has been completed by one [particular means], the others do not deserve to be employed. Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

In a certain specific ritual action, it is heard [in scripture]: "They praise with the *ṛc*; they praise with the *sāman*.

There is a doubt: should one praise with a *ṛk* or with a *sāman*, or rather, only with a *sāman*? What, then, is the prima facie view? It is an option—either with a *ṛk* or with a *sāman*;
for this sentence is seen as distinct: "When they praise with a *ṛk*, the Asuras followed after that."

Thus, when the praise is being performed with a *ṛc*, the Asuras followed along; we see that the sentence is complete at this point.
