The verse should be employed only when it is already chanted (*pragīta*), not when it is not chanted (*apragīta*). Why? Because of the scriptural statement (*vacana*).

What is the statement? "With this [verse], *prayaṃ sahasramānavaḥ*,"—here the word "this" (*etayā*) refers to what has been introduced in the context; and in the Sāmaveda, that which is chanted is what is introduced. Therefore, it is connected with the word "this."
"Even *namo 'pragītā* is recited there. True; however, that [recitation] is for the purpose of establishing a connection with the *pragāṇa*.

One cannot establish a means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) regarding what has already been recited. Regarding the purpose of the *ṛc* and the *sāman*: the study of the *ṛc* is understood to be for the sake of the *sāman*; the accomplishment of the *sāman* does not occur without the *ṛc*.
However, even without the *sāman*, the *ṛc* is accomplished; the *ṛc* does not depend upon the *sāman*.

Thus, therefore, when it is stated in the Sāmaveda that one "stands near" (*upatiṣṭhate*) or "praises" (*stauti*), the understanding refers only to the verse that is set to melody (*pragītā*), not to that which is not set to melody (*apragītā*).

[The opponent] says: "If the understanding refers to the melodic verse because of the context (*prakaraṇa*), then by virtue of the explicit statement (*vacana*), it would refer to the non-melodic verse as well; for that non-melodic version is also recited in another recensional branch (*śākhā*), and that [would be part of] the context."

"If it were [the case], it would sublate [the injunction] by means of the sentence (*vākya*). Commentary: Here, some recite with a threefold accent (*traisvarya*), while others recite with a fourfold accent (*cātuḥsvarya*). What do they do? They study after skipping one *khara*-interval. Your doubt is this: is there a combination (*samuccaya*) of the *caisvarya* and other qualities, or is it an option (*vikalpa*)?
What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Because the injunction of performance (*prayoga-vacana*) requires the inclusion of all auxiliary elements (*aṅga*), there must be a combination.

Thus it being established, we reply: "Now, because the purpose is one, there would be an option; for the single purpose of all [rules] such as the threefold accentuation (*traisvaryya*) is the accomplishment of study; therefore, there is an option. "By virtue of the womb and the season? It is said: we shall explain this by taking a certain example.

If the substitution of *ai* is performed first, then the singing occurs according to the phonetic nature of the preceding vowel;

however, if one observes the long palatal vowel (*bṛhantālavya*) in the subsequent portion and performs the substitution of *ai* there, then the singing occurs according to the phonetic nature of the following vowel.
"What, then, is to be done here? [It is] by means of the power of the womb-color (yonivarṇa). How so?
We shall investigate that portion of the letter *e* where its state as a womb (*yoni*) is known: what is performed there? The letter *e* is not uttered; rather, it is the letters *ī* and *ā*. "

"In the *mimitā* [verses]," it is said; if this is so, then in the subsequent [verses] as well, that syllable which occupies that same position must not be pronounced, and the vowels *ī* and *ā* must be supplied. Thus, when there is a correspondence between the *yoni* and the subsequent verses, it becomes connected with those subsequent verses. Therefore, one should sing according to the syllables of the *yoni*.

Moreover, if it were not so, the *gīti* (melodic chant) would not be established; otherwise, something might perish, since a *gīti* belonging to many syllables is sung upon few syllables, and in that case, it would clearly perish and be replaced by a *gīti* consisting of subsequent syllables.
Therefore, it must be performed according to the original number of syllables.
Furthermore, in some cases the sequence is obstructed where there is no phonetic modification (*ādeśa*) for the preceding part;
and in some cases the archaic form (*ārṣa*) is obstructed, where the Prakrit insertion (*prākṛtāgama*) is simply not performed. In such instances:

At the time of recitation (*svādhyāya*), singing is performed; however, at the time of ritual action (*karmakāla*), singing must be performed without contradiction [to the rules]. Therefore, it should be performed according to the *yoni* [verse]; thus, there is a modification in the *sāman* section (such as the insertion of *āībhāva*, etc.), which is dependent on that (i.e., dependent on the *yoni*). Bhāṣya: [The author] considers that [the formation of *aikāra*] should be performed according to the sequence of the *avarṇa* (the sound *a*), and not according to the sequence of the *yoni-bhāga* (the source-part). Why? Because that which was made into a single entity (*aikabhāva*) in the original form (*prakṛti*) is neither an *āgama* (an augment) nor is there an elision of the vowel *e* there; rather, what is called *ekāra* consists of both *avarṇa* and *ivarṇa*. Furthermore, *avarṇa* is contracted (*saṃvṛta*), while *ivarṇa* is expanded (*vivṛta*); yet both are sounds (*dhvani*).

From those two improper [sounds], a proper *sandhyacara* (euphonic combination) is produced. In your case, the long *a* and *ī* have been separated; nothing new has been introduced, but a certain unprecedented *guṇa* has been made of them. In all such matters, direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is the authority; that is so in this instance as well.

In one portion there is another vowel, not a *sandhyacara* (conjunctive vowel); in that case, since there is no remainder [of the same sound], a separation (*viśleṣa*) cannot be made. In the other portion where a *sandhyacara* occurs, a separation is made because of that.
Thus, it is done for both the *yoni* and the subsequent two verses.
For just as a separation was made between two things joined within the womb, so too here is there a separation of two things joined;
otherwise, something distinct would have to be imagined.
In this regard, the reading *īśvarasya* found in some manuscripts appears to be correct. The same applies to the subsequent passage.

"One sings the Rathantara on the *kavatī* verses; one sings the Rathantara on the two subsequent verses; whatever is sung on the model verse (*yoni*), that is sung on the two subsequent verses. Now, the following point is deliberated here: are the *stobhas* (interpolated musical syllables) indicated [by the rule], or not? What is the prima facie view? They are not indicated. Why?

For the *gīti* (the act of singing) is the *sāman*, not the *stobhas*; that which is the *gīti* is what is indicated by the rule, "He sings that [verse] on the two following verses just as it was on the original verse (*yoni*)," because of its connection with the word "sings" (*gāyati*). Furthermore, a *stobha* being connected with the meaning of the word "direction" (*dik*) would be purposeless; therefore, for this reason also, it would not be indicated. Moreover, there is a scriptural statement in some cases: "The *Avabhṛtha-sāman* belongs to Indra."

In that case, there would be an inconsistency, for Indra is understood from the supplementary passages (*vākyaśeṣa*) to be characterized by cold actions; he could not have a connection with the word "he heats" (*tapati*).

Therefore, the *stobha* syllables are excluded when there is another *ṛc*, just as the syllables of the *ṛc* itself are excluded because they are not to be sung (*agītitvāt*), so too are the syllables of the *stobha*.
"But there is an extension of everything; the modification would be like that in common worldly usage" (Sūtra 35).

This is not so—that there is a cessation of the *stobhas*—for indeed, there is an extension of everything: "The *koma*, produced by the two sounds *auṃ* and the word *hāya*, has arrived at its own nature."
"He causes it to grow," says Mādhava.

The word *sāman* denotes a song characterized by the practice of specific *ṛk*-verses, *stobhas*, musical notes (*svara*), and temporal measures (*kāla*).

How is this understood? From its usage therein; for if the *stobhas* were excluded, the specific distinction [of the song] would not be grasped in reality, and thus the term [sāman] would be contradicted. Therefore, the *stobhas* [are included].

[The opponent might argue that] they would be prescribed [as meaningless]. Let it be so; however, if the *stobhas* were not connected with the meaning of the words of the *ṛc*, they would be purposeless. To this we reply: "As in common worldly practice (*lokavat*), they will not be purposeless.
For example, in the world, when singers insert certain musical embellishments (*aṅgavastuka*) into their songs—

Those [syllables] are for the purpose of counting the time of the song (gītikāla), they are not uttered for the sake of connecting the meaning; the time of the song is easily determined by means of the syllables. Or rather, the connection [of the statement] would be an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda). (Cāturhotṛka-nirṇaya, sūtra 38)

Or rather, the *stobhas* are of that same nature; for we do not perceive the form of Indra as something directly perceptible. And as for the statement in the supplementary portion of the text (*vākyaśeṣa*), that is merely an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*). 8.2.100.

It is said: that which is additional to the syllables of the *ṛc* and is not of the same phonetic quality (*savarṇa*) as them is called *stobha*; for it is in such cases that people in common usage employ the word *stobha*. However, regarding what has been spoken with much exaggeration by those who prattle on— namely, that which is more than what is found in the explanatory passages (arthavāda) and is discolored by them— it is precisely upon reflecting on this that people speak in such a manner.

"Is it sufficient, or excessive, or discolored? He said: "No; for there is something that is excessive but not discolored, such as repetition—'yādri-vādri';

Because the dharma is produced by its purpose, there is a connection with the injunction in the prohibition of the transformation and displacement of substances and qualities, due to their inherent relation. 40.

In the Vājapeya sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "He offers a charu of wild rice (nīvāra) for Bṛhaspati, consisting of seventeen śarāvas. Now, there is the sprinkling (*prokṣaṇa*) of *brīhi* rice which is part of the archetype (*prakṛti*); does that [sprinkling] apply to the *nīvāra* grains, or not? Such is the doubt. Likewise: "Verily, the Udgātṛ becomes exhausted at this point when the Pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha concludes; he should not speak much nor question another."
"One should say, 'Recite the Bhāgya hymns,' or, when the sacrifice has been completed, one should have him eat honey, or this [hymn]"— thus it is seen in the Mīmāṃsā.

Regarding the consumption of honey and the consumption of clarified butter, there arises the doubt: do the duties pertaining to the six-day sacrifice (ṣaḍaha) apply or not? Similarly, in the Rājasūya it is heard: "For the sake of warding off the Nairṛta, [the grain] is winnowed by the nails. In the archetype, there is the sprinkling of the mortar and pestle, as in: "One threshes with the sprinkled mortar and pestle. Does this [sprinkling] apply to the nails or not? This is the doubt. Likewise, in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices it is heard: "On the enclosing sticks... [the text continues].

Regarding the injunction "one should employ [it]," there arises a doubt: should the characteristics of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) be performed on the enclosing-stick (*paridhi*), or should they not?

Similarly, regarding the rule, "One should not say 'girā gireti'; if one were to say 'girā gireti', he would thereby draw death upon himself; having made it *aira*, [he should say] 'iyam'," there arises a doubt: do the characteristics of the word *girā* apply to the word *ira*, or do they not? What, then, is the prima facie position (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? The properties stated for rice (*vrīhi*) and so forth do not apply to wild rice (*nīvāra*) and so forth.

Therefore, they should not exist in those [substitutes]. This being the position reached, we reply: in the case of *māṣa*-beans and the like, there would be a "connection with the injunction" (*codanānubandha*), for that original (*prākṛta*) property is inherent in them.
Indeed, that [property] is prompted by the transcendental result (*apūrva*), not prompted by Brahman and the others; for by this, it is distinguished from the transcendental result.
This is a specific means of accomplishment; it has been established that this property resides therein [in the *nīvāra*] and not in rice (*vrīhi*) and the like.

Furthermore, it is understood that *nīvāra* and other such grains perform the function of rice and so forth, as there is an injunction regarding the substance of the *nīvāra*: "A sacrificial pap (*caru*) of *nīvāra* must be prepared. And that [preparation] cannot be accomplished by any other means.

The *nīvāra* grain assists the sacrifice, with the exception of the production of rice; this is understood through direct perception that it performs the function of *vrīhi*. Therefore, the properties of *vrīhi* should apply to the *nīvāra*.

Thus, when there is an injunction stating "one should worship for six days," once it is understood that "the six-day period has concluded" (meaning it is no longer worshipped by means of the six-day period), it is then understood that "one should worship with honey and ghee."
When the absence of one thing results in the occurrence of another, that [substitute] is understood to take its place;
since the text prescribes the eating of honey upon the cessation of the six-day period, it is understood to prescribe it for the function of the six-day period.

Therefore, the duty of the six-day rite—whether it be the vow (vrata) or the restriction (niyama)—occurs at the end of the Madhu-pressing.
Due to the absence of the sacrifice, the cups (grahas) contingent upon it do not proceed; for [the rule states], "having taken a cup, or the goblet (camasa)."
Because there is no *graha* or *camasa*, the *stotra* does not take place;

because there is no *stotra*, the *śastra* does not take place according to the rule "he recites the *śastra* following the *soma* that has been pressed. Due to the absence of the *savana*, the *savanīya* offerings do not proceed; thus, such things as these do not take place, while the vows (*vratas*) and observances (*niyamas*) do proceed.

And as for the other [text], "that which is not rendered useless by its purpose is not [to be used] after being purified by the nails," it is not otherwise that they become purified by the nails; if they were not purified by them, then it would follow that the nails are prescribed for the purpose of removing the husks. Therefore, it is understood that the mortar and pestle are connected [to this context].
Likewise, the statement that the *paridhi* performs the function of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is quite explicit: "the *paridhi*..."
"They employ the *padma*," it is said; therefore, there should be only one enclosing-stick (*paridhi*).

Similarly, regarding the passage "One should not say *girā gireti*; having made it *aira*, one should utter [the word]"; here, both are not being enjoined, for there would be a prohibition and a remote application, and thus the sentence would be split.

The impossibility of using the word *girā* applies to the Supreme Self; however, the split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*) remains as it was. What, then, is the established conclusion? That it should be employed without modification. From that, they first consider this: it is employed with the intention of expressing the quality of "green. It is understood that [the mantra] must be recited. There exists a mantra that expresses the quality of being green; therefore, the quality of being green must be recited. [Objection:

Furthermore, this [word] *dvayoḥ* is not seen in the Vedic language (*chandas*) with a plural ending; thus, if this mantra were employed [with such an ending], it would be nothing but a corruption (*apabhraṃśa*), not a Vedic form (*chāndasa*). Nor does the plural number express the meaning of the suffix *hit*."

It is obtained both in worldly and Vedic usage; and when two [entities] are intended to be expressed, a dual number occurs. For example, in the case of "it must be done by Devadatta and Yajñadatta," duality is already established by the two words "Devadatta" and "Yajñadatta" themselves, and is not further intended to be expressed by the case-ending (vibhakti);
nevertheless, the dual number alone is used, not the plural. Therefore, it should be modified [by substitution] in the *vikṛti* (modified sacrifice). 18.3.4a0.
Sūtra-bhāṣya:
In the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma (Agnīṣomīya-paśu), the section concerning the modification of the singular number and the singular gender denoting the animal.

In the case of a conflict of views, there would be an option because of their equality; however, when it concerns a subordinate element, there can be no assumption of an improper alternative, because it is only a part [of the whole]. (Siddhānta Sūtra 15)

There is the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, as stated in the text: "He who, having been initiated, immolates the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. In that context, both a mantra expressing the singularity of the tether and a mantra expressing the plurality of the tether are recited; of these two, which one [expressing singularity] is [connected] to the context?

Does it apply [to the context], or is that which denotes plurality to be extracted from the context, or do both apply within the context? What is the prima facie view? That which denotes plurality should be extracted. Why? Because it is the releaser of many nooses.

Furthermore, there are not many *pāśas* (fetters) in this context; therefore, being unconnected within this context, it should be applied where there are many *pāśas*. For example: "One should perform the *pratipad* with the verse 'For you two are good lords' for two sacrificers," and "These drops have flowed forth."
"Thus one should perform the *pratipad* for many sacrificers"— this is the injunction regarding the *pratipad* from the Mīmāṃsā-darśana. [Page 290]

It is displaced. Just as the consecratory formulas (*anumantraṇa*) addressed to Pūṣan, Savitṛ, Sarasvatī, Dyāvāpṛthivī, and others are displaced, so too is this formula denoting a plurality of nooses (*pāśa*).
This being the position reached, we reply: "In the case of a conflict" (*vipratipattau*). What is the conflict?
That in the archetype (*prakṛti*) there is a single noose, yet the mantra denotes a plurality of nooses; in this situation...

[Regarding] the case of a discrepancy: is the mantra to be displaced [from its context], or not? It is said: it should not be displaced. [Objection: But there is another mantra in the archetype (*prakṛti*)?

It is said: there will be an option (*vikalpa*) with that one. Why? Because the meaning of the nominal stem *pāśa* (rope) exists in the archetype, displacement is not logical. [Objection: But [the word *pāśam*] expresses only a single rope...

The mantra [speaks of] a single noose in the archetype; therefore, it is argued that it cannot apply there [in the ectype]. To this it is replied: by speaking of many nooses, the mantra indeed manifests the substance characterized by plurality. If it did not manifest this, plurality as qualified by the nooses would not be understood. If it does manifest it, that much serves our purpose, for it is the release of that [substance] which is being performed.
It does not refer to plurality, nor to the form of the noose. Therefore, its manifestation must be performed;

this will be done by the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), and it is not to be displaced. "For there indeed exists a nominal stem ending in the singular number, and that will effect its manifestation. To this, it is replied: No.
For this [word] here is different from that; if the nominal stem ending in the singular number were not desired.
It is said that [the rule] applies by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), meaning that the excellence of the whole [is intended] as "this very same thing.

Now, one might argue: "The plural number has its purposeful application in the use of many nooses; therefore, it must be displaced [from its original context]. And when it is displaced, because it is a part [of the whole], it displaces the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) as well. To this it is replied: "But in the case of a subordinate element (*guṇa*), there is an unjustifiable assumption [of displacement]."

Furthermore, the quality (*guṇa*) is the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*), while the primary substance (*pradhāna*) is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*). A specific qualification of the nominal stem's meaning is expressed by the case-ending; and since there must be a case-ending's meaning when there is a nominal stem's meaning, and since the nominal stem does not exist in the modified form (*vikṛti*), [the case-ending] must refer back to the original form (*prakṛti*), even though it was not explicitly mentioned in relation to it.

It enters [the discussion]; how much more so, then, when it is explicitly stated in the archetype (*prakṛti*) itself? Therefore, wherever there is the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*), there the meaning of the case-ending (*vibhakti*) will apply.

"But surely, even in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), the nominal stem and the meaning of the nominal stem are obtained through the extended application (*codaka*). Certainly; however, the extended application is remote, whereas the provider of the plural number is immediate.

The nominal stem (*prātipadika*) will not be superseded by the injunction. Therefore, because it is a part [of the whole], the plural number will supersede the singular nominal stem. Furthermore, the plural number is not meaningless in the archetype (*prakṛti*); for it establishes the connection with the ritual action in the case of releasing that which has been made into a noose (*pāśākṛtika*).

Therefore, the "unjustified assumption" (*anyāyakalpanā*) applies to the quality (*guṇa*) when there is a plural number, not to the primary meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadikārtha*). But what is unjustified? It is that which is called "unexpressed" (*avivakṣita*) despite being understood; let that be assumed. However, one should not assume an unjustified failure of the nominal stem to express its own primary meaning (*prātipadikārtha*) in the original context (*prakṛti*). For this quality—the plurality—is indeed unexpressed in the modified form (*vaikṛta*), because of the absence of proximity (*sannidhāna*). Therefore, even that which ends in a plural suffix finds its place in the original context.
Sūtra and Bhāṣya:
And because of the specific context. (16) (Yukti)

And from the specific context (*prakaraṇaviśeṣāt*), it is determined that the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) attracts the plural number; it is not that the nominal stem is displaced by the plural number.
For the meaning of the nominal stem is present in the *agnīṣomīya* animal sacrifice, [and] the plural is its support (the reading *bahu-samarthakam* is found in the Ka0 Saṃ0 Pu0).
[The phrase] *canyāvyakalpanā* is found in the Kā0 Krau0 Pu0.

Because it is sought for the sake of preservation in the modified forms (vikṛtis), for this reason as well, that which ends in the plural number finds its place in the archetype (prakṛti).
As for what was stated—that there might be an increase [of the rite] as in the case of the *dvirātra* sacrifice—that must be refuted.
Sūtra and Bhāṣya:
"But this cannot be so because of the absence of purpose; the other is merely a subordinate element. (17)
(Śrauta-nirṇaya)

It is logical that the injunction for the *pratipad* verses is elevated [to a higher status], because in the original model (*prakṛti*), there is neither duality nor plurality of sacrificers; therefore, these two *pratipads* would not apply there.

In this case, however, there is no mere quality (*guṇamātra*) nor plurality; rather, the purpose of the plural number is its connection with the word "muc" (liberation), and it is not the case that [the injunction] lacks a purpose due to one particular purpose among many.

It is applied. For it is not the case that because a torch is not applied for the purpose of illumination, it is therefore not applied for the purpose of producing ash. Therefore, this [objection] is inconsistent with the two steps [of the argument].
If it is argued that it is so because of the two [verses] beginning with "dyāvā," [we reply: No. (0)

Now, as for what was stated— that just as there is a displacement (utkarṣa) of the consecratory formulas (anumantraṇa) such as those addressed to Heaven and Earth, so too there should be for this [formula]— that must be refuted. Sūtra Commentary.
Because it is a word denoting non-origination. (Ābhāsa-nirṇaya 19)

This is not equal to the case of the *anumantraṇa* (subsequent recitation). For there is no scriptural statement regarding the origin of Heaven and Earth and the other deities in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), whereas here there is indeed a scriptural statement regarding the origin of the *pāśa* (noose). Therefore, it is dissimilar to the *anumantraṇa*. (Sūtra 2.2.50) Saṃkarṣa-kāṇḍa.

In the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa, which is designated by its name in the world, the application [of the mantras] is established; therefore, there is an occasion for modification (ūha) in the case of the *mandra* [tone].
However, in the case of what is *apūrva* (unprecedented), there would be no modification, as it is understood from the specific injunction (*pradeśa*). || 20 ||

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, they prescribe: "Having sprinkled [the materials], place them; place the sacrificial grass (barhis); set down the ladles (srucaḥ); cleanse them; and go out with the wife. In this regard, it is considered whether one should lead the wife [out] or not, for there exists a sacrificer who has but one wife.

It has already been settled by the *Pāśādhikaraṇa* that, because the word "patnī" (wife) is uttered there after having understood the application of everyone, it is subject to modification (*ūha*). However, this point is now being deliberated: in a performance involving one wife or many wives, should the word "patnī" be modified, or not? What is the prima facie view? Since its purpose is denotation, the word should be modified accordingly.

This being the case, we reply: "But in the case of the *apūrva* (the unprecedented rite), it should be used without modification in a ritual that is not preceded by a model sacrifice (*aprakṛti*). Why? Because this word ending in the vowel *ī* denotes the wife (*patnī*) alone; therefore, whether in a rite with two wives or many wives, when the word *patnī* is employed, the dual or plural number would follow by implication due to the connection with multiple wives. However, because of the force of the singular number [in the original injunction], it is restricted to the singular. Nor is duality or plurality intended here, since the word *patnī* is heard as a mere indicator (*lakṣaṇatvena*), and not because of a single wife."

In the case of the *dīpanīka* application, there is an extension (*atideśa*) from the primary application; as it was with the number there, so it is here as well. Therefore, the word *patnī* is used without modification.
Even if, in this case too, singularity were somehow intended to be expressed, nevertheless, in the *dīpanīka* application—

Because there is no common understanding [of the singular number], the singular number is used for the sake of the singular meaning; thus, in a ritual application involving multiple wives, it is employed as if it were modified by the desire for plurality. (2.2.10)
S:
Even when there are two wives, since the mantra exists [in the archetype], there is no modification [of the mantra] in the case of the ritual application;
and this also applies to the modified form (vikṛti), because of that specific statement. || 21 ||
Now, the meaning of the word *patnī* (wife/partner) is being investigated: is it seen in the *dvipanīka* sacrifice, or in the *bahupatnīka* sacrifice?
[Page 294] Mīmāṃsā-darśana.
And regarding the employment of the word *patnī* (wife), should it be used in the singular or not? The word *patnī*, which denotes one or many,

ought to be employed here in either the dual or the plural, since its application as a dual or plural is not sublated by a specific injunction in this context, and there is no such restrictive recitation [of the singular] present here.

This being the case, [the conclusion is]: "In the modified sacrifice (vikṛti) as well, there is no modification; such is the purpose. Why? Because of that scriptural statement: "Whatever is performed in the archetype (prakṛti) should be performed in the ectype (vikṛti).
That is the scriptural statement. And since singularity was not intended to be significant in the archetype, here too duality [is not intended].

Neither plurality nor singularity is intended to be expressed; therefore, there is no modification. Alternatively, even if that very [singularity] is intended, it is determined that there is indeed no modification because it is not restricted to a single leaf. (8.2.00) Sūtra.
The mantra "Agni is the foremost of those who have mastery over their own selves" is for the *adhvar* sacrifice;
if it is of the same injunction as that which applies to the *savanīya* offerings, then it is so. 22.

In the *Bhāṣya*: Regarding the animal sacrifice to Agni-Soma, there is the text: "When one who is initiated sacrifices the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma. Similarly, this [formula] arises for the Adhvaryu priest: "O Ambika, bring the grass; spread the sacrificial straw; the mother follows, the father follows, the brother follows," and so forth. But when the animals dedicated to Agni-Soma (*agnīṣomīya*) and those belonging to the Soma-pressing (*savanīya*) have different ritual prescriptions (*asamānavidhāna*), then this is deliberated: Should the words "O Ambika" and so forth be modified (*ūhitavya*) or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?

Thereupon, an extended application (atideśa) is made, namely, "the first [is] not that. In this regard, whatever was the prima facie argument (pūrvapakṣa) in the section concerning the modification of the cooked rice (pattādhikaraṇa), that is the prima facie argument here;

whatever was the established conclusion (siddhānta), that is the established conclusion here: "there is abandonment" (jahati) is the prima facie argument, and "no modification" (avikāraḥ) is the established conclusion.

Sūtra: "And in the case of a substitute, because there is no modification" (23). (The prima facie view.)
Mādhava:

There is a substitute when the substance prescribed in the scripture is unavailable, according to the principle: "Or there is the introduction [of another], because there is no difference in the purpose of the injunction" (Jaimini Sūtra 6.3.18). And that [substitute] is innate, being based on commonality...

[This refers to] the desire to perform that [rite]. Thus, when *nīvāra* grains are taken as a substitute for *vrīhi* rice, then the mantra prescribed for the *vrīhi*—namely, "I prepare a pleasant seat for thee; I fashion it well with a stream of ghee.
Sit upon it, O immortal one, and take thy stand, rejoicing in the essence of the *vrīhi*s"—is [applied].

Thus, regarding this, there is a doubt: is the word *vrīhi* used for *nīvāra* grains by abandoning its primary meaning (*jahat-svārtha*), or without modification (*avikāreṇa*)? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That the word *vrīhi*, when employed without modification, cannot denote the *nīvāra* grains which are to take its place.
Since they are to be manifested, the word *novāra* (wild rice) should not be employed when those [rice grains] are to be manifested.
Therefore, the day must be performed.
This being the position reached, we reply: "And in the case of a substitute, because there is no modification. In the case of a substitute...

The *Nyāyamālā* should be consulted here, beginning with the passage "the *calācikā* is performed" and concluding with: "In the ultimate sense, since all [mantras] are the essence of the *ājya* and *paśu*, there is indeed a modification (*ūha*) of the dual and singular endings according to the principle of the *pāśa*.

And thus, it is understood that no modification (*ūha*) should be made. What will happen in this way?
In this manner, there will be no alteration; therein, the Vedic tradition (*ārṣa*) will be upheld. Therefore, there is no modification.
Sūtra.
Bhāṣya:

On account of its not being mentioned in the sacred texts, it would lack scriptural authority; furthermore, this would be so because of the absence of anything else [to the contrary]. (Sūtra 24, Purvapakṣa).

And this is not the case— that it would be "without modification" (anūha), and thus "without substitution" (amūha)— if the word *vrīhi* were not recited in that mantra; for, as it is said, "due to the absence of the other," if this [word] were not present...
It would have to be called *nauvāra*, yet neither of these two conditions exists; therefore, this is a designation, and the word *nauvāra* must be inferred. That is so.
Or rather, it may be designated by that [name] because it is for the sake of that, since it is not distinguished from the purificatory rites. (Sūtra 25, Purvapakṣa-Nigamana)

The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position; it is not the case that there is a "dropping" (jaha), but rather the usage [of the term] remains without modification. Why? Because of "being for that purpose" (tādarthyāt). The purpose of the *nīvāra* grains is the same as that of the *vrīhi* rice: whatever purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*), such as the sprinkling of *vrīhi*, are performed upon the *vrīhi*, this word *vrīhi* applies to the *nīvāra* because it is not distinguished from them by those purificatory rites, just as the word *vrīhi* applies to other grains characterized as *vrīhi*.
The same applies to these *nauvāra* grains; therefore, it should be employed without modification.

[Page 297] Chapter 9, Section 9:
The section concerning the modification of the mantra beginning with "himavatsu saṃbhūtādi" in the Himavat sacrifice.
And because, in the case of combined [substances], the dimension of the object is not fixed. (Siddhānta)
In the *abhigupraisa*, there are interconnected meanings, such as "the eye, the breath," and so forth, in the passage: "Make the eye go to the sun; release the breath into the wind.
Regarding the animal sacrifices (*paśuyāga*) such as the *hipampa* and others, it is asked: should [the formula] be modified (*ūhitavya*), or not? It is said in reply:
"Indeed, because it is a non-archetypal recitation (*anyāyanigada*), this should be modified; for the word *cakṣuḥ* ends in the singular."

For it is heard [in scripture]: "It is said that the movement of the sun is spoken of with reference to two substrata; for the sun does not move upon two substrata, since the word refers to its radiant rays, and that radiance is one.
Therefore, this is merely a figurative expression (anyāyanigada). And in the case of modified forms such as the two-humped camel and the like..."

In ritual applications such as "One desiring union with the waters and plants should sacrifice a white animal to Varuna and a black one," since a difference in the animals is perceived, a modification (*ūha*) of the *tejas* [mantra] would follow. However, this is not the case even when there is a single animal, due to the difference in its substrates.

"It is precisely the brilliance [of the eyes] that is intended"—this is not so; it is said: because of the statement "May he lead his eye to the sun," it is the brilliance of the animal that is intended, not the distinction of the substratum, since there is modification (*ūha*) due to the difference in the brilliance of the eyes in other animals.
This being the position reached, we reply: "And because, in the case of combined things, the measure of the object is not fixed."

Although there is a distinction between the individual rays among those objects that are in contact, nevertheless, their rays become unified through that very contact of the rays; just as water, oil, or clarified butter, though distinct when in different locations, become one when they occupy the same location, so it is with the rays.

[Question: Is it so? [Answer: It would be bound by the summary (uddāna). Because it is not a constituent part of the summary, it is understood as "this is not a summary. It is connected with a single purpose, namely the Agnihotra.

Since the fire is subordinate to the act of kindling, the connection of the expiation (prāyaścitta) with its purpose is established through that very [kindling], just as in the case of the army. In that context, once it has been drawn out, it becomes impaired if it lacks that purpose.
It does not bring it about. In that context, the purpose of drawing out the fire intended for the *agnihotra* is the performance of the *agnihotra*;

When the drawn-out fire has gone out and is unfit for its own purpose, it is rendered fit by means of an expiation (*prāyaścitta*). And while performing that expiation, one assists the *agnihotra* itself. As for that which has been stated...

One who is performing the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices might benefit the *agnihotra* by making [the fire] fit; one who is making the fire fit for the purpose of the *agnihotra* benefits the *agnihotra*. Therefore, the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) is for the sake of the *agnihotra*, when the fire has been well-prepared. But how is it known that the connection of the expiation is with the fire, not with the act of kindling? By means of the fire as the qualified object.

It is understood from the statement that "the connection is with the *uddāna*," or rather, from the sentence "it is not sought when the *uddāna* is absent"; since direct audition (*śruti*) is more authoritative than syntactic context (*vākya*), the connection with the *uddāna* would follow.
To this it is replied: because the connection with the *uddāna* cannot be avoided, [the rule] applies even when [the *uddāna*] is present.
It attains its very purpose; and because it has the status of a *bhaṭṭa* (an auxiliary), there is no connection with that which is not required (*anākāṅkṣita*).

When the *ambī* is connected with the expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the sake of the *uddhāna* (the act of drawing out), then upon the occurrence of a mishap (*vyāpatti*), there is a connection with that which is required, and there is also a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatā*). Therefore, the *ambī* drawn out for the sake of the *uddhāna* is connected with the expiation. [This applies] where the fire drawn out for the sake of the *darśapūrṇamāsa* follows after [the main rite].

In that case, the fire of the *agnihotra* belonging to another has been extinguished. Since it is the fire of another, there would be no expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for it. Moreover, there is an indicative mark (*liṅga*).
What is it? It is the restatement: "The *agnihotra* is performed with one's own fire. For this [restatement] would be a prescription only if [the fire were not one's own].

Otherwise, there would be the consequence of a syntactical split (vākyabheda). If the lifting [of the fire] were for the purpose of the Agnihotra, then it would follow from that— [Page 330]— that it is not independent.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, it is prescribed: "The Prāyaṇīya [offering] is a pap of rice cooked in milk for Āditya. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should the properties of the milk be performed for the sake of the cooking, or not? If this milk is intended for the purpose of offering...
Therefore, they should be prepared; however, for the purpose of mixing [the milk], they should not be prepared. How does the doubt arise?

From the use of the locative case, it is understood that the milk is for the purpose of mixing. But when the milk is heard of as the locus for the sacrificial oblation (caru) connected with a deity, there arises the suspicion of a syntactical split (vākya-bheda); therefore—
[The topic of] dependence.

What, then, is the prima facie view? That it is for the purpose of offering. How so? Because the Āditya [cup] is mentioned separately, and since that [cup] consists of milk, if multiple purposes were enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*).

Moreover, both of these [the substance and the deity] are understood here from the sentence; if one of these two were enjoined, then the other would be understood as not being enjoined. Therefore, there is no split of the sentence (*vākyabheda*). One must explain how there is no split of the sentence: in that case, when the connection with the sacrificial base (*adhikaraṇa*) is being enjoined, the understanding of the connection with the deity is not possible, because it has not been established by any other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

But when the connection with the deity is being enjoined, the *caru* and the milk which are specified— by the force of that specification, they are understood to be conjoined by syntactical connection (*vākya*) and thus connected with the deity;
in that case, by implication (*artha*), the *caru* becomes the receptacle for the milk.
He said: "By the word, the two—*caru* and milk—are understood, but not their conjunction.
[The reading *apane* is found in the Ānandāśrama and Somanātha manuscripts; likewise in the Bhāṣya.
[The reading *cādityaḥ prāpacchoṣaḥ* is found in the Kāśī Sanskrit Series manuscript.]
It is said:

when these two are understood, their simultaneity is understood through the injunctive statement (*prayogavacana*); therein, by implication, there is a connection (*saṃsarga*), and because they are singular, there is a conjunction (*samuccaya*) of the two words. Therefore, in this case, it is the mere indication that is intended, not a relationship with a locus (*adhikaraṇa-sambandha*), even though such a relationship is implied.

It is thus prescribed; however, this instruction is given so that it may be understood how the rice-mess (*caru*) and the milk (*payas*) are to be combined. In that case, when the rice-mess mixed with milk is offered, the milk is necessarily offered along with it; therefore, there is for this [offering] the "observation of its presentation" (*pradānadarśana*). Of that [rice-mess], which is being cooked by means of the milk...

The seventh [case-ending] is indicated in order to show how the offering (*pradāna*) is to be made. Therefore, this milk is for the purpose of eating and for the purpose of sacrifice; or rather, he says this because of the similarity [of the word *bhojana*] with "eating. Consequently, since the milk is for the purpose of offering, the characteristics (*dharma*) of milk are connected [to it].

Objection: "Sacrifice is not merely the act of giving; it becomes a sacrifice only when an offering is made directed toward a deity. Reply: This [act] also consists of an offering being made directed toward Aditi as the deity. Objection: "Aditi is not the deity of milk, nor is she the deity of mere gold."
That which is heard [in the scripture] is the deity for that [offering];

curd is heard, not milk. [Objection: No, because both are specified, the deity is connected with both, as in a mixture like honey and water, just as in the case of "curd, honey, ghee, and parched grains."

Water, when mixed with that, becomes *prājāpatya*; it should be viewed in this very same way. Although it is indicated by the locative case (*saptamī*), because the meaning of the locative is not the cause of the injunction and only the mere indication is intended—just as in the expression, "having added curd to rice, it should be consumed"—the rice is [the locus].
Only the instruction is being expressed, not the status of being a locus; it should be understood in this way here as well.
Therefore, since the milk is for the purpose of offering, the properties of the milk must be performed for the sake of the offering.

Having thus established this, the prohibition of certain preparatory rites for those things to be offered becomes logical.

"He performs the *bahiṣpavamāna* with the *yajus*, he causes the cow to be milked with the *apavitra* [mantra]"; for a prohibition applies only when there is something already established. Sūtra: "And in the case of its prohibition, because that which is of such a nature is excluded. (2.3.34)

This [is the case] when there is a prohibition of milk; even that which has become like milk is avoided in common worldly usage, as in "milk sprinkled with milk" (payasā siktaṃ payaḥ). And this is not a property of the substance whose purpose is victory.

Just as water is for the purpose of drinking, yet when that [drinking] is prohibited—as in the case where it is declared, "Water must not be drunk"—then gruel is consumed instead; and because such [water] is thus avoided, milk alone remains for the purpose of drinking in the world. For it is just as in the world: [milk is used] for the purpose of eating. Indeed, as in the world...
"Just as [the inference] regarding milk [is established], so too should it be here"; thus is "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyatodṛṣṭa) designated.
It is unrighteousness because of non-giving; because it is prescribed for a superior purpose, there is no connection due to inequality. (Siddhānta Sūtra 35) — Bṛhadāraṇyaka Bhāṣya.
The meaning is that "the nature of being milk" belongs to the milk itself; its properties should not become the properties of the substance to be offered (*pradeya*).
Why? Because there is no offering; for this [milk] is not offered. [Objection:

It is said that the cooking in milk is for the purpose that when the sacrificial cake (*caru*) is being offered, it will thereby be offered. [Reply: No, he says, because it is a cooked *caru* (*śṛtavarūḥ*).

For it arises for the purpose of [asking] "How shall it be sweet? Therefore, there is a requirement for rice grains, and not otherwise, as in the case of the final [offering]. However, it is not heard that this should be given with milk already offered. How so? Because it is prescribed for the sake of what is being cooked. But [an objection is raised]: "In this way, there would indeed be a split in the sentence. [Reply: This is precisely the accepted position; thus it becomes the sacrificial oblation (*havis*).
Thus it has been stated. It is replied: "Because of non-weighing, there is no commingling; [this is] according to the reading in the Kāṭhaka-saṃhitā manuscript.
In the case of the *caru* and the milk, they are not weighed.

[Page 336] Milk is heard of as the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) through direct perception, whereas the *caru* is [heard of] as the substance to be offered (*pradeya*). When the status of being the substance to be offered is understood for the milk by means of the *dākya*, that [status] is set aside by its status as the locus. As for that which...

Regarding the objection that it would result in a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), [we reply]: in that case, there will not be a connection such as "the sacrificial pap (*caru*) is in the milk. How then? It will be "the Āditya [deity] is in the milk"; both [elements] will be connected with the word "Āditya"—namely, "Āditya in the milk" and "the Āditya-pap. Thus, both the words "pap" and "milk" will have Āditya as their primary referent, and so there will be a single sentence; there is no risk of a syntactical split. The Āditya deity will be the receptacle for the milk. Therefore, in this case, [it is not milk].

Since this meaning is permanent...

It restates [the fact]. It is not because it is not to be given that one speaks with the *yajus* formula; rather, they are removed, and the cow is not milked in the vessel containing the *pavitra*. "But surely, a constant restatement (*nityānuvāda*) is purposeless. It is said in reply: we do not investigate whether there is a purpose or no purpose; what [is the point]?

Let us examine whether this is understood from this statement: "From this sentence it is understood that the omentum is not cooked with a Yajus formula, nor is it purified with a Pavitra; and because it is not to be offered, the Yajus and the Pavitra are not applicable to it."

Or rather, it is a prohibition of what has been enjoined. (Śrautaniyama 2)

Alternatively, the prohibition should be understood as applying specifically to that which has been prescribed—for some, it is prescribed: "He removes the clods with a *yajus* formula," and "Burn me in the purifier";
thus, the prohibition of that [prescribed act] becomes meaningful.

Now, as for what was said—that when milk is prohibited, that which is sprinkled with milk and that which is mixed with milk are also to be avoided—we reply: it is indeed appropriate in common worldly usage to avoid that which is mixed, for it is precisely that which is prohibited there; however, milk that has become a subordinate element in a meal is not [prohibited].

That which is practiced, and that against which there is practice, makes a prohibition meaningful; for that which is not practiced, a prohibition would be purposeless because its non-occurrence is already established. [Objection: "But surely milk is consumed even by itself in the world. That [curd] alone is used, but this [milk] is not abundant; therefore, because milk is generally subordinate, the prohibition of milk is stated for the purpose that one should not eat it even when it is mixed with milk.

And because of the duty of the vow, like the smeared [remnants], (Śrauta-sūtra 3.5.38).

Commentary: Now, why is this other solution stated? It should be regarded as being like a religious vow (*vrata*); just as when it is said that a student (*brahmacārin*) must not eat meat, they avoid even the smearings that have come into contact with the sacrificial ladle (*darvī*), so too here, when it is said that milk must not be drunk...
"They will avoid what is sprinkled with milk and mixed with milk."
Or rather, there is a prohibition of [the mention of] taste, because it is a quality of the person. (Sūtra 40) (0 ni)
Commentary: Nor is this a refutation; rather, the word "or" (*vā*) signifies another refutation.

Why? Because the vow is a duty of the person (*puruṣadharma*). For the student (*brahmacārin*), the non-eating of meat is for the sake of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭārtha*); therefore, even one who eats it—even as long as the taste of the meat is known—incurs a fault. It does not depend on any visible effect, such as the provocation of the humors (*doṣa*) and so forth.

17. ... [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. [Mahāmati asked: "What, O Blessed One, is the imagined self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is that which is grasped by the ignorant through names and characteristics, based on the forms of the dependent self-nature; it does not exist as a real entity, yet it is clung to as such. This is called the imagined self-nature. [Mahāmati asked: "What, O Blessed One, is the dependent self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the manifestation of the mind (citta) appearing as objects due to the habit-energy of beginningless false discrimination; it is like a dream or a reflection, and it is devoid of the characteristics of grasped and grasper. This is called the dependent self-nature. [Mahāmati asked: "What, O Blessed One, is the perfected self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the state in which the dependent self-nature is completely free from the imagined self-nature; it is the non-dual nature of reality (dharmatā) which is always thus. This is called the perfected self-nature. [Mahāmati asked: "What, O Blessed One, is the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the storehouse-consciousness (ālayavijñāna) which is the seed of all phenomena, and it is the basis for the arising of the seven consciousnesses. It is the realm of the Buddhas, which is profound and subtle, and it is the womb of the Tathāgatas. It is neither eternal nor impermanent, because it is the support for the arising and ceasing of all phenomena, yet its own nature is eternally unchanging. This is called the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. [Mahāmati asked: "O Blessed One, is the Tathāgata-garbha not the same as the Ālayavijñāna, which is taught by the various teachers of other schools? [The Blessed One replied: "No, Mahāmati, they are not the same. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata-garbha is taught by me as the cause of liberation for those who fear the absence of self (anātman), whereas the Ālayavijñāna is the cause of birth, death, and transmigration. However, Mahāmati, I teach the Tathāgata-garbha as being identical to the Ālayavijñāna in order to lead the followers of other paths, just as a potter makes various vessels out of the same clay.

Therefore, Mahāmati, you should abandon the views of the externalists and cultivate the insight into the non-self of both persons and phenomena. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Having heard the words of the Blessed One, the venerable Mahāmati and the great assembly rejoiced and carried out what he had taught. Thus ends the first chapter, titled "On the Characteristics of All Dharmas," in the Laṅkāvatāra Sūtra in ten fascicles. 17. ... [End of Chapter 1].)

188. Then one should inquire: "Is the other [offering] for the sake of the deity, and the *caru* for the sake of the sacrificial purpose, as well as the curd and milk? He says: "But surely the *caru* also has a connection with the deity, and the curd and milk likewise;
thus there will be no split in the sentence. It cannot be so; the division must be made, as in the previous sentence.

"One should divide the stalks and the vessels," it says; immediately following that, there is this sentence concerning specific divisions: "Those which are the most excellent, let us offer them to Indra Pradātṛ; those which are the least excellent, let us offer them to Viṣṇu Śipiviṣṭa. Since there is no distinction here, the division of both curd and milk must also be stated. And if curd and milk were to be divided while being mentioned for the purpose of the *praṇītā* water, then the sentence would be split; therefore—

The prescription for these two [words] is for the sake of the *prayāja* offerings. And since the sense of the locative case is not being prescribed, the nominal stem-meaning is compounded with the deity by virtue of the syntactic force (*vākya-sāmarthya*).
Both *dadhi* and *payaḥ* are connected with the deity; [then] the *caru* is offered with them—first the *caru* in *dadhi*.

"The portion for Indra becomes [the one] for Pradātṛ. Just as when various substances are being divided, it might be said: "The jewels are to be collected from the golden vessel; one portion is Devadatta's;
the other portion, gold placed in the silver vessel, is Viṣṇumitra's"—since the two portions are understood through the two vessels because the statement is intended to specify a particular division.

And because the curd and the whey are distinct, the sense of the locative case is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*). Likewise here, since the sentence is intended to convey a division, and because the curd and the whey are distinct, it is understood that "one portion" refers to both together.
Furthermore, since this meaning is already established by implication, it will be a restatement of the sense of the locative case.

Therefore, this must first be examined: Is the choosing [of the priests] in the *satras* merely a ritual duty (*dharma*), or is it for the purpose of hiring (*parikraya*)? If it is merely a ritual duty, it should be performed in the *satras*; if it is for the purpose of hiring, it should not be performed. What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? The *udavasānīya* [concluding sacrifice] should possess its own specific ritual properties (*dharma*), because it is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of that [sacrifice]; and thus, that gift would be merely a ritual duty (*dharmamātra*).

There is the *udavasānīya* sacrifice, concerning which it is said: "Having concluded the *sattra*, they should perform the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* *jyotiṣṭoma* with a thousand-fold sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). In this regard, there is a point of doubt: is the giving of the fee merely a ritual duty (*dharma-mātra*), or is it for the purpose of hiring services (*parikrayārtha*)? Furthermore, there is another dichotomy: is the *udavasānīya* a subsidiary part (*aṅga*) of the *sattra*, or not? If it were a subsidiary part of the *sattra*...

The gift is merely a ritual act; it is not, therefore, a part of the *satra* sacrifice intended for the purpose of hiring (the priests). What is the prima facie view? That it is a part of the *satra*. Why? Because of the context (*prakaraṇa*) of the *satra*; it is heard in scripture that it is to be performed after completing the *satra*, and from the context of the *satra*, it is understood that it refers to the *satra*. Furthermore, the *udavasānīya* rite is prescribed as belonging to the *satra*. Moreover, since the *satra* is for the sake of a result, it is not understood to be for the sake of the *udavasānīya*. Nor does the *udavasānīya* belong to the time of concluding the *satra*, for in that case there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And if it were not a part [of the *satra*], a separate result would have to be postulated.
Therefore, because of its immediate sequence and its connection as part of a single syntactical unit (*ekavākyatā*), the *udavasānīya* is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) [of the preceding rite].
Having completed the sacrifice as described, one should not rest content, nor should one consider the task finished merely by having performed it;
rather, another auxiliary must be performed for it—the *udavasānīya*. Such is the connection.

It is performed as follows: "Having piled the fire, one should sacrifice with the Sautrāmaṇī," and "In the Vājapeya, one should sacrifice with the Bṛhaspatisava. "It must be performed. But here, having abandoned the *sattra*, the *udavasānīya* is to be performed; thus, "having risen from the *sattra*" (the meaning being "having departed"). Bhāṣya: This very same is the illustrative example: "Having emerged from the sacrificial session (sattra), they should sacrifice with the Pṛṣṭhaśamanīya Jyotiṣṭoma involving a thousand-fold sacrificial fee. In that regard, this meaning has been established:

should that be performed by them collectively, or by each one individually? What is the prima facie view? It is "collectively. Why? Because plurality is heard in the injunction regarding the sacrifice as something to be adopted.

And if it were performed by a single person, there would be no performance connected with plurality, as in the case of "the twice-born," for example: "By this [rite], a king and a domestic priest, desiring union, should sacrifice.
Even though the king and the domestic priest are mentioned merely as defining characteristics (*lakṣaṇa*), nevertheless, [the text says] "they two should sacrifice" (*yajeyātām*).

Thus, the sacrifice is presented as that which is to be undertaken; and with regard to the sacrifice, this duality of agents is heard in the scriptural injunction: "The two should sacrifice" (*yajeyātām*).
Thus, they should perform the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* sacrifice; therefore, they should employ the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya* collectively.

Thus much has been established for now, though it is not yet concluded; we shall first describe the sūtra concerning the intermediate [rite] within the interval—namely, the section on whether others may act as officiating priests at the *udavasānīya* sacrifice when there are no *satriṇas* present. (This is a deliberation involving doubt.)
And that [offering] should be performed by other officiating priests (ṛtvij).
Bhāṣya: In this very example, this matter is doubtful: "Are those same sacrificers to be employed, or should others be chosen? What is the prima facie view?—those same ones. Why?

For it is understood that there is a commonality of agent, as in the statement, "Having settled down, they should sacrifice. The cognition arises that those very ones who are the settlers are themselves the sacrificers. Just as, by the authority of the direct injunction (*vacana*), the unity of agent obtained through the general rule (*codaka*) is set aside and a plurality of agents occurs, so too, by the authority of the direct injunction, those very same persons [settle], setting aside the other officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) obtained through the general rule.
"They ought to be so.

This being the position reached, we reply: "And one chooses other officiating priests (ṛtvij) for that [sacrifice]. There would be some deficiency [in the performance]; moreover, there are other officiating priests (ṛtvij) obtained through the force of the injunction (codaka).

Furthermore, in this case, as far as the fruit of the action is intended for the agent, so far those alone are the agents; this is understood from the specific use of the middle voice (upagraha-viśeṣa). And the officiating priests are not [the agents].

[Page 414] Furthermore, the fruit of the action in a sacrifice is intended for the agent; therefore, in the Ārtvijya [priestly office], those very priests are the agents. First, we understand the agents in the principal portion [of the rite] to be the *mijaḥ* (the sacrificer's own kin).
Furthermore, others are to be chosen. (10.2.130)
But [the objection is not valid] because there is no contradiction in each case individually, and because the primordial matter (prakṛti) is connected with only one [effect] at a time.

They should not perform [the rites] by joining them together as a collective whole (*saṃhatya*), but rather "one by one" (*ekaikaśaḥ*). Why? Thus it is said. And in that case, even a single person becomes an *āhitāgni* (one who has consecrated the fires); since the sacrifice belongs to those who have piled the fire-altar (*cit*), the sacrifice is prescribed for each individual, while the piling of the altar is prohibited [for others].

"Therefore, it does not apply to each one individually. This is not a fault; for even the individual is not excluded, and thus, by the force of the *codaka* (the extended injunction), one should sacrifice one by one.
He says: "The performance connected with many cannot be carried out by a single person."

Even so, there is no fault; for here the plural number is not being prescribed. Those who have performed the *udavasāna* (the concluding rite) are the ones for whom this sacrifice is intended, and they are many; thus, this is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of those many who are already established [in that status]. Furthermore, each one of them individually is an *udavasātṛ*. Therefore, their sacrifice shall take place in that very same manner, just as it was for them collectively at the time of the *udavasāna*.
The plural number [is used] because, in the same way, it will apply to the *bāga* as well, even though they are not combined.

Now, if it is argued that the plural number is not a restatement (*anuvāda*) because it has not been previously established—since the plural number is not established for the *bāga* when the word is uttered—[we reply: "But now, in this case, it is indeed so. Regarding the departure (*udavasāna*).

[Page 415] It is said, "The *āmala* is for the *mahāvrata*"; this applies extensively to their *mudavakha* [offering], but not to the *yāna*. [Objection: "But will it not also apply to the *dyāga*? [Reply: No, he says.

And this sacrifice has already been connected with the plural number [of the word]; therefore, at that stage, the *udavasānīyā* (concluding rite) is not obtained through the sentence. However, one then takes up many [participants]. From that—

The plural number refers to the *udavasātṛ*s (those who have withdrawn) mentioned in another passage; therefore, the performance should be carried out in connection with plurality, as in the case of the *Dviyajña* and the *Satre*s.

[The opponent] says: This is not so. Where a restatement (*anuvāda*) is possible by some means, there it may be either a restatement or an injunction (*vidhi*). Furthermore, since it is something new (*apūrva*), elsewhere it would be an injunction rather than a restatement; nevertheless, in this case, it ought to be a restatement of plurality. Thus...
The connection with the sacrifice does not belong to the plural number; in that case, there is only a visible purpose.
In the other alternative, if the connection with the sacrifice were [made] through the plural number, an unseen result would have to be postulated.
Therefore, it is a restatement (anuvāda). And here, even in the case of the singular, the same [conclusion] follows.

[Khaṭi: It is said: there is a distinction [between these], such as "the *cāvera* [is] from the forest," "the king and the domestic priest should sacrifice together," and "those desiring food [should eat] the *satrabādha*. Where a word has a fixed gender, two usages are considered possible; however, because the same form is heard, it is by that very fact that the usage of the other gender is precluded.

The verbal root-meaning alone is enjoined; likewise, the employment [of the word] is by the agent, and it is accompanied by that [agent]. In this way, all of this—when being enjoined as the meaning of the verbal root—is merely restated as something already established. And in the case of the *diś* and *vac* roots, the verbal root-meaning is enjoined, the employment is also by the agent, and it is accompanied by that [agent].

Likewise, the group itself has been obtained in that manner. For one cannot say that the application of the term "king and domestic priest" (rājapurohitau) is intended to express a dual number there; rather, it is the singular form used for them. Similarly, "[those] desiring prosperity" [is said].

Here, however, [the rule is] "therefore, each one individually should sacrifice with the *Pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*."
But it is not so.

In the Sārasvata Sattra, there is a sacrifice for the fulfillment of desires: "Having reached Śācīpralavaṇa, he offers a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Kāma; at that [sacrifice], a mare and a man [are offered]."

"Having given a cow to the Dhenuka, he descends into the water at the bathing-place on the Yamunā. What, then, is the prima facie view? Just as in the *pṛṣṭhaśamanīya*...
The word "also" (ca) implies that this is likewise the case here for the purpose of purchase (*parikraya*). Why?

Because of the word "giving" (*dāna*); there occurs the word "giving" in the passage: "Having given a mare and a man as two milch-cows (*dhenuke*) to her. It has been stated that when laborers are present, the word "giving" signifies the purpose of purchase.

And this is not a *sattra* sacrifice; rather, it is a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the *sattra*. Furthermore, by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), the *sattra* itself possesses the status of being the performer (*kartṛtā*), whereas the subordinate parts possess it through the priests obtained by extension (*codaka*). Thus, the *sattra* is endowed with its qualities.

In a Sattra sacrifice, it is beneficial to oneself; otherwise, being deficient without other officiating priests (ṛtvij), it would not be effective even if performed. Therefore, in this case, the giving [of wealth] is for the purpose of hiring (parikraya).

• Or rather, it is a statement because of its being for the sake of acquisition.
(Siddhānta) Bhāṣya:

By the word "or" (vā), the alternative view is set aside—the gift here is not for the purpose of hiring, but is merely a religious duty (dharma). Why? Because of its being for the sake of acquisition (sacatvāt); for when there is acquisition, the act of hiring has ceased.

[The opponent] says: "It has been stated that this is not true, nor is it a constituent part of truth. It is replied: It is not untrue; rather, it is a constituent part of truth, for it falls within the scope of truth. Furthermore, regarding the human agency of truth, while that [agency] is being established, the agents of the various [elements] are proven. And there is no purpose served by what is heard through traditional scripture (āgama).
"But the gift must be considered as having only a spiritual purpose.
(10.2.15–50) This is the section concerning the fact that the gift at the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices has no visible purpose.
And there should be no reproach regarding what is blameworthy; it would result in the removal of the sacrificial fee. || 46 ||

In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, this is prescribed: "If one should overturn a potsherd while performing the Saṃyāja offerings, one should offer a Vaiśvānara cake on twelve potsherds; a one-year-old cow is the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); he should give that at the very time [of the offense]. In this regard, there is a doubt: is the gift of the one-year-old cow for the purpose of purchasing [the services of] the priests, or is it merely a ritual duty (dharma)?
What is the prima facie view? [The word *daryā*] is for the purpose of purchase (*parikraya*), because the suffix *triṅc* occurs in the sense of purchase.
This being the prima facie view, we reply: "And in the case of the *dakṣiṇā*, the gift is a religious duty (*dharma*)," according to this scriptural statement.
It is heard [in the scripture]. Why? Because there is no injunction [to that effect] regarding the deities and the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*);
for one who is to be given [as a gift] does not become an officiating priest, according to the principle that "one should not transgress against an officiating priest or a teacher.
When there is no purpose served by the very act of giving, then what is the significance of the term *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee)?
Will he do so? Moreover, for the purpose of hiring, the *dārvīndra* [should be used].

In the Mīmāṃsā system, that which is obtained through the general injunction (*codaka*) would be set aside in the case of the *anvāhārya* rice, and thus the injunction itself would be contradicted; therefore, the gift of a one-year-old cow as a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) must be given to the *anūkti*.
