16th Adhyāya.
The section concerning the bones of those who are living: The bone-sacrifice belongs to others because there is no prohibition; it would otherwise be like [the sacrifice] of the living.
Because of the prohibition, there is no standing [of the rule]. (Siddhānta 87)

This is prescribed: "If one who has been consecrated (dīkṣita) should die, having cremated him, they should place his bones upon a black antelope skin; then, having initiated the nearest relative in his stead and performed the sacrifice with him, they should thereafter, after a year, collect the bones. And so it is said.

The sacrifice takes place in the year; it deliberates: "What [benefit] shall there be for these bones while they are living? What is the logical conclusion? That it is for the bones, because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). What is this coreferentiality? It is that the bones are the very objects of the act of officiating at the sacrifice. [Objection: But bones are insentient; they do not have the capacity to speak for themselves. How [can this be]?

"Would those [acts] belong to the agent in the performance? It is said: "Their primary status is heard in scripture; therefore, there are others who are the instigators, and they will cause these acts to be performed."
He says: "For one who does not perform [the action] himself is called an agent when he causes it to be performed; indeed, the instigator of the agent is the cause.
And these [factors] are not able to bring about the action through their own activity.
It is replied: "By virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement, to the extent that the sacrificer is capable of causing [the action] to be performed, to that extent [he is the cause]."
They will cause [the rites] to be performed— such as "The Udumbara post for me," "The sacrificial stake for me," and so forth.
[Page 419] Chapter 10, Section 2.

Water, being merely the primary substance (pradhāna), is not able to perform the auxiliary acts; it serves only as a means for the journey. To this it is replied: "Because of the deficiency of the assembly [of factors], that specific substance will be accepted as the victim; those purchased for its sake will perform the sacrifice; such is the case."

"The renunciation of the substance will be based on the explicit scriptural statement. [The opponent] says: "If this is explained in such a way, it would follow that the agency is taught for the one who is ignorant (bāla) alone. It is replied:
By this method, agency is indeed taught for the one who is ignorant; it is not the case that [agency] belongs to the agent who causes another to act.
Let it be granted that the status of being the cause and the agent are already established in the village; they are merely restated.

For instance, while "one desiring a village should perform the Saṃyāja" is an injunction, "one who desires a village should sacrifice" is a restatement of what is already obtained as a cause. And he shows this [in another case]: "In the Stotra, one places the horse-pot. In this very way, the status of being the sacrificer is observed. Thus it is for him.

Regarding the question, "Is it not to be released? we reply: It should be for those who are alive, for they are capable of action; for them, the sacrifice is not prohibited, whereas for those [who are dead], it is prohibited. The relinquishment is performed mentally toward the village, and in this case, there is no mental intention [of ownership] remaining. As it is said: "The priests shall take the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)."

"Having accepted it, those who have performed the ritual perform the renunciation; thus, there is a scriptural injunction for renunciation. This is not so; for when "one should sacrifice" is stated, that statement would become meaningless if it were merely a prohibition against eating.
Indeed, that statement means "one should perform the renunciation," and otherwise it would be purposeless.

Thus it is said. Nor does this follow from the authority of the verbal statement: "Whatever substance is [offered], that is accepted," for it is not as if it were given by means of bones, nor is there a purchase in the absence of giving.

Furthermore, the meaning of the mantra is not understood from the injunctive word, because when the matter has been determined by another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), [the mantra serves only as a reminder].

The word "cow" is connected [to the animal], just as in the case of "the *mora* is to be sacrificed," where the *mora* is sacrificed as qualified by the genus (*jāti*) of *mora*; it is not a single individual, for in the debate one says, "this cow is a *vācoka*.
[Page 420]
The term "Vāhīka" is used figuratively; therefore, in the injunction for the abandonment [of the priests], there would be no other way to act.

Furthermore, it is not possible for these [priests] to have property of their own such that they might think, "We have been hired by this [sacrificer]. Therefore, in no way can the verses (*ṛc*) become non-owned.

Therefore, grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is not intended here. And it has been said: "This sentence is meaningless because it speaks of what is already connected. We say: "No, for a statement becomes meaningless only when its meaning is already understood; therefore, by this much alone [it is not meaningless] regarding the performance of the *Vājapeya* sacrifice after a year."

A certain meaning is understood from the sentence; that is what is intended here. The connection "one should cause one who is not sick (asklīni) to sacrifice" is not being enjoined. [Objection: "Is 'asklīni' a corrupt reading? [Response: We say it is not a corrupt reading. For that alone is not a non-corrupt reading which serves the purpose of an injunction and expresses the primary sense; even when expressing a secondary sense as a restatement (anuvāda), it attains consistency through its own expression and does not become a corrupt reading. In that context, regarding those who are not sick...
The word "year" (abda), while expressing its primary meaning [of time], does not fit within the sentence if taken literally;

however, as a restatement, it will fit through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). Therefore, the phrase "and after a year he should sacrifice" will refer to the subject under discussion—the living person—and for that purpose, the word "bones" (asthi) will be applied [metaphorically] to him.

"Thereafter, in that year, one should cause him to sacrifice. Who are "those" (asmin) in this context? They are those [sacrificial rites] which have been commenced by him. Therefore, for whomsoever those [necessary] implements exist, and by means of those implements it is possible to complete [the rite], for him there is the sacrifice while living.
The application [of the rule] should be as far as has been stated. (0 ni0) || 48 ||

Now, as for what was stated—that it shows the act belongs to the sacrificer (yājamāna) by saying, "He places the eye-shaped jar on the eye"—this does not belong to the sacrificer; for it has been said that this is not connected to the sacrificer. Therefore, by the authority of the scriptural statement, this ritual act takes the form of belonging to the sacrificer.
[Page 421]
The second quarter of the eighth [chapter].

To the extent that there is a scriptural statement, it must be exactly so; it is not possible to attribute all of that to the patron of the sacrifice (*yajamāna*). Therefore, the merit belongs only to those who are living. (10.2.10) n.

The section concerning the non-permission of recitation (*japa*) and other rites in the case of the *pārthiva* fire; and the section concerning the touching of the *audumbarī* post. (This is the deliberation.

"But if, by virtue of the scriptural statement, their recitation and consecration are omitted because they are rendered purposeless, [then it is] with the sacrifice, since that is for its sake. (Sūtra 48)

Here, the purification (*saṃskāra*) of the muttered prayers (*japa*) and the sacrifice (*iṣṭi*) are considered. In that regard, the purification of the muttered prayers is considered by the latter half of the Sūtra, while the sacrifice is considered by the remainder. The muttered prayers are injunctions such as "he mutters here," and the purifications are [rites] such as "he shaves his hair. The doubt is: should the purification of these be performed, or not? Now, it has been stated that "there is no sacrifice for those who are living in this [rite]."

It is stated: [this is] the desire for a portion. Having considered that they are not [to be used], the purpose of the preceding section is investigated in this manner: if the sacrifice were to be performed with them, would a purificatory rite (*saṃskāra*) be performed or not? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? "In the absence of a specific injunction, by extension (*atideśa*), the ritual action should apply to all cases" (10.1.10).
"By this reasoning, it should be performed.

This being the position reached, we reply: if, however, on account of a scriptural injunction, the sacrifice were to consist of those [grains], then the preparation of those [grains] would be excluded as its purpose is already fulfilled; yet by means of them, one does not pray, nor does one [shave] the hair and beard.

It cannot be maintained that the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) does not extend [the requirement] because it is impossible; regarding this, the latter half of the verse states: "The *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice must be performed, because it is for that purpose. The inquiry is: should the *dīkṣaṇīyā* sacrifice be performed? What is the prima facie position (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It should be performed in order to favor the *codaka*.
*Vajrayāga*, according to the *Kāśyapasaṃhitā*, chapter 2, part 2.
[Page 422]

This being the case, we reply: no mental preparation (apasaṃskāra) should be performed [for the deities], for they would perish. Why? Because that [preparation] is for their sake; the sacrificer undergoes initiation (dīkṣā), and initiation consists of vows and restraints, which are mental acts; and these [deities] possess no mind.

The performance of the *iṣṭi* sacrifice is understood from its connection [with the consecration], as it is stated: "One who is being consecrated should offer an eleven-potherd cake to Agni-Viṣṇu. Therefore, the *iṣṭi* is also excluded.
However, it should be performed for the sake of the sacrifice (*kratvartha*), because it is a subordinate element.
(10.2.18) This very point is doubted in the case of the *asthiyajña*: "By the sacrificer, [the post] made of Udumbara wood..."
Likewise, [it is said]: "The sacrificer takes hold of the *śukra*. Regarding this *vāmā* (the left), should such an action be performed or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?

There is no independence (*svātantrya*) in all these actions for those who are without a retinue; therefore, when the ritual procedure (*ekācāra*) is the same and there is a single taking hold (*ekārambhaṇa*), many performers (*kartṛ*) may participate.

This being the case, we reply: it should indeed be performed for the sake of the sacrifice, because it is subordinate to it. Whatever is of such a nature as to be for the sake of the sacrifice should be performed, because it is subordinate; for in that context, the sacrificer is subordinate, and the purpose of the *audumbarī* post is to ensure the preservation of the sacrificer’s measure. Thus ends the section.

The section concerning the performance of optional rites (*kāmya-karma*) is established herein. (Brahma-siddhānta) Sūtra 50: But optional rites do not exist [in the case of one who has renounced], because desires have ceased, just as [they do not exist] for another when they are not being performed.

Commentary: There is the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, and regarding it, it is heard in scripture: "If he desires that Parjanya should rain, he should fix the sacrificial post low," and so forth. This is the case here [Page 423].
In the tenth book, second chapter:
[Sūtra 367] Is that which is obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction) and is optional (*kāmya*) to be performed? This is the doubt. [The answer is: For the sake of favoring the *codaka*.

How so? [The opponent asks: "The *janyathīni* (the verses for the sacrificer's wife) do not desire anything; they are items whose purpose is caused by the desires of the sacrificer. To this it is replied: There is no need for the sacrificer to desire them here. The meaning in this context is: "When the *sadas* is measured low, rain occurs. Therefore, if there is a need for rain, the *sadas* must be measured low.
The view will become purposeful.
Thus, when [this is established], rites performed for specific desires (*kāmya*) of this kind should not be performed.

Why? Because if the sacrificer should desire prosperity, then while the *sadas* is being measured, prosperity occurs. For, due to the specific dedication (*upagraha*), the ritual act yields fruit for the sacrificer;
it cannot possibly bestow it upon other desirers. Furthermore, prosperity does not belong to the sacrificer [in that context].

It is understood that there is a result; for just as in the case of another living sacrificer, a desire, even if present, does not come to fruition if it is not expressed—how much more so, then, for those who have no desire at all? Therefore, optional rites (*kāmyāni*) should not be performed. (9.1.20)
In the case of the bones, there is no *sūktavāka* because of the absence of a desire for results, as in the case of the injunction regarding the performance [of the ritual]. Sūtra 51 (Nirṇaya).
Commentary.

There exist the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, which serve as the archetype (prakṛti) for those rites such as the Prāyaṇīya that are obtained through extension (codaka). In those [latter rites], the *kravāk* (the call of the ritual procedure) is obtained by extension;
therein [are recited these mantras]: "This sacrificer seeks long life; he seeks a good dawn; he seeks all that is dear."
"By means of this mouth, he prays for the oblation; may he eat that, may he consume that, may the gods grant that to him"—thus [it is said].
"He does not become one who has no mouth"—this is an additional reading in Ka0 Saṃ0 2.0.1 [Page 424].
In the Mīmāṃsā—[like] a blade of *darbha* grass—this question arises: "Are these things to be performed, or are they not to be performed? This is the point of doubt.
What, then, is the prima facie position? [It is that] those desires which exist among the *svakravāka* birds in the herd...

They too would not exist. What is the reason? "Because of non-existence": for one who desires does not desire what is already possessed; this has been stated. Therefore, they should not be performed. Regarding the term *kravāke*, since it is to be diminished (*cayitavye*), it is explained as being like a word (*vākavat*).

How is it described in this way? It is said: "The suffix *ti* should be understood as having the sense of *īha* (effort or purpose). For example, in the *Indovyatikrama-cūḍā*, there is the statement regarding the origin of the mantras: 'The sacrificial vessel (*kapāla*) should be modified according to the specific utterance of the mantra. Therefore, there is no reproach against the author."

[Objection: "They are for the sake of praise (arthavāda), because they are mere commendations" (Pūrvapakṣa Sūtra 52). [Bhāṣya: This which you have stated—that desires arising from delusion should not be performed—is not so;
for these desires are merely commendatory statements (arthavāda). They are indeed commendations.

Why? Because they are explanatory statements (*arthavāda*). These—"He prays for long life; he prays for good offspring"—are explanatory statements, not injunctions (*vidhi*). Since they are explanatory statements, the impeller (*codaka*) brings them into effect through the ritual action. In this way, there is favor toward the impeller.
Therefore, we see that these desires are to be performed.

And this is not so—that which was stated by you, that desires should be pursued for such purposes. Why? Because they are designated as "wishes"; these desires are designated as "wishes."

Commentary: This is not so, as you have stated—that those desiring gold should perform [the rites]; they should not be performed. Why? Because "it is for his sake" (tadāśīṣṭvāt). This [blessing] is for his sake; it is for the sake of the sacrificer. For it shows that the blessing has the sacrificer as its object, according to the text: "Whatever blessing whatsoever the priests invoke during the sacrifice, all of that is for the sacrificer."

And since there is no sacrificer here, and inanimate bones lack the capacity to desire [the results], and it is said that "only one who is both desirous and capable is entitled [to perform a rite]," according to the principle that "because of the connection with the Vedic text, the injunction must be understood as applying to the agent in its entirety," we therefore see this in this [context].
"One desiring the *homa* should not perform [the rite]"—having raised this doubt, the purpose is not stated. "Because it is for the sake of that blessing" (10.2.22).

Even when the sacrificer has gone to the other world, there is the completion of the *makhārā* sacrifice; however, for the *sarvasvār*, there is no completion upon the death of the sacrificer, because the ritual is connected with one who is alive. (Pūrvapakṣa) 56.

By means of that, one should sacrifice for him who desires, "May I go to the heavenly world free from disease."

In this regard, there is a doubt: when the sacrificer has met his death (diṣṭagati), should the ritual action be abandoned at that point, or should it be brought to completion? What, then, is the prima facie view?—In the Sarvasvāra sacrifice, since the sacrificer has met his death, the ritual action should be abandoned at that point, because "the action is connected with living" (karmaṇe jīvasaṃyogāt); for the action is performed by one who is alive, not by one who is dead. Therefore, this conclusion follows: in the Sarvasvāra, one should perform the sacrifice until the point of the sacrificer's death.
It may be so for both, because it is taught by direct perception [of scripture]. (Siddhānta) || 57 ||

Mādhava [says]: "akhādā" marks its completion; for both the season and the completion are perceptible. Furthermore, this is also stated: "while the *prastāva* of the *Ārbhava* [stotra] is being chanted, the *audumbarī*..."

"Having wrapped [the fire] all around with a fringeless cloth, and having issued the command, 'O Brāhmaṇas, complete my sacrifice,' he enters the fire. It is prescribed as follows: "If they should carry off the Soma, one should say, 'Run! Hold the umbrella!
Now, as for what was said—"One who is living is an agent, not one who is dead"—we reply: no; the instruction was given by one who is living, namely, "Complete the undertaking."
Therefore, its completion occurs only at that very moment.

To this, it is said: "When the self (ātman) has initiated [the action], at that time the completion was not yet effected by it; when the completion occurs, then the self is no longer present. Who, then, is the agent of the completion?"
The reading in the Kāśīmudrita-puṣpaka (Kā0 kī0 pu0) is "sanprāptidvāralakṣaṇyā," but it is more appropriate for the reading to be "sampreṣaṇadvārā lakṣaṇyā."

[Page 428] Thus it is said. It is replied: this is equally true for one whose doubt has been removed—that you consider the agent to be one who lives with his doubts removed—it is equally true for him as well who brings [the action] to completion.

At the time of the completion [of the rite], he is still living; even his life at the time of completion is of no assistance [to the performance], since his status as an agent is established solely by the previous injunction (*praipa*). And that previous injunction is the same for one who is living and for one who is dead. Therefore, this person also is as if living.
As for the argument that "agency is established because [the self] exists while living," this too is exactly the same: even while living, it is the person (*puruṣa*) who is the agent, not the body;
and that person exists even when the body has fallen away. Therefore, he alone is [the agent] at the completion [of the action].

Regarding the word "karma": now, it might be argued that—"Since it is impossible for the sacrificer [to perform them] after his death, it is impossible to carry out the subsequent ritual procedure (tantra) once he has gone to his destination; therefore, the injunction (codaka) does not extend it to him. This is not so; it will extend [the procedure] with the exception of those acts pertaining to the sacrificer himself; therefore, there is no fault. By the very power of that [text], it will constitute a ritual act performed by the sacrificer. (10.2.23a)

Now, when the sacrificer has actually passed away, what is to be done? This is the question.

It appears and there is a connection; it occurs even when [the object] is not well-known. For example: "What is the name of this mountain? What is the name of this river? What is this fruit? In the case of the sacrificer, there will be an action characterized by "bone-glory" (*asthiyaśas*). Just as in the *Asthiyaśas* sacrifice, that which is for the sake of the ritual (*kratvartha*) is performed by the bones and nothing else, so too when [the sacrificer] has gone to his appointed destination, one should cause the ritual purpose to be accomplished with speed and nothing else; as it is said: "The sacrificer takes hold of the *śukra* cup."
"The Udumbara post is joined with the sacrificer. (10.2.24)
On every occasion, even when the patron is in distress, this is the means for attaining longevity and meditative concentration.
The word "living" is not [required] in the formula for longevity, because that [formula] has the purpose of expressing a blessing. (Pūrvapakṣa 59)

Commentary: In the Sarvasvāra sacrifice itself, while the sacrificer is still alive, there certainly arises this doubt: regarding the formula "O sacrificer, may hope be yours," should it be an invocation for long life, or not? What is the prima facie view? There is no mention of an invocation for long life while he is living. Why? Because that [invocation] is for his sake [only when he is dead].

When the officiants bestow the *prastara* [grass-bundle] while saying, "The sacrificer desires such-and-such a life-span," it must be made known: "How may the sacrificer obtain that? Yet this sacrificer here has contrary desires—he desires death. Therefore, the prayer for long life should not be uttered there.

Commentary: There is the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), [prescribed] by the injunction, "Those desiring prosperity should perform the twelve-day sacrifice. Is this not so? What is the prima facie conclusion (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It has been stated that because one is performing the act oneself, the *varaṇa* (selection) and *dāna* (giving) are excluded; furthermore, there is no other scriptural injunction stating that these must be performed. To the extent that there is a fault in deviating from what is explicitly heard in the scripture, to that same extent there is a fault in assuming what is not heard. Therefore...
Regarding the term "kāvya":
this being the position reached, we reply: "The action should be for the sake of dharma," for that which is indeed superior...
Or, the gift is not for the sake of excessive acquisition; therefore, it does not come into conflict even when one is personally impoverished.
Consequently, the ritual action should be performed for the sake of favoring the person who enjoins it. (10.2.26 Śrauta Sūtra)

Commentary: There are Pavamāna-iṣṭis at the establishment of the sacred fires (agnyādheya), as stated: "He who should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna, to Agni Pāvaka, and to Agni Śuci."

In the absence of that [ladle], should the pouring out [of the oblation] also not be performed, or should it be performed? Which is it?

[Objection: "Is it attained [that the rite must be performed]?—As it was heard, that [rite] cannot be performed, nor is there any purpose served by performing it otherwise than as heard. Therefore, one who lacks the [required] qualities should not perform it.
This being the position reached, we reply: "And even upon the omission of the subordinate elements (guṇa), the performance of the primary element (mukhya) shall take place."

The *guṇa* (subsidiary) is the *agnihotra-homa*, and the *pradhāna* (principal) is the *nirvāpa* (offering). If the *nirvāpa* were impossible, then, due to that impossibility, the *agnihotra-homa* would also become impossible and thus cease;
however, it is not the case that the principal ceases simply because the subsidiary is omitted. Therefore, the *nirvāpa* must be performed.
And since its being the means for the *āgnihotra* ladle is not possible, that [application] is set aside.

There is the Vājapeya sacrifice, concerning which it is heard: "One desiring sovereign rule over the earth should proceed with the Vājapeya in autumn.
In that context, it is further stated: "The sacrificial pap (caru) consists of seventeen measures of wild rice (naivāra) in milk."

Thus it is said. However, there exists in the archetype (prakṛti) the injunction regarding the handfuls: "He offers four handfuls. Both [the sacrifice and the handfuls] are thus obtained through the extended application (codaka). In this regard, there arises a doubt: is it that the sacrifice is to be favored at the expense of omitting the handfuls, or is it that the handfuls are to be favored at the expense of omitting the sacrifice? Or rather, is it the omission of the sacrifice? Or is it the omission of both the sacrifice and the handfuls? Or is it the omission of one or the other? What is the prima facie position? It is the omission of one or the other—if...
Or in handfuls, or on a cart. Why?
Because there is an absence of any word that imposes a restriction, there is no fixed rule.
This being the case, we reply: there should be an omission of the handful (muṣṭi), because it is for the sake of favoring the measure (mātrā).
Why? Because the number is primary; for the measure falls first, and it is understood first, and at the time of that understanding, it does not obstruct the cognition of the measure.

There exists some cognition; when that non-contradictory cognition of "one" is attained, the cognition of "a handful" (muṣṭi) arises. That [cognition of a handful] ought not to act as an obstacle to the cognition of number. Therefore, because it is subordinate, there is the omission of the handfuls; because it serves the primary purpose, the number is upheld. As it has been said: "Or rather, the primary [is followed], like the injunction regarding the first [offering]."
This being the case, we reply: "The omission of the fist is justified by my [omission].
Why? Because of its quality; for the quality of the fist is heard in my [text]: "four fists.
The number is uttered so that the fists might be characterized by the number four—how else could they be? Thus, the number is pronounced.
It is not for its own sake. Therefore, the number previously mentioned is as if it were not mentioned at all;

for it is uttered solely for the purpose of qualifying the subsequent element, and thus no benefit need be accorded to it. When the handful (*muṣṭi*) is omitted, that which was its substratum (*adhikaraṇa*) ceases to exist due to the absence of that substratum. If another substratum were employed, it would not be like the original model (*prakṛti*).
Furthermore, in the discourse on numbers, the handfuls (muṣṭi) are the substrata for the scattering (nirvāpa); this is the ninth quarter of the tenth chapter.

The handfuls do not cease [to be performed]. Therefore, because they are subordinate qualities (guṇa), the name [of the sacrifice] would cease, but not the handfuls; as it has been said: "And when there is a conflict between a quality and its purpose, [the quality ceases]."
[Objection: No, because it is a remnant of the offering. [Siddhānta: 64. (Siddhānta) Because it is a remnant of the offering.
1.1 How then? It is not so; the number is not heard in connection with the handfuls. If it were heard in connection with the handfuls, [then it would be as you say].
It would cease because it has been fulfilled. Where, then, is it heard? At the act of pouring out (nirvāpa).
How so? The connection is not made thus: "four handfuls," [but rather] "he pours out four";
for the pouring out is qualified by the handfuls and qualified by the sacrifice.
It is explained as follows: for when there is a connection with an action, the accusative case-ending occurs. How so?

Because that is a case-ending denoting a *kāraka* (grammatical participant), and a *kāraka* belongs only to an action, not to a substance. Therefore, while "four handfuls" (*catuḥ-sakhā*) is understood through direct audition (*śruti*), it is [further specified] by syntactical connection (*vākya*) as belonging to the handfuls (*muṣṭīnām*).
Direct statement is stronger than syntactical connection; therefore, for the sake of favoring the primary element, there must be the omission of the handfuls.
But as for the number, because it is common to the injunction, it is a modification of that [handful], and because of its connection, it applies to the handfuls last of all. (Sūtra 65, Pūrvapakṣa)

The word "tu" (but) in the commentary sets aside this position. It is not that the favor [of the deity] is lost through the omission of the handfuls; what then? That which is "by me" is what ceases—the handfuls [themselves].
How so? Because of the "commonality": in the archetype, the substance used as the means for the pouring out (*nirvāpa*) consists of handfuls; of those...

The number four is a delimiter; here it is heard that there is a sacrificial vessel (*śarāva*) consisting of seventeen substances. In that case, the handful (*muṣṭi*) substance intended for measurement is replaced by the sacrificial vessels intended for measurement; and the number seventeen intended for measurement is replaced by the number four intended as a delimiter. For example: "This is curd, this is ghee, this is vegetable, these are rice-grains"—it is appropriate that the reading should be "is replaced" (*nivartate*).

"Devadatta is to be fed; like Devadatta, Yajñadatta [is to be fed] with oil. In this regard, whatever can be accomplished at the meal with ghee is done with oil. Therefore, even though it is not explicitly heard that "he is to be lubricated with oil," nevertheless, because the function is the same, [the substitution is valid].

Oil serves as the substitute for clarified butter; likewise, while performing [the rite] with "mayā" (me), it ought to serve as the substitute for the very number [of measures] used in the delimitation. Furthermore, the substance "bharu" is the substitute for "suṣṭi" because of their conjunction. Therefore, [the rule applies] to the original "mayā."
And the ordinary substance is set aside.
It is not a substance, because it is connected with an injunction; rather, it is the subject under discussion, because it is associated with a purificatory rite. (Siddhānta Sūtra 66)

This is not so. By "injunction" (*codanā*), we mean the sacrifice (*yāga*). For the number seven and the substance *śarāva* are connected to the sacrifice; whereas in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the number four and the substance *suṣṭi* are connected to the preparatory rite of pouring out (*nirvāpa-saṃskāra*). And that which is performed elsewhere, even if it has the same function, [does not apply].

Furthermore, something becomes a sublater (nivartaka) when the function of that which is obtained through the general rule (codaka), as perceived by direct observation, is brought to completion; and when that sacrifice is performed, the function of the offering (nirvāpa) is thereby set aside. Therefore, nothing whatsoever obtained through the offering is set aside by this [act].
However, when examined through the four handfuls, the substance being measured does not amount to seventeen *śarāva*s;

therefore, due to this contradiction, one of the two must be set aside—either the substance or the measure. In that case, since the four handfuls are to be maintained, it is more reasonable that the measure (the *śarāva*) be omitted. (10.2.28)
The section concerning the fact that words such as "cow" in injunctions like "one should sacrifice a cow" denote the animal [and not the product].
But in the case of that which is produced by its own nature, there would be a modification of substantiality, because it is not an effect.

"Vatsamaindram ṛṣabham" (a calf, a female of the Indra-lineage, and a bull). Regarding this, there is a doubt: are these a goat-cow and a bull, or are they cows? What is the prima facie view? They are goats, in order to favor the extended application (*codaka*). Those words are based on qualities; those qualities are to be introduced into the substance already obtained through the extended application.
"Is it not the case that these words denote qualities in a cow? True, they do;

however, this is not by means of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), nor by explicit statement (*vacana*), nor by the extended application (*codaka*). Although this word denoting a quality expresses the quality as residing in the cow through its primary sense (*mukhyā*), it nevertheless refers to the substance to be seized (*ālambhadravya*) through syntactical connection (*vākya*)."

Furthermore, because of the absence of a divine substance (*godravya*), it is the sentence of the injunction (*śrālabhati*) itself that is grasped, not the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Moreover, these words denote age and physical state; since qualities are formless (*amūrtatvāt*), they cannot be connected with an action, but rather have a connection only with a substance.

And the substance is obtained through the general rule (*codaka*); therefore, there is grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between them, as in: "He gives two ewes as milch-cows; for him, a human female is the milch-cow as the sacrificial fee."

Likewise, in the case of the statement, "He wears the skin of a goat-bull here," the word denoting a part of the body (*dhāma*) is connected only with the substance mentioned within that same single sentence. Similarly here as well, it is connected with the substance obtained through the *codaka* (extended application). Therefore, [the animals are] a she-goat, a milch cow, and a bull.

This being the case, we reply: "In this *autpattika* [inherent] instance—referring to a quality-word (*guṇa-śabda*) that is distinguished by genus from its very origin—there would be a modification according to the substance; it would modify the substance as well, not merely the quality. That which is the act of cutting (*dhāna*) or weaving (*vaya*) distinguished by genus does not apply to goats and sheep."

That fear belongs only to the cowherds. [They might argue: "Well, whatever can be introduced here will be introduced; what cannot be introduced will be omitted, just as in the case of the cows, calves, and bulls at the end of the day. To this it is said: In that case, it is clearly expressed by the word *aja* (goat).

The cows and other items form a single syntactical unit; however, in this case, when there is a conflict with the *codaka* (the general rule of transfer), the *codaka* does not bring about the substance of goats. Nor is there a contradiction regarding the substance of the cows and others.

As for the relationship: the case-ending of the agent (*kāraka-vibhakti*) itself establishes the relationship. Alternatively, there would be a direct scriptural mention (*śruti*) regarding the cow, whereas the connection with the substance would have to be established through syntactical connection (*vākya*); thus, because the substance is not directly heard [in that context], when the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is connected to the *ākhana* (the hole) as qualified by that [cow-ness], it is impossible for it to be made from the substance of a goat. Furthermore, the directly perceived genus (*jāti*) cannot be set aside in favor of the indirect implication (*codaka*).
Therefore, cows such as milch-cows and others may be eaten.
According to the Bhāṣya, the section concerning the sacrifice [is established] by this [text]: "One should immolate a white [animal] dedicated to Vāyu."
But in the case of a contingent rite, because it is something to be performed, it should belong to the archetype, since that [archetype] is what is attained. || 68 ||
They prescribe this: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu.
Here there is a doubt: should the goat (*aja*) be the animal here as well, or is it another [animal]?
It is said: this word "white" refers to the quality of whiteness in its final sense; therefore...

Whatever is connected with the quality of whiteness is to be understood as "white"; for the word "white," being directly perceived, cannot be excluded from any white substance by means of a restrictive injunction. Therefore, whether it be a goat, a cow, or something else, that which is white is to be understood as "white."

This being the case, we reply: when this word "white" (*śveta*) occurs as having an occasional cause (*naimittika*)—namely, the quality of whiteness—it denotes only the quality; it does not denote an individual (*vyakti*) qualified by a genus (*jāti*). For that which serves as the means of apprehension (*upalakṣaṇa*) is precisely what is to be delimited.

This is understood from the direct statement (*dākya*). Furthermore, whatever substance for this [rite] is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*), which would otherwise apply by default (*bhūlyā*) provided it is not contradicted by an incompatible factor—that very substance this word "white" (*śveta*) will delimit. [Objection: "But can this [word] not also delimit other substances? [Reply: We do not say that it cannot; however, it does not [delimit them] in that manner.

The section concerning the rule that the *sāmala*, the *citrā*, the *khalevālī*, and the threshing-floor must be made of *khadira* wood according to the traditional scriptures.
Because of that statement, there would be the removal of the natural qualities when one practices what is contrary [to them],
and by that, there is a connection with the ritual action.

In the Sādyaska sacrifice, it is heard in scripture: "The threshing-floor post (khalevālī) becomes the sacrificial stake. Regarding this, there is a doubt: should that [stake] which is obtained through the extended application (codaka) of the *khadira* wood be made into a threshing-floor post?

Now, if it is not obtained, should the threshing-block (khalevālī) be made of khadira wood or of some other wood? Similarly, regarding the Citrā sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "Curd, honey, ghee, sour milk, parched grains, and rice—this mixture constitutes the offering to Prajāpati. In that case as well, there is a doubt: "Are the rice-grains to be prepared according to the injunction for the *śrīhyas* (rice), or not?"
Are large or small grains of rice to be taken?
What, then, is the prima facie view? The threshing-floor post (khalevālī) should be made of *khadira* wood and so forth, and its pegs (*śūla*) should be made of large [grains];
for by the extended application (*codaka*), the *khadira* wood and other materials as well as the *johu* [grains] are prescribed.

They obtain [the properties]. In this way, there will be favor toward the extended application (codaka); for those [properties] already obtained, the threshing-fence (khalevālī) is enjoined as a substitute: "That which is smoke, that should be made the threshing-fence.
For it is possible to make smoke the threshing-fence, but the threshing-fence cannot be made [into smoke] by any means whatsoever.

It becomes a sacrificial post (*yūpa*); for a sacrificial post is made from woods such as *khadira* through consecratory rites like cutting and so forth, but not from others. Thus, the statement "it becomes a sacrificial post" would mean that it takes on the function of a sacrificial post; in that case, there would be a figurative usage (*lakṣaṇā*) of the word, even in the case of the *proṣṭhīs*.
One [group] has attained [the state of ancestors] through the water offered with the *tac-chukrā* formula; regarding those who have become such, having established their status as *pitṛ*s,
there is the *Mīmāṃsā-darśana*.

The connection with the deity is established; therefore, the *khādira* wood and so forth must be transformed into the state of a threshing-floor post (*khalevāsī*), and the rice-grains must be transformed into the state of that [post].
This being the prima facie view, we reply: "In the case of such a conflict (*vipratiṣedhe*), there should be an omission of the original quality.
How is there a conflict? Because of that specific injunction: the state of being a sacrificial post (*yūpatā*) is enjoined for the threshing-floor post."

The *khalevālī* (threshing-post) is not [merely] that which exists in a threshing-floor; rather, because it is connected with the word "is" (*bhavati*) without any intervention, this is a direct statement (*pratyakṣa-vākya*). Otherwise, if it were connected by an intervening term, it would be an indirect statement (*parokṣa*). And the word *khalevālī* is the designator of that which functions as a barrier in a threshing-floor; such a thing is then employed for the purpose of the sacrificial post (*yūpa*), in the sense:
"That which is a *khalevālī* is the sacrificial post. And it is indeed possible [for it] to serve the function of the sacrificial post.

[The opponent says: "Let it be so—the word *yūpa* (sacrificial post) is for the purpose of indicating its function (*kāryalakṣaṇārtha*). Even with the intervention [of the term], it is better [to accept this]; for direct [application] (*pratyakṣa*) exists in the case of indication (*lakṣaṇā*), whereas verbal expression (*vākya*) is indirect (*parokṣa*) in the case of intervention.

Therefore, whatever kind of tree the *khalevālī* (the threshing-post) is made of, that same kind of tree should be employed for the function of the sacrificial post. The general rule (*codaka*) cannot restrict this to a specific [tree], for the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) would be contradicted by the general rule in that case. Therefore..."
"The restriction [concerning the sacrificial post] is that it must be made of *khadira* wood or the like. (10.2.310)
The section concerning the performance of the *calevākhā* and the *tacacācana*.

[Objection: There would be a prohibition of others. (Siddhānta) Bhāṣya: In the case of the *sthālīpāka* offering, there is indeed a doubt: should the ritual acts such as "piercing," "scorching," and "raising" be performed there, or not? What is the prima facie view? They should be performed in order to favor the extended injunction (*codaka*).

This being the case, we reply: "There should be a prohibition of others. For when the application to the ritual action of such a nature has been performed, the purpose of the scripture (śāstrārtha) is fulfilled;
one need not strive for another quality beyond that purpose of the scripture. Moreover, [this applies to] those beginning with *tat*.

There are thirty-eight reasons why the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) is not to be employed here; for that which is not a sacrificial post must be employed for the purpose of a sacrificial post.

And because of the prohibition. (Sūtra 71) (Hetuvākya)
In this case, they should not be fashioned; otherwise, a contradiction would arise.

While they are being fashioned, that threshing-post (*khalevālī*)—which is so called because it was used as a post for separating grain from chaff in the threshing floor—must be taken up exactly as it is. If it were to be destroyed during the process of carving, another substance [would have to be substituted].
How could it arise? For [the term] is not applied to the *khalevāraṇa* (the threshing-floor post).

As for the heating (*joṣaṇa*), its occasion has already passed; for that heating was intended solely for another purpose—namely, for trees, and not for a modification. Furthermore, the raising (*ucchrayaṇa*) is impossible for something that is already raised. Therefore...
The *tap* augment and the others are not to be applied. (10.2.32–50)

In the *bhāṣya*,

there is a doubt regarding the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*) itself: whether the actions performed on the earth— such as the sprinkling with water by the Maitrāvaruṇa, the firm pressing down, the digging, and so forth— are to be applied [to the post].
Should the sacrificial post (yūpa) be prepared, or not? What is the prima facie view? It should not be prepared;

for it has been stated that "there would be a prohibition regarding others. Just as it functions in the case of threshing on a threshing-floor, in that very same manner the sacrificial post should be employed for the purpose of fumigation, and [not] for the purpose of the sacrificial post itself.
The preparatory rites obtained by injunction would cease to apply to that [post].

This being the position, we reply: "In the absence [of the purpose]"—if, in the case of the threshing-floor post (*khalevālī*), the purpose for which those preparatory rites exist is not present, then the status of being a sacrificial post (*yūpatva*) itself would be their sole cause [for performance].
They would not exist in the saline soil; however, there is a task for the earth through equal treatment, namely by sprinkling with water and by applying strong pressure,
for that [soil] is indeed capable of being held in check by force.
It does not exist [as a separate entity], nor do they destroy the status of being a threshing-floor fence (*khalevālī*). Therefore, they ought to be performed.

Even the labor, when performed as obtained by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), provided it is non-destructive, would lead to an additional excellence and not to a fault. Therefore, that too ought to be performed. (10.2.33a)
The section concerning the performance of the scattering and the placing of the parched grains in the Mahāpiṣṭayajña.
And if there were a reversal [of cognition] due to the object, then because it would have that as its purpose, it would indeed be reality itself.
There is a great ancestral sacrifice (*pitṛyajña*): "To Soma accompanied by the ancestors, [an offering] on six potsherds;
parched grains for the ancestors upon sacrificial grass; and to those [ancestors] who have entered the fire, [an offering] from a cow that has recently calved."

Regarding the phrase "mantha in milk," there is a doubt concerning the *dhānās* (fried grains): should the act of *hanti* (threshing) be performed upon them, or not? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? It should not be performed. Why?
Because of the contradiction; for if *hanti* were performed, the nature of the *dhānās* would be destroyed, as they are [already] threshed.
"Therefore, they should not be performed.

This being the position reached, we reply: that which does not obstruct the primary injunction should be performed as a subordinate quality, just like the *āñjana* (anointing). It is argued: "But the *āñjana* does obstruct the primary injunction, for it obstructs the grinding of the grains (*dhānā*). To this it is said: it is not obstructive in the way you suggest.

It shall be done in such a way that it is reversed accordingly, yet it shall not be destroyed. Although the sequence of the ritual steps is not performed in its original order, the essential meaning of the substance does not cease to exist. Therefore, when the secondary quality is set aside, the primary action still takes place. Consequently, the act of striking must first be performed.
For in that case, the root *han* will have the sense of cooking; it does not denote mere support.
Thus ends the second quarter of the tenth chapter in the Mīmāṃsā-bhāṣya composed by Bhaṭṭa Śrī Śvarasvāmin.

Chapter 1, Section 3:
The section concerning the non-removal of the archetypal procedure, such as the *sāmidhenī* verses and others, from the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
In a modification, because the primary element possesses the same verbal designation, there is an addition of qualities due to their proximity. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 1 ||

In the *Bhāṣya*: "There is the animal sacrifice dedicated to Agni and Soma, as it is stated: 'He who, having been initiated, immolates the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma. Regarding this, the following is established:
'He offers eleven *prayāja* oblations; he offers eleven *anuyāja* oblations. Likewise, [there are the] *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices."

"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Cāturmāsya [sacrifices]," it is said; and regarding that, it is further declared: "He offers nine fore-offerings and nine after-offerings. Likewise, "One desiring offspring should sacrifice a white animal dedicated to Vāyu"; and regarding that also, it is declared: "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning..."

"Thus he establishes the Āghāra [libation]. Similarly, regarding the *Avabhṛtha* (concluding bath), it is stated: "In the waters, he establishes the Āghāra of men. Regarding these, there is a doubt: Is the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of the archetype not obtained [in these cases], so that when it is unobtained, these are enjoined as distinct acts;
or is it obtained, such that they are injunctions of accessory qualities (*guṇavidhi*) when it is already obtained? What is the prima facie view? It is not obtained.
Thus: "In the modifications," that is, in those [rites], as in the case of the word [itself], the primary [element] has its subsidiaries;
in such [rites] as the Soma-sacrifice and others, there is the origination of additional subsidiary actions.
Because it "causes to exist" and "establishes the conduct," these are enjoined as distinct actions.
For in this way, the Śruti becomes supported; and by those very means, they [the Vedas] become possessed of their limbs (sāṅga), according to the Mīmāṃsā system.
Therefore, the procedure belonging to the archetype (prakṛti) is not obtained; for that [procedure] is proximate in the archetype, and it will not bypass the proximate archetype.
And there is no contradiction of that [rule], as in the case of the original form. (Yukti-sūtra 2)

And thus there will be no contradiction. What is the contradiction? It is the assumption that it is "like the archetype" (*prakṛti-vat*). That word *codaka* (the injunction) would have to look back to this archetype, which is not nearby but separated by many sentences; therefore, other rites are enjoined—the *prayāja* sacrifices.
He performs it; he performs it nine times; he establishes the foundation; he performs it with the words, "The embryo of the diamond has come forth for the sake of turning. Thus he does.
And because of the authority of the injunction. (Sūtra 3) (Śrāddha-nirṇaya)

In response to the objection regarding the portion (*bhāga*), the following is stated: "But surely there is no capacity to enjoin an action in this way. How so? Because from that sentence it is understood: 'He makes a portion. How then [is it enjoined]? 'He makes eleven portions.'"
"Because it brings about the possession of qualities (*guṇavat*), upon hearing the word 'quality' (*guṇa*), if the existence of the sacrifice were being brought about [as the primary object],
the hearing of the word 'quality' would be purposeless. Therefore, these words are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*)."

It will be explained that these [words] possess the power of impelling (*codanā-prabhava-sāmarthya*); they are capable of impelling action. Why? Because these are verbal forms (*ākhyāta-śabda*), and it has been established that verbal forms are impellers of action, according to the rule: "Words denoting action have the sense of becoming" (PMS 2.1.1).

These [words] will enjoin the primary action (*karma*) together with its subsidiaries (*samūha*). Just as in the case of "we go to the sacrifice" (*yāmaḥ karṇāvthaḥ*) and "with eleven [sacrificial cakes]" (*ekādaśapāla*), so it is everywhere. Therefore, these words are injunctive of the action; they do not [enjoin] the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
He attains it.

But the principal act, when conjoined with its subsidiaries, would likewise be of such a nature as to produce an unprecedented result (*apūrva*), because it is characterized by an injunction; for every injunction that possesses a prior [corresponding rite] is set in motion without distinction. (Siddhānta) || 4 ||
Bhā[ṣya]: Let this not be so—that no procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained from other rituals.
The primary [action], being archetypal (*prākṛta*), "joined with its subsidiaries" (*aṅgasaṃyukta*), would likewise be known as having an unprecedented result (*apūrva*).
This has been stated: "The ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) indeed proceeds in the case of an injunction just as in the archetype; for thus..."

"Because of the observation of [the term] *ciṅga*. The "rule" (*vidhi*) of that archetypal (*prākṛta*) rite is observed in some of the modified (*vaikṛta*) rites. Therefore, every rule from the Veda is understood through the *codaka* (transference injunction) as being "preceded by the archetype" (*pūrvavat*), because it is set in motion without distinction.

Therefore, even here, the archetypal procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained. As for what was said—that "because [the sacrifice] is rendered complete by the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, the archetypal procedure is not obtained"—this would indeed be so if the sacrifice itself were being enjoined; for when the sacrifice is being enjoined...

The words "eleven," "nine," and "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre"—what purpose could these serve? It cannot be said that "eleven" and the others are merely being restated (anūdya), for they are heard as something previously unknown (apūrva) and must therefore be enjoined; and they are enjoined in connection with the sacrifice by means of the sentence. Now...

A sacrifice is enjoined, and [if] "by me" were also enjoined in that sacrifice, then the sentence would be split. Therefore, since the procedure is already established, these are injunctions of accessory qualities.
Therefore, the archetypal procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not obtained; for that [procedure] is present in the archetype, and one will not bypass the present archetype.
And there is no contradiction of that [rule], as in the case of the original form. (Yukti) || 2 ||

And in this way, there will be no contradiction. What is the contradiction? It is the assumption that [the rule] applies as in the archetype (*prakṛti*). That word of the injunction (*codaka*) would have to depend upon an archetype situated at a distance, separated by many sentences;
therefore, distinct rituals are enjoined—such as the *prathājāga*.
He performs it; he performs it nine times; he establishes the foundation; he performs it with the words, "The Golden Embryo (Hiraṇyagarbha) arose in the beginning."
Sūtra:
And because of the authority of the injunction. (0.3.0) (0.3.1) [Nirṇaya]

This is the response to the objection: "Indeed, it lacks the capacity to enjoin the ritual act (*karman*). How so? It is not understood from this sentence that 'one performs a sacrifice'; rather, how then? It means 'one performs eleven fore-offerings (*prayāja*) at the sacrifice.'"

"Because one honors the sacrifice with qualities, upon hearing the word 'quality' (guṇa), if the existence of the sacrifice were being enjoined, the hearing of the word 'quality' would be purposeless. Therefore, these words are injunctions of qualities.
To this it is replied: These possess the capacity for the power of an injunction; and they originate from ritual action.

To urge [the opponent]: Why? Because these are verbal nouns (*ākhyāta-śabda*); it has been established that verbal nouns are denoters of action (*karmaka*), according to the rule: "Words denoting action have the meaning of becoming" (*bhāvārthāḥ karmaśabdāḥ*, 2.1.1).
[The phrase] "he does this" (*naya karoti*) does not appear in the second manuscript of the Kāśikā Mañjarī.
In the reading "prabhu," it is appropriate that [the word] "bhavitum" (to become) should be supplied.

in this chapter, from the beginning.

Therefore, these words will enjoin the ritual action (*karman*) as a whole—such as "the *yāma* sacrifice" or "the eleven-fold [stoma]," and so on in all cases. Consequently, these words are injunctive of the action (*karma-codaka*); they do not [enjoin] the procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
He attains it.

But the primary act, when conjoined with its subsidiaries, would likewise be such as to produce an unseen result (*apūrva*), because it is characterized by an injunction; for every injunction that possesses a prior [result] is set in motion without distinction. (Siddhānta 4)
It must not be thought that the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is not obtained for other rituals.

Even though the primary ritual (*pradhāna*) is archetypal (*prākṛta*) and "connected with subsidiaries" (*aṅgasaṃyukta*), such an unprecedented (*apūrva*) modification (*vaiśasa*) would arise from itself. This has been stated: "In the case of an injunction, the end of the procedure (*vidhyanta*) proceeds according to the archetype; for thus..."

"Because of the observation of indicative marks (liṅgadarśana) [Sūtra 7.1.100]. The "injunction" (vidhi) of that archetypal (prākṛta) rite is observed in some of the modified (vaikṛta) rites. Therefore, the entire injunction from the Veda is understood to have been "initiated previously" (i.e., preceded by the archetype), as it is "set in motion" by the impelling force (codaka) without distinction.

Therefore, here too, the archetypal procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained. As for what was said—"Because [the sacrifice] has no further expectancy due to the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, the archetypal procedure is not obtained"—this would indeed be so if the sacrifice itself were being enjoined; for it is when the sacrifice is being enjoined that...

The words "eleven," "nine," and "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre"—what purpose could these serve? Nor can it be said that "eleven" and the others are merely being restated (anūdyante), for since they have not been previously enjoined, they must necessarily be enjoined, and they are enjoined in relation to the sacrifice by means of the sentence. Now...

The sacrifice is enjoined, and if the number were also enjoined in the sacrifice, the sentence would be split; therefore, since the procedure has already been established, these are injunctions of accessory qualities.

Mīmāṃsā-sūtra 2.1.5: Furthermore, an injunction regarding a subsidiary part would not apply to that which is not a subsidiary part. (First pūrvapakṣa)

Therefore, these are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). For there would be no specific injunction regarding a ritual action that lacks constituent parts (*anaṅga*); yet there is indeed a specific injunction: "The *prastara* [grass-bundle] is made of *āśvavāka* grass.
If the *prastara* did not already exist, this specific quality of the *prastara* would not be enjoined; and as for the [mention of] the pan...

Just as no son exists for one who has no father, nor are toys made for him; so too here, the state of being a sacrificial grass-bundle (prastara) and a horse-sacrifice (aśvamedha) would not be enjoined [as primary acts]. Therefore, these are injunctions of subordinate qualities (guṇavidhi).

Sūtra: And because of the single word [denoting] the action, when there is proximity, the injunction would be a combination [of the action] with the accessory; the modification [of the action] would be by means of that accessory, because the word is directed toward the injunction and the accessory is what is to be taught. (Second Pūrvapakṣa)
But there is this further distinction: because of the "single-word-utterance" (ekaśabdya) regarding the subordinate action by means of the principal action.

For by a single word—the injunction of performance (prayogavacana)—both the subsidiaries and the principal acts are expressed. Therefore, since the subsidiaries are present within that which expresses the principal, this is the designation of a quality-rule (guṇavidhi) with respect to those [subsidiaries] that are thus present.

Having grasped [the connection], there arises a relationship: "That sacrifice which belongs to the *prayāja*s is the quality (*guṇa*). Thus, in every sacrifice, by means of the quality, there would be a modification of that; by means of the *sāmnāyya* and the mantra, one mantra and another mantra would be modified; this applies to the injunctions for the *prayāja*s and so forth.

Indeed, the word "hi" [indicates] that a quality (guṇa) is to be enjoined; a redundant repetition is not purposeless. Therefore, the procedure (itikartavyatā) is obtained, and once it is obtained, there are injunctions of qualities (guṇavidhi).
Sūtra: And because the name is not something to be produced. (Third Yuga)
Nor can it be said that this relationship with me is being enjoined as something previously unestablished.

For indeed, there would be a different mode of expression (*vacanavyakti*) when the relationship between word and meaning is being prescribed; for the sentence "He makes eleven offerings, and they consist of the *prayāja* and *anuyāja*" would be contradicted by that mode of expression. Now, however, in this case...

The utterance of those names which are already well-known is for the purpose of prescribing accessory details; therefore, from this as well, the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) is obtained, because these are prescriptions of accessories.
And the predominance is equal with respect to the quality. (Sūtra 1.1.8)
Bhāṣya: This [section] follows certain words. What are those words?
It is that which was stated: "Since the *praiṣas* and *anuyājas* have not been prescribed, it is not possible to prescribe their *guṇa* (accessory details)"; that must be resolved.
To this it is replied: "This very power of yours, which impels toward the qualities, will cause the natural qualities to be reached;
and once those qualities have been reached, [the text] will be intent upon the injunction of those qualities."

In this context, the *vākya* (syntactical connection) is considered more authoritative. When there is a conflict between what is produced (*utpanna*) and what is brought forward (*prāpta*), those who hold the view that words denote qualities (*guṇavacana*) do not accept it; for them, the bringing forward of what is already produced is stronger.
A word, having fulfilled its purpose by bringing forward the archetypal (*prakṛta*) elements, is not capable of producing new ones. This is [the case].

If it is argued that the word [denoting] the present time is productive [of the action], we say no; this is not so, because that [word] is heard merely for the purpose of connecting with a quality (*guṇa*) within the word denoting the quality. Therefore, even in these cases, they are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*) regarding actions already established. Now, as for what was said—that these verbal forms (*ākhyātaśabda*) are the enjoiners of the agent (*kartṛ*), and that the meaning is the action (*bhāvārtha*)—[we reply:]...
"From those words, an action would be understood. (Pāṇini 2.1.10). The reading "tukhā" or "bā" is an additional passage found in the second manuscript of the Kaśikā-vṛtti.

In the Mīmāṃsā system,

these words such as "prabhūta" possess authority; for those [words] which are capable of enjoining both a quality and a substance when accompanied by a word expressing a quality are all the more capable of enjoining the quality alone.
For it is said that one who eats grains [produces] "draṣatkarāva" and "mudraku";
therefore, these are also injunctions of qualities (guṇavidhi).
Sūtra: If it is argued that everything is thus [composed of] Pradhāna. (2nd Adhyāya, 3rd Pāda, Introductory)
If you say, "The word 'bhā' will enjoin the quality," then in that case,
everything would be primary, because it is denotable by a verbal form (ākhyāta-śabda).
Sūtra: Likewise, through conjunction with that which has become so, there would be injunctions for various purposes.

For an object does not become primary or secondary merely by being denoted by a verb; rather, an object that is secondary by its own nature does not become primary simply because it is denoted by a verb. When there is a connection with such [a verb], the injunctions regarding the objects would occur according to their actual status. That which is primary—[is the object of the injunction].
That which is primary remains primary; that which has become subordinate remains subordinate.
And thus, the status of being an injunction is indeed non-distinct; because the archetypal acts are joined with the modified acts, therefore everything is for the sake of the primary act.

381: Therefore, we see that these are injunctions of qualities (*guṇavidhi*). Why? Because "the nature of being an injunction is not distinguished" between the archetypal (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*); the connection with the purposeful action (*arthavāda-karman*) is not differentiated. Just as in the archetype, [it is said]: "One sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt for the stability of the sacrifice. Thus, whatever [is prescribed] in the archetype...
That very same [passage] becomes an explanatory supplement (arthavāda) regarding a modification: "He sacrifices to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt;
he thereby establishes the sacrifice itself. Likewise: "These two butter-portions (ājyabhāga) are indeed the eyes of the sacrifice."

Thus it is in the archetype; and in the ectype, [it is said]: "He offers the two *ājyabhāga* oblations; thus he does not exclude the eyes. Therefore, everything of this kind is for the sake of the primary rite, existing as a subordinate element (*guṇabhūta*).
And because that [result] arises from equality, there would be qualification through the formative impressions (saṃskāras).

From this also we see that not everything is the Pradhāna; rather, there is something even for the sake of the Pradhāna. For the order of origin of the Prayājas and Anuyājas is indeed the same: by the very same order in which the performance of the preparatory rites (saṃskāras) of the Prayājas and Anuyājas occurs in the archetype (prakṛti), by that same order they are seen to exist in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti). How so? "Prajāpati created the sacrifice; he created clarified butter (ājya) at the beginning, the animal (paśu) in the middle, and the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) at the end. Therefore, by means of the first...

"The fore-offerings (prayājas) occur at the beginning; with the animal [offering] in the middle; with the speckled butter (pṛṣadājya) [in the middle]; and the after-offerings (anuyājas) occur at the end"—this observation of the curved sequence of the fore- and after-offerings is appropriate if they are for the sake of the principal [sacrifice], but not if they were themselves the principal. Therefore, not everything is the principal;
there is also something that exists for the sake of the principal. (10.3.1)
