"Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ" and so forth; this mantra constitutes the primary locus for the subsequent discussion regarding the support of the universe.
Hiraṇyagarbha [is the deity] of the first [verse], because of the indicative mark of the mantra. (Pūrvapakṣa)
Bhāṣya: There is an animal sacrifice dedicated to Vāyu, [stated as]: "One desiring prosperity should sacrifice a white animal to Vāyu.
In that context, it is heard: "With the verse 'In the beginning, he who was the embryo of the waters,' one pours the Āghāra libation.
Regarding this, the following meaning has been established: since the Āghāra libation is already established [by another rule], this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi) for it.

Thus it is said. But this is now considered: Is this an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) regarding the first base (ādhāra), or regarding the latter? What is the prima facie view? Because of the indicative mark (liṅga) of the mantra "Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ," this is an injunction of a quality for the first base. Why?

"From the indicative mark of the mantra (*mantraliṅga*)," thus it is understood for the sake of the meaning of the mantra: in the mantra, "He who was Hiraṇyagarbha at the beginning of creation, he established the earth," there is this statement, "He was the sole lord of beings once born," and "the one" (*eka*) is a designation for Prajāpati.

Thus, because it precedes the possible birth of offspring, it is understood that he is not yet joined with the exhaustion of the birth of offspring; therefore, this very mantra is capable of addressing Prajāpati,
and since the practice of Prajāpati preceded, he is capable there of accomplishing the task.
In this [latter] case, it is a prescription of a quality for the preceding [element], because it is heard [therein].
And because there is no modification of the original form. (Yukti) 14.

If it is argued that "it is like the archetype," then there will be no subversion of the *codaka* (the rule of transfer), because in the subsequent case there is no removal of the support (*ādhāra*), whereas otherwise it would be removed; this is indicated by the mantra "jā'adhvaraḥ.
Therefore, for this reason as well, the preceding [passage] is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*).
Chapter 10, Second Pāda, Section 383.
Or rather, it belongs to the latter, because of its requirement for a mantra. (Siddhānta) || 15 ||

Commentary: The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. It is not that there is an injunction of a quality for the preceding [act]; rather, a quality is enjoined for the subsequent [act], and not for the preceding one, because it serves the purpose of another.

How so? It is thus taught: "One pours the Āghāra-libation with [the verse] 'Hiraṇyagarbhaḥ samavartatāgre'. What is the meaning? One recites this Ṛg-verse during the Āghāra-libation. When it is recited, it produces a specific Vedic cognition as a subordinate element (aṅga), namely: "To which god shall we offer worship with oblation?"—the meaning being "to one god," by means of the elision of the letter *e*.

From the cognition of this word, there arises the understanding of this meaning: "The oblation is to be given to a single deity. Now, in the preceding substratum (the *āghāra* offering), there is no scripturally enjoined (*śruta*) cognition that serves as a subordinate member (*aṅga*);

rather, such a cognition would have to be postulated—that a scripturally enjoined cognition exists as a subordinate member—and that it must be performed by means of the verse, "Hiraṇyagarbha arose in the beginning. In the case of such a postulation...

There is no authoritative basis [for this]. For this sentence prescribes a specific function of the mantra, rather than regulating the general function of the mantra. The general function of the mantra is merely optional. If it is argued that "this is a prescription for a specific function within that optional context," [the reply is] that it would be purposeless (*ānarthakya*).
The meaningfulness of our position and of the instruction [is established] because it has as its object that which is to be supported;
therefore, the latter is an injunction of a subordinate quality (guṇavidhi).
As for what was said—that this mantra, denoting Prajāpati, is not capable of addressing Indra—[that is incorrect].

"It will come to be"—this is not so. For just as Prajāpati is praised as "one" because of his designation by the word *prajāpati*, and it is said that "Prajāpati was one before the birth of creatures," so too is Indra; for since the word *indra* denotes sovereignty, he is designated as "the unborn" (*aja*) in order to produce everything: "Who shall praise him? Who shall offer oblations? Who..."
And he establishes the boundary when the bounteous one, possessing all wealth, strikes down one after another like a footman hurling his blows.
"East and west by thy powers" (RV 10.60.470). Likewise: "Who indeed among the ancient seers reached the limit of the measure of thy greatness?
For thou didst bring forth at once both mother and father from thy own body" (RV 10.54.3).

Thus: "Who shall praise him? Who shall satisfy him? Who shall sacrifice?"—this verse, though addressed to Indra (*aindra*), by virtue of its statement, is [applied] as an *aindrī* verse. "Who is able to praise him? Or who gives to him?
Or who sacrifices?"—there is a universal application here; for it is He alone who performs all this, just as:
Someone walking places the right foot first and the left foot second; in this way, he performs all these actions. If it is said that "he performs all," then prior to the cause, he is one.
Likewise: "Who indeed [is capable] of encompassing your entire greatness?"—who can grasp his whole majesty?

Even the seers of our forefathers were able to reach the end [of this matter], seeing that since even one's mother and father are born from one's own body, they are prior even to the parents; how much more so, then, than any other person? Thus, its oneness is established. Furthermore, before the creation of all things, it was indeed one alone.
This *ṛg* verse refers to Indra; therefore, there is no contradiction.
On account of the extension of the injunction, there would be a modification of that which is heard [in the model sacrifice], because the qualities are intended to be taught. (16) (10)
This is taught as an injunction regarding qualities (*guṇavidhi*); in that which serves as the substratum (*ādhāra*), there would be a modification (*vikāra*) of the mantra, for here,
in the subsequent substratum, there is a specific difference in the mental state (*manas*) compared to the preceding ones.

The specific knowledge of the mantra recited at the time of the *śrīta* [offering] is: "For vigor, the sacrifice that touches the sky, the great word of the Lord of Sacrifice, accompanied by Indra, for the sake of the sight of the honeyed ghee—*svāhā*. This [mantra] is the means for the knowledge that serves as an auxiliary to its constituent parts; thus, it is addressed to Indra.
However, on page 457...
10. This is the tenth quarter.
The injunction "Hiraṇyagarbha" is Śrauta; it pertains to the function of that great Śrauta knowledge.

It is capable of performing [the function] by virtue of its inherent power; for example, "curd, ghee, vegetables, rice, and meat—Devadatta should be fed with oil like Devadatta," where the optative suffix (*liṅ*) indicates the purpose of assisting in the act of eating. Thus, the substitute (*pratinidhi*) is able to accomplish the task of the original (*prakṛta*); such is its function.
It is employed for the purpose of supporting; for its capacity to produce a physical effect is common [to both].

Here too, the mantra being recited produces a specific result within the original scriptural injunction, and that [result] becomes a subordinate factor (aṅga) toward the subsequent [act], serving as the means for the cognition of its meaning, but not toward the preceding one. Therefore, it is an injunction of a quality (guṇavidhi) with respect to the subsequent [act].
And because it is seen that in the preceding case there is an absence of a mantra. (Sūtra 17) (Second Yukti)

In the *pūrvārdha* section, it demonstrates that there is indeed no mantra; one performs [the rite] with "svāhā," and the mantra does not contain "svāhā. Therefore, this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the internal [rite]. (1.4.3.210).

In the *Cāturmāsya* sacrifices, regarding the placing of the *soma* vessels, it is an application of the original subordinate qualities (*prākṛtaguṇa*). It pertains to the scope of the modified rite (*vikṛti-adhikāra*).
But in the case of a *saṃskāra*, there is another action, because it is that which enjoins [the performance].
|| 18 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||

Bhāṣya: There are the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, and it is heard [in the scripture]: "They place the whey (vājina) on the utkara heap; they bind the animal to the enclosing-stick (paridhi). Regarding this, the meaning is subject to doubt: "Is the placing of the whey possible on the utkara, which is a heap of earth five cubits wide? Or is it possible to bind the animal with a cord on the paridhi, which is as thick as a finger?"

The expositor [says]: Is this a separate act of placing (*āsādanāntara*) and a separate act of tying (*niyojanāntara*), or is it an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the original acts of placing and tying? This must first be examined: Are the acts of placing and tying merely ritual duties (*dharmamātra*), or do they have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭakārya*)? If...
Dharmācārya says: first there is a distinct action, then a visible purpose, and then an injunction regarding a quality;

therefore, since both are doubtful, they are considered together—namely, whether it is merely a religious duty (dharma) as opposed to another action, or rather a visible purpose, or an injunction regarding a quality? Thus, both are examined in conjunction.
What is established? Because of the height and sharpness of the *utkara*, its visible function—namely, the act of scattering—is impossible to perform;
likewise, because of the narrowness of the *paridhi*, its visible function—namely, the act of tying—is impossible.

Therefore, it is merely a ritual act (*dharmamātra*). Just as in the context of the Sautrāmaṇī sacrifice, the statement "he places [the vessel] upon the head of a Brāhmaṇa" refers to the act of placing as a mere ritual act, so too here, if it were a separate action consisting of a mere ritual act, then both the placing and the tying would be enjoined; in that case—

It will be enjoined by the direct Vedic statement (śruti); otherwise, the syntactical connection (vākya) would have to be the enjoining agent. Furthermore, in our view, the two [terms] regarding the placing and the joining will not function as indicators of a subordinate injunction (guṇavidhi), whereas in your view, they would indicate a subordinate injunction. Therefore, one is a distinct action and the other is distinct, because of its being the enjoiner; for it is not as in the case of a verbal suffix (bhāvapratyaya) occurring within its own word following another word.
There is an injunction regarding qualities in the substrate; likewise, there is one in this consecration consisting of the acts of placing and binding.
And [the words] are by nature without any limiting condition. (Yuktidīpikā 18)
Commentary: And thus, what would prevent the application of the archetypal (prakṛta) dharma?
[The texts state]: "He places the oblations," and "They bind the animal to the sacrificial post. For this reason as well, it is a different action.
[Page 459] But because there is an injunction regarding that [state], when there is doubt, the word shall have the meaning of that [which is enjoined]. (Siddhānta 20)

But the word "tu" (but/however) sets aside the previous position. It is not that there is a separate placing down (*āsādana*) and a separate tying (*niyojana*); rather, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the original acts of placing down and tying.

And this is for the following purpose: [it concerns] the two acts of placing and directing which have a visible effect. Why? Because the effect is visible; "placing" means bringing near, and its visible purpose is the accomplishment of the oblation (*homa*).

If it is argued that even in the case of the act of tying, there is no departure from the animal [itself], then for this reason, one is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) and the other is something else. Why? Because "of the injunction" (the injunction of placing and tying) "that" is seen there, since it is already obtained there by the *codaka* (the extended application). "In the case of doubt"—namely, whether it is an injunction of a subordinate quality or a separate ritual action (*karmāntara*).

The injunction of another action is not logical, for an injunction (*vidhi*) is the making known of what was previously unknown; and since the preparation and the assignment have already been made known by the extended application (*codaka*), the word must therefore be uttered for the sake of that specific quality (*guṇa*) which the *codaka* does not convey. Thus, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Now, as for the objection that "the direct statement (*śruti*) is injunctive in this way, whereas in your view it is a syntactical connection (*vākya*)," it is replied: even though...
Even so, there will be a much smaller assumption of unseen results (adṛṣṭa) through inference,
insofar as it is only a quality that is being enjoined, and not a quality conjoined with an action.
And there are also the conjunctions of the nose with the impressions and their potencies. (21) (Candranirṇaya)

Now, as for what was said— "Because the *utkara* has a sharp edge and the *paridhi* serves as a support, it is not possible to perform their visible functions, namely placing and assigning"— to this it is replied: [the text in the Ādarśa manuscript reads *yāvatī*.]

[Page 460] Is this a different act of placing (*āsādanāntara*) and a different act of binding (*niyojanāntara*), or is it an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the original acts of placing and binding? First, this must be examined: are the acts of placing and binding merely ritual duties (*dharmamātra*), or do they have a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭakārya*)? If they are merely ritual duties, then they are separate acts; if they have a visible purpose, then they are injunctions of a quality. Therefore—

Since both are doubtful, both are taken together and examined: Is one a mere property (*dharmamātra*) and the other a distinct action, or do they serve a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭakārya*), being an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Because of the height and sharpness of the *utkara*, its visible purpose is the act of placing [the offering].

It is not possible to perform [the rite] in that manner because of the proximity; since the tying (niyojana) has a visible purpose, it cannot be performed as a mere ritual act (dharmamātra). Therefore, it is merely a ritual act. Just as in the context of the Saucāmaṇī sacrifice, "he places [it] on the head of the Brāhmaṇa" is merely a ritual act of placing, so too here it is merely a ritual act.

It is a distinct action; and this being so, the placing (*āsādana*) and the tying (*niyojana*) will be enjoined, and in that case, they will be enjoined by direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). Otherwise, the syntactical connection (*vākya*) would be the enjoining agent. Furthermore, in our position, the placing and the tying will not function as indicators of a subordinate injunction (*guṇavidhi*), whereas in your position, they would indicate a subordinate injunction. Therefore, it is a different action in one case and another in the other.

Because it is prescriptive; just as there is no injunction of a quality in the substratum with respect to the abstract suffix (*bhāvapratyaya*) occurring within its own word and following another word, so too it is not the case here in this preparatory rite known as *āsādana* (placing) and *niyojana* (tying).
And because there is no obstruction to the original nature [of the sacrifice]. (Sūtra 18) (Yukti)
And thus, the water that brings about the ordinary ritual act is not poured out [at this stage], as in the cases:
"He places the oblation on the sacrificial grass" and "They bind the animal to the sacrificial post. For this reason also, it is a different action.
[Page 461] But because the injunction exists there, when there is doubt, that for which there is a word shall have that as its meaning. (Siddhānta) || 20 ||

The word "but" (tu) sets aside the previous position. It is not that there is a separate placing down and a separate tying; rather, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*) regarding the original acts of placing down and tying.
In that regard:

For this reason: because the actions of placing (*āsādana*) and tying (*niyojana*) have visible effects. Why? Because the effect is visible; placing means bringing near, and its visible purpose is the accomplishment of the oblation (*homa*);
tying also has the visible purpose of keeping the animal from wandering away. If this is so, therefore, it is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) for the other [action].

[The opponent says: "Otherwise, why? Because that [action] is seen in the injunction" (namely, the injunction for placing and joining), since it is already obtained there by the *codaka* (the rule of transfer). "In case of doubt"—whether this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*) or a separate ritual act (*karmāntara*)—it is not proper to enjoin a separate ritual act; for an injunction is the making known of what was previously unknown, and when [something] is already known...

Because there is an injunction for the purpose of enjoining [the quality] through the impeller (*codaka*), therefore the utterance of that which is the impeller of a quality must be for the sake of that [quality]. Therefore, it is an injunction of a quality (*guṇavidhi*). Now, as for what was said—"In this way the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is the enjoiner, whereas in your view it would be a syntactical connection (*vākya*)"—it is replied:
even if it is a syntactical connection, nevertheless it will involve a much smaller assumption of an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*). This is the extent of the argument.
It is the quality alone that is being enjoined, not the quality conjoined with the ritual action.
And [the production of sound occurs] through the conjunction of the air-currents with the capacity of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*). (21) (Candrananda’s Commentary)

Bhāṣya: Now, as for what was said—"Because of the sharpness of the *utkara* and because of the proximity (*upaśaya*) of the *paridhi*, it is not possible to perform the placing and the assignment for a defective rite"—to this it is replied: [The reading in the Ādarśa manuscript is *yāvatī*.
[Page 462]
It shall be done in such a way that the acts of placing and binding can be performed upon both the *utkara* and the *paridhi*;

namely, we shall make the *utkara* broad and the *paridhi* large. Therefore, through its connection with the qualities of being broad-tipped and large, it possesses the capacity for the purificatory rites (*saṃskāra*) of placing and binding.
It will come to be; therefore, it is not a separate action.
Because of the contradiction, [the term] "sthātṛ" (one who stands) should apply to the context of action. (Yuktidīpikā 22)
Commentary:

Now, as for the objection that just as in the *Sauccāmaṇī* section the bringing about [of the result] is merely a property (*dharma-mātra*), so it is here as well—that must be refuted. To this, it is said: in the *Sauccāmaṇī* section...

Because of contradiction, it is not possible to perform the attainment of a visible result; therefore, only the action itself, which has an invisible result, would remain within the context of the *Saumya-āmanī* sacrifice, for here it is impossible to have an action with a visible result.
Therefore, this is an injunction of a subordinate quality (*guṇavidhi*). (10.3.350)
Commentary:
In the construction of the fire-altar (agnicaya), there occurs both the archetypal (prākṛta) and the modified (vaikṛta) procedure; this is the section concerning their performance.
• "He causes the six to beg" refers to a modification of the mantra for them, because of its connection with the Vedic revelation. (Pūrvapakṣa 23)

And there is this [text] regarding the fire-altar: "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar. Regarding the initiations: those of the archetype and those of the modification—[as in]: "To intention, to Agni, to the impeller, svāhā! (1)
To the mind, the intellect, and the impulse, Svāhā! (1) To the consciousness, the known, the fire, and the lord, Svāhā!
(2) To the speech, the arrangement, the fire, and the impulse, Svāhā! (3) To Prajāpati, to Manu, Svāhā!
(4) To Agni Vaiśvānara, Svāhā! (5) All have chosen the friendship of the divine leader; all—
"O King, you awaken; choose the pure for your nourishment, svāhā! (Taittirīya Saṃhitā 4.9.20)—thus it is recited.
Likewise, from the Vaidyati: "To Ākūti, to Mayu, to Advi, svāhā.
[Page 463]
Having set out, [he went] on foot.
To Medhā, to Manas, to Apravī, to Sācī, to Dīkṣā, to Tapas, to Agriya, Svāhā! To Sarasvatī, to Pūṣan, to Agraṇī, Svāhā! To the divine Cāpo, to Bṛhatī, to Viśvaśambhuvau, to Dyāvāpṛthivī!

"May all the gods, the great lords, accept this oblation with Svāhā! O All-Gods, you who are the masters of the path, drink this; O All-Gods, may you choose for me wealth and prosperity, for the sake of a male child, Svāhā!

(Taittirīya Saṃhitā 1.2.20). Having recited these, they hand them over, saying, "He brings them forward. In this regard, there is a doubt: is it that the modified (vaikṛtī) mantras are to be employed and the original (prākṛtī) ones are excluded, or is there a combination of both the original and the modified? What [is the conclusion]?

Is it obtained? [The answer is: "He initiates with six"—this constitutes a modification of the mantras of those original (prākṛta) verses; by this, the original ones would be set aside because of the connection with the direct Vedic statement (śruti). For there is a connection with the direct statement regarding the six Vaiṣṇava mantras, as six Vaiṣṇava mantras are prescribed in the text. Therefore, there is a sublation of the original ones, not a combination.
But [the repetition] belongs to the principal [act], because of practice. (Siddhānta) || 24 ||

The word "tu" (but) excludes the contrary view—that there is a sublation (*bādha*) of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) elements; rather, there is no sublation, but rather a combination (*samuccaya*). Why? Because of possibility. For where the archetypal and the modified (*vaikṛta*) cannot coexist simultaneously, there the archetypal is sublated by the modified. However, in the case of combination, there would be a repetition (*āvṛtti*) of the principal act (*pradhāna*).

Thus it is said. Furthermore, where a repetition is heard as something that must indeed be performed, there this fault does not arise—that is, the objection that "repetition would result. But here, a repetition of the principal oblation is heard in the injunction, "He offers twelve times. Therefore, because it is possible, there is a combination [of the two].
And the mantra-rite should be performed while ascending. (25) (0)

This is not so— that there is a combination— because the archetypal elements obtained through the *codaka* (extended application) would be sublated by the directly stated (*pratyakṣa-śruta*) modifications. Now, as for what was said— "when possible, they should not be sublated"— to this it is replied:

There is no possibility [of the original mantras being used]. How so? The six modified (vaikṛta) mantras are enjoined for the original (prākṛta) oblations by direct scriptural hearing; and since these are the oblations, they must be accompanied by the modified mantras, because of the repetition [of the act].

Furthermore, since those same oblations are performed, and if they are indeed oblations, they must be accompanied by the modified (vaikṛta) mantras. Therefore, "the mantra-ritual should be repeated"; consequently, the original (prākṛta) elements are necessarily set aside.
Or rather, because each mantra is distinct, there should be no omission of the original mantras;
and repetition [of what has already been performed] would be improper. (Ca0 Ni0 26)
Alternatively, the word "or" (vā) serves to exclude the previous position. There are separate recitations for each mantra.

And due to repetition, there are twelve [offerings]; for both the archetypal (*prākṛta*) mantras are obtained through extension (*codaka*), and the modified (*vaikṛta*) ones are obtained through direct audition (*śravaṇa*). Furthermore, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), which grasps all constituent parts (*aṅga*), includes both sets.

Since simultaneous combination (*samuccaya*) is impossible, there is either sublation (*bādha*) or option (*vikalpa*); combination is not possible, because if there were sublation, the application of the extended rule (*codaka*) would be lost. Moreover, the modified mantras are not heard as being extracted separately for the accomplishment of the oblation (*homaniṣpatti*); therefore—

If the *homa* (oblation) has occurred, then it must be concluded that the performers are those who have undergone modification (*vaikṛta*). For regarding initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*), they are heard of as being "learned" (*vaidya*)—as in the text, "He initiates with six. However, the injunction for the performance of the *homa* takes up, by virtue of its inherent capacity, those [formulas] ending in *svāhā* which are intended for offering and are present [in the context]. Both [sets of formulas]...

And since both the archetypal (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*) [mantras] are present, there is no reason for a definitive determination that "one should recite these" and "not those. Furthermore, it has already been stated that repetition of the primary [element] here does not constitute a fault; therefore, there is no omission of the archetypal mantras. Moreover, "repetition is improper when the purpose has been accomplished"—since the modified mantras are recited only once, and by them the consecrated person (*dīkṣita*) is to be prepared, once the consecrated person has been prepared by them and the purpose achieved, [there is no need for further recitation].
Therefore, for this reason also, there is no abandonment of the natural [state].
Furthermore, repetition is not logical.
[Page 465]
And the feet are on the left side.
It is not tenable through repeated practice in a temporal sequence, because it is dependent on specific causes.

Furthermore, there are the passages: "He offers six with the word *pūrva* (prior), and he offers one with the word *uttara* (subsequent). A sequence of prior and subsequent cannot logically apply to the Vaidyanāman formulas when they are being repeated as isolated units;

for the term *uttara* is dependent on a prior cause (*pūrva-nimitta*), and the term *pūrva* is dependent on a subsequent cause (*uttara-nimitta*). Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no omission of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) formulas.
And he shows that it is distinct from that: || 28 || (20) ||
Mādhava: From this we see that there is neither exclusion (nivṛtti) nor combination (samuccaya). Why? Because it shows the distinctness of those mantras: "He offers both—the āgnikī and the ādhvarikī.

If there were a combination of both sets of mantras, then because they possess both the nature of being āgnika and ādhvarika, this designation would be appropriate; otherwise, all of them would simply be āgnikī, and in that case, there would be no distinction.
It would not be possible! Yet it exists separately; therefore, there is no exclusion, but rather a conjunction.

And there would be no designation on account of non-distinction. (Sūtra 28) [Interpretation: For this reason also, there is no cessation [of the previous rule], but rather a combination. Why? Because of the designation; there is a designation.

"It occurs: 'First [there is] the Adhvara, then the Āgnīdhra; this action is the Āgnīdhra-action. The designation 'first the Adhvara, then [the Āgnīdhra]' is appropriate for a conjunction, not for a mere distinction.
Therefore, it is a conjunction. (10.3.4)
[Page 466] They would be sublated. Now, as for what was said—namely, "When there is possibility, they are not to be sublated"—it is replied:
there is no possibility. How so? Because the six modified mantras do not apply to the original (prakṛta) oblations.

The oblations are enjoined by direct perception through the act of hearing [the scriptural text], and these are indeed oblations; therefore, they must be accompanied by the modified (vaikṛta) mantras.
When there is repetition, those same oblations occur again, and if they are oblations, they must necessarily be accompanied by the modified mantras.
Therefore, "the ritual action of the mantras should occur through repetition"; consequently, the original (prākṛta) elements must indeed be set aside.

Or rather, because each mantra is distinct, there should be no omission of the archetypal mantras; moreover, repetition would be improper once [the rite] has been performed. (Sūtra 26) (Candranārāyaṇīya-nibandha)
The word "or" (*api vā*) serves to set aside the previous position. There are separate *śrāta* (directly stated) mantras for each [action].

Due to repetition, there is a total of twelve; the archetypal (*prākṛta*) mantras are obtained through the *codaka* (transfer rule), and the modified (*vaikṛta*) ones are obtained through direct scriptural statement (*śravaṇa*). Furthermore, the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), which encompasses all constituent parts, includes both sets.

Furthermore, since a combination is impossible due to the presence of a contradiction, a combination cannot occur; for if there were a contradiction, the application of water would be precluded! Moreover, the modified (vaikṛta) elements are not heard of as being extracted [from the archetype] once the oblation has been accomplished; therefore, if the oblation does indeed occur, one must conclude that the modified elements are the means of accomplishment. For those modified elements are heard of in connection with the initiation (*dīkṣaṇa*), in the statement: "He offers with six [verses]. But the injunction regarding the performance of the oblation—
One grasps the offerings intended for presentation, which terminate with the utterance of *svāhā* and are present by virtue of their functional capacity;

and since both the original (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*) ones are present, there is no reason for a definitive selection—namely, that "one should grasp these" and not "these. Furthermore, it has already been stated that repetition of the principal act is not a defect here; therefore, there is no omission of the original mantras. Moreover, [it would be] unjust...

"Once performed, there is no repetition"—for the modified mantras are recited only once, and by them the consecrated person is to be prepared; once the consecration has been accomplished by them and the purpose achieved, a further repetition is not logical.
Therefore, for this reason as well, there is no omission of the archetypal (prakṛta) elements.
Bhāṣya,
Chapter 10, Pāda 2.
It is not tenable [that the soul is eternal] through the practice of prior and posterior [moments], because it is dependent on causes.
Moreover, the terms "prior" (*pūrva*) and "subsequent" (*para*) are used [in the scripture]: "He offers six prior [oblations]; he offers six subsequent [oblations].

In the absence of a specific reason for restriction (*vinigamanā*), whichever connection one might exclude,
in that very case the suffix would be sublated; therefore, the collection beginning with "cow" (*gavādi*) must be connected with the sense of measure (*mātra*).

In this manner, the unity [of the measure] will not be disturbed.

Otherwise, the application [of the measure] occurring through the sentence, failing to produce a specific activity regarding the substance, would—by virtue of the context—be disturbed for the sake of the sacrifice, since it does not effect a specific activity. For that [sacrifice]...
"The sacrificial fee for the Kratu consists of one thousand and ten. Therefore, for a single type of sacrifice, the sacrificial fee is twelve hundred.
And the meaning of the word is also [determined] as in common worldly usage. (Yukti 44)

Moreover, this should be viewed as being like the world: for in the world, when a designation is applied without qualification, it gives rise to a cognition of a single class. Why? Because otherwise, linguistic usage would be impossible. In the absence of a specific distinction regarding a class, the number "parārdha" is applied to all [the items] together;
and then, a transaction is carried out with that "parārdha" by means of other distinct entities.

[Page 482] Those things which have a relation with any one of several [factors], their series enters into that [relation] by depending on one related factor; that single related factor must be either explicitly mentioned or understood from the context.

Because "there is a distinction from the origin," and because there is an original distinction regarding the use of the term "animal" in common transactions.

They are saved [from this difficulty] by such expressions as "purchased with five horses" or "purchased with five cows"; for in worldly transactions, the specific individual divisions of rice and so forth are not taken into account. The statement is intended either as a general reference (nigada) or as a measure (māna); for it is not the case that [the meaning is restricted to] "with five [individual grains]."
Regarding the statement "purchased for five māṣas," it occurs that [the price] is measured by five āḍhakas, drōṇas, kuḍavas, or prasthas of māṣas; in that case,
with the words "āḍhaka" and so forth being unuttered, the sentence remains expectant and incomplete, and thus lacks authority regarding any specific object.

"Now, why is it that a purchase is not made here even with beans through an absolute division? To this it is replied: When there is a price, a specific distinction is stated regarding the purchase, namely, "the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) consists of twelve hundred"; and twelve hundred [coins] are not mentioned as the wage for seeds such as rice and the like.

It is appropriate for the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*); the fee (*bhṛti*) is established in three ways: by way of activity, by way of fruit, and by way of scriptural injunction.
First, regarding activity, the fee consists of twelve measures of *māṣa* seeds.

For laborers performing work receive even a quarter [of the produce]; indeed, the correspondence with the fruit is not perceived. However, when wages are paid, the statement is intended to specify a particular measure. For that wherein even a quarter is not obtained as a reward does not constitute a sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), nor is it such.
In that ritual, one should perform it with skill; out of affection or by some other means, one should perform the work for the entire day, not merely being enticed by twelve hundred measures of rice.

Vāha says: "If someone, at any stage, is enticed by twelve hundred measures of rice, would that [rice] constitute his sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)? We say: "No. For a sacrificial fee is that which makes one capable (*dakṣa*); capability is strength. That which does not produce satiety is not [a true sacrificial fee].

It is that which produces strength; therefore, that which does not produce satiety is not a sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*). The subject matter of the scriptural statement concerns the superiority of that which produces satiety.

He says: "Even in the case of rice seeds, one should give twelve hundred, as much as makes one feel satiated. To this it is replied: This so-called "strength" is relative; for it is the same person [who is the subject].

One person may be stronger in relation to another, while another may be weaker; in that regard, as long as one has not yet reached the state of being "one who has eaten" (*āśitambhava*), there is weakness, for it is by eating that one becomes strong.
Thus, the production of strength occurs after the act of eating; therefore, that substance which constitutes the state of having eaten is the wages (*bhṛti*).

That is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); since the status of being a sacrificial fee is established as superior to that, it exists by virtue of the authority of the scriptural statement. In the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) of the *tapas* [rite], by the authority of the scriptural statement, even the offering of a small amount of meat (*alpa-vasa-karaṇa*) is prescribed in place of the sacrificial fee; that is the *soma-cup* (*somacamasa*), which is established through its dependence on the primary rite (*āśrayāt*). As for the animals, however, they are all [to be offered].
The primary capacity lies in the soil; when these exist, the seeds of rice and other grains will not sprout through the power of illusion (māyā).

The word "bhā" excludes non-restriction. There should be a hundred and twelve cows. Why?
Because they possess a share; for cows are share-holders, highly fortunate, and [capable of] great service.

The meaning is "he conducts himself. There will be a greater benefit for the officiating priests; assistance must be rendered without fail. To act toward the greatest and most beneficial assistance is "vartaka" (conducting oneself); and it is the practice of the virtuous that those who are being assisted must in turn assist [others]. In this way, the practice of the virtuous will be upheld.

If a greater number [of animals] is given by me to those of great fortune, and cows are indeed of great fortune, then let twelve hundred of them be given. Horses would be more beneficial, for in their case, knowledge, acceptance, and sale are not prohibited; whereas [it is said], "one does not give a maned beast."
The Śruti states, "He does not accept from one who has not become [an owner]," and also, "She does not sell. Therefore, there should be one hundred and twelve cows.
[The suffix] *bhā* is used after a verbal root [to form an abstract noun]. (Yogavibhāga 48)
Or rather, it is a prohibition of the question. Why? Because of the cognition.
For when the primary elements are being employed for the accomplishment of knowledge, and when they are being taken up along with their respective purposes, the cows are first cognized;
therefore, they are connected with the evening [sacrifice], and there is no contradiction therein.

The indicative mark (*liṅga*) indeed demonstrates this very point. What is the indicative mark? It says as follows: "A thousand is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). "O Iḍā, Kāmyā, Candrā, Vyotiraditi, Sarasvatī, Mahī, Viśrutī—these are your names;

may they bring me happiness from the gods through what has been done. Thus he speaks regarding these names of cows as a great sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*): "These are your names," if she is indeed a cow.

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, cows and other items constitute the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); regarding this, it has been established that "the cows are the designation. Now, the following point is deliberated: should the sacrificer himself divide the portion according to its size and distribute that much [to each], or is it divided by the assembly (*pariṣad*) itself? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That it should be divided and distributed by the sacrificer himself.
Or rather, it should be given; for this much alone is heard: "it should be given," not that it must be divided or undivided. Therefore, there is no fixed rule.

This being the case, we reply: it should be given by dividing [the property]. That is the very nature of what is to be given;
namely, the production of another's ownership through the relinquishment of one's own ownership. And that must be performed by the sacrificer himself.
Therefore, in the case of personal performance (*svayaṃ-prayoga*), [the fee] belongs to him. Whoever participates in a particular [rite], he is not [considered] unassigned to that [rite].

It cannot be connected with that [general term]; therefore, when he specifies it, he brings about the gift. And the gift must be brought about by the sacrificer. Therefore, the sacrificer should specify it by dividing it, "because of the separation of the gifts. In the absence of division, the effort cannot be connected with its own portion. Therefore, the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) should be given after having been divided.
And because of the purchase, it is like one's own [wealth]. (01)

Furthermore, there is a gift for the purpose of hiring, not merely for the sake of merit; and for the purpose of hiring, one must bargain with a servant. And if it were said to the assembly, and the assembly were to accept it—

It is not divided together with the owner; in that case, there is no purchase at all. Just as in the world, when something is given to wood-carriers who have forgotten [their wages], the wood-carriers cook it together with the owner, and the owner points it out to them after dividing it, saying, "This for you, this for you."
The same should be understood here as well; therefore, one who is capable should give the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā).

"Having searched for them, he gives the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā). Likewise: "He gives first to the Śrīdh; he thus pleases the ancestors who have Agni as their mouth; he gives to the Brahman; he gives to the Prasṛtas;

In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, the Sāman is chanted with the words, "The cow, the horse, and the mule.
Regarding this, the following point has been established: it should be distributed. Now, the question arises concerning the method of distribution:
is the division equal, or is there a disparity based on the work performed, or is it based on the scriptural word?
Thus [the question arises]: what is the prima facie conclusion? The share should be equal, because no specific distinction is heard;
where no specific distinction is heard, there an equal division ought to take place. How so? It follows that everything should be given to one, provided it were not to be given to another.

It happens thus: as long as when giving to one person another is not being shared with, so long it should not be given to that one alone; it should be given without distinction, and likewise to each individual.
Therefore, since no specific distinction is heard [in the scripture], the deity is the same.

[The sacrificial fees] should be fourfold in the purchase; the unevenly named [fees] are prescribed by rule because of the purchase, for it is not possible otherwise, as there is no distinction in the scriptural observation.
Likewise, in the case of prosperity (siddhānta):
"It is not the case that there is a hundredfold inequality in the ritual action; rather, it is a matter of benefit.
That benefit is understood through direct scriptural statement (śruti); therefore, the inequality is established by scripture, and by that [inequality], they are 'not four'."

They would exist in the context of a purchase; for their participation is unequal: some are "half-sharers" (*arddhinaḥ*), some are "third-sharers" (*tṛtīyinaḥ*), and some are "quarter-sharers" (*pādinaḥ*).
Those whose mark is half are the "half-sharers. And how is it half for them?

[Is it] so? If [the fee] is given to them as well. Likewise, the scriptural injunctions regarding the rules for initiation (*dīkṣā*) known as "those who receive a third" (*tṛtīyinaḥ*) and "those who receive a quarter" (*pādinaḥ*) would not be tenable if there were a disparity caused by the hiring (*parikraya*) for the performance of the ritual. Where, then, is this distinction observed? In the *Abhyudaya* [rite], in the *Abhyudaya*.
Thus we describe the twelve-day rite as having the fruit of spiritual prosperity (*abhyudaya-phala*). "The Adhvaryu initiates the Gṛhapati;

the Brahman initiates the Udgātṛ, and then the Hotṛ. Thereupon, the Pratiprasthātṛ, having initiated himself, initiates the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*): the Brahmaṇācchaṃsin by the Brahman," and so forth.
The Neṣṭṛ initiates the Prastotṛ after the Udgātṛ, and the Maitrāvaruṇa after the Hotṛ; having initiated them, he then initiates the Pratihartṛ with the Tṛtīyina cup.

"The Subrahmaṇya belongs to the Udgātṛ, the Gāvastuta to the Hotṛ; then another person, either a student (brahmacārī) or one sent by the teacher, delays him"—this is a restatement regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) concerning those who receive "half-shares" (arddhinaḥ), "one-third shares" (tṛtīyinaḥ), and "one-fourth shares" (pādinaḥ).
If, in the archetype (prakṛti), these portions were assigned according to their respective designations, then...

The observation [of the term] is appropriate in the case of the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*). In the case of "tasya dhenuḥ" (his cow), because it is a derivative of a nominal stem (*vibhakta*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the suffix *-ikā* would apply due to its general nature, just as in the case of an *iṣṭi* sacrifice [named] by means of a word denoting a quality. (Pūrvapakṣa)

Regarding this, they recite: "Now, the *bhū* [verse] belongs to the Viśvedevas; whatever is all-encompassing and all-pervading is the *stojīyā*; the cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). Now, by combining these two [statements], a formal inquiry (*adhikaraṇa*) is conducted: Is the cow (*dhenu*) a substitute for the distribution of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) in the archetype (*prakṛti*), or is it a substitute for the entire sacrificial fee?
What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? Since the word "cow" (*dhenu*) is mentioned in the phrase "its [the cart's] cow," the cow [is a substitute for the distribution].
Regarding the term "nivarttikā":
first, this point must be examined—namely, that in the archetype (prakṛti), the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is divided.
What does "divided" mean here? It means that each individual substance among the cows and so forth constitutes the sacrificial fee. How so?

Regarding the rule "The cow or the mule is the sacrificial fee" (*gauś cāśvataro dakṣiṇā*), in the archetypal rite (*prakṛti*), the word "sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*) is completed with each [item] beginning with the cow individually, for the cow and the others are specifically designated, not their collective aggregate.

In this context, the word *ca* has the sense of conjunction (*samuccaya*), but it does not designate the conjunction itself; rather, it employs the conjunction for the purpose of qualifying the subsequent term. For if it were to designate [the conjunction] directly, [it would apply] to actions and qualities.

The conjunction (*samuccaya*) would be connected [with the preceding term]— that is, it would be as in "the conjunction is beautiful" or "the conjunction is to be seen," or likewise, "it is both beautiful and to be seen. Furthermore, just as the genitive case occurs here between two things being conjoined— as in "the conjunction of the *dhava* and *khadira* trees"— so too [would it occur] with the *dhava*.
It would have been as if there were a *khadira* tree, but it does not exist. Therefore, we say:

It indicates a collective [grouping]; and it is logical that there be syntactic unity with what is indicated by direct audition (*śruti*), not with a collection indicated by secondary implication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, the connection is "the cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)" or "the horse is the sacrificial fee. For having enumerated the cows and so forth, their status as the sacrificial fee is enjoined; and that, being subordinate, would differ for each primary element! Furthermore, the word "and" (*ca*) will thus be justified.

"—the cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), or [the word] 'sacrificial fee' [refers to] cows and so forth. It does not mean that it is accompanied by respect (*gaurava*) and the like, nor is it a collective compound (*samāhāra*) of cows and other items. If the state of being a sacrificial fee were already established [by the general rule], then the phrase "the cow is the sacrificial fee" would be mentioned again for the sake of specification: "that which is the cow as the sacrificial fee is a milch-cow (*dhenu*)," thereby excluding others.
By not altering the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) and by maintaining their original state, there will be an adherence to the extended injunction (*codaka*).
By the word itself, this quality called "cowness" (*dhenu-tvam*) is expressed in the case of the cow; for it is the cow alone that is the "milch-cow" (*dhenu*), and nothing else.
"According to the sacrifice" means "by means of a word denoting a quality"—one should establish a connection with Sūrya [in the phrase] "one should offer to Sūrya.
When the substance is intended to be expressed, the application based solely on the act of offering (*nirvapaṇa*) is indicated by the word;
thus, from this application which includes the offering, the ritual pertaining to the sacrifice (*aiṣṭika*) is conveyed by this word "offering" (*nirvapaṇa*).

Just as the end of the injunction is restricted, so too here, by the word *dhenu* (cow) which expresses a specific quality, a modification of the cow-gift (*godakṣiṇā*) is effected; it is not that the gift itself is modified.
Alternatively, because of the connection with the seasons, there is unity for the entire purpose of the sacrificial fee;
since the purpose of the subordinate elements is one, the scriptural statement should apply to the modified form in that sense.
Therefore, [the connection] is through inherence (samavāya) by means of actions. (Sūtra 57; Siddhānta)
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the alternative view. It is the sublater of "all," namely the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).
The phrase "is restricted" (*niyamyate*) does not appear in the Ka0 Sa0 manuscript.

It is promised that "the cow [is the sacrificial gift]. And this is intended as the entirety of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). What is this "entirety of the sacrificial fee"? It is not the case that the term "sacrificial fee" is connected to each individual item—such as "the cow is the sacrificial fee," "the horse is the sacrificial fee," or "the mule is the sacrificial fee."

How, then, is it that "cows and so forth are the sacrificial fee" (*dakṣiṇā*)? For it is not the case that, with reference to cows and so forth, a connection to the sacrificial fee is enjoined in the sense that "those which are cows and so forth are the sacrificial fee. For if it were for the purpose of enjoining a connection to the sacrificial fee for cows and so forth—expressing a relationship already inherent through the use of the plural—the term would have to be in the plural form, as in "cows and so forth are the sacrificial fees" (*gavādayo dakṣiṇāḥ*). This is just as in the case of qualifying words such as "these two are the deities," or "prāṇa and apāna came into being together."

The gender and number of words arise from their substrata; how then is it that cows and other items are prescribed with reference to the *dakṣiṇā* (sacrificial fee)? What is the *dakṣiṇā*? It is cows and the like. The term *dakṣiṇā* is derived from the root *dakṣ*, which means "to encourage"; thus, the *dakṣiṇā* is that which encourages. That is one quality, and it—

The cow and other items are intended to be expressed primarily as qualifiers of that [gift]; for words denoting qualities take their gender and number from their substratum, whereas words denoting substances do not follow the gender and number of the qualities they qualify, as in the expression "the Viśvedevas are the deity. What, then, is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*)? It is "the cow, the horse, the mule"—here the word *dakṣiṇā* is connected with the act of giving, meaning "he gives to the priests," and not with the cow and other items themselves. For one purpose of the sacrificial fees is the securing of the priests; they become gratified by it, and furthermore, by means of greater gratification.

In the absence of the original purpose, even for cows and other such items, there is a single function, namely, being the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). When the entire nature of the sacrificial fee is present, then in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), that cow— which has become the subject of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*)— in place of that original purpose on earth, accomplishes the original function through its connection with the ritual.

For it is heard: "The cow is the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*) for that [sacrifice]. When that has been completed, everything obtained through the *codaka* rule—that which is inferential—is set aside, because she is directly connected with the rituals by means of direct scriptural statement (*śruti*).

Furthermore, even in the Mīmāṃsā system, it is understood that the "cow" (godravya) is the object of the fourfold sacrifice along with its attendants; yet its connection to the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā) is established by syntactical connection (vākya), and direct audition (śruti) is more authoritative than syntactical connection. Therefore, first—
There is no connection [of the cow] with the ritual action; rather, there is a subsequent connection with the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

The items such as cows and so forth, being mutually connected, are related by way of being the sacrificial fee. Therefore, the milch-cow (*dhenu*) is that which sets aside the entire gift of the sacrifice.
There would be a restriction [of the injunctions] by means of a mark that does not depend on other injunctions.

Regarding what was stated—that "the *iṣṭi* [is designated] by means of a word denoting a quality"—it is now replied: among the archetypal injunctions (*codanā*) for the Āgneya, Upāṃśuyāja, and Āgnīṣomīya sacrifices, there is no single effect such that one injunction might depend upon it;
in that regard, it will be stated that a single ritual action takes over the ritual procedure (*vidhyanta*) of another ritual action. Ta.

In the doubt as to who shall take [the animal], a restriction is made by means of the optative suffix (*liṅ*). But here, the reason is what has been enjoined: since there is a single purpose for the cow and the other animals, namely the status of being the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*), the *dhenu* (milch-cow), being directly stated in the scripture (*śruti*), is able to set aside those [animals] obtained through the general rule of transfer (*codaka*). This is the answer to what was stated [previously]. As for the claim that "one and five [cows] are the indicators of the entire sacrifice and thus exclude [the others]," in this regard, "some," however, are excluded from the purpose—namely, some cows are excluded from the exclusion.

Regarding this expression, "He gives one; he gives five," the connection is not made in this way: "He gives one sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇām). How then? It is "one cow. For the connection with the word "cow" is stronger due to its primary sense. Moreover, the direct connection of the name is with the word "sacrificial fee" (mojadena), whereas its connection with the word "cow" is indirect because of the intervention of the word "sacrificial fee"; thus, the word "cow" retains its primary meaning.
Otherwise, the alternative view would be that there is one cow and [one] horse, etc.

Therefore, by means of the specific gender of the cows, the number is applied to the cows; and thus, when none of the horses and so forth are excluded, there will be an adherence to the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) in accordance with the original model (*prakṛti*). Consequently, there is one cow and five cows.

In the Aśvamedha sacrifice, it is heard: "He gives two golden prākāśas to the Adhvaryu.

Regarding this matter, is the meaning based on the mantra such that the two prākāśas exclude the entire set of fees (dakṣiṇās) prescribed in the Taittirīya school, or do they exclude only the portion belonging to the Adhvaryu? Why is there a doubt?

If this "Prakāśa" (the light-vessel) is connected with the verb "dadāti" (he gives), then it is the displacer of the entire sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*); if, however, it is connected with the "Adhvaryu," then it displaces only the Adhvaryu's share. What is the prima facie view? That it is connected with the verb "dadāti. In that case, the word "Prakāśa" is construed with the verb "dadāti."

"It is connected. Why? Because if the connection with the verb *dadāti* (he gives) is thus enjoined, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is upheld; whereas if the connection were with the *adhvaryu*, it would be a mere syntactical connection (*vākya*). Furthermore, the accusative case-ending in *prākāśau* is a kāraka-vibhakti (case-ending denoting a grammatical relation), and by its very force, it is connected with the verb, not with the noun;
therefore, the connection is with *dadāti*. Moreover, if there were a connection with the *adhvaryu*, the word *adhvaryu* would have taken a genitive ending.

Therefore, it is also connected with the act of giving (*dadāti*). Having defined the act of giving, two subsequent elements (*prākāśau*) are enjoined; in that case, the act of giving cannot be enjoined by the Adhvaryu, for the sentence would then be split.

[The sentence] would be split. Moreover, even though there is a qualification, if the verb *dadāti* (he gives) is connected with another word that is not itself qualified, it results in an unqualified action; for even when being employed, the [qualification] does not qualify the qualificand at the outset. Therefore, the *adhvaryu* intended here is the one who "joins the sacrifice" (*yo 'dhvaram yunakti*). Consequently, the two *prākāśas* are the sublater of the *kalā* belonging to the ritual giver.
Sūtra: But rather, because it serves the purpose of a part and because its original form is distinct, there should be a modification of the quality "this-ness" (idantā). (Conclusion) Bhāṣya:
The word "but rather" (api tu) indicates a reversal [of the prima facie view]. The *prākāma* [offering] is for the sake of the function of a part of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*).

One does not seek the entire purpose of the sacrificial gift (*dakṣiṇā*), for their portions have been divided—this portion belongs to the *adhvaryu*, these others belong to the rest. Therefore, there should be a modification of the vowel-quality (*guṇa*) and the dental sound (*danta*). What is this "modification of the vowel-quality and the dental"? The vowel-quality is the *guṇa*, the dental is the *da* sound; the modification of that vowel-quality and dental is "modification of the vowel-quality and dental. The two *prākāśas* (mirrors) are the displacers of the *adhvaryu*'s portion. How so? For this is one [gift].

Regarding the statement, "The two golden *prākāśas*," this is the first [sentence]; nor is there a connection with the verb "to give" (*dadāti*), by which they might function as the purpose of the sacrificial fee (*dakṣiṇā*). What then?
It is the second [sentence], which is connected precisely with "gives. Thus, there is one sentence: "He gives the two golden *prākāśas* for the sake of the sacrifice."

Regarding the statement "he gives" (*dadāti*): because of the connection between the two [terms] through the act of giving (*dadāti*) where the Adhvaryu is the recipient, it excludes the portion belonging to the Adhvaryu's act of giving. When the act of giving, qualified by all its attributes, is enjoined as something unprecedented (*apūrva*), then, since it serves a visible purpose (*dṛṣṭārthatva*), it supersedes other purposes related to the arrival of the Adhvaryu.

Now, as for what was said—that "the connection with the two lamps is enjoined, for in this way the direct Vedic statement (śruti) is upheld"—that is not so; for the Vedic statement does not depend upon inference (māyā).

The genitive case (*ṣaṣṭhī*) is not considered appropriate when there is no immediate sequence with the verb *dadāti* (to give). It is stated: "A case-ending (*kāraka-vibhakti*) is fit to be connected with a finite verb (*ākhyāta*). It is understood by the Adhvaryu priest through the sentence. [The opponent] says: "In this case, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) is the fourth [in order of strength], and thus it sets aside the sentence (vākya). [The respondent replies: No, that which is not being enjoined cannot be set aside.
How then is it heard in reference to the recipient (sampradāna) when it is being enjoined? It is by virtue of its inherent capacity (sāmarthya).

Because it is a restatement of what has already been established, there is no fault. Or rather, the gift qualified by all the specific attributes is what is being enjoined. In this way, when other elements are not set aside, there will be the favoring of the *codaka* (archetypal rule) regarding the state of remaining as in the original model. "He would commit a falsehood by giving [the animal]. Thinking thus, he says, "The Soma-cup is the sacrificial fee.

Accordingly, it is heard in this context: "The priests proceed with red garlands, red garments, and wearing the sacred thread around the neck (*nivīta*). In the archetype (*prakṛti*), there exists the rule: "The *nāriṣṭha* [oblations] are offered while wearing the sacred thread around the neck."

"The *prācīnāvīta* is for the ancestors; the *upavīta* is for the gods; he wears it over the left shoulder (*upavyayate*), for he thereby makes it a mark of the gods. This [rule] is obtained here by the force of the general injunction (*codaka*). In this regard, there arises a doubt: is there a cessation of the *upavīta*, or rather no cessation, or is there a combination? Likewise, it is heard in the context of the *pṛṣṭhya-ṣaḍaha*:

"One should have him drink honey or ghee. However, in the archetype (prakṛti), it is stated: "Curdled milk for a Brāhmaṇa, rice-gruel for a Kṣatriya, and gruel for a Vaiśya. This [archetypal rule] is extended here by the force of the injunction (codaka). Regarding this, there is a doubt: is there a suspension of that [archetypal rule], or no suspension, or rather a combination?
[Page 505] 5 Together.

#25 What is attained? It is the cessation of the [general] rule. Directly stated *upahoma*s and the like are the sublaters (*nivarttaka*) of those [rites] obtained through *codakā* (extended application) that are inferential. Furthermore, there occurs a modification of the archetype (*prakṛti*), as in the cases of "he offers" (*juhoti*), "they lead forth" (*ninayanti*), "they proceed" (*pracaranti*), and "he should establish" (*ādadhyāt*).
Just as, for example, when it is said, "The sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* reeds," people substitute *kuśa* grass [for the original].

This being the case, we reply: there is a combination [of the subsidiary acts]. Why? Because of the connection with the primary act through its own indicative mark (*liṅga*). For these subsidiary offerings (*upahoma*) and so forth have no connection with the purpose of the primary act; that [connection] occurs either through direct observation, as in "just as in the *Nairṛta* sacrifice," or through the prescription of a specific state, as in "what is this breath now? [and so on].

And there occurs the statement: "I am the priest; [the sacrifice] concludes with the *pṛṣṭhya* [stotra]. One should not speak much, nor ask another, unless it be for the sake of [obtaining] honey, meat, or ghee. Or it occurs by way of modification (*vikāra*), as in: "The rice-oblation (*caru*) is cooked in milk for those purified by the nails. Or it occurs by way of a specific rule (*khamada*), as in: "He should yoke the two side-horses. Or it occurs by way of prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), as in: "One should not..."

"One should say 'girā nireti'; he who says 'jirā gireti' swallows his own self; therefore, having made it 'aira', one should sing. Or rather, there is nothing here by which it can be understood that a natural function is being accomplished. And this much [is not sufficient].

There is cessation [of the original rule], based on the thought: "This is heard directly in the text," and "This is obtained through an injunction. Cancellation occurs when there is a connection with the characteristic marks of the archetype (*prakṛti*), and not otherwise. Now, one might ask: "Is there indeed such a connection with the characteristic marks of the archetype here?"—namely, in the cases of "he offers," "wearing the sacred thread around the neck," "they proceed," and "he should cook. It is replied: "Of these..."

These intervening rules, beginning with "muhū" and ending with "hoti," are now being prescribed. In that regard, first of all, the *juhoti* sacrifice has an invisible purpose (*adṛṣṭārtha*); how, then, could it be understood that it should be performed for the sake of the original (*prākṛta*) purpose? Likewise, the *upavīta* has an invisible purpose; how, then, could it be understood that the *nivīta* should function in its place? Similarly, [the same applies to the others].
[Page 506] It is not known at all that the vow for the purpose of dancing consists of eating honey and eating ghee;
therefore, there is no connection with the characteristic marks of the archetype (prakṛti).

Now it is argued: "The subsidiary offerings (upahoma) are not a separate class of oblations; rather, the mantra is prescribed for the primary oblation. This is not correct, because there is no injunctive statement. Since the sentence "He offers after that" has already reached its conclusion, there is merely the mention of the mantra alone; there is no explicit injunction.

"Thus he offers"—these are distinct sentences. "He offers after that" is an injunctive sentence (*vidhi-vākya*), whereas "To Anadṛṣṭe svāhā! To the Kṛttikās svāhā! and so forth are mantra-sentences. Therefore, the repetition of the word *juhoti* (he offers) is not for the purpose of enjoining the mantras. In the case of enjoining the oblation (*homa*), the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is the enjoining authority; in the case of enjoining the mantras, it is the syntactical connection (*vākya*). For this reason as well [it is not for the purpose of enjoining the mantras].

Therefore, there is no combination [of the two] because of the rule regarding the mantra. Both are obtained through authoritative means: direct perception (*pratyakṣa*) is an authority, and the stated [textual injunction] is also an authority; since they do not prescribe the same action, there is no contradiction between them.
Consequently, just as they do not sublate the *prayāja* offerings and so forth, they likewise should not sublate the *nāriṣṭa* oblations.
Thus, such a type of ritual refinement (*karmasaṃskāra*) should be additional in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Commentary:

When there is a connection with an indicative mark in the injunction, that modification should be understood [as applying] because of the proximity to the archetype. (Sūtra 2, Śābarabhāṣya, Adhikaraṇa-nirṇaya)

Now, as for the statement, "The sacrificial grass (barhis) consists of reeds (śara)," it might be argued that just as reeds exclude the kuśa grass, so it is here as well. To this it is replied: It is appropriate in the case of the reed-made [grass], for there is a connection with the word "barhis" through its natural characteristic (prakṛtiliṅga), such that the barhis becomes qualified in that manner.
"Or rather, [the term] 'barhis' functions in the sense of its effect; but here there is a connection with the indicative mark of the Prayāja offerings;
therefore, it is dissimilar to the case of the *barhis*. (10.4.10)
In the *Kaśmīra-saṃskṛta-pustaka*, it reads "cādamāsiṃyoge" at the beginning; likewise,
there is a break after the tenth section of the fifth chapter.
The section concerning the increase of the *kaumāra* [period] through the contemplation of the burden of existence; (the first [section], which is purposeless).

Or it is thus: this is enjoined—"One practicing exorcism should offer a sacrificial cake of black rice to Soma and Indra. And with regard to this, it is heard: "The sacrificial grass consists of *śara* reeds."
And herein arises the doubt: "Is the time set aside, or not? What is the prima facie view? Since both are understood through authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), they should be combined.
This being the position, we reply: "In the case of a connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of an injunction (*codanā*), it should be understood as a modification thereof.
For there exists in that context a connection with the word *barhis* (sacrificial grass) as used in the archetype (*prakṛti*); therefore, [it is] the archetypal [grass].
"Cessation."
In the Vājapeya sacrifice, there is a section concerning the sublation of both the darbha-grass and the mantra by the sound of the chariot and the sound of the drum.
(The second section)

Or thus: there is the Vājapeya sacrifice, [prescribed] with the text, "One desiring sovereign rule should sacrifice with the Vājapeya in autumn. In that context, it is heard: "He begins the Māhendra-stotra with the sound of a chariot;
he begins the Māhendra-stotra with the sound of a drum. And there exists...

In the archetype, it is stated: "With the words 'Come hither,' he introduces the stotra with two blades of darbha grass. This is extended here by the rule of transfer (codaka). Regarding this, there arises a doubt: "Is it that the sound of the chariot and the sound of the drum—which is the noise—replace the mantra, while the substance [of the offering] replaces the two darbha blades; or does both replace both?"

"What is the remover of both? What is the prima facie view? Sound, by virtue of its general property as sound (*śabdatva*), is the remover of the mantra; the substance, by virtue of its general property as substance (*dravyatva*), is the remover of the *darbha* grass. [Objection: "But this is a *tatpuruṣa* compound;
therefore, the utterance is for the sake of another, as a qualification of the chariot's noise, and not as a designation for its own function."

It is replied: even the designation "Indra" is of such a nature that this meaning also follows there—namely, that the chariot will not be mentioned for the sake of another; for otherwise, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) would be abandoned and there would be a figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
[Page 508]

Furthermore, the connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the injunction would be sublated; therefore, the substance of the two *darbha* grasses is for the purpose of removing impurities from the mouth.

This being the case, we reply: "In connection with a mark [indicative] of the injunction, one should recognize its modification. In both instances, the mark of breaking is mentioned, not that of each individual separately; for it is heard in the scripture as "with the sound of the chariot" (rathaghoṣeṇa), not as "with the chariot" and "with the sound" separately.
Thus, the sound qualified by the chariot is the means for the driving forward of the animal.
And regarding the *darbha* grass and the mantra, [the opponent] says: "But will it not be indicated right now?
This is not so; for if it were thus, there would be a dual number, whereas the indication is made with a singular number.
That singular number is the defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), and that is the sound (*ghoṣa*); for by means of that, there is a co-utterance (*samabhivyāhāra*) with one's own [mantra].

"But surely there will be co-utterance with the aggregate; for it is not the case that the aggregate has the meaning of *śraddhā* (faith). If, however, the aggregate were to be indicated, then it would be admitted that [the mantra] is the subverter of both.
But surely the mantra itself is expressive, as in: 'Upāvartadhvam'."

It is said: "No. The mantra is the designator of the mere *upāvartana* (turning toward), and the mere *upāvartana* is not the commencement (*upākaraṇa*) of the hymn (*stotra*). Even if it were a designator, nevertheless there is a direct Vedic injunction (*śruti*) that it should be performed by means of its indicative mark (*lakṣaṇa*), namely, "it should be commenced," rather than [by] the designation, "it should be commenced."
The injunction (*codaka*) and the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*); the direct statement is stronger than the injunction.
Therefore, both the sound of the chariot and the sound of the drum are excluded. What will be the result? If [the sound of] the chariot...
It is not a qualification of the sound; for even a sound that is not distinguished by being [the sound] of a chariot might be understood there as an accessory to it.
The section concerning the combination [of the cups] for the ordinary Indra-Vāyu and others, based on the arguments of Pratiṣedhin, Bāḍhamati, Pracārin, and others.
But in all cases, the seizing of the cup should be performed additionally, as in the archetype.

Chapter on the Path.
In the Bṛhaspatisava, it is heard: "He takes up the cup dedicated to Bṛhaspati; he takes up the cup for liberation. In the Mahāvrata, it is said: "He takes up the Śukra cup. In the Aśvamedha...
"One takes the two *mahimāna* cups with gold and silver [ladles].
However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there are the *aindravāyava* and other cups; these are extended here by the rule of transfer (*codaka*). In this regard, a doubt arises:
are they set aside by the modified elements (*vaikṛta*), or is there non-removal and a combination? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)?—[It is] direct perception (*pratyakṣatā*).

The modified (vaikṛta) [elements] ought to exclude the archetypal (prākṛta) ones obtained through the rule of extension (codaka), for they possess a connection with the word "cup" (graha) that deviates from the archetype.
This being the position reached, we reply: in each and every instance, the instruction regarding the cups (grahāmnāna) ought to be additional.
"There is no exclusion of the archetypal [elements]. Why? Because both are understood through authoritative means;
for the injunction (*codaka*) is an authority, and there is also direct scriptural hearing (*pratyakṣa-śravaṇa*).

If it is argued that 'the word *graha* is a term of reference (*pratividhi*)', it is not so; if the accessory (*guṇa*) were enjoined after uttering the word *graha*, then the archetypal [elements would remain]."

In this way, the cups (grahas) would possess the qualities of the knowledge. Now, if the *arka* is enjoined in connection with the cup, then, by functioning as the task of the cup, it would exclude the original (archetypal) element, just as in the case of the statement, "The threshing-fence post is the sacrificial post" (*khalevālī yūpaḥ*).
However, this other word "cup" (*graha*) signifies the act of taking; it produces a cup named *arka*.

Regarding the statement "the one named *mahimānī* takes [the draught]," a previously unestablished act of taking (*grahaṇa-kriyā*) is enjoined here. Therefore, in this case, the word *graha* (draught) is an indicator of the injunction; for among things that serve a single purpose, there is either an option (*vikalpa*) or a combination (*samuccaya*), but there is no single purpose in the case of optional alternatives.

"Namely, because the purpose of the sacrifice is one, all [the offerings] have a single purpose through that very fact. It is said in reply: "With respect to the sacrifice, these [offerings] act in combination; not each one individually, independently, is the sublater [of the other], nor is there a separate connection of the subsidiary parts with the sacrifice—such as 'one may offer with the *śukra* cup' or 'one may offer with the *manthin* cup.
How then is the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) the grasper of these? And that [injunction] applies to those that have been prescribed, not [to others]."
"At the equinox, [the rule is] 'by the sun' (viṣuvatyārka)," according to the reading in the Kātyāyana-Śrautasūtra-Paddhati.
Since there is a distinction in proximity, therefore [this applies] to all, both the archetypal (prākṛta) and the modified (vaikṛta).

The collector [of the cups] is "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*). Just as in the archetype the drawing for Indra-Vāyu is enjoined, and the drawing for Mitra-Varuṇa is enjoined again, so too the division [of the soma] is for the sake of an unseen effect (*adṛṣṭa*), as is the consecration and the assignment of the deity; because the result is unseen, it is not known whether the former serves the purpose of the latter.

Furthermore, because they are grasped by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), there is a combination [of the two], not merely [the inclusion] together with those for Mitra-Varuṇa and others.

"Even by means of the Aṃśu and Adābhya vessels, which are studied outside of the specific context (*aprakaraṇādhīta*), so too in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*) there ought to be a combination (*samuccaya*). [The opponent] says: 'But surely a quality is enjoined after having taken up the cup (*graha*), as in: "In the Aśvamedha, [the cups] are made of gold and silver. To this it is replied: those two are not the original (*prākṛta*) cups. "The name... [is the response].

"Because of the connection with the origin [of the rite], the two acts of drawing [the cups] are distinct. He says: "In that case, the statement 'He draws the Bārhaspatya cup' must be for the purpose of enjoining a deity. It is replied: When two things are being enjoined, direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is favored; and regarding the deity, direct statement is more authoritative than syntactical connection (*vākya*).

He asks: "Is it not like the case of Agni? Just as in the *Agniṣṭut* sacrifice, where the statement 'the cups belong to Agni' serves as an injunction of the deity, so too here, even though the singular ending is used, the number is not intended to be significant."

Just as in the case of "He cleanses [it]," which prescribes the cleansing of all the cups (*grahas*), so too here the deity of all the cups is prescribed. To this it is replied: This has already been stated—that [the injunction] is due to the superior force of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*). However, the sentence "The cups belong to Agni" is not in conflict with that direct statement.

For it is not the case that the existence of the *āgneya* [offering] is sublated there by the sentence "he takes the *yahna*," since that [sentence] is not in contradiction with it. Therefore, the *vārhaspatya*, which is distinct from the archetypal [offerings], is combined with the archetypal ones. Just as in the archetype one takes the *adābha*.

Just as in the case of "he should sacrifice with a horse-sacrifice, he should sacrifice with a Mitravindā," where an irrelevant [rite] is combined with relevant ones, so too here the Vaidya-statuses would be combined.
