Chapter 10, Part 4.
And because it forms a single syntactical unit with the additional [words]. (Yukti 4)

From this as well, we understand that there is a combination [of cups]. Why? Because this [text], which is beyond doubt, forms a single syntactical unit with the mention of "more than" the Soma-cups. How so? [Because] it says: "These seventeen cups are drawn."
In the *Dvādaśāha* sacrifice, there are cups for the Prajāpatis (*prājāpatyā grahāḥ*) and cups for the Surās (*surāgrahāḥ*).
Among those cups for the Surās, which exceed the number thirty-six, the term "ending in *ṭā*" (*ṭānte*) is enjoined as a rule (*codyate*), not merely restated (*nānūdyate*).
The word "ending in *ṭā*" (*ṭānte*), being uttered only once, is connected with all the cups. Therefore, by this [text], there is a separate injunction (*codanāntara*) regarding the cups.
By means of what is beyond doubt, other things as well are understood in exactly this same way.
Bhāṣya:

And because of the observation of an indicative mark (liṅga). (Sūtra 5) The indicative mark also demonstrates that meaning. What is it? "This sacrificial rite is indeed without a chariot... [and so forth].

"One attains the Vājapeya, the Toga, the Agniṣṭoma, the Ukthya, and the Ṣoḍaśin, but does not reach the Atirātra. The word *viraddha* occurs in the sense of "extended," as for example when it is understood that "the joints of the ribs are widely spaced" (*viralyāni*); if there were a conjunction [of rites], such would be the extension.
It is not tenable in the case of contradiction; therefore, for this reason as well, there is a combination. (10.4.3) [Sūtra]
Bhāṣya: The section concerning the combination [of offerings] with the animals dedicated to Prajāpati in the Vājapeya sacrifice.
And because it is heard [in the scripture] among the Prājāpatya offerings.
There is the Vājapeya sacrifice, [enjoined] by the text: "One desiring self-sovereignty (khārājya) should sacrifice with the Vājapeya.
In that rite, there are animals dedicated to Prajāpati, [as stated]: "He immolates seventeen animals dedicated to Prajāpati."
However, there are animal-sacrifices belonging to the archetype (prakṛti), which are extended here by the rule of transfer (codaka). In this regard, a doubt arises:
are those animal-sacrifices of the archetype set aside by the Prājāpatya sacrifices, or are they combined with them? What [is the conclusion]?
Is it obtained?—that the *prājāpatya* animals, being directly perceived, would set aside the sacrificial animals (*kratupaśu*) obtained through the *codaka* (archetypal injunction).

This being the position reached, we reply: "And in the case of the *prājāpatya* animals, there should be a combination. The word "and" (*ca*) has the sense of an addition (*anvācaya*). For the sacrificial animals are indeed enjoined: "The exponents of Brahman say..."

"It is neither the Agniṣṭoma, nor the Ukthya, nor the Ṣoḍaśin, nor the Atirātra. Now, why are all the sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) encompassed by the Vājapeya? One should say: "By means of the animals. When he immolates the animal dedicated to Agni, he thereby encompasses the Agniṣṭoma; by the one dedicated to Indra and Agni, the Ukthya; and by the one dedicated to Indra, the Ṣoḍaśin.
"By means of the Sārasvatī [offering] one performs the Atirātra; by means of the Mārutī, the Bṛhat-stotra. So many indeed are the sacrificial rites (yajñakratu);

through the animals, he secures them all"—thus it shows their combination (samuccaya). "But surely this is merely an illustrative teaching (darśana); what is the underlying logic (nyāya) here? It is replied: the connection with the indicative mark of the archetype (prakṛti-liṅga-saṃyoga). "But as for the word 'animal' (paśu)..."

[Objection: "It is a modification of the original form (*prakṛti*). [Reply: No, he says; for here no deity is enjoined by way of restating the sacrifice, because there is no hearing of the word *māyā*. Since a separate number and a separate deity are heard, this is a distinct ritual act (*karmāntara*).

Because it is established separately, there would be a difference in the ritual acts due to the *māyā*. Therefore, as in the case of the cups (*graha*), there ought to be a combination (*samuccaya*). (10.1.4.4)
The section concerning the combination of the *anuyāja* offerings with the *sāṅgrahaṇī* and *kīṭa* oblations through the *cāmama-homa*.
Because the indicative mark is seen in the case of the Śrāmaṇaka [offering]. || 7 ||
There is the Sāṃgrahaṇī sacrifice, [instituted] with the injunction: "One desiring a village should offer the Vaiśvadevī Sāṃgrahaṇī.
In that context, it is heard: "He offers three oblations with the formula, 'The gods are worthy of honor.
However, there are three after-offerings (anuyāja) in the archetype (prakṛti), and these are extended here by the rule of transfer (codaka). And therein—
The doubt is as follows: do the after-offerings (anuyājas) cease because of the āmanahāmans, or are they combined with them? [Page 513] 10th Adhyāya, 4th Pāda.

Thus [it is asked]: what is the conclusion? The inferred *anuyāja* offerings should be set aside by the *āmīkṣā-homas* which are directly heard in the text. Moreover, there is a connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*).

This being the case, we reply: there should be a combination (*samuccaya*) with the *śrāmaṇaka* [offering]. Why? Because of the observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*). For an indicative mark demonstrates this matter. What is the indicative mark? "The fore-sacrifices (*prayāja*) and after-sacrifices (*anuyāja*) are indeed the outer self (*bahirātman*), while the deity is the inner self (*ātman*). If one were to offer the fore-sacrifices and after-sacrifices either before or after [the main offering], he would place the outer self among his kinsmen; but since [they are offered] in the middle..."

"He offers [the oblation] in the middle; thus he establishes himself among his kinsmen"—this shows the non-cessation of the after-offerings (*anuyāja*s). [The opponent] says: "But surely there is a connection with the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the archetype (*prakṛti*) in the word *tri* (three). [The author] says: No, for it is not possible to enjoin a quality by merely restating a number, since there is no number that does not belong to something. Therefore, there is no connection with the indicative mark of the archetype.

"This observation of an indicative mark (*liṅga*) has been cited, and it must now be explained how [the action] is established. It is replied: By the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), "He offers the *āghāra* oblation," the possession of the *āghāra* is established; by the sentence (*vākya*), there is the injunction of the mantra; and the number is understood as a restatement (*anuvāda*). However, distinct sacrifices (*yāgāntara*) accompanied by specific numbers and mantras are enjoined.
Since these are known through both means of valid cognition, their combination (*samuccaya*) is logical. (10.4)
In the case of a great multitude, there is a section on the combination [of metaphors] consisting of the metaphor of the subject with the metaphor of the object.
In the secondary rites (upaga), it should be as in the case of the arrows, because of the connection with the characteristic marks of the archetype.
|| 8 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||
In the Mahāvrata, it is heard: "The wives sing along with ladles; the female slaves [sing] with water-pots"—this is the reading from the Mādhava-sadman.
[Page 514]

"They sing; they accompany with lute-like instruments (*kāṇḍavīṇā*) and so forth; they accompany with *śrāpāṭalikā* [instruments] and so forth. However, in the archetype (*prakṛti*), there is the rule: "The *vijas* accompany. This is what is obtained here by the extended application (*codaka*). In this regard, a doubt arises as to the meaning: do the wives "accompany"?
Thus, it is considered whether the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*) are turned back while singing, or whether they are not turned back.
Furthermore, this point is deliberated: is this "singing along" (*upagāna*) a form of vocal singing, or is it a form of instrumental accompaniment?
And in that regard, there is a twofold distinction: is it a singing along of singing, i.e., *gānopagāna*, or...

Is it "singing and accompanying singing" (*gāna-upagānam*), or "singing for the sake of accompanying singing" (*gānāpagānam*)? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? That the original (*prākṛta*) [singing] is set aside. To that, this is explained: it is "accompanying singing of the singing," meaning the wives augment the singing of those who are singing; the original singing is already established, and "augmentation" (*upacaya*) is the sense of the prefix (*upasarga*).

It is prescribed; therefore, the *upagāna* (accompaniment) belongs to the *gāna* (singing). Or rather, the *gāna* itself is the *upagāna*, for the word *gāna* is well-known in common usage as vocal singing (*śārīrī gīti*);
therefore, this *gāna* is the *upagāna*, or the *upagāna* belongs to the *gāna*. When one of these two [is intended]...

At that time, the wives perform the duties of the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*). Therefore, due to the connection with a specific indicative mark (*liṅga*), what is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) is set aside by the directly stated injunction (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), "just as in the case of the *barhis*. Just as the rule "the sacrificial grass is made of *śara* grass" sets aside the *darbha* grass obtained through the extended application because the *śara* grass is directly stated, so it is here as well.
But because [the other] would be purposeless, there should be an addition. (Siddhānta) Sūtra 9.
The word "but" (tu) in the commentary sets aside the previous position—that there is no cessation—and instead asserts that there should be a combination.

Consequently, this is considered: there exists such a thing as the *upagāna* (choral response) of instrumental music, namely, where there is instrumental music—as in the phrase "the drums resound in the quarters"—the *upagāna* of that is the *upagāna* of instrumental music.

How so? For by means of the suffix (pratyaya), the verbal root (bhāva) and existence (sattā) are expressed through direct audition (śruti); whereas [the connection with the agent] is remote (viprakṛṣṭa).
[End of Chapter 10, Section 4, Part 1].

Because the meaning of the prefix (*upasarga*) is remote from the meaning of the verbal root (*santa*), it is weak. Therefore, the prescription of the verbal root’s meaning along with the prefix is sublated by the prescription of the verbal root’s meaning alone.
Alternatively, this singing (*upagāna*) is subordinate to the singing (*vādi*); thus he says: "The others sing in accompaniment (*upagāyanti*)."

"They sing along with *kāṇḍavīṇā*s and so forth. Here, the *kāṇḍavīṇā* and similar instruments serve as the point of comparison; furthermore, the word "singing" (*gāna*) is applied to stringed instrumental music. Therefore, this is instrumental accompaniment (*upagāna*). And whether it be instrumental accompaniment or vocal accompaniment, in either case—

It occurs as something distinct from the original meaning; therefore, there is a combination. Why? Because "it would otherwise be purposeless"—the meaning is that in this way the force of the injunction (*codaka*) will not be rendered useless, and the injunction will be upheld. Therefore, there is a combination. (10.4.6)

The section concerning the combination [of substances] such as collyrium for anointing the eyes and fresh butter for anointing the body with ointments made from the marrow of the *māṅgula* plant and so forth.
Nor [is there a connection] with the consecrated [fire], because of its conjunction with another. (Siddhānta) || 10 ||

Commentary: There is a forty-nine-night sacrifice named Añjanābhyañjana. In that context, this is prescribed: "At the morning pressing, one anoints oneself with guggulu resin and recites over oneself; at the midday pressing, with pailadāru; at the third pressing, with saugandhika. However, in the archetype (prakṛti), there exists [the following rule]:
Anointing with fresh butter is obtained here by extension (*codaka*). Regarding this, there is a doubt:

is that [anointing] set aside by the modified [rite], or not? What is the prima facie view? Because it is directly heard [in the original injunction], and because in the modified rites [the words] "he anoints" and "he anoints over" are connected with specific indicative marks (*liṅga*), it is set aside.

Thus it is said. [The opponent] says: "But surely, in the *sattra* sacrifice, the anointing (*añjana*) and the smearing (*abhyañjana*) take place at the time of the Soma-pressing (*sutyā*), whereas in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the smearing with fresh butter (*navanīta*) takes place at the time of initiation (*dīkṣā*). Since the times are different, it serves a different purpose; therefore, there should be no sublation (*bādha*). It is replied: "Like the *prayāja* offerings, even though the time is different, it must be understood that its function is indeed the same."

[Page 516] Time alone is different, but the substance remains the same; just as in the case of the statement, "They perform the *prayāja* offerings while the animal is standing," the *prayāja* offerings, being performed while the animal stands, serve exactly the same purpose as when it was previously lying down.
The same should be understood here as well.

This being the case, we reply: in the case of *saṃskāra*—namely, bathing and anointing—there should be a combination with the original (archetypal) rite. Why? Because of the connection with something else; this [rite] occurs at a different time and serves a different purpose.
In this way, the one who offers the gift will be benefited; therefore, there is a combination [of the two].
If it is argued that "it is like the *prayāja*s," then that which was stated must be refuted.
• Not so, because there is no difference in the meaning. || 12 || (0 ni0) ||
Commentary:
"And it cannot be like the *prayāja* offerings. Why? "Because the purpose is different":

at the beginning, fresh butter (*navanīta*) is used for the sake of easy movement [of the tongue]; once the ritual action has commenced, [the substance] is [to be used] at the time of the pressing (*sutyākāla*).

The anointing with guggulu resin for the purpose of removing skin discoloration is a visible act that serves another function; therefore, it is not capable of displacing the original [anointing]. (10.4.70).
Furthermore, in the Mahāvrata rite, there is an injunction regarding the wearing of new garments together with the tārya and other materials.
But in the case of the covering, because of the unity [of the action], there should be a modification of the original. 13.
In the Mahāvrata it is heard: "The sacrificer puts on a *tārya*, and the wife [puts on] one made of *darbha* grass.
Mādhava states that what is smeared with ghee is called *tārya*; [it is] a woolen blanket (*kambala*).
[Page 517] Chapter 10, Section 880.

Thus it is said. However, there is a rule in the archetype: "He puts on unwashed cloth"; this is obtained here by the extended application (codaka). Regarding this, there is a doubt: "Is there a cessation of the unwashed cloth, or not? What is the prima facie view? "But in the case of covering, there should be a modification of the archetypal [cloth]."
Why? Because they serve the same purpose (*ekārthyāt*). The purpose of both the original (*prākṛta*) and the modified (*vaikṛta*) [text] is one: to cover the private parts (*kaupīna*).
Covering is performed both in the archetype (*prakṛti*) and in the ectype (*vikṛti*).
That which is obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) is set aside by the directly stated text (*pratyakṣa-śruta*).
Or rather, it is not excessive, because its purpose is something else. (Siddhānta) || 14 ||
Śrā0:
Therefore, the word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position; this [offering] is "additional" to the ordinary āsana.

"It ought to be so. Why? Because that which is a remover [of something] is such that it cannot establish itself without first removing it; however, that which is able to exist even without removing [something] does not remove it. For if it were to remove it while remaining non-prohibitive, it would sublate the *codaka* (the general rule) that has been obtained. Now, one might object: "In the case of covering the private parts, one says 'he puts on,' but not when it serves another purpose. To this it is replied:

This is not so; for even in the case of an upper garment, the term "he puts on" (*paridhatte*) occurs, as in "he puts on a woolen blanket" (*kambalaṃ paridhatte*) or "he puts on a ruru-skin" (*rauravaṃ paridhatte*). The expression "he puts on all around" (*sarvato dhate paridhatte*) arises from the well-known etymological derivation of the word's parts. Therefore, there is no exclusion of the unwashed garment; rather, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) of both.
And it shows the conjunction [of the two]. (Yu·) 15.
And [the author] shows the "combination" by means of the word *vāsas* (clothing) in the plural form:
"He takes off the garments and the boar-skin sandals," and "With the black antelope horn, the garments..."
"He causes [the fire] to deviate; then the Adhvaryu puts it on. This indicates non-exclusion and a combination [of the two acts]. (10.4.80)
Therefore, we also observe that in the Mahāvrata sacrifice, there is a section concerning the combination of the Rathantara and other Sāmans with the Ślokā and other Sāmans.
Sūtra 16: Because another meaning is heard [in the case] of the Sāman, no modification should be perceived.
In the Mahāvrata, it is heard: "They praise in front of the Sadas with the Jhoka, and with the Aghu-jhoka."

"Then, looking at the *cātvāla* pit from the *krauñca* [position] within the sacrificial hall (*sadas*). Now, there are archetypal (*prākṛta*) *sāman* chants which are extended here by the rule of transfer (*codaka*). In this regard, a doubt arises:
"Is there an exclusion of the archetypal *sāmans*, or is there no exclusion, or is there a combination? What is the prima facie view?

Regarding the phrase "they chant" (*stuvate*), when there is a connection with the gender of the archetype (*prakṛti*) and a direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-śruti*), the *sāmans* obtained through the extended application (*codaka*) are set aside. For example: "The *kautsa* occurs;
the *kāva* occurs; the *aurṇañjani* occur; the *śuddhāśuddhīya* occur; the *bhargayajñasī* occur. [And] the *krauñca*s...

Just as in the case of the Vedic texts beginning with "they come into being," those [elements] obtained through the force of the general rule (codaka) are set aside, so too should it be understood here.

This being the case, we reply: when such [injunctions] as "In the Sāmans, one praises with the *loka* in front" are heard, there should be understood to be no modification (*avikāra*) of the archetypal elements. Why? Because of the hearing of a different meaning (*arthāntaraśruteḥ*). For in such cases as "They praise in front of the *sadas*," a connection is heard through a different meaning; and that word which is connected by another word as a qualifier...

That which is uttered [once] deserves to be connected with another word; for example, in the case of "the king's wife" and "Devadatta's man," the word "of the king," being employed as a qualifier of "wife," is not again connected with the word "man. Similarly, [the word "praise"] being connected with "they praise before the assembly," does not deserve to be connected again with "they praise by means of the world."

If the praise were enjoined with respect to the region and "and by the world" were merely restated, then it would be possible for there to be a single sentence. However, when two distinct things are enjoined, then the sentence is complete; in that case, "and by the world" must also be enjoined, which results in a repetition of the injunctive force (*vidhi*).
The fourth quarter of the first chapter on the Probandum (sādhyādhikaraṇa).
The heart [mantra] is to be brought; it is to be uttered for the purpose of bringing the heart. Yet, it has not been uttered;
therefore, either that which is unuttered must be conceptualized, or the utterance itself must be conceptualized.

Furthermore, in such a construction, the word would be contradicted! Therefore, it is not so. How then?—The praise qualified by both [place and time] is enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). And when a connection with one [qualifier] has been established, it is not necessary to further imagine another sentence once the sentence is complete; for when the praise qualified by both qualifiers is enjoined by direct scriptural statement, the sentence is then complete, and no further connection with anything else need be imagined for the sake of which something [else] might be required.
If it were so intended, then this would be enjoined as a separate praise; the original [practice] is not set aside, but rather there is a combination (samuccaya). Thus it is said.
But when no specific purpose is heard [in the text], there should be a modification of the archetypal [element] because it is a subsidiary. (Yukti 17)
Commentary:

Now, as for what was described— namely, that there is a cessation of the archetypal [rites] by means of such [injunctions] as "the kautsa occurs," "the kāṇva occurs," and "the two janitras of Vasiṣṭha occur"— 1.
Thus, that must be refuted. It is replied: it is logical that the archetypal (prākṛta) element is set aside where no other meaning is heard, for there only a supplement to the archetypal is heard;
therefore, in that case, the archetypal is set aside by the directly stated (pratyakṣa-śruta) Vedic element. But here, because another meaning is heard...
It has been stated that there is no cessation [of the injunction], because it would result in a split in the sentence.
The section concerning the modification of the original substance by Kautsa and others.

(Second Section) Or rather, it is heard in some places: "There is the *kautsa*, there is the *kāṇva*, there are the two *janices* of Vasiṣṭha, there are the *śuddhāśuddhīye*, there are the *bhargayaśasī*, and the *krauñcāni*."
In the Mīmāṃsā system, it is said:
"It exists"; however, there are indeed Sāmans in the archetype (prakṛti), and they are obtained there through the injunction (codanā).
Are those [original elements] set aside? Or not? This is the point under consideration. What is the prima facie view?
That there is no setting aside, but rather a combination. Why? Because only the sāman is enjoined;
there is no connection with the characteristics of the archetype (prakṛti) such as "it is its own. Therefore, it is an addition.

The prima facie view having been thus established, we reply: when no specific purpose is heard [in the text], there is a modification of the archetypal [element] because it is a subordinate constituent.
It may be so. || 17 ||

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the previous position: even though the specific meaning is being heard, there should be a modification of the archetypal (*prākṛta*) element, for in the archetype the *sāman* is a subordinate (*śeṣa*) element; this [new] *sāman* is also heard, and by virtue of the commonality of being a *sāman*, it ought to take the place of the original *sāman*. For example: curd, ghee, and vegetables.

In the case of "The rice is to be fed to Devadatta" and "Yajñadatta [is to be fed] with oil like Devadatta," although the phrase "it is to be served with oil" is not explicitly stated, nevertheless, it occurs in the very same way as with oil, because of its capacity for that purpose; likewise, even if it is not directly stated that "one should prepare [the rice]."
It is heard [in scripture]; nevertheless, because it is capable of that, the *sāman* deserves to be applied only to the consecration (*saṃskāra*).
The section concerning the sublation [of the Vedic injunction] by the *Bava* and other [lunar days], as established by Kautsa and others.
[The rule applies] to all [the fires], because there is no distinction. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 18 ||
In some places it is heard: "Time becomes the cause;
for one devoted to the birth of Vasiṣṭha, those two become Bharga and Yaśas, and the Kāñcanīs come into being."
Thus, there are indeed the *prākṛta* (archetypal) *sāmans*, and those are obtained through the rule of extension (*codaka*); this concludes the fourth quarter of the [fourth] chapter.
It has been established that these are the sublaters of the archetypal (prakṛta) elements. Now, this point is being clarified:
do all [of them] sublate all [the archetypal elements], or does one [sublate] one, and two [sublate] two?
"Many [mantras] for many [deities]? What, then, is the prima facie view? That all [mantras] belong to all [deities].

Why? Because there is no distinction; indeed, there is no specific reason by which it could be understood that "this one is the displacer of this [deity], and not of another. Therefore, every [mantra] is the displacer of every [deity].
Or rather, it belongs to one [deity] alone, because of the force of the direct scriptural statement and because there is no modification of the archetype.
|| 18 || (Siddhānta) ||

Let it not be thought that all [prohibitions] are the sublaters of all [rules]; rather, one [prohibition] sublates one [rule], two [sublate] two, and many [sublate] many. Why? Because of the capacity of the Vedic revelation (śruti-sāmarthyāt), as in the case of the "kola" [passage].

The scripture, having established the derivation for each one individually— saying "there is Kākha" and "there is Bhava"— is thus both capable and meaningful. Likewise, when the derivations of two [names], such as "Vaśiṣṭha and Janitra" and "Śuddhāśuddhīca and Bhārgava," are being established, the capacity of the scripture is demonstrated.

It occurs thus: by the rule "there are three *kṛñca*s," having set aside three [verses] with the three [stomas], the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*) achieves its purpose. If, when one [verse] is pressed out, only one is set aside, then this very [verse] which was intended for the archetypal *sāman* becomes [the substitute] for that many; so it is in all cases.

How could this be so? There would be no modification of the original form (*prakṛti*); the remaining original elements (*prākṛta*) would remain as they are, and thus the stated rule would be upheld. Therefore, one [element] belongs to one [word].
"Nivartaka, he, daye, mahani, and bahūnām" [Pāṇini 6.3.100].
Commentary:
Regarding the various types of knowledge, there is a section concerning the obstruction or non-obstruction of the objects of perception in accordance with their respective order.
But the *stomaviddhā* should be greater; it is a modification of substance (*dravyavikāra*), because the other is not heard [in the scripture]. || 20 ||

There are sacrifices (*kratavaḥ*) with increased *stomas* and those with non-increased *stomas*, such as: "One should cause one desiring progeny to sacrifice with an *atirātra* having thirty-one [verses]; one desiring vigor with a thirty-four-fold [sacrifice]; one desiring stability with a thirty-three-fold [sacrifice]. Likewise: "The *pavamāna* [laudations] of the *abhiṣecanīya* have thirty-two [verses].
In that regard, there are nine *rājasāman*s, eleven *rājasāman*s, and the *valaughatras* of Vasiṣṭha.
And [the verses] beginning with *janitri* are recited together with trembling sensations; both the *maṃtra* and the *upapada* regarding purity and impurity;
likewise, the two methods for the chariot and the oblation of the *punaḥstoma* sacrifice; and likewise, the rites involving honor (*apaciti*) of the *punaḥstoma* sacrifice.
"Furthermore, the middle pressing of the Stoma is traditionally known as the twelvefold;
both the preceding and following pressings should consist of nineteen-fold Stomas."

In this regard, in some cases the number of original (prakṛti) stotras is increased, and in others it is decreased. In that situation, there is a doubt: when there is an increase or a decrease, is there a cessation of the original sāmans, or rather, is there a cessation upon decrease, but no cessation upon increase? What is the prima facie view? There is cessation in both cases; for that which is obtained through the extended application (codaka) is set aside by what is directly heard in the scripture. Furthermore, the production of the sāmans will be purposeful when they are performed in connection with the new (apūrva) rites.

This being the case, we reply: "In the case of an increase in the *stoma*, there should be an addition [of verses]. Why? Because the completion of the number is stated by means of an addition—as in the rule: "Or it may be by addition, because repetition is not prescribed in the scripture" (10.5.23); in this way, there will be compliance with the *codaka* (the archetypal injunction).
However, in the case of "no increase," the original [archetypal] would be excluded; for only by its exclusion is that [required number] fulfilled."
To that extent, the archetypal rule (prakṛta) should be set aside; otherwise, it would remain merely archetypal. Why? Because of the other [rule], Chapter 10, Section 4, Part 10.

Because it is not heard [in scripture], the other is not heard; that is, it is not heard in the statement "the Āgama should be performed. Therefore, there is no addition in those sacrifices where the *stoma* is increased, and in those where the *stoma* is diminished, only as much as is required.

It must be set aside. Now, as for what was said—that the originative injunction will be meaningful—it is replied: let the Vedic text be sublated by the extended application (*codaka*), since it is distinguished only by its accessory details; for the extended application pertains to the accessories. (10.4.11)
The section concerning the addition and subtraction of Sāmans in the Pavamāna [laud], which is indeed characterized by various stomas and kratus.
These two [verses] should belong to the Pavamāna; they are to be inserted therein because no specific occasion for their application is observed.
Commentary: The *daha* sacrifices and those with increased (*vivṛddha*) and non-increased (*avivṛddha*) *stomas* serve as examples;

these are the very same ones cited in the preceding section. Therein, this point was established: that there is no removal (*anivṛtti*) in sacrifices with increased *stomas*, but there is removal (*nivṛtti*) in those with non-increased *stomas*. Now, the following is doubted: should there be an insertion (*āvāpa*) of any [verse] whatsoever, and a removal (*udvāpa*) from any [verse] whatsoever?

"Or rather, should the insertion (āvāpa) and the removal (udāpa) occur only during the Pavamāna [laud]? What is the prima facie view? "Because there is no specific distinction, there is no restriction.
This being the position, we reply: "The insertion and the removal should take place during the Pavamāna."

Why? Because these two are indeed seen in this very [text]: "There are three wombs of the sacrifice: the Gāyatrī, the Triṣṭubh, and the Anuṣṭubh; in these they scatter the seeds, and from these alone they draw them out.
[Objection: But let this be considered a mere observation (*darśana*); let it be called an attainment (*prāpti*). [Reply: It is said—
But the scriptural statements [are authoritative] because they convey something not previously known. (Sūtra 1.2.22)
In the absence of a logical rule, these words themselves must be so interpreted; therefore, the *pavamāna* alone is the place for insertion and removal. (10.4.120)
[Page 524] We say: The section concerning the designation of the deity by the word expressing the injunction itself.
If a word of injunction were a mantra, there would be a state of being [of that injunction] through it; for by it, there is the impulsion [to action].
(Bhāṣya 23)
Regarding the New and Full Moon sacrifices, it is stated: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the New and Full Moon sacrifices.
In this context, the following is recited: "The cake for Agni on eight potsherds is constant at the New Moon and the Full Moon. And there are designations for Agni, such as Agni and Śuci.

"Pāvaka," "dhūmaketu," "kṛśānu," "vaiśvānara," "śāṇḍilya"—these and others [are names]. Regarding this doubt: in the Vedic texts (nigamas), should the designation of Agni be made by any name whatsoever, or by the specific term "agni" as prescribed by the injunction? What is the prima facie view? That it may be by any name whatsoever. Why? Because of the indication of another meaning; for the sacrificial cake (purōḍāśa) is prepared with another purpose.

It must be nourished; the deity must be honored with effort; at the time of renunciation, it must be designated, and that [deity] can be designated by means of this word; therefore, it should be designated by that [word]; it can be designated by any one of these words; consequently, the designation should be made by whichever [word] among those spoken in the Vedic recitations (nigama).

This being the case, we reply: the material should be designated by the word of injunction itself—that is, by the word "āgneya"—and not by another term such as "cyādi. Why? Because "by that there is an injunction"; by that word of injunction, the connection of the oblation with the deity is enjoined. How so? "The āgneya is to be performed."
The meaning is that one must perform [the sacrifice] for a deity without setting this aside.

But what, indeed, is this so-called "deity"? First, there is one opinion: those who are celebrated in the Itihāsas and Purāṇas as Agni and others, the inhabitants of heaven (nākasads), they are the deities.
To this it is replied: among those deities, there is no inclusion of the day and so forth, or of the months and so forth.
And the status of being a deity is attributed to words denoting time, as in: "from words for time [the suffix occurs], 'the month is the deity,' 'the year is the deity.
[Page 525]
Chapter 10, Pāda 4.

Another opinion is as follows: "Those [beings] in whom the bliss of the deity is heard in the Mantras and Brāhmaṇas— such as 'Agni is the deity,' 'Vāyu is the deity,' 'All are the deities,' 'The Moon is the deity,' and so forth— they are what is expressed here by the word 'deity'."

Furthermore, there would be no inclusion of the *acara* verses and so forth. Moreover, because a word with a general meaning lacks specific application in common worldly usage (*laukika-vyavahāra*), the meaning would remain unestablished.
Therefore, [the verse] "The offering of the *śukra* and its division belong to the deities. Which ones are the recipients of the *śukra*? "[This hymn of praise for the great Jātavedas...]"

"Draw me hither with your wisdom as one draws a chariot; for auspicious is his providence in our assembly. In your friendship, may we not suffer harm. Thus [it is said] regarding the oblations (*havirbhiḥ*): "One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni; [one should offer] a cake on eleven potsherds to Agni-Soma. He says:
if the deities are [defined] by the oblations, then the potsherds (*kapāla*) would also have the status of deities.
He obtains those as well, being afraid. If that is so, then that deity is the one toward whom [the offering] is directed;
for even in the case of a compound, it is exactly the same. For here, the deity is the recipient.

A thread is consecrated as having Agni as its deity, and an oblation is consecrated as having Agni as its deity; likewise, [an offering] has the guest as its deity, or the ancestors as its deity. In this way, whether they are embodied or bodiless, conscious or unconscious, and whether they are intended for some purpose by means of the Vedic text, they will possess the status of a deity, and the use of a general term will also be justified.

What follows from this? If you say that a deity is established when a great effort is made with the thought, "I shall designate this sound as the designator of that [deity]," then it would follow that,
such being the case, one could even more easily designate it by any word whatsoever.

It is replied: This would indeed be so if the word "fire" were uttered for the purpose of conveying a meaning, and if that meaning were also intended to be connected with the oblation; however, in this case, the word "fire" is not uttered for the purpose of conveying a meaning, because by that [conveying of meaning], all the required function is accomplished. In that regard, it is not for the purpose of conveying a meaning.

[Page 526] It is so; there is no purpose in the actual object, but rather the effect must reside in the word itself. In that case, it is the word alone, by virtue of its connection with the effect, that must be made known. Furthermore, the status of a deity as an instrument of sacrifice does not exist through its form, but rather through the related word. Just as the *adhvaryu* priest assists by means of two hands, so too the deity assists by means of the word, as in the case of the sacrificer.
Just as in the injunction, "He spreads [the grass] with the hand after double-anointing," it is the *hotṛ* priest alone who benefits despite the connection to the hand;
likewise, a deity that benefits through a related word is understood to be the benefactor.
Even when a beneficial deity is enjoined, its integration into the sacrifice belongs to the word alone. And therefore—

A word is uttered for the purpose of conveying a meaning; if that meaning were in turn to convey the word, it would indeed result in a circular definition. What then? The word itself is connected with the oblation; through that connection, the meaning will also become the deity, for the word belongs to that [meaning] which possesses the oblation.

That deity is connected by way of being for that purpose; since the operation [of the word] is impossible with respect to the object, it is understood that the operation pertains to the object. But here, the operation is possible with respect to the word itself. Therefore, the word is not for the purpose of conveying the object. As the author of the *Vṛtti* has said: "Or rather, the comprehension of the object is preceded by the word; therefore, the accomplishment of the object [occurs]. If this is so, there is no connection of the oblation with the word *agni*.

There would be the undesirable consequence [of applying this] to words such as "pure" (śuci) and so forth. Therefore, the word expressing an injunction (*vidhi*) must be employed in the case of mantras.

It is said: "In this way, it follows that the word itself would be the deity. To this we reply: this is not something we must avoid; for what is being stated here does not contradict our position, and it certainly does not result in the undesirable consequence [of applying the rule] to words such as *śuci* and so forth.
Because there is a single injunction for the remaining [subsidiaries], therefore it is heard in all cases.
The statement regarding the *ratas* (the remaining ones) should be made in the words by means of the term "rule" (*vidhi*). Why? Because of the "remainder" (*śeṣa*).
[Page 527, Verse 217]

The word for the mantras is one and the same, and it is indeed this word of injunction; that very word is heard everywhere—in the *apāṅkāra*, in the *ubjiyā*, and in the *svāhākāra*: "O Apālā, [bring] the dear abodes; O Soma, [bring] the dear abodes; O Indra, [bring] the dear abodes."
In the case of the *apāṅkāra*, [the mantra] "I have won the victory of Soma among men; may I win the victory of Soma" is used as a constant (*nitya*);

and in the case of the *svāhākāra*, [the mantra] beginning with "Svāhā to Agni, Svāhā to Soma" is used. Thus, these *apācikā*s will be heard as if they were constant, just as the principle has been taught by us. Therefore...
“If a word of injunction were to be a mantra, there would be [an inconsistency] regarding its state. (10.4.1–3 Śrauta-sūtra)
The section concerning the designation of the deity by the injunctive word itself, even in the case of extended application (atideśa).

There are several names for the sun: Sūrya, Āditya, Bhāskara, Savitṛ, and Divākara. And the meaning of "Sūrya" must be proclaimed in those [mantras], and that may be proclaimed by any word whatsoever denoting the sun; therefore, there is no restriction. This being the case, we reply: "And likewise in the subsequent weaving, because it has that as its archetype. Just as in the archetype, so too in the subsequent "weaving" (tati)—that is, in the act of weaving—it should be performed, because it follows that same procedure.

The Bhāṣya states: "The fire-installation [is enjoined] by the text, 'He who, knowing thus, installs the fire. In that context, the Pavamāna oblations are heard: 'One should offer a cake on eight potsherds to Agni Pavamāna;
[one] to Agni Pāvaka; [and one] to Agni Śuci. Regarding this, a doubt is raised: what..."
Should the recitation be performed with qualities (saguṇa), or without qualities (nirguṇa)? What is the prima facie view?
That it should be performed "with qualities," as the original [recitation] was without qualities.
Or rather, there would be no modification, because the object and the word do not depart [from their nature], just like a substance.
Commentary:
"Or it may be without modification"—that is, the designation is devoid of qualities. Why?
Because "the word does not deviate from its object"; thus, the word remains non-deviating from its object, whichever that may be.
He is indeed Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci. Whatever deity is to be designated, that one should be meditated upon. This is the quarter-verse.

It is indeed indicated even when there is no word expressing a quality, as in: "Like a substance, like speech—this very goat-ewe is sacred to all deities; one desiring prosperity should sacrifice a goat-ewe.
And when the rite is enjoined by the word "goat-ewe," the desires become subordinate to it through the word "desiring."
Just as one says "the word is not devoid of meaning," so too should it be understood here; therefore, the designation must be made by means of that which is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa).

Likewise, because of the non-inherence of the undertaking [in the substance], there should be a designation by means of what is enjoined, since the purpose is inherent in the direct Vedic statement; for if it were not so designated, the scripture concerning the accessory would be purposeless. (Sūtra 28) (Uttara-pakṣa)

Alternatively, it might be argued that [the deity] is denoted by the "impelled" [word], i.e., as possessing qualities. Why? Because of the non-connection with the commencement: for the deity does not enter into the ritual action through its commencement; nor is the deity's status as an instrument in the ritual action established by its own form. For if it were connected through its form, [then the word would denote it].

That being the case, since even *pavamāna* would not be conveyed by the word *agni*, the designation of the quality (*guṇābhidhāna*) would not be performed. How, then, is the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) established? Because of its "inherent connection with the Vedic revelation" (*śrutisamavāyitvāt*), the relationship between the deity’s purpose and the word for the deity is directly stated; that word whose relationship [to the object] is thus expressed [is the means].

The word must be uttered so that this connection is established. And if the expression of the quality were not performed, the cognition of the quality would be purposeless. For it is for this purpose that the word is pronounced there: "How might this [word] be connected with the ritual action? In that case, if the quality were not connected, [the utterance would be futile].
The description of qualities would otherwise be meaningless; therefore, the designation must be made by means of that which possesses qualities.
Because it proceeds toward the commencement of substances, "modification" (vikāra) refers to the object by implication.

Commentary:

"Or it may be without modification"—that is, the designation is devoid of qualities. Why? Because of the non-removal of the meaning and the word; for in this way, that very [designation] becomes meaningful and free from deficiency.
Agni is indeed Pavamāna, Pāvaka, and Śuci. The deity who is to be designated belongs to the tenth chapter, the [tenth] quarter.

It is taught that even in the absence of a word expressing a quality (*guṇavacana*), [the term] "like a substance" (*dravyavat*) applies; for example: "That very same [animal] dedicated to all deities is the he-goat and the ewe; one desiring prosperity should sacrifice them to Vāyu.
In the ritual act enjoined by the words "he-goat" (*ajā*) and "ewe" (*avaśā*), the *nigamas* (Vedic citations) occur using the word "goat" (*chāgā*).

The meaning is not separated from the word; this is the *kalā* (aesthetic/artistic element). It should be understood in the same way here as well: that very [meaning] must be expressed, just like sugar in molasses.

Likewise, because there is no inherence in the commencement, the designation would have to be by means of what is enjoined; for the meaning is inherent in the direct audition [of the word], and if it were not so expressed, the scripture concerning the quality would be purposeless. (28) (70)

Alternatively, it might be argued that [the deity] is denoted by its qualities when impelled. Why? Because of the "non-inherence in the commencement"—for the deity does not enter into the ritual act through its commencement; indeed, it has been stated that the deity's status as a means (*sādhanabhāva*) in the ritual act is not by way of its own form. For if it were to enter into the act by way of its form, [it would follow that the form itself is the means].

That being the case, since the word *agni* would also denote *pavamāna*, there would be no mention of a specific quality (*guṇābhidhāna*). How, then, is the status of being a means (*sādhanabhāva*) established? Because the meaning of the deity is directly connected to the Vedic revelation (*śrutisamavāyitvāt*), the relationship between the word for the deity and the sacrificial oblation (*haviḥ*) is explicitly stated; that word which has this relationship [is the one that functions as the means].

The word must be uttered so that this connection is established. And if the denotation of the quality were not performed, the instruction regarding the quality would be purposeless. For it is for this purpose that the word is pronounced there: "How might this be connected with the ritual action? If, therefore, the quality were not connected, [the instruction would be futile].
The description of qualities would otherwise be purposeless; therefore, the designation must be made by means of [the deity] as possessing qualities.
Since it pertains to substances as that which is to be produced, "modification" (vikāra) refers to the object by virtue of its capacity.

The Āgneya cake should be prepared as "Budhavat" (possessing *budh*); thus, by virtue of the deity being endowed with the quality of *budh*, the Āgneya becomes "Budhavat. But this is not so—that the designation is with qualities (saguṇa) and that it should be performed without qualities (nirguṇa). For they explain it thus: "This is a specific indication of a mantra. Why? Because this word has the form of a specific mantra: "That which is dedicated to Agni—whether specified or unspecified—is to be made *budhanvat*, not Agni himself. Now, if Agni is made *budhanvat*, then Agni *budhanvat* becomes the deity.

It might be argued that if it were [the case], then because it would be dependent on "belonging to Agni" (*āgneya*), there could be no designation by means of a secondary derivative (*taddhita*); for there is no formation of a compound (*vṛtti*) with qualifiers. Nor, indeed, is a qualifier applied to that which has already been compounded.
Therefore, the state of being accompanied by *budh* is not a qualifier of Agni. What, then, is qualified by the state of being accompanied by *budh*?

It belongs to Agni; its mantra is addressed to Budha, and by that, this sacrifice becomes "possessing Budha" (budhanvān), as in: "Awaken Agni with a hymn, kindling him with fuel. Alternatively, the mantra itself is connected [to the sacrifice], such that it is called "this [sacrifice] possessing Budha" (budhanvān).

Now, as for what was said—that because [the deity] is already expressed by the word "form" (rūpa), the mantra would be obtained [by implication] and need not be prescribed—it is replied: this is stated for the purpose of excluding whatever other designation might otherwise be obtained. It must be performed with the term *budhanvat* [as in], "Awaken Agni with Soma"; if it were otherwise, there would be no specific mention of the deity. Therefore, the designation of the deity must be performed without [other] attributes.

The *codaka* (the rule of transfer) brings about what is required; for it is not the case that whatever exists in the archetype (*prakṛti*) must necessarily be performed in the ectype (*vikṛti*)—this is not established by anyone. Rather, the *codaka* brings about that which was intended to be performed in the archetype and is explicitly stated by the word, rather than being obtained merely by implication. Therefore, the designation is not by whatever [word] one pleases, due to the capacity of the injunction (*vidhi*).

Commentary: There is the *avabhṛtha* (concluding bath) sacrifice, [established by the rule]: "They go to the *avabhṛtha* with an oblation of one potsherd for Varuṇa. Regarding that, it is recited: "He sacrifices to Agni-Sviṣṭakṛt and Varuṇa. In this regard, there is a point of doubt: should the word *asviṣṭakṛt* be used in the *nigama* (invocatory formula), or the word *saviṣṭakṛt*? In this matter, first this is examined: Is it prescriptive (*sāṃvidhāyika*)...?

Is the word *sviṣṭakṛt* conventional (*rūḍha*), or is it derived [etymologically] as "one who makes well-offered" (*sviṣṭaṃ karoti*) and thus applied by virtue of this quality? If it is conventional, a statement lacking the word *sviṣṭakṛt* must be made; if, however, it is etymologically derived, then it must contain the word *sviṣṭakṛt*. What is the conclusion? It is not conventional.

"It is explained. Why? Because Agni has not yet performed the *sviṣṭa* (well-offered) act, and yet at that very time he is called "the one who has performed the *sviṣṭa*" in the injunction, "He sacrifices to Sviṣṭakṛt. For the two [the fire and the act] are not capable of being endowed with the quality of being "well-offered" (*prādeśika-guṇa*) through their own inherent refinement (*svarasaṃskāra*). It is Agni alone who is denoted by the word *Sviṣṭakṛt*, as he is the one among those two who has performed the *sviṣṭa*. When it is a case of conventional designation (*sāṃvidhāyika*), then a statement containing the word *asviṣṭa* must be made. Why? Because of the deity Agni's... [text fragment].

The designator [of the deity] does not apply to Agni and Varuṇa; since the deity Agni is absent in the *vidyati* [offering], it is excluded from Agni-Varuṇa. Therefore, a statement containing the word *sviṣṭakṛt* must be made.
Or rather, it is conjunction [that is the cause], because the expression [of the meaning] arises from the action [of the speaker], as established by presumptive testimony (*arthāpatti*).

Commentary:
It is not the case that a statement expressing praise (praśaṃsā) must be made; rather, a statement expressing blame (nindā) must be made. From this, the following purpose is established:

This designation is secondary (gauṇa). It is understood that [the word] *sviṣṭakṛt* [is used] because of the performance of a well-offered sacrifice (*sviṣṭakaraṇāt*). It is not reasonable to assume that what is already understood is unintended; for its being based on an action is understood from the constituent parts of the word. Furthermore, since the whole is not used in common worldly usage [independently], it possesses the status of a conventional name (*abhidhānatva*) for the fire.

It is not determined; therefore, it is not based on a formal injunction (*sāṃvidhāyika*). If this is so, then a statement containing the word *sviṣṭakṛt* must be made, [on the grounds of] "presumption" (*arthāpatti*): for the sake of Agni, Agni-Varuṇa are heard [in scripture], namely, "He sacrifices to Agni-Varuṇa as the *Sviṣṭakṛt*. And because of their connection with the action, the word *sviṣṭakṛt* applies to Agni and Varuṇa. Therefore, there must be a statement containing the word *sviṣṭakṛt*.

"It must be performed. Now, as for what was said—"The word [kṛtvā] refers to one who has performed the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering, and Agni has not performed the *sviṣṭakṛt*"—to this we reply: in my view, the past tense would be lost; in your view, however, that [past tense] is the meaning of the verbal root accompanied by its prefix. Agni has performed the sacrifice well. (10.4.180)

[Page 538] Furthermore, regarding the fire (*agni*), is there a loss of qualities (*guṇalopa*) only in the case of the *khiṭaka* (the specific sacrificial vessel) among the ritual injunctions (*nigama*), such that it exists according to its original form (*yathāprakṛti*), or is there a loss of qualities everywhere? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)?—When a loss of qualities is heard for the fire which possesses qualities in the case of the *khiṭaka*, it is stated by way of illustration; thus, there would indeed be a loss of qualities. And in the sacrifice, it is stated: "He sacrifices to Agni" (*agniṃ yajati*). In the sacrifice, [it refers to] the fire intended for the *muṣala*.
If a loss of qualities were observed in all the recensions (nigama) while they are being recited, then what would not have been heard [in the original] be assumed?

Whatever fault there is in such an abandonment [of the qualities], that same fault exists in the assumption of what was not heard [in the original]. Therefore, the loss should indeed occur only in some [recensions], and not in all recensions.
But rather, [the entire rite is to be performed] because of the unity of purpose. (Siddhānta) 37.
Or rather, the word *agni* in the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—even for one established in the Vedic tradition (*nigama*)—would apply as a subordinate quality (*guṇa*).

Why? Because of the unity of the ritual action (*ekakarmyat*). This quality would not apply only to the *sviṣṭakṛt* sacrifice itself, but rather to the performance of the sacrifice (*yāgaprayoga*). How so? Because it is precisely in the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*), namely "he sacrifices to Agni" (*agnim yajati*), that this occurs.

The word [sviṣṭakṛt] would apply to every performance of the sviṣṭakṛt offering, for other sviṣṭakṛt recitations also pertain to the sviṣṭavat sacrifice itself; therefore, there is omission everywhere. (10.4.18)

The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are under consideration; therein it is stated: "He offers the Sviṣṭakṛt with the Anūyāja. Regarding this, there is a doubt: is the Sviṣṭakṛt action an indirect auxiliary (ārādupakāraka), or is it a purificatory rite (saṃskāraka)? What is the prima facie view? It is an indirect auxiliary.
Why? Because this is well-known as the function of ritual acts, namely that they provide assistance from a distance (ārādupakriyā),
as stated in the tenth chapter, first quarter.

For indeed, [in that case] there would be the status of an established fact (*bhūta*) for the *bhavya* (the thing to be accomplished), and the injunction would be by means of direct Vedic statement (*śruti*).

Otherwise, there would be the status of an established fact for the *bhavya*, and the injunction would be by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*). Therefore, it is an indirect auxiliary (*ārādupakāra*).
This being the case, it must certainly be that [the mantra] belongs to the *āvāpa*, not to the speech itself.

What is this "belonging to the *āvāpa*"? The *āvāpa* is the intermediate space between the two *ājyabhāga* offerings; that which exists therein is "belonging to the *āvāpa*" (*āvāpika*). As for the *anuyāja* offerings, they belong to the ritual procedure (*tantra*) outside the *āvāpa*. But as for...

The deity of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is precisely that same principal deity who is subject to the *āvāpa* (insertion); therefore, it is called *āvāpika*. And when this is the case, it would be a *saṃskārakarma* (a preparatory rite), for it thus possesses a purpose, as it assists the fire which itself possesses a purpose. Furthermore, [rites] are of two kinds.
The subsidiaries are of two kinds: those that assist from afar (*ārādupakāraka*) and those that are integral (*sāmavāyika*).

Among these, the integral subsidiaries are more important than those that assist from afar, for in their case there is a direct syntactical connection (*vākya*); whereas among those that assist from afar, there would be a mediated syntactical connection with the primary rite (*prakṛta*). Therefore, it is a purificatory act (*saṃskārakarman*).
The section concerning the fact that the *yājyā* and *puronuvākyā* verses in the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) serve as sanctificatory acts (*saṃskāraka*).

"Like the recitation" (śastravat)—just as the acts of "praising" (stauti) and "reciting" (śaṃsati) in the case of a hymn (stotra) are primary actions because their status as things to be performed is understood, so too should it be seen here.

"This is an improper recitation regarding the archetype (*prakṛti*), for in the archetype Agni and Soma are the deities; this [offering] also belongs to Agni. This being the case, we reply: that which is heard as "other than the *rathantara*" for the sake of the *pṛṣṭha* chant—that *kalarathantara*—should have its source in the *rathantara*; for the *vaiśvaja* sacrifice is preceded by the *jyotiṣṭoma*, and in the *jyotiṣṭoma*, the *pṛṣṭha* chant is established upon the source of the *rathantara*. It is so, because of its distinctness; for here a distinction is understood, as in the case of the statement, "The *kaṇvarathantara* is the source of the *rathantara*. Why? Because the word *rathantara* is heard in connection with the *kaṇvarathantara*;

therefore, it is understood that the *kaṇvarathantara* is a specific variety of the *rathantara*. The term *kaṇvarathantara* would apply to something else only if the properties of the *rathantara* were not present; since those properties do exist, its application is justified, just like the word "incense" (*dhūpa*).

Just as in the case of the statement, "The incense is made of udumbara wood," for the substance of the incense was not mentioned in the original archetype (prakṛti); thus, this word is applicable because it has the property (dharma) as its cause. Likewise here too, the word "rathantara" is applied to the *ṛk* and the *sāman* because of that property, and not otherwise.
Or rather, it is from its own source, because it is common to all; this is the siddhānta (conclusion). (Sūtra 44)

And this is not the case—that it should be sung in the *rathantara-yoni*; rather, it is "in its own *yoni*. Why? Because of "universality": for the word *rathantara* denotes that which is qualified by all its specific attributes; namely, the entire [hymn] consisting of the *prastāva*, *udgītha*, *pratīhāra*, *upadrava*, and *nidhana*, together with the *stobha*s, accents, and repetitions, receives the designation "the *kasa-rathantara*. Therefore, the *yoni* is also a qualifying attribute.
Furthermore, if there were another meaning for the *kasa-rathantara*, of what would the word *rathantara* be the name? Therefore...
It should be sung in its own source.

If it is argued that it is like the sacrificial post (yūpa). (Sūtra 45) (Objection)

201. If you view it thus— that the word *rathantara* refers to what is to be sung in its own source (*svayoni*), and therefore [the application] is justified because, when the properties of the *rathantara* are present, it is applied like incense (*dhūpa*)— then [we reply]:...
Not so, because of the connection with the ritual action. (0 Ni.)

Commentary: It is thus: "From connection with a ritual act" (the term *yūpa* refers to) the state of being a sacrificial post for a piece of wood; for in common worldly usage, there is no tree whatsoever that is designated by the name *yūpa*. That which possesses those consecrations (*saṃskāra*) is the *yūpa*; therefore, the statement "the sacrificial post is made of Udumbara wood" is based on the consecrations. But here, the word *kaṇvarathantara*, qualified by such specific attributes, exists in the world itself; it does not belong to the Kaṇvas.

The term *kaṇvarathantara* refers to a specific modification (*kalā*) of the *rathantara*. If either the *rathantara* itself or its connection with Kaṇva were being enjoined [as a primary element], a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*) would result. Therefore, the word *kaṇvarathantara* is a name based on a ritual injunction (*sāṃvidhāvika*); for this very reason, it is sung in its own original source-melody (*svayoni*). (10.4.2–3)
The performance of the ritual action and the subsequent yoga are not dependent upon a substratum.
• Because it is an effect, it should proceed according to its original nature, as in the case of the subsequent [offering] (Pūrvapakṣa). || 47 ||
In the Kala-rathantara itself, there is a doubt regarding the mantras: "The Uttarā is sung.
Does this mean that the two Uttarās belonging to the Rathantara-sāman are to be used, or rather the two Uttarās belonging to the Bṛhat-sāman? Or does it mean both sets of Uttarās?
What is the prima facie view? It is that either the two Uttarās belonging to the Bṛhat or the two Uttarās belonging to the Rathantara are to be used.

Why? Because of the favor accorded to the general rule (codaka). In that case, the fault does not arise—namely, "How can the *rathaṃtara* have its own source as its injunction?"—because the duty of the *uttarārcik* must necessarily abandon its own source. Therefore, the context (*prakaraṇa*) must be taken into account.
[Page 544] Or rather, it belongs to the same deity, because there is no division of the triplet of verses (tṛca). (Siddhānta) ||48||
Commentary:

This is not the case—that it should be sung on the *rathantara-yoni* and the subsequent [verse], or on the *uttara* and the subsequent [verse] of the *rathantara*; rather, it should be sung on its own *yoni* and the subsequent [verse]. Why? Because of the word *ṛcaḥ* (of the verse).
It has been stated that the term *tṛca* (a triplet) applies without qualification to those [verses] that have the same meter and the same deity;
therefore, since the general injunction (*codaka*) is set aside by the direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), it should be sung upon the two verses following its own original source (*svayoni*).

Sūtra 48: When there is a difference in the deities of the cups, there should be no modification [of the formulas] for the Stotra and Śastra, because they are the primary acts. (The Established Conclusion)

Commentary: There is a one-day sacrifice called the *Agniṣṭut*; regarding it, it is heard in the scripture: "The cups (*grahas*) belong to Agni. In this regard, there is a doubt: should there be modification (*ūha*) of the original *stotra* and *śastra* mantras according to the respective deities, or should there be no modification? This is stated in order to set aside the notion of modification: "Of the cups..."
If there were a change of deities, there would be no modification of the *stotra* and *śastra*, because they are principal acts (*pradhānakarma*).

But whose idea could this possibly be that one should set aside [the original deity]? It would be the idea of someone of dull intellect who thinks that the designation [of the deity] will be accomplished; for even instruction given to those of dull intellect is fruitful.

It occurs. Furthermore, everyone is of dull intellect in comparison to someone [else]. But if there is still no satisfaction with this, then it is described otherwise: that very topic (*vṛtta*) which is the subject matter (*adhikaraṇa*) in the second chapter, [sūtra 9.4.50], has this as its purpose-sūtra:

"When there is a change of deities for the cups (*graha*), there should be no modification [of the stotra and śastra] because they are acts. If the stotra and śastra are preparatory acts (*saṃskārakarman*), what happens?

What is the purpose? [The answer is: In the *agniṣṭud-ekāha* sacrifice, there is modification (*ūha*) according to the respective deity; however, if these two were principal acts (*pradhānakarman*), then, because the cups (*graha*) have different deities, there would be no modification due to the two being acts of praise (*stotra*). (10.4.2–5)
And in the Cātunīstra [texts], the word *avya* means "sheep" (*avika*), and it is not subject to the rule regarding the substitution of *repha*.

In the case of the *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter), because both [milk and curds] are drunk, there should be an indication of the curds in the ritual recitations (*nigama*), since it is the drinkable substance that is indicated. (Sūtra 50, Purvapakṣa)

There are the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, [established by the injunction]: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Cāturmāsyas. In that context, having introduced the after-sacrifices (anuyājas), they prescribe: "He performs the after-sacrifices with speckled butter (pṛṣadājya).
However, in the archetype (prakṛti), there is an invocation: "Bring the gods who drink the oblations!"

Thus, it is obtained here by the rule of extension (codaka). In this regard, there is a doubt: should the invocation (āvāhana) be performed without modification, or with modification (ūha)? If it is to be performed with modification, then should one say "O drinkers of clarified butter" (ājyapān), "O drinkers of curd" (dadhipān), or rather "O drinkers of speckled butter" (pṛṣadājyapān)?
What is obtained? Even "the soma-draught" (*datraḥ*) would be an "indication" (*upalakṣaṇam*) of the clarified butter (*ājya*) as well. Why?

Because of "the drinking of both"—for both of those are offered with reference to the deity; and that which is offered is stated by the mantra to be "drunk," and thus that which is to be drunk is indicated, as it was in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

Regarding the phrase "śrāvyapān": here, both curd (*dadhi*) and clarified butter (*sarpiṣ*) are heard to be for the purpose of the *śrāva* offering—[as in the text]: "Now he takes the speckled butter; this [world] is indeed twofold, namely clarified butter and curd; a pair is indeed productive;
thus a productive pair is created"—in which case the curd is equal [to the clarified butter].
Clarified butter is mentioned as the primary substance; therefore, both should be understood as required—namely, the curd and the clarified butter.

Or rather, it is not so, because it is for the sake of another, like the *yajñapati* (the master of the sacrifice). (Purvapakṣa-siddhānta 51)
Or rather, it is not thus—that curd is to be indicated as the secondary mark. Why?
Because it is for the sake of another; for the substance to be drunk is for the sake of another, and the drinking is the indication of that [substance].
If it is indicated by means of the clarified butter (*ājya*), the purpose is accomplished, and therefore the curd is not to be indicated again, "like the patron of the sacrifice" (*yajñapati*).

Just as in the case of the mantra, "May you favor this sacrifice and strengthen the lord of the sacrifice," the mention of the "lord of the sacrifice" (yajñapati) is for the purpose of praising the human sacrificers who are the performers of the rite, and is not intended to glorify him for his own sake; thus it is employed with a figurative sense and does not imply special regard for every individual sacrificer— so too here, the mention of that which is to be drunk is for the purpose of characterizing the drinker.
It is employed, not for its own sake; since even a single one of them, whichever it may be, suffices as a protector, a second should not be employed.
It should belong to the invocation, because it is for that purpose. (Cātur-māsya-sūtra 52)
Commentary:
"He should stand" is an elliptical expression referring to the curd; he should not stand like the master of the sacrifice (*yajñapati*).
For the word "master of the sacrifice" is not uttered for its own sake; it is uttered for the purpose of praising the *iḍā*. As for the invocation (*śrāvāhana*), however...
For the sake of remembrance, that which is to be drunk must also be remembered; therefore, another drink should be indicated in order to favor the injunction.
Sūtra 53: Or rather, it is not so, because it is a word denoting a consecration (saṃskāra). (Śrāvaṇa-nirṇaya)
Or rather, curd should be indicated; for here the word for a preparatory refinement (*saṃskāra*) exists in the case of the clarified butter (*ājya*), namely:
"He performs the after-sacrifices with *pṛṣadājya*. The meaning is "with variegated *ājya*";
for by means of the refinement [of mixing], the prepared *ājya* becomes variegated. And that variegation—
It produces curd directly from perception. Therefore, it should not be drunk for the sake of another (for the purpose of producing *ciṇatāsa*), and consequently, it should not be stored.

Or rather, it may be so, because of the designation of a substance. 54. (0)

"Let there be curd"—here, "curd" is an indicative mark (*upalakṣaṇa*); for curd as a substance is equal to clarified butter (*ājya*), and it is taught as being the primary element. Thus we have said: "Now he takes the speckled butter (*pṛṣadājya*);
this world is indeed twofold—clarified butter and curd; this is indeed a pair, a productive union; verily, this is a productive pair."

"It is performed"; does this mean that *pṛṣadājya* (speckled butter) is taken? No; rather, it means that the sacrifice is to be performed with both clarified butter (*sarpiḥ*) and curd (*dadhi*). *Pṛṣadājya* is not denoted as a separate substance; therefore, the curd is to be indicated [as an ingredient].

But the *dabha* grasses should be [the subject] of the *nigama* formulas because they are subordinate; their subordination follows from the Vedic revelation (*śruti*), since the clarified butter (*ājya*) is the primary element. (Siddhānta 55)
But this is not the case— that curd is equal to the clarified butter (*ājya*) in being a primary substance;

for it is equal to the clarified butter only with respect to its being taken up (*grahaṇa*), not with respect to the sacrifice (*yāga*), since the sacrifice is heard of as being distinct through the word *citra*.

Therefore, because the *śruti* (direct Vedic statement) establishes that the clarified butter (*ājya*) is the primary element, the curd (*dadhi*) would be subordinate with respect to the sacrifice; for indeed, the curd is not heard as being mentioned in relation to the sacrifice by the word "cup" (*graha*).

Thus, the curd mentioned in connection with the taking of the cup does not serve the purpose of the sacrifice; moreover, by direct statement (*śruti*), the clarified butter is the instrument (*karaṇa*), whereas the curd is so only by syntactical connection (*vākya*).
For what purpose, then, is the mention of curd (*dadhi*) there? It is because [the deity] becomes directly perceived through that which is being taken.
Therefore, the invocations should be addressed to the drinkers of the *ājya* (clarified butter), and one should not employ the curd as a secondary designation (*upalakṣaṇa*).
Or rather, curd should be the primary substance, because of its connection with both the beginning and the end of the clarified butter. (Sūtra 56, Purvapakṣa)
Commentary:
This is not the case; it is not intended here that the recitations (nigamas) should be audible, nor is this a mere figurative indication.
[Page 548]
Mīmāṃsā: Regarding the injunction "the sacrifice (darśapūrṇamāsa) is to be performed," it must be performed exactly as with curd; here, "curd" alone is the "primary" element.

Why? Because of the connection with the first [act] regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*): the first connection is the spreading (*upastaraṇa*), and the other connection is the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*). As it is said:

"If one should sacrifice with *priyaṅgu* grains, he should spread twice and pour over once; for *priyaṅgu* grains are indeed herbs, and thus he establishes the cattle in the very herbs. And: "If one should sacrifice in the rainy season, he should spread once and pour over twice."
"In cutting the sacrificial animals, he takes them for himself"—here, another [substance] is placed there to serve as a base (upastaraṇa).

In this context, the meaning of the word is for the sake of another; it does not denote mere taking. By means of the act of taking, the word "he spreads" (upastṛṇāti) refers to the preparation of a receptacle for something else. Likewise, "he pours over" (abhighārayati) does not mean mere taking; rather, it is understood that he pours over something else by facing toward it. How could that other thing be unconnected with the clarified butter?

Thus, by the two terms "spreading" (*upastaraṇa*) and "sprinkling" (*abhighāraṇa*), it is understood that the curd is the primary substance, while the clarified butter (*ājya*) is subordinate therein.
Therefore, in this case, the spreading should be performed with curd alone,
not with clarified butter.
But rather, because the clarified butter is the primary substance, the other substances are subordinate;
thus, in this designation, the term "consecration" (saṃskāra) must be used figuratively. (Sūtra 57: Purvapakṣa-Nirṇaya)
Commentary: Or rather, it is not thus—that curd is the primary element and it is that which must be characterized.

The clarified butter (ājya) alone is the primary element, for it possesses a purpose due to its connection with the sacrifice—as in "he sacrifices the after-offerings with speckled butter" (pṛṣadājya). That upon which it is spread is prepared by this [butter], and therein it comes to completion.

Furthermore, when curd is spread, it serves as the substratum for what is placed upon it according to the scriptural rule, "the support of what is to be supported," as seen in the case of the darbha-grass and the potsherds.
Chapter 10, Section 1, Verse 800.

The refinement (*saṃskāra*) is understood as the refinement of the curd, but the purpose of that which has been refined is not "control" (*dama*); rather, the visible variegatedness (*citratā*) being produced is stated to be the purpose, for at that time, the speckled color (*pṛṣat*) is heard [in the scripture]. Furthermore, the curd cannot be the instrument (*karaṇa*) in the sacrifice, as it is obtained through the syntactical connection (*vākya*).

Since the opponent has already established through scripture that [the butter] is for the purpose of spreading (upastaraṇa), it follows that the spreading is indeed for the sake of taking the clarified butter; thereafter, the taking of the curd will occur.

Thus, by implication, in the relationship between the receptacle and what is to be placed within it, the term *upaskṛṇāti* is employed in the sense of "spreading," just like the act of spreading; likewise for the term *abhighārayati*. Therefore...

In the sense of the quality expressed by the word "great" (*mahat*), this term for consecration (*saṃskāra-śabda*) is used figuratively (*abhaktyā*) even where there is no formal designation (*avyapadeśe*), as in: "He spreads [the grass] beneath," "He sprinkles [the butter] over," "He establishes the animals in the very plants," and "He anoints the animals upon the trees. Therefore, these are indeed figurative applications (*nigamāḥ*).
"May they be."
Or rather, because this [term] is not a modification, it should serve as a secondary indicator (upalakṣaṇa) by means of that.
Commentary: The phrase "api vā" (or rather) serves to set aside the previous position. The *nigamas* (invocatory formulas) for the *ājyapās* (ghee-drinkers) should not occur;

rather, it should be stated as "pṛṣadājyapān" (those who drink the speckled ghee). Why? Because there is indeed a modification of the name, and therein a mixture of curd and clarified butter is prepared. In that case—
Whatever quality arises, that which is mixed and endowed with that quality receives a specific designation, such as "speckled butter" (*pṛṣadājya*), just as [one speaks of] "the *khāḍava* sauce."

Regarding the term "surā": for in that case, we perceive a single word used figuratively. In that state, because there is no longer any duality of what is to be attained, it is non-conceptual (*avikalpa*). Here, one might ask: "Should that very thing already begun be brought to completion, or should something else, not yet attained, be undertaken?
By bringing that to completion, one makes it heard (*śruta*); by abandoning it, one lets go of what has been heard. Thus, it is "begun."

It is understood that [the ritual] must be brought to completion. Now, once that has been accomplished, since the purpose of the statement regarding the optional [elements] has been fulfilled, it is logical to follow the sequence rather than following the meter.

Now, once that [commenced rite] has been concluded, the optional [alternative] becomes available since its purpose has been achieved; therefore, it is proper to follow the sequence [of the original], not to follow the meter (*chandas*).

Commentary: Here, the sacrifices characterized by pierced stomas (*viddhastomaka*) serve as the examples: "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the twenty-one-fold *atirātra*; one desiring splendor with the twenty-seven-fold; one desiring stability with the thirty-three-fold. In this regard, there arises the doubt: Is it by the repetition of the original (*prākṛta*) stomas themselves? Or...?

Is it to be fulfilled by the repetition of those already present in the archetype (*prakṛta*), or by the introduction of new ones? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? There is no restriction, because there is no specific distinction stated. To this we reply: "In the increase of the *stoma*, the number is fulfilled by repetition," for in this way there is the inclusion of what is archetypal; otherwise, it would be an action of what is non-archetypal. For the number...
The archetypal [elements], being primary, are mentioned as subordinate factors (*guṇabhāvena*), not as primary ones;

nor is any other substance for the *sāman* enjoined by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*). And as great is the fault in abandoning a meaning that is directly stated, so great is it in assuming what is not stated. Therefore, the archetypal elements must be repeated.
Just as the *sāmans* are [placed] at the pole, so are the *sāmans*.
