Or rather, because repetition is not heard in scripture. (Sūtra 16)
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the previous position. [The view is that] for the non-archetypal sāmans, the deficiency must be filled by "addition" (āgama). Why?
Because no repetition (abhyāsa) is heard in the scripture.
This much is heard: "One should cause one desiring progeny to sacrifice with the twenty-one-fold Atirātra.
And as great is the fault in abandoning what is explicitly stated in scripture, so great is the fault in assuming what is not stated.
[Objection: "But even the traditional authority (āgama) for this is not heard. [Reply: It is said: when both are not heard, [the latter is more reasonable].

The completion by means of traditional scripture (āgama) is logical; in this way, the number filled by scripture will be consistent, whereas otherwise, a number filled by mere repetition would be inconsistent. Therefore, it must be completed by means of scripture.
And because number is established as distinct from [the other categories]. (17) (01)
And from this, it follows that there must be an addition [of letters].

Why? Because a designation applies to distinct entities, as in "the cows are many" or "the jars are many"; through repetition, they would not remain distinct. Therefore, it must be completed by means of an addition.
Thus [it is said].
Sūtra-bhāṣya:
Because of the word "parāc" (turned away). (18) (02)
"Because of the scriptural statement. Why? Because there is the word "parāc" (backward/away), as in:

"They praise with the *vahiṣpavamāna* [laud] in a backward direction. And that word denotes non-repetition; just as in the case of "He recites the *sāmidhenī* verses in a backward direction," it is understood that they are not repeated. Therefore, for this reason also...
The scripture.
Bhāṣya: And because of the stated absence of modification. (18) (03)

Furthermore, there is scriptural authority for this: that which has been thus stated becomes "unchanged" (*avikāra*). What is this "unchanged"? It means non-repetition; therein the fault of redundancy (*jāmitā*) will not occur.
For if there were repetition, there would be this [fault]: "This sacrifice is rendered redundant when one thing is performed again."
If it is argued that this is not so because of its being a scriptural statement. (20) (0)

is to be refuted.
There may be a science of measurement for those things that have been brought forth by purpose. 21.
Commentary (Āraṇyaka-nirukta):
The *sāmans* are enjoined by means of a purpose. By what purpose? "By means of the twenty-one-fold [stoma]."
This is because of the meaning of such sentences as "One desiring offspring should sacrifice with the Śratirātra";
for these numbers cannot be consistently applied unless the Sāmans are understood.
Therefore, the scriptural statement has fulfilled its purpose by providing this instruction on the measurement of those [Sāmans] that have not been previously enjoined.

"One should cause one who desires offspring to sacrifice with the twenty-one-night Śratirātra"—this [injunction] cannot prevent the acquisition [of the required number of days] that follows from the sense of the matter; therefore, the completion is achieved through traditional scripture (āgama).

Furthermore, we see that there is scriptural authority for this, for there is a statement regarding insertion: "There are indeed three bellies of the sacrifice—the Gāyatrī, the Bṛhatī, and the Anuṣṭubh; for into these they insert [the hymns]."
"For this very reason, it does not fall away"; this is not possible in the case of repetition. Therefore, it is also scripture (āgama).
And because of the capacity for the origin of the Sāmans [as indicated by the word *sāman*]. (Yukti 5) || 23 ||

Furthermore, there is scriptural authority (āgama). Why? Because the origin [of the Sāmaveda] is meaningful only thus: "Ten thousand and fourteen hundred Sāmans, along with their auxiliary limbs and secret doctrines, which the chanters of the Sāman sing;
the Pavamāna consists of eighty hundred and four hundred."
"The Sāmavedins sing twenty-seven [verses] belonging to Indra.
Otherwise, the origin of these [verses] would be purposeless. Therefore, for this reason as well, there is sacred tradition (āgama).

Now, that which was described above—namely, the existence of smoke in the absence of fire—that must be refuted.

Commentary: This is not correct. For in the case of the *dhuri-sāmans*, repetition is indeed their characteristic, due to the authority of the scriptural statement: "They chant the *dhuri-sāmans* repeatedly; he worships with the *pṛṣṭhas* after they have been repeated. Because of that statement, it is performed there. But here, no such statement exists.

Regarding the sacrifices characterized by increased *stomas*, there is a doubt: in the *vahiṣpavamāna* chant, is there an addition (*āgama*) of verses, or is it repetition (*abhyāsa*)? According to the previous principle, it is an addition.

This being the case, we reply: it is not so in the case of the *vahiṣpavamāna*; rather, there is an addition (*āgama*) [of verses] there. Why? Because "the *sāman* is one. How so? Because in the two subsequent *pavamānas*, he utters the *hiṅkāra* for each triplet (*tṛca*). Now, why does he utter the *hiṅkāra* only once in the *vahiṣpavamāna*? One should say: "Because there is only one *sāman* there; it is a singing (*gāyana*) in the *khāra* scale."

From this statement, it follows that when the unity of the *sāman* is known, the required number must be completed by the addition (*āgama*) of *ṛc*s; thus, the *sāman* itself must also be repeated. (10.5.70) This concludes the section concerning the completion of the number of *sāmiṣenī* verses by the addition of those remaining.
"But by repetition, there is a completion [of the number], because the recitation of the *sāmidhenī* verses is of the nature of a model (*prakṛti*). (Pūrvapakṣa 27)

In the *Bhāṣya*: The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are [the subject]; therein are the optional ritual variations for the *sāmidhenī* verses: "One desiring stability should recite twenty-one; one desiring spiritual luster (*brahmavarcasa*) should recite twenty-four;
one desiring food should recite twenty-one; one desiring stability should recite twenty-two."
"One should recite twenty-six for one desiring cattle," and so forth. Regarding this, the matter to be determined is as follows:

in the case of the *sāmidhenī* verses, should the required number be completed by means of insertion (*āgama*), or by repetition (*abhyāsa*), or by repeating as much as has been prescribed and completing the remainder by insertion? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? [It is] by the former.
Mīmāṃsā: According to the logic of Harṣa, it is scripture (*āgama*). Furthermore, the object is non-distinct, for it is being fulfilled through repetition.
It would not be consistent; therefore, it is scripture (*āgama*).

This being the position reached, we reply: "But the fulfillment [of the number] is by repetition (*abhyāsa*). The word "but" (*tu*) excludes the previous view—it is not scripture, but rather repetition. Why? Because "repetition is the primary cause."

In the archetype (*prakṛti*), the number is fulfilled through repetition (*abhyāsa*), as stated: "He recites the first three times, he recites the last three times. How so? There is the scriptural injunction (*śruti*) that "there are fifteen *sāmidhenī* verses," yet eleven have arrived [in the text]. Since the number must be completed either by repetition or by additional verses (*āgama*), repetition is prescribed; by the rule "he recites the first three times, he recites the last three times," it means that repetition of the first and the last must be performed. When their repetition is performed as many times as required, [the number] reaches fifteen.
The intention is that one should exhale as many times as it takes [for the breath] to be filled;
for in this way there is a visible purpose (dṛṣṭārthatā). If it were intended for an invisible result (adṛṣṭa), what would be the point?
Therefore, here too, because it follows that same archetype, the two [breaths], being practiced as many times as required, are filled in the manner previously described by me.
It should be practiced that many times.

If it is argued that [the rule does not apply] because there is no distinction, we say no. (28) (0)
Thus, that which has been stated must be refuted.
Because it is its inherent property, it should be repeated like the original, until the completion of the prescribed number. (0 Ni.)
There should be repetition. Why? Because the nature of the archetype (prakṛti) exists;

therefore, it must be repeated "until completion. In this way, it will be performed "according to the archetype" (prakṛtivat), and repetition must be accepted as being situated within the context of the injunction (codaka). Therefore, there is repetition.
Thus [it is said].

48.3 Or rather, it is as much as has been stated, because a limit has been established. (Siddhānta) || 30 ||

The word "or" (vā) in the commentary sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that the first and last [verses] are to be repeated until the number is completed; rather, having repeated as much as has been prescribed, the remainder is to be filled by means of [additional] verses.

Why? Because the measure of the repetition has been fixed. For the measure of the repetition has indeed been established: "He recites the first three times, and the last three times. And this number three is accomplished through repetition.
The number intended is not for the purpose of filling out a count; thus, the direct Vedic statement (śruti) would be upheld, whereas otherwise there would be figurative indication (lakṣaṇā).
As for what was said—that "in this way, the meaning becomes defective"—this is not so; it must be respected.

Indeed, there is no insistence on [the specific] number; for even by two or four [repetitions], it is completed by me. Nevertheless, the threefold repetition of the first and the last [verses] must be performed, because the number is to be completed by that. Here too, the number is completed by that very repetition; for that also serves to complete the number here, since in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the first and the last were repeated three times and the number was thereby completed. Here too, it should be done in exactly the same way: the first and the last are to be repeated three times, and the number is to be completed by me, not as in the archetype.
It is understood from the meaning of the word that by this repetition the number is to be completed;
it is understood from the explicit statement that "repetition is to be performed," and from the functional capacity (sāmarthya) that "the number is to be completed.
And that [number] was completed in the archetype (prakṛti) by implication; and that which is done by implication is not the meaning of the injunction (codanārtha).

Therefore, the opponent (codaka) says that the number must not be completed by this repetition; rather, having repeated [the rite] as stated, the remaining [verses] are to be introduced. Thus, it is "as much as has been said."
And because more [than one] is seen. (Yukti) || 31 ||

if one were to conclude with a Jagatī, one would cause the meters to depart; therefore, one should conclude with a Triṣṭubh.

therefore, it is also an addition (āgama).

And [it is] not so, because it has already been explained. (Sūtra 33, Śruti-nirṇaya)

therefore, one should repeat as much as is stated and complete the required number by the introduction (*āgama*) of the remaining [verses].

The section concerning the archetypal nature of the *ṣoḍaśin* cups.
Sūtra: The Ṣoḍaśin is a modification (vaikṛta), because its complete prescription occurs therein.
|| 34 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||
The ordinary [text], the Bhāṣya:
There is the *ṣoḍaśī*, introduced with reference to the *Jyotiṣṭoma*: "He who, knowing thus, takes this *ṣoḍaśin*, prospers in himself; his rival is defeated."

In this regard, there is a doubt: is this [the Agnicayana] archetypal (prākṛta) or modified (vaikṛta)? How so? Because it is taught in the context of the Jyotiṣṭoma, it would seem to be modified; for it is stated regarding a modification: "It is taken on the middle day of the three-night sacrifice. However, one might think that there is indeed a statement even in the archetype: "A Kṣatriya should have it built at the Agniṣṭoma, a Brāhmaṇa at the Atirātra," since such a statement exists by virtue of its force even in the modification.
[Page 579] Chapter 10,
Section 4, Verse 85.

It is expected that [the *śatirātra*] would occur in the modified form (*vikṛti*). Because it is not mentioned in the original form (*prakṛti*), and because the *śatirātra* exists in the original form, there arises the doubt: "Is it archetypal (*prākṛta*)? Therefore, there is uncertainty.
Why? Because therein—
How so? [The prima facie view is:
"What is obtained is this: the *ṣoḍaśin* should have the nature of a modification (*vaidyatva*).
Because it is prescribed in its entirety; for in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), it is prescribed in its complete form."

Having stated, "The learned man should take up this Ṣoḍaśin," it is further enjoined, "It is taken up on the middle day of the Chaturmāsya sacrifice"; and since syntactical connection (*vākya*) is stronger than context (*prakaraṇa*), when the context is thus set aside by the syntactical connection,
the statement "for a Brāhmaṇa at the Atirātra" refers to the modified (*vaikṛta*) Atirātra.

It is understood; therefore, although this [ṣoḍaśin] is not heard in its entirety within the *vidyā* because it is prescribed with reference to the *jyotiṣṭoma*, nevertheless, it is indeed prescribed in its entirety. Consequently, the *ṣoḍaśin* is to be taken up in the enumerated *vikṛtis* (modified sacrifices), but not in the *prakṛti* (archetypal sacrifice).
And because non-existence is observed in the case of primordial matter (prakṛti). (Sūtra 35) (Commentary 1)
"From this, it is known that [the *ṣoḍaśin*] is not [part of the sacrifice]. Why? Because its absence is observed in the archetype (*prakṛti*).

How so? It is explained in the second chapter (2.4) that "of the *saṃstuta* verses, two exceed the *virāj*"; this refers to the absence of the *ṣoḍaśin*, for it is stated that "two *stotrīya* verses exceed the *virāj*."
2 (0) | For this reason also, the Ṣoḍaśin is a modification.
And because there is a statement regarding the non-performance of the sacrifice. (Sūtra 36) (Second Yuktivāda)

And for this reason also, it must be a modification (vaikṛta): for there is such a statement as, "They say that there is no sacrifice named the Ṣoḍaśī. Now, it is not the case that the Ṣoḍaśī does not exist in the archetype (prakṛti), the Jyotiṣṭoma;
rather, this statement [is made] because if it did not exist in the Jyotiṣṭoma, then [the statement] would be appropriate. Therefore, for this reason also—
It is understood as "transformed" (vaikṛta).
[Page 580] Or rather, it is according to the original nature, because of the remaining [of the rule]. (Siddhānta 37)
Commentary: The word "or" (*vā*) sets aside the previous position—it is not the case that the *ṣoḍaśin* is [optional] according to the Vedic text;

rather, it should be archetypal (*prākṛta*). Why? Because it is heard in the archetype, the *Jyotiṣṭoma*, and by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), it would form a single syntactical unit with the *Jyotiṣṭoma*; this remains so even when it is mentioned in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
It does not depart [from the context]. For this statement is not a prohibition regarding the archetype (prakṛti), but rather an instruction regarding the modification (vikṛti).

Therefore, since it is neither enjoined nor prohibited in the archetype, the Ṣoḍaśin cup ought to be present there. Furthermore, its establishment is not based on the context alone, but also on the direct statement (vākya).

"So be it; [the rule] 'In the Agniṣṭoma, a Kṣatriya should take [it]; in the Atirātra, a Brāhmaṇa'—this is not possible in the archetype (prakṛti), for it is observed in the Atirātra and can thus be inferred [to apply there]. Therefore, the Ṣoḍaśin is an archetypal element."
And because of the perception of the primordial nature (prakṛti). (38) (0)

The observation of this *ṣoḍaśin* occurs in the archetype (*prakṛti*), namely: "Three [verses] remain over from the *virāj* of the hymns. It has been stated that when the *ṣoḍaśin* is taken up, the observation of these three *stotrīyā* verses becomes possible. Therefore, the *ṣoḍaśin* belongs to the archetype.
The *śrāmrāta* is for the purpose of cleansing. (0ni0 1) || 38 ||
Commentary:

Now, regarding the point that "where there is a modification (vaikṛta), it is because of the complete prescription [of the ritual]," it has been stated: "That statement does not prohibit the archetype (prakṛti). [The objection is: "If [the details] are already obtained through the extended application (codaka), for what purpose is it stated again? Thus, in the case of connection with time, the fifth case-ending is used, not the ablative; it should be understood in the same way here as well;

0. Because of the connection with the Uktha and the Āgniṣṭoma, it should be without Stotras and Śastras, for there is indeed a difference in the final form (saṃsthā). (Pūrvapakṣa) || 48 ||

"the village"; it is stated that the *ṣoḍaśī* cup is to be drawn at the *agniṣṭoma* sacrifice and at the *ukthya* sacrifice. and this scriptural statement would be contradicted: "For a Kṣatriya, the Ṣoḍaśin and the Ukthyas follow the Agniṣṭoma.
[This applies] to the Jyotiṣṭoma qualified by the Agniṣṭoma.

It is said: [the stotra and śastra] are indeed auxiliaries (aṅga) of the Agniṣṭoma alone; for a sacrifice cannot be an auxiliary of the stotra and śastra by its own nature, because the sacrifice possesses a fruit while the other two are fruitless. Furthermore, it is only through this [connection with the stotra and śastra] that it becomes an Agniṣṭoma, which is a form (saṃsthā) of the Jyotiṣṭoma, and not otherwise. Therefore, it should be accompanied by stotra and śastra.
[Sūtra 50] Or rather, it is accompanied by the Stotra and Śastra, because they are its constituent parts. (The Siddhānta)

The Bhāṣya says: "Or [the Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice] may be without the Stotra and Śastra. Why? "Because it is a subordinate part of that"—for the Stotra and Śastra are indeed subordinate parts of the sacrifice, being the causes for the drawing of the cup (graha). How so? Because when the occasion has arrived—according to the rule, "Having either taken up the cup or having brought forward the bowl, he introduces the Stotra"—it must necessarily occur.
Because it is based on an indicative mark, therefore the Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice should consist of the Stotra and Śastra.
And because of the observation of indicative marks. (51) (0)
An indicative mark (*liṅga*) also shows this meaning: "The *ṣoḍaśī* sacrifice has its *stotra*s and *śastra*s recited.

How so? "Some sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) conclude uprightly, others conclude crosswise; those which conclude with the *hotṛ* priest are upright, while those which conclude with the *acchāvāka* priest are crosswise."

How is this established as a mark? This is what is meant: sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) belong to the two [officiants] alone—those which conclude with the *hotṛ* and those which conclude with the *acchāvāka*. If the *ṣoḍaśin* were accompanied by both *stotra* and *śastra*, then it would likewise conclude otherwise, namely with the *adhvaryu*.
For this reason also, the Ṣoḍaśī sacrifice is accompanied by both Stotras and Śastras.

Because it is absent [in other contexts], it is taken up in the *atirātras*. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 53 ||
There is a two-night sacrifice belonging to the Aṅgirases; regarding it, this is transmitted in the scripture:
"The Vaikhānasa Sāman is performed on the previous day, and the Ṣoḍaśin on the following day. In this regard, the meaning is subject to doubt:—

Is this the injunction of the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup], or is it a restatement (*pariṣaddhyāna*) of what is already established? What is the prima facie view? It is the injunction of what is not yet established; for the inferential *codaka* (archetypal rule) does not apply once [the rite] has been enjoined, and it has already been enjoined by the statement: "In the latter day of the two-day sacrifice, the *ṣoḍaśin* is drawn."
By virtue of the statement; therefore, since the impeller does not cause [the action] to be reached, it is understood that this is an injunction of what was previously unobtained.
Sūtra and Bhāṣya:
Or rather, it belongs to the Śrāmaṇyā because it is prescribed as an independent injunction. (Siddhānta) || 54 ||

Or else, there is "connection" (*anvaya*): this hearing [of the text] regarding the *ṣoḍaśin* cup is for the purpose of delimitation within this sacrifice, namely, "The *vaikhānasa* chant is on the previous day; the *ṣoḍaśin* is on the following day. How is there connection? Because it is an "unattached injunction" (*anārabhyavidhi*). What is the unattached injunction? It is: "On the following day..."

Regarding the statement, "It is taken at the Dvirātra," this serves as a restrictive specification (upasaṃhāra) of what was previously established: that which is taken at the latter part of the Dvirātra is taken at the Dvirātra of the Aṅgirases,
and not otherwise.
Alternatively, it is established as follows: "It is taken at the Atirātras because of its absence.

This taking of the Ṣoḍaśin cup at the archetypal Atirātras, which is optional, is obtained by way of that very option for all Dvirātras; it is then restricted by the rule: "It is taken on the latter day of the Dvirātra."

When its application has been made, there is an absence [of it] in other two-night sacrifices; because of that absence, the *ṣoḍaśī* is restricted as being taken in the latter two-night sacrifice of the Aṅgirases. Or rather, it is a connection established independently [of the context].

"Because of the injunction": the subsequent [rites] are connected with the *ṣoḍaśin* in all *dvirātra* sacrifices, because they are heard directly in the statement, "The subsequent *ṣoḍaśin* is taken at the *dvirātra*," by means of an injunction not restricted to a specific context (*anārabhyavidhāna*).
[Objection: "But is it not the case that the concluding summary (*upasaṃhāra*) or the exclusion (*parisaṅkhyā*) applies to the *ṣoḍaśin* in the subsequent [sacrifice]? [Reply: It is said, no.
It is possible to measure the direct hearing [of the text] by means of specific statements; for the elders have declared that there are three defects:

grasping one's own meaning, imagining another's meaning, and the sublation of what has been established. Nor is there a restrictive application (upasaṃhāra), because the two sentences are distinct. For what purpose, then, is this [mention of] the Ṣoḍaśin cup in the latter [section]? This is certainly not an injunction.

for it is prescribed that "that Vaikhānasa Sāman occurs on the previous day," while the Ṣoḍaśin is merely restated for the following day, since its application is already established by a general injunction (anārabhyavidhāna). Sūtra: On every fourth day, because of the repetition "of the Ahīna," it should be understood as a repeated performance, like the eating [of the Soma]. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 55 ||

With reference to the *ṣoḍaśin* sacrifice, they declare in the Bhāṣya: "It is taken on every fourth day of the *ahīna*. In this matter, the following point is subject to doubt: Is the *ṣoḍaśin* to be repeated on the fourth day within a single *ahīna* sacrifice, or on the fourth day of one *ahīna* sacrifice [relative to] another *ahīna* sacrifice?

"Is it to be practiced thus: 'on each day [of the Ahīna] they take [the draught]'? What is the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa)? It should be practiced on one [day]. Why? Because it is said, 'of the single Ahīna'; if it were applied to various Ahīnas, that would be redundant; in this view, there is the direct scriptural statement (śruti). Moreover, if it were applied to various Ahīnas, the purpose of the mention of the seed-syllable would be lost, since by the mere words 'on the fourth day of the Ahīna,' that [purpose] would already be achieved."
It is established; however, in a single [instance], the repetition becomes meaningful. Therefore, in a single *ahīna* sacrifice, there is a recitation of a quarter-verse (*pāda*).

It is to be practiced like eating; just as in the expression "Devadatta eats every fourth day," having eaten on the fourth day, one proceeds again on the fourth [subsequent] day— this being understood in one sense.
The same should be understood here as well; therefore, it is said: "in one who has not fallen away."

Or rather, because it possesses a numerical quality, it is taken in various *ahīna* sacrifices; like the *paca*, because there is no purpose for a completion (*saṃsthā*) in a single [sacrifice]. || 56 ||

"In the Ahīnas," or rather, it is performed on the fourth day; thus it continues until the performance is completed—meaning "on the fourth day. In one Ahīna, there is one fourth day, and the other becomes the eighth. As for what was said—that the word "Ahīna" will be based on direct Vedic revelation (śruti)—it indeed exists.

For that is indeed a direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), yet nothing is established by hearing it, because there is no fourth [category]. In our view, however, it is an indicative mark (*lakṣaṇā*), and by it, [the result] is established. Furthermore, it is not an indicative mark; rather, the singular number is intended to express the class (*sāmānya*). As for the objection that "repetition would be purposeless," it is not so; the meaning of the word must be conceived such that purposelessness does not ensue. There is a doubt: are the ritual properties (dharmas) taught with reference to the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha) in both its forms—the *samūḍha* and the *vyūḍha*—or are they taught with reference to the *samūḍha* form, while the *vyūḍha* is a modification (*vikāra*) of it? Regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it is traditionally taught: "The *Prāyaṇīya* and *Udayanīya* days have the *Aindravāyava* cup first; so does the tenth day. Now, among the other nine days: the first has the *Aindravāyava* cup first, then the *Śukra* cup first, then the *Āgrayaṇa* cup first, then the *Aindravāyava* cup first, then the *Śukra* cup first."

Now, regarding the rule: "Then the Śrāyaṇa is first; then the Aindravāyava is first; then the Ekāgra is first; then the Śrāyaṇa is first"—this is obtained by extension (codaka) in the Gavām Ayana sacrifice. In that context, many *vyanīkā* sequences must be rotated, and thus repetition is established by the requirements of the purpose. 10. Pathāye || Pāda:
Should the repetition be performed according to the *dakṣakalita* method, or is there an increase in the number of recitations? Thus [the question].

"How should it be like the Daṇḍaka-khila, or how is there an increase in its own place? Thus, since the section concerning the *pari* [sacrifice] has been concluded, when the first nine days have been completed—even though they are threefold—the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) brings them forward; this being present, it applies to the purpose of the Aindravāyava cup.
"The first day is for the Śukra," it is said. When those nine [days] have been completed, this again presents itself: "The first day is for the Aindravāyava.

Thus, there is a repetition like that of a staff (daṇḍaka). Now, if there were no reference to the days, then the interval between the Prāyaṇīya and Udayanīya would be filled by nine sections (anīka); likewise, in the Gavām Ayana, it would be filled by nine sections.
It should be filled; when that is full, there is no returning again, so it would not be like the "measured-stick" (daṇḍakalita) repetition,
nor would there be an expansion in its own place as if it were being filled by something else in the interval.

But what is established? That there is a repetition like that of a staff (daṇḍakalitavat). In this regard, there is no further authority; for it is heard thus: "The first day of the *Rudra-vāyavya* sacrifice is [to be performed];

now, as for the work (*kārya*), because of the context, it is understood to be the day (*ahar*). Therefore, the day is the subject of the discussion. Consequently, in the *Gavāmayana*—which consists of twelve months and thirty-six days—the *anīka* (sets of hymns) are obtained through the force of the general rule (*codaka*). Therein, the *anīkas* are [repeated] at the end of each day, just as in the case of the *Rudra-vāyavya*. (Note: The text appears to be a fragment from a commentary on Jaimini Sūtra 10.5.24–25 concerning the repetition of ritual elements in the Gavāmayana sacrifice.)

The *pānīkā* and the *pariṣṭuti* [are to be performed] at the two ends; that is, in the middle of the two days—the *prāyaṇīya* and the *udayanīya*—the remaining fourteen *nakṣatra* verses are to be inserted.

Since the entire *saṃvatsara* sacrifice occurs between the *prāyaṇīya* and the *udayanīya*, these [verses] must be filled in. Regarding that filling, as previously stated, a group consisting of nine days is established within the *pariṣṭutis*. Thus, the repetition (*āvṛtti*) is obtained, and its twofold nature is observed, just as in the case of the *dakṣiṇā* day and the *bhūman* day, where the sequence is determined.

One method is that the teacher recites the beginning, middle, and end, and then the student repeats it; [the teacher says], "My path does not have the capacity for such daily study"—this is one way. Another way is as follows:

just as students who wish to repeat a text read each portion individually, so too should one proceed with each individual day within the collection of days; this is called "the performance according to the sequence."
Thus we understand: the repetition is like that of a measuring-stick (*daṇḍakalitavat*). Among the principles of repetition, the "measuring-stick" [is the first].

This is logical; thus, there is conformity with the sequential order (*krama*). For example, when someone is told, "Recite the *anuvāka* three times," he recites it like a staff-stroke (*daṇḍakalita*) for the sake of conforming to the sequence;
so too should it be understood here. Just as in this very *Gavāmayana* sacrifice, there is the *ekādaśinī*.
When practiced, it is practiced like the striking of a staff, not by increasing the duration in its own place.
Because it is directly perceived as a number residing in its own location.

"Or rather, there is an increase in its own place, not a repetition like that of a *daṇḍakalita* (a staff-like sequence). And this is because it is the governing factor (*adhikāra*) for the days. Why? Because the days are not directly perceived; the days are not directly perceived as nine days, and [the rule] 'beginning with the Aindravāyava' is being enjoined.

How is it that the day is not enjoined? Because of the consequence of a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*): the sentence would be split into 'the first [day] begins with the Aindravāyava' and 'that [is] the day, not a collection of days.'"

Therefore, the mention of "first" (agra) is merely a restatement (anuvāda). If this is the case, then for the sake of maintaining the sequence, one must resort to an expansion in its own place (svasthānavivṛddhi), such that after making the Āgrayaṇa-graha the first, the Aindravāyava-grahas must be made the first.

"The *pṛṣṭhas* and the *trayastrimśa-stoma*"; this very [rule] is established according to its own position (*svasthāna*) in the tenth chapter, first quarter.
[The ritual] is performed with the *daṇḍaka* and the *spita* reversed. How so? In the first fortnight, the *vyanīkā* (intercalary sequence) revolves three times;

However, [if the rule were otherwise], the Triṣṭoma would reach the Mahendra cup with the Aindravāyava as first, and in that case, this observed fact would be contradicted. Therefore...
"Increase in its own place."

This much must be examined: Is "he should look at his son" a supplement to the sentence "one should close one's eyes when the Rathantara is being chanted," or is "he should look at his son," etc., a separate sentence?
Thus [it is asked]: what is the prima facie conclusion? That there is a connection between the subsidiary (aṅga) and its purpose, and that this constitutes a separate sentence.
Why? Because it is understood as distinct; this is perceived as distinct: "One should look toward the sun. [Objection:
But a connection is also observed, namely: "When the Rathantara is being chanted, one should close one's eyes."

Having thus established [the injunction], it is restated that "one should look toward the sun. To this it is replied: When both [factors] are understood, a distinction must be grasped; that distinction is contradicted by that which is being grasped.

However, the understanding of only one or the other arises from the conflict between injunction (*vidhi*) and restatement (*anuvāda*). And in that case, the principle of injunction applies because of its novelty (*apūrvatva*), for "mere restatement is purposeless" (Jaimini Sūtra 1.2.19). Furthermore, because of the understanding of the injunction, the injunction is understood in the words "one should look"; thus the direct Vedic revelation (*śruti*) itself is supported by the statement, "toward the sun."

The injunction "one should look" is prescribed for the purpose of looking toward the solar battle (*svaryuddha*). Through the word *svardṛk*, there is a connection with the sacrifice (*yāga*) which is the means [to that end]; otherwise, the word *svardṛk* would merely denote a quality.

Furthermore, when there is a conflict between direct statement (*śruti*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*), direct statement is the more authoritative. Therefore, there is a relationship between the subsidiary (*aṅga*) and its purpose (*prayojana*).

Alternatively, the relationship between the subsidiary (aṅga) and its purpose (prayojana) is as follows: "one should look toward the sun. In this way, the word "sun" (svardṛk) serves as the means for the act of looking; thus, the vikrama [accent] is also supported, as is the sentence itself, because the word "sun" is heard. Therefore, there is indeed a relationship between the subsidiary and its purpose.

This being the case, the position is as follows: "The observation for one who sees the sun should be at the time of the *kāṭamātra* (the duration of a finger-snap)," because it is for the sake of another; this is not so, however, in the sense of a relationship between a subsidiary and its purpose, but rather, by the word *svardṛśaṃ*, there would be a relationship of time with the *vīkṣaṇa* (observation). Why? Because speech is for the sake of another.

however, this is so provided that no attainment of the matter through another means of knowledge is perceived. This is established by direct audition (*śruti*) itself; and it has already been understood that direct audition is more authoritative than indicative mark (*liṅga*) and syntactical connection (*vākya*). Alternatively, the syntactical connection (*vākya*) would not be sublated here, for a syntactical connection is that which conveys a relationship, and such a relationship is of many kinds according to the circumstances.

The relationship is understood from the sentence—sometimes as a relationship between an action and its factors (*kriyākāraka*), sometimes as a relationship between a qualifier and a qualified (*viśeṣaṇaviśeṣya*), and sometimes as a relationship between the indicated and the indicator (*lakṣyalakṣaṇa*)—such are the various types of relationships. In this case, since the relationship between the indicated and the indicator is prompted by a purpose, that specific type of relationship is indeed accepted; thus, the sentence is not contradicted. As for the Mīmāṃsā argument that "even though there is the word *darbha* [in the mantra], there is an acceptance of the indicative mark (*liṅga*) because of the use of the root *dṛś* (to see)," we do not find that even this is well-founded regarding the established meaning. For when the root *dṛś* is employed in its own primary sense, it would imply seeing; it does not [imply] another's purpose. However, in the word *svardṛk*, the root *dṛś* is understood as subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the prefix *sva-* which functions as a qualifier (*upapada*), whereas in other cases it is the principal element (*pradhānabhūta*). And the agent is not what is being expressed here.
It is designated as having the nature of a wave-cause;
however, because it is absolutely transcendent, this [Self], being denoted as the agent, does not at all enter into a relationship with the waves through conjunction.

If this meaning were taught—that "one should wave for the sake of the Self-seer"—then, not knowing who that Self-seer is for whose sake the waving is taught, we would certainly not determine the action. Now, if this is the meaning—
"One should perform the looking at the sun"—even so, because it is not understood [from the context], that same fault remains.

Thus, when such a connection is accepted by the Āśvalāyana, neither the indicative mark (liṅga) nor the syntactical connection (vākya) is supported; for in the case of a definition-based connection, this "looking" would mean "one should look" at the time of its utterance.

There may indeed be some logical connection; however, even for one who asserts that the agent is expressed [by the suffix], this does not contradict the connection with the praise. Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), one accepts a relationship of qualifier and qualified through the act of praising—as in the passage, "the Lord of heaven, the beholder of all, who stands over the firm. Therefore, we say: since there is a connection for the sake of praise, as in the case of "one should look toward Śam," the purpose here is ritual action (*kāryārtha*).

What is the purpose? When there is a relationship between the subsidiary and the principal, as in the case of the extended application (*atideśa*) "one should sing the *Rathantara* on the two *Uttara* verses," then this [rule] is extended: "One should close one's eyes while the *Rathantara* is being sung. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), because the word "simultaneously" (*saha*) is absent from the *Uttara* verses, there is no restriction regarding the closing of the eyes. However, in the final view (*siddhānta*), when there is a connection with the night, because the time is not lost during that portion, the restriction "one should look toward the sun" becomes established.

Because whether these two *sāmans* are combined or separated, the expression "the *ṣaḍaha* period has the *pṛṣṭhya* [stotra] with the *rathantara-sāman*" is applicable in both ways. Therefore, this is the inquiry: Is this a *bahuvrīhi* compound containing a *dvandva* within it?

Regarding the phrase "one for whom the *vṛhat* and *rathantara* *sāmans* [exist]," is it a multi-word *bahuvrīhi* compound—meaning "the *vṛhat* belongs to him" and "the *rathantara* belongs to him"? If it is a *bahuvrīhi* with an internal *dvandva*, then the two *sāmans* are combined every day;
if it is a multi-word *bahuvrīhi*, they are distinct.

What, then, is the prima facie position?—namely, that [the compound] applies to the whole. Therefore, this is explained: [it is] an *indaga* (dvandva) *bahuvrīhi*. Why? Because of the immediate sequence of the two words ending in the suffix *vṛddha*, because the view of *vṛtti* (compound formation) has been adopted, and because in the case of *vṛtti* a compound is obligatory. Furthermore, in a *dvandva*, there is the expression of its own meaning, the non-requirement of direct hearing (*śruti*), and internal proximity (*antaraṅgatā*); otherwise, both would [not apply].

It would be contradicted. If the *indra-gīta* (Indra-songs) were indeed a *bahuvrīhi* compound, then both *sāmans* would have to be performed together every day. Why? Because of the existence of the *dvandva* compound which denotes mutual conjunction (*itaretarayoga*).
That which is the *rathantara* is accompanied by the *bṛhat*; this simultaneous injunction is what constitutes mutual conjunction.

Therefore, it says "daily in their entirety. Regarding the phrase "like a single day"—just as one speaks of a person suffering from consumption (*śyogāmayāvin*) using the word "eating" (*aṭatti*), so too there is a compound of the two words "Bṛhat" and "Rathantara"; this should be understood in accordance with the *Tantravārttika* which states, "that [compound] belongs to both."
One should perform both at a *saṃsava*; one should perform both at an *apaciti* sacrifice as well; and one should perform only one at a *vṛddhi* sacrifice.
Or rather, [the rule applies] even when [the substance] is divided, because the injunction is for the whole; thus, in its division, the prohibition [of the offering] is suspended. (Siddhānta) || 5 ||

And this is not the case—that "day after day there are two Sāmans" means that on some days the *rathantara* is used and on others the *bṛhat*, such that both Sāmans are not prescribed for the whole [period]. Why? Because the expression "having the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* as Sāmans" is applicable to both alternatives, namely, that the two Sāmans are distinct.

This is logical. Why? Because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *pṛṣṭha* stotra was accomplished by means of one [sāman], and in the ectype (*vikṛti*) as well, it must be accomplished by means of one, in order to favor the extended injunction (*codaka*). This being the case, both the cause for the *bṛhat* and the cause for the *rathantara* will be fully realized. Now, if the collection of the *bṛhat* and *rathantara* together accomplishes the *pṛṣṭha*, then neither the *bṛhat* nor the *rathantara* would be the means of accomplishment.
If it were the means (*sādhana*), that [specific] cause would not be applicable, and in that case, there would be a contradiction with the injunction (*codaka*).

Not only would that cause not be applicable, but the state of having the *bṛhat* as the *pṛṣṭha-stotra* would not be applicable, nor would the state of having the *rathantara* as the *pṛṣṭha-stotra*; because of this disparity, there would indeed be a different performance altogether.

Moreover, when the entire back-chant (*pṛṣṭha*) is figuratively designated as "the *bṛhat* back-chant" or "the *rathantara* back-chant," this serves as an indicative mark (*liṅga*) for the expression of that collective whole. Furthermore, the word *bṛhat*,
requiring a connection with the word *sāman*, would not be connected with the word *rathantara*.

And the immediate proximity [of the word *rathantara*] is equal to that of the word *sāman*. Furthermore, if one relies on the view of secondary derivation (*vṛtti*), there is all the more a lack of semantic competency with the word *indra*; nor indeed is composition (*samāsa*) mandatory in the case of derivation, for the venerable Pāṇini teaches it as optional (*vibhāṣā*). And there is the direct audition of the word *sāman*.

In this way, much of the original form will remain unaltered, and thus the injunctive rule (*codaka*) is upheld. For this reason as well, there is no connection of the verbal root (*dhātu*) with the *sākara*. (10.6.30)
*The reading "dadhiśakā" is found in the manuscript of the Ādarśa.
[Page 630] Here begins the section concerning the modification of the Soma-matasya sacrifice in the case of the "Cidagniḍoma."
If there were no *citi* (consciousness), there would be a modification of all enumeration through existence alone. || 22 ||

(Prima facie view) The Bhāṣya states: It is heard thus, "The Agniṣṭoma is threefold" (*trivṛd agniṣṭomaḥ*). Regarding this, there is a doubt: does the "threefold" (*trivṛt*) serve as a means for the Agniṣṭoma in general, or is it restricted to the subject of Soma?
Thus [the question arises]: what is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? Since the word "cit" (bricks) is heard [in the text], there should be a modification consisting solely of bricks.

Why? Because in common usage, the word *trivṛt* is employed in connection with "citi" (piling/arrangement), as in the expression "a threefold golden necklace. Here too, in the phrase "the *agniṣṭoma* is *cit*," it is stated that the *agniṣṭoma* is to be performed in connection with the *citi*. And that *citi*-nature [is established] by means of delimiting the sacrificial implements of the *agniṣṭoma*.

What is meant is that it is connected with that [Agniṣṭoma], not directly, because number is a quality (*guṇa*). Nor is any specific number belonging to it mentioned here. Since there is no such specification, whatever number is connected with the Agniṣṭoma should be delimited by the number; thus, one should measure out the whole.

By virtue of its commonality as a substance fit for sacrifice (*saddhyātva*), one should transform it into that [substance]. Just as when it is said, "Devadatta should be fed with curd, ghee, and rice," and "Yajñadatta should be fed with oil like Devadatta," the oil is employed only for the purpose of lubrication due to the commonality of being a lubricant, and not for the purpose of providing nourishment;
in the same way, by me as well, it is employed only for the purpose of the sacrifice.
Or rather, it belongs to the Stoma, because it possesses its characteristic mark. (Siddhānta) || 23 ||

And this is not the case that the modification applies to everything; rather, one should modify only that which pertains to the *soma*. How so? Because the *triṣṭubh* meter is seen elsewhere in relation to the *stoma*;
just as in the case of "the *bahiḥpavamāna* is *triṣṭubh*," its application to the *stoma* is determined, so too [is it here].
In the expression "the *agniṣṭoma* is threefold" (*trivṛdagniṣṭomaḥ*), that very same word is uttered, referring back to that very same related entity—
[as discussed] in the tenth chapter (pāda).
One should bring [the mantra] into proximity with the intellect through pride; therefore, because of the characteristic of Soma, one should modify that which belongs to it.
To this it is replied: this is not tenable; for words have unrestricted applications, and by whatever [entity] they are connected, they denote that very thing as real.
This has already been demonstrated in the case of the "threefold gem. Therefore, [the term applies] to the *ahiḥ pavamāna*.

"Because of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it enumerates the *stoma*; furthermore, whatever else is to be enumerated will also be enumerated by it; therefore, even the status of being a characteristic mark (*liṅga*) of the *stoma* is not a reason for its restriction. To this, it is replied: "In this context, this word *trivṛt*, having transcended its worldly meaning..."

In the case of something unknowable, a specific number is employed; for example, regarding the *stoma* consisting of nine [verses], as in "the *bahiḥpavamāna* is threefold," after stating "the *bahiḥpavamāna* is threefold," nine *sūktas* are mentioned, by which it is understood that the term applies to them. The same applies to the subsequent case as well.
It is observed: "The pile [of bricks] consists of nine potsherds, accompanied by the *trivṛt* hymn; it is the ninefold nature of the Agniṣṭoma.

By stating that the pile is honored with the *trivṛt* hymn through the nine potsherds, this shows the established usage of the word *trivṛt* in that context. Therefore, because of its usage as an established term and because of the observation of grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it is determined that this is its meaning. Even in common worldly usage, the determination of meaning occurs either from the application of coreferentiality or from established usage, as in the case of "This is Devadatta."

Thus, since this word *ciṣṭh* is seen elsewhere to have as its object a specific number of things to be measured, when it is employed here as well, it brings to mind by means of its indicative power (*liṅga*) that very object for which it was seen [elsewhere]; therefore, it must be restricted to the subject of the *stoma*. As for what was said—that "number has a fixed scope and everywhere enters into a relationship"—this is already refuted by the rejection of the meaning of the individual components and the acceptance of the collective whole. And thus, there is no cessation of the numbers belonging to other [contexts].
"There will be favor toward the instigators" (10.6.70).
[Page 632] The section concerning the combination of both the Bṛhat and Rathantara [Sāmans].
In both cases, there should be a division like that of the Viśvajit sacrifice. || 24 ||
(Pūrvapakṣa)

There are sacrifices common to both [the Rgveda and Sāmaveda], such as: "One should perform both at a *saṃsava* sacrifice; one should also perform both on a single-day (*ekāha*) sacrifice. In this regard, there is a doubt: do the two [chants] occur separately when the *rathantara* is used, or together? Why? Because it is understood that they are combined; or why would they be separate? It is said in reply: this very statement suggests both meanings.

How so? The sacrifice must be connected with both of these; whether they exist in combination or separately, in either case the sacrifice becomes connected with them. And this appears to be the case in the statement. What is appropriate? That they are separate. Why?

For in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *pṛṣṭha* stotra is accomplished by either one of the two, the *ṛkṣāma* or the *rathaṃtara*; here too, it is understood that for the sake of favoring the extended application (*codaka*) according to the archetype, it must be accomplished by either one. And thus, when the actions connected with the *pṛṣṭha* proceed according to their respective functions, the scriptural injunction will be favored;

for since both accomplish the *pṛṣṭha*, they are prescribed as alternatives to one another, and one would fall into a different performance—neither "the *rathaṃtara* is the *pṛṣṭha*" nor "the *bṛhat* is the *pṛṣṭha*"—since the meaning of the statement is established in both ways, and there is no sublation of what has been stated.
There is a reason for this; therefore, just as in the Viśvajit sacrifice there is no single placement of all [the Sāmans] such as the Bṛhat and so forth, so it is here as well.
Or rather, it is for the sake of the back [of the cart], because it serves that purpose. (Siddhānta Sūtra 25)

This is not the case—that [the *sāman*s] are to be used separately; rather, they are to be used together in their entirety. Why? Because in the archetype (*prakṛti*), the *pṛṣṭha* stotra was accomplished by means of the *ṛc* and the *śāntara* *sāman*, which were optional alternatives;
here, in this modification (*vikṛti*), since those two have already been understood as having that nature, they are obtained precisely in the form of an option.
[Page 633] Chapter 10 (Pāda: 14.5)
This statement is merely for the purpose of enjoining; namely, that one "should perform both the Bṛhat and the Rathantara.
And thus there is totality [of the two], provided those two Sāmans do not abandon each other.
Since these two are heard as things to be adopted, the hearing of the dual number and the hearing of the compound are indeed intended to be significant.
Therefore, wherever the *Bṛhat* occurs, it must be accompanied by the *Rathantara*, not alone. This might be argued: "The conjunction of these two is subordinate to the primary action;

thus, even when they are performed separately, their conjunction is not contradicted. For example, when the cooking of Devadatta and Yajñadatta is mentioned as being done together, one of them performs a portion of the work."

"Furthermore, there is something else: it is not the case that what is performed by one is performed by another; rather, one *sāman* will accomplish one hymn (*stotra*), and another [second] *sāman* will accomplish another. Since their conjunction depends upon the assistance rendered to the primary act (*pradhāna*), the connection of the whole will not be contradicted. To this, it is replied: "This is indeed so in cases where there is a conjunction between two things that are mutually dependent."

It is logical that [the injunction] applies to the two [parts] taken together, not separately, by means of whichever constituent part of the action—whether the beginning, the middle, or the end—it is connected with. Why? Because just as it is understood that "it must assist by this [part]," so too is it understood that "it must assist when accompanied by the other. As for the claim that in common worldly practice, even when the totality of the factors of action (*kāraka*) is expressed, their operations are seen to be distinct—that is due to the impossibility of the matter; for one cannot perform a further act of placing [fuel] on a pot while it is already being placed upon the fire, because such an action would contradict the purpose. Thus, one does not do it.

But that [conjunction] is not enjoined by the word; for whatever is to be performed must be done by means of both together, and not otherwise. However, in this case there is no impossibility, because the *Bṛhat* and *Rathantara* are enjoined as embellishments (*saṃskāra*) of the *ṛc*, and these two, when combined, are capable of embellishing the *pṛṣṭha*; therefore, of those two—

Only the [interpretation of] proximity (*sāhitya*) is appropriate; as it has been said: "When both [interpretations] are possible, it is logical to favor the direct injunction (*codaka*); for there is no [scriptural] observation [to the contrary]. (Note: This is the reading found in the Kāśī edition).
In the Mīmāṃsā system,
there will be no establishment of the means for knowing dharma; and that [dharma] is not perceived through direct perception.
Since the entire injunction is being set aside by the *codaka* (the general transfer rule), no fault arises.
And because of the vision of variety. (Sūtra 26) (Yukti)

And he shows the indicative mark (*liṅga*), namely that the application [of the two] is simultaneous and not separate. What is the indicative mark? He says this: "In the Mahāvṛti, the *Ṛk* and the *Rathantara* are completed with the *nidhana*; when the two *Ṛks* meet, there is no separation, nor is it broken apart."

From the mention of a distinction in the *nidhana*, it is understood that there is a single location (*ekasthānatā*). If the two were in different places, then the distinction in the *nidhana* would be established by the very nature of the case; however, if they occur together, then the mention of a distinction in the *nidhana* becomes meaningful. Therefore, for this reason as well, there is non-difference. Likewise, another [reason]: *hiṃ*.

"The *rathantara* is indeed the fore-axle, and the *bṛhat* is the hind-axle"; by this connection through a single axle, it shows their unity as a single axle. Therefore, both [sāmans] are to be placed in the region of the back (*pṛṣṭha*).
The section concerning the six *ṛc*s of the middle [portion] of the two [verses] consisting of eight [syllables], which are not *anudātta*.

On the thirty-third day, when the sacrifice has concluded, one should partake of the food containing meat, because it follows immediately after that [day], just as in the archetype (prakṛti). (Pūrvapakṣa) 27.
In a certain specific ritual, it is heard in the scripture: "The Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha consists of three Trayastriṃśa stomas.
Regarding the Dvādaśāha, there is a statement: "When the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha has been concluded, one should cause [the sacrificer] to consume honey and ghee."

Thus it is said: "Bā. This very honey-mixture and ghee-mixture, being obtained through the force of the general rule (*codaka*), are now subject to doubt: should they be performed on the thirty-third day, or at the end of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Regarding that, the commencement is as follows: "In the six-day period, the meal of savory food is prescribed; on the thirty-third day... [Page 635]
Chapter 10 (Pāda)
It should be performed in brief. Why? Because of its immediate sequence: in the archetype (prakṛti), the consumption of the soma-remnants occurs immediately after the thirty-three-fold [offering];
therefore, performing it here according to the archetype, one should do so immediately after the thirty-three-fold [offering].
It performs [the action] and favors the prompter (*codaka*). Now, if another master were to act immediately thereafter, he would obstruct the prompter;

for immediate succession (*ānantarya*) is indeed sequence (*krama*), and it has been established that this is the cause for a specific relationship. And this immediate succession of the consumption of the *rasa* is observed together with the thirty-third; therefore—
It is performed immediately after the Trayastriṃśa.
Or rather, [the time for the offering] is determined by the time [of the preceding act], because it has been performed previously. (Siddhānta 28)

Commentary: This is not the case—that the consumption of the *rasa* occurs immediately after the *trayastrimśa*; rather, it should occur at the conclusion of the *ṣaḍaha*. Why? Because it is said, "when the *ṣaḍaha* has concluded," and not, "when the *trayastrimśa* has concluded. The conclusion refers to the completion of the *ṣaḍaha*, not to the commencement of the *trayastrimśa*. Thus, the *ṣaḍaha* reaches its end across the six days of the *ṣaḍaha*, not on a single day such as the *trayastrimśa*.

As for what was said—that because the *trayastrimśānantarya* (the sequence of thirty-three) was observed there, one must likewise eat here for the sake of that very [sequence] as in the original model—this is not correct. In that case, the *trayastrimśānantarya* occurred by implication. Why? Because on that day, the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) concluded within that twelve-day period (*dvādaśāha*).

In this case as well, the meal will take place where the [six-day period] concludes; therefore, the connection with the meal is characterized by the conclusion of the six-day period—as in "when the six-day period has ended"—and not by the conclusion of the thirty-three-fold [stoma]. As for the argument that "sequence is the cause for a specific connection," it is true that it is a cause, but it does not prevail where it is contradicted by a stronger means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Here, however, it has been stated that the injunction is made at the conclusion of the six-day period by means of a direct statement (*vākya*); therefore, since there is a specific connection established by the direct statement, [the meal occurs then].
The immediate sequence alone is not the cause; therefore, the meal should take place at the end of the six-day period.

(20141270) || The Discourse on the Great Virtue of the Bodhisattva Avalokiteśvara || The Buddha was staying in Rājagṛha, on Vulture Peak Mountain, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Ānanda: “Ānanda, if there are good sons or good daughters who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, single-mindedly take refuge in him, then if they should fall into a great fire, by virtue of the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s spiritual protection, they will all be delivered from that great fire. If they should fall into a great flood, by virtue of the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s spiritual protection, they will all be delivered from that great flood. If they should encounter robbers or bandits, by virtue of the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s spiritual protection, they will all be delivered from those robbers and bandits. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good sons or good daughters who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, single-mindedly take refuge in him, then if they should enter a great ocean, by virtue of the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s spiritual protection, they will not meet with any evil winds, nor will they be harmed by sea monsters, dragons, or other aquatic creatures; they will safely reach their destination and arrive at the shore. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good sons or good daughters who, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, single-mindedly take refuge in him, then if they should be imprisoned or bound in shackles, chains, or stocks, by virtue of the power of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara’s spiritual protection, they will all be delivered from those bonds. For this reason, Ānanda, you should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great spiritual power and great virtuous merit. At that time, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, why is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva named Avalokiteśvara? The Buddha told Ānanda: “If there are sentient beings who suffer various afflictions, if they single-mindedly call upon the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, he will immediately deliver them from their suffering. Because he can thus observe and deliver all sentient beings, he is named Avalokiteśvara. At that time, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who wish to worship the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, how should they perform their worship? The Buddha told Ānanda: “If there are good sons or good daughters who wish to worship the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, they should offer incense, flowers, necklaces, garments, banners, parasols, and various kinds of music. They should also recite his name with a single mind. By doing so, they will obtain immeasurable blessings and virtues. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good sons or good daughters who wish to see the Buddhas of the ten directions, they should single-mindedly take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to manifest in various forms according to the needs of sentient beings—sometimes appearing as a Buddha, sometimes as a Śrāvaka, sometimes as a Pratyekabuddha, and sometimes as a Brahmā, Indra, or a world-protecting deity—to deliver all sentient beings. Therefore, Ānanda, you should know that the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses such great spiritual power and great virtuous merit. At that time, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Buddha, saying: “World-Honored One, if there are good sons or good daughters who, having heard this Dharma-door of the Great Virtue of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others, what kind of merit and virtue will they obtain? The Buddha told Ānanda: “If there are good sons or good daughters who, having heard this Dharma-door of the Great Virtue of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others, they will obtain immeasurable blessings and virtues. Furthermore, Ānanda, if there are good sons or good daughters who, having heard this Dharma-door of the Great Virtue of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, receive, uphold, read, recite, and explain it for others, they will be protected by the gods of the four great kings, the Trāyastriṃśa gods, the Yāma gods, the Tuṣita gods, the Nirmāṇarati gods, the Paranirmita-vaśavartin gods, and the gods of the Brahma heavens. They will also be protected by the gods of the sun and moon, the gods of the constellations, and the gods of the great oceans, mountains, rivers, forests, and trees. They will also be protected by the gods of the earth, the gods of the wind, the gods of the fire, and the gods of the water. They will also be protected by the gods of the great void, the gods of the great compassion, and the gods of the great kindness. Commentary:
The Mīmāṃsā System of Philosophy.
Even when there is a firm attachment [to one's own view], the section concerning the performance of that [practice] by those who have lost their middle course is as follows.
And in the case of repetition, there is a repetition of that [action], because of the repeated performance of the ritual act. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 28 ||
It is heard in the scripture: "They perform the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha in rotation.
In this regard, it is obtained through the *codaka* (extended application rule): "At the conclusion of the Pṛṣṭhya Ṣaḍaha, one should eat honey or ghee.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: should the eating be repeated with each rotation of the Ṣaḍaha, or only at the end of the Ṣaḍaha?

Should it be performed only once? What is the prima facie view? When there is a repetition of the six-day period (ṣaḍaha), the eating should also be repeated. Why? Because of the "repeated performance" of the rite; for that rite is repeated, and by its repetition, whatever is connected to it should also be repeated, just as [the following].
Just as the hymns (*stotra*), the recitations (*śastra*), and so forth, which are connected to the sixfold [ritual], are repeated, so too is the meal connected to the sixfold [ritual] repeated.
Or rather, it should be at the end, because its time has been fixed [by another rule]. (Siddhānta) || 30 ||

Commentary: This is not so, as was stated—that eating should also recur through the repetition of the six-day period—but rather, it should be performed all at once at the end of the six days. Why? Because "the time has been fixed":
for the time for eating has indeed been fixed by the statement, "when the six-day period is completed" (*saṃsthite ṣaḍahe*). Completion (*saṃsthāna*)...

The "conclusion" (paryavasāna) is the cessation of the six-part activity; however, one who is performing the six-day rite is not said to have ceased from the activity pertaining to the six-day rite, nor does the six-day rite terminate for the agent as long as he has not ceased [from that activity]. For number [in this context] implies either indifference toward the action or the performance of another activity.
[This refers to] the previous ritual action. Furthermore, one who performs the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*) does not maintain indifference;
the reading "he should return to eating" (*bhojanam āpadyāvarteta*) found everywhere is not correct.
[Page 637]
1. On the day of the full moon (pāda).
Nor does it perform another function; rather, it effects a repetition of that very same act.
Therefore, it is not concluded. And since there is no number when something is not concluded, it is indeed as if unhearing were wisdom.
It is not performed.

As for what was said—that just as other properties of the six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*), such as the *stotra* and *śastra*, are repeated, so too the eating (*prāśana*) should be repeated—that is not correct; for those [other properties] are connected to the days.

The phrase "repetition of the *śrāma*" means the repetition of the *stotra*s and so forth; for those [the *stotra*s] are not enjoined in connection with the days by way of a concluding connection (*avasāna-saṃyoga*). But here, the reason stated is that the eating is enjoined in connection with a concluding connection; therefore, a repetition of the eating is not appropriate.
Furthermore, if this eating were a subordinate part (*aṅga*) of the six-day rite (*ṣaḍaha*), then [it would follow] from the repetition of the principal [rite].

It would recur, yet this is not an auxiliary (aṅga). Why? Because there is no cause that makes known its status as an auxiliary. Its status as an auxiliary could arise either from context (prakaraṇa), or from syntactical connection (vākya-saṃyoga), or from the observation of a visible benefit (pratyakṣopakāra); however, we do not perceive any such cause among these in the case of the *dṛhadhana*. As for context, it belongs to the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*).

It does not belong to the *ṣaḍaha*. Even the connection with the sentence—"when the *ṣaḍaha* has concluded" (*saṃsthite ṣaḍahe*)—teaches that the eating occurs upon the conclusion of the *ṣaḍaha*; for a *ṣaḍaha* is only "concluded" when no further constituent part remains of it. Furthermore, the consumption of honey, meat, and ghee does not provide any perceptible benefit [to the sacrifice].

[Regarding] the *bar̤aha*: Why? Because [the procedure] has ceased; for by whatever means and to whatever extent the satisfaction of the performers is accomplished, one might assist those preceding rites by generating their efficacy; but this does not apply to the *bar̤aha* which has already passed. Furthermore, even those reasons such as order (*krama*) and so forth, upon assuming a connection with another means of knowledge, [apply] only to a specific relationship.

The causes [of the rule] exist, but not independently. Therefore, the act of eating for persons is enjoined at the time marked by the conclusion of the six-day period; hence, the eating should not be repeated. (10.6.10)

In the Gavāmayana sacrifice, it is heard in the scripture: "Four Abhiplava six-day periods, six Pṛṣṭhya six-day periods—this constitutes one month; that is the second, that the third, that the fourth, and that the fifth. In this regard, by means of the *codaka* (the rule of extension),...
It has been established: "On the sixth day, whether condensed or expanded, one should cause him to eat honey or ghee.
Regarding this, a doubt arises: should the consumption of the liquid (rasa) be performed every month, or should it be done only once at the very end?
What, then, is the correct conclusion? It is as stated by the aforementioned principle: [it should be done] repeatedly.
At the very end, he desists from the activity of moving through the *vahni*, not before;

even after having performed six *ṣaḍahas*, he indeed exerts himself again for another six *ṣaḍahas*. Nor does that six-day period become completed until he exerts himself once more for its sake. But at the absolute end, he does not [exert himself] again.

One exerts effort; therefore, it follows that one should perform [the act] at the end of all [six]. This being the position reached, we reply: "But there must be repetition because of the intervention and the difference in time. There should be a "repetition" of the consumption of the *rasa*, not a single performance. Why? Because of the repetition of the occasion (*nimitta*); the completion of the six [days] (*ṣaḍaha-saṃsthā*) is the occasion, and that six-day period repeats itself. Since that [period] repeats, the occasion—the completion—repeats; therefore, [the act] should be repeated.
As it has been said: "For at the very end, he ceases from the six-day period, not before;
even though he has completed it, he again exerts himself for that purpose. To this it is replied:
Even though he proceeds again, nevertheless, having completed that [first cycle], he begins anew, and again...
He completes [the rite], not according to the previous procedure of the *ṣaḍaha*; thus there is a repetition of the *pṛṣṭhya* for one who has not ceased [the sequence].

Here, it is separated by four *abhiplava*s; therefore, because of the intervention of another intermediate action, the reading in the Ādarśa manuscript is "pṛṣthagato 'punaranu" (having gone separately, he does not repeat).

The distinction is that it is understood that the operation has reached its completion. And as long as that [operation] is not completed, it is impossible to perform the act of eating; for it has already been stated that there are two modes of action: the state of indifference and the intervention of another action. Therefore, every month, the [period of non-eating] recurs with an interval; and while that is recurring, the eating occasioned by the conclusion [of the vow] also recurs.
Thus, for this reason, it returns every month. (10.6.1150)

In the context of the twelve-day sacrifice, it is heard: "On the abbreviated six-day [sacrifice], one should eat honey or ghee.

Regarding this, there is a doubt: should those who have been consecrated eat honey or not? What is the prima facie view? That they should not. Why? Because they are consecrated and are thus celibates (brahmacārins), and honey is forbidden for a celibate.
It is prohibited by the statement, "One should avoid honey and meat. Therefore, they should not eat it. [Objection:

"But surely this statement would override the general prohibition. [Response: We say it does not override it. How so? If this [specific rule] were not overriding [the general], it would be purposeless in the context of the *dvādaśāha* sacrifice; therefore, it would have to override it. But it does not.

[The opponent says: "It is meaningless. How so? Having accepted the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) as being of both kinds [Sattra and Ahīna], both [substances]—clarified butter (*ghṛta*) or honey (*madhu*)—must be prepared. In that case, the consumption of clarified butter will pertain to the sacrificers (*satriṇaḥ*), while the application of honey will pertain to the officiating priests (*ṛtvijaḥ*) in the Ahīna; thus, both will be connected to the twelve-day sacrifice through a distinction of scope. No.
And thus there will be conduct that is contradictory; therefore, they should not undertake [the vow].
Or rather, it should be consumed, because of its purpose [in that context]. (Siddhānta 33)

Commentary: This is not the case that "honey must not be eaten by those who possess power" (sacins); rather, it must be eaten. How so? It is stated without distinction for one who is performing [the rite], having accepted both modes.

Regarding the statement, "When the six-day period of the Pṛṣṭhya has concluded, one should eat honey or ghee for twelve days," both options are alternatives (vikalpa) and not to be applied according to a fixed rule of performance; therefore, even those who are initiated (sacins) may eat honey. As for the objection that—since they serve a purpose through different applications—it is not right to set aside [the prohibition], and that in this way the absence of honey during the twelve-day period is not contradicted—it is replied: when the six-day period has passed...

When it is stated without distinction that one may eat honey or ghee, whether in connection with the *saca* (the sacrificial session) or not, or whether in connection with the *ahīna* (the multi-day sacrifice) or not, by what means do we establish a restriction? If you say "by contradiction," no; for injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) are established through a difference in their scope: the prohibition pertains to the human purpose (*puruṣārtha*), while the injunction pertains as a constituent part of the ritual (*karmāṅga*).
Moreover, if the superiority of the prohibition were accepted here, the scriptural statement would be rendered entirely meaningless.

If it is argued that [the two statements] have different meanings, we say no, because their objects are distinct. For an option (*vikalpa*) occurs between two statements that have the same purpose and the same object, not between those with different purposes. And here, a difference in purpose is perceived. Why? Because the injunction has as its purpose the completion of the ritual action (*karmasaṅguṇya*), whereas for the prohibition, the accomplishment of the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) for the person results from the performance of the restrictive rule (*niyamānuṣṭhāna*). Therefore, they should offer the *prāśitra*. (1.4.29–70)11
