Regarding the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*), it is heard [in the scripture]: "With this vessel, containing the waters of the ocean, he takes the mental day (*mānasaṃ manaḥ*) for Prajāpati, saying, 'To Prajāpati, thee, the pressed! Concerning this, there is a doubt: Is the mental day another day distinct from the twelve-day sacrifice, or is it a constituent part (*aṅga*) of the sacrifice? [The reading in the Nyāyamālā is: "With this vessel, containing the waters... This is the meaning: the earth...
"Pārka, samudraḥ, somaḥ, prajāpatiḥ as the deity; for such a word-form, the suffix *bhama* is the means of formation; this is the *āja-sa* [suffix]," so they say regarding this grammatical operation.
[Page 641] 10th Chapter (Pāda: 2)

Thus it is said. And here, certain grounds for differentiation appear; wishing to refute them, the Teacher presents [the following]: "There might be another mental mahāh. Why? Because of designation by way of distinction—it is designated as distinct from the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha).

How so? Because it designates the Mānasa as not being included within the Dvādaśāha, stating: "Speech is the Dvādaśāha; the mind is the Mānasa. This is because of the praise of speech in the phrase "Speech is the Dvādaśāha," and the praise of the mind in the phrase "The mind is the Mānasa. Just as a difference between speech and mind is understood from the facts, so too is there a difference between these two—the Dvādaśāha and the Mānasa—since they exist separately and are distinct.
There is a designation [of it], and not otherwise; it is understood from the designation that "this day is distinct" because it is heard [in the scripture].
And because of familiarity with that. (35) (01)

"Therefore, there is another day. Why? Because by that mental day, the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is praised. How? [It is said: "Indeed, the days of the twelve-day sacrifice have been shaken off and are devoid of essence."

"They swell those very meters by means of the mind alone"; by stating that "in the twelve-day sacrifice, those meters which have lost their essence are swelled by means of the mind," it shows [the sacrifice] to be distinct from the twelve-day [sacrifice]. How so? "Because of the praise," for it is not by its own self that it [is praised].

There is praise (saṃstuti). Why? Because of the absolute difference between the object of praise and the act of praising; for Devadatta is not praised by Devadatta himself, but is praised by means of distinct parts such as his head, feet, and so forth. Similarly here, because of the praise that "the twelve-day sacrifice is praised by the Mānasa [cup]," a distinction is understood.
And there is an injunction subsequent to that which follows the word *aharantāt*. (02)
Commentary:

From this also, it is understood that [the action] occurs immediately after the end of the day. Why? Because it is enjoined as being subsequent to the "end of the day" of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha), stating: "Having performed the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings, having moved eastward, they proceed to the Mānasa [offering]."
In the Mīmāṃsā system, it is said:

"They proceed. If this were an injunction regarding the qualities of the twelve-day sacrifice (dvādaśāha), then the rule that the twelve-day sacrifice ends with the Patnīsaṃyāja offerings would apply; however, if it pertains to another day, then this property belongs to other days and not to the twelve-day sacrifice, so there will be no fault. This is also because of the distinctness [of the case].
It is understood that this is the perfection of the essence of dhāraṇā.
Commentary:
Next, [the rule] regarding number is like that of a thousand.
(Candrananda’s Nyāyaviniścaya) This is the refutation of an objection. What is this objection?—Is it not thus?

The expression "twelve days" (*dvādaśāhaḥ*) is not applicable to thirteen days. To this it is replied: when it is understood through another means of knowledge that the word is employed in reference to such a meaning, then, due to its proximity to the number, the usage is established by figuratively attributing the quality [of being twelve] to the thirteen. This is just as in the case of the statement, "The *atirātra* consists of a thousand days;
one should sacrifice with the *atirātra* which accomplishes a thousand," even though there are more [days].

The word "thousand" is seen to be used for a thousand; likewise, here too, it will apply to something greater. Alternatively, this is a name for a collection of rituals: it is determined that the term "Dvādaśāha" denotes as many rituals as are undertaken and employed. All [the rituals] are included by virtue of the context.
There is no fault, for through its application it will be expressive of all.
Or rather, it is like a wheel, because there is an absence of impelling force. (Siddhānta) || 38 ||
Commentary:
There would be an injunction of a quality for the tenth day, not an injunction of a distinct day.
Why? Because there is no statement that establishes another day. How so? First, it is as follows:

It is heard [in scripture]: "With this vessel, which has the ocean as its essence, I accept the libation for Prajāpati; thus he takes the Manograha, the libation belonging to Prajāpati. Since this is an injunction regarding the taking of the libation (graha) by accepting the tenth day, and since the rule for the consecration (saṃskāra) is given as "he consecrates," there is no difference in the ritual action (karman) due to a difference in the consecration.
And it has been stated that "the modakas are conditioned phenomena," yet the substance is intended to be heavy; thus, in this manner, the section concludes.
555 (2|1|350) Action is not the primary factor. Just as the *Aṃśu* and *Ādābhya* offerings, when prescribed,
do not divide the action but rather occur within the *camas* rite, so too are the other two cup-offerings (*graha*).

They are understood not as separate actions; for even if this were a mere coloring [of the rite] rather than a separate action, such a conception would still result in the undesirable consequence of having to resort to inference based on unseen factors (*adṛṣṭānumāna*).

Because there is a connection with the morning [rite], there is no introduction of something not under discussion nor the performance of another action; therefore, it is not a different day, but rather a prescription of an accessory on that very tenth day.
The tenth [chapter] is for the purpose of stating the emission (*visarga*). 38. (01)

For this reason as well, there is no separate day, and it is merely an injunction regarding the qualities (guṇavidhi) of that very same [day]. Why? Because of the statement concerning the "emission of the tenth" (daśamavisarga); for there is indeed a statement regarding the emission of the tenth: "This, namely the Mānasa [sacrifice], is the emission of the tenth day. By stating that "this Mānasa is the end (anta) of the emission of the tenth," he shows that this is the conclusion of the tenth through that which possesses an end, and not that this is an independent rite.
Therefore, it is understood that this too is a limb of the tenth [chapter], and not a separate subject matter.
And because of the scriptural statement regarding its quality, [the rite] occurs on the tenth day. (Sūtra 40) (Yukti 2)

The limb [of the sacrifice] is to be performed. How so? Because in this way the scripture will be properly construed: "On the tenth day they proceed with the Mānasa [offering]," and "On the tenth day they praise with the Sārparājñī verses. This is because the tenth position is indicated as being of primary importance.
Because the cup (graha) is that which is to be established, this quality belongs to its hymn (stotra); thus it is understood that this is not a different matter from the tenth [chapter].
• Because of the consistency of the number. (41) (03)
According to the Sūtra, the reading "daśame 'van" would be appropriate.

Mīmāṃsā Darśana Bhāṣya:

And if this were a secondary quality (guṇa), then the expression ‘dvādaśāha’ would be consistent with me; otherwise, since there are thirteen [days], the term ‘dvādaśāha’ would be an inconsistent designation for me, because it could not be so designated. As for what was said—that it is by way of a figurative application (guṇavṛtti) like the word ‘sahasra-sādhya’—that is incorrect.

That it "will come to be" is untenable. Why? Because in that case, since the number [one hundred] is apprehended through another means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), it is determined that the word "thousand" is used in a figurative sense (*gauṇī vṛtti*) with respect to something additional; however, here there is no evidence for anything additional to the thing to be named (*saṃjñeya*), by which a figurative usage might be resorted to.
As for this statement, "With this vessel, thee," that too is because of the injunction regarding the consecration (*saṃskāra*) of the cup (*graha*).

It has been established that on that day one prescribes the practice of the sacrifice (*yāga*), and not a different ritual action (*karmāntara*). If this is so, then this direct scriptural statement (*pratyakṣa-vacana*) does not establish another day, nor does any other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇāntara*) apply; by which we could determine that the use of the word [denoting the sacrifice] applies to something additional. Therefore, it is not [the case].
The application [of the name] is by means of a more direct function (*vṛtti*).

As for the argument that, because it is the name of a group of rituals, those many [subsidiaries] will be accepted by virtue of the context (*prakaraṇa*), and thus repetition will occur through the form of the name—that too is not correct; this is true.

This is the name of a collection of rites (*karmagaṇa*), not by virtue of an association with something other than its actual meaning; for these twelve rites, being delimited by the *śrautasūtras* and brought together as one, constitute the name of that collection of rites in this form, and not merely by way of their sequential order. For indeed, in all cases...

Among the names of ritual acts (*karmanāmadheya*), the term "name" (*nāma*) occurs as a restatement (*anuvāda*) through its connection with the meaning [of its constituent parts], rather than by mere technical convention (*paribhāṣā*) while disregarding worldly meaning—just like the terms *dvṛddhi* and *guṇa*. For example:
*agnihotra*, *śyena*, and *jyotiṣṭoma*; likewise, the term *dvādaśāha* [is so called] through the connection with its meaning.
It is not [a case of] name, but rather due to the absence of an object; therefore, this is not a valid objection.

And because, when there is a difference from the animal, [the cognition] exists for one [of them]. (42) (04)
Commentary:

From this also, it is understood that [the animal] is an additional element (āraṅga). Why? Because, beyond the [standard] animals, it shows an excess of "one," not two. How so? "The animal which is left over shall be dedicated to Indra and Agni."

Having prescribed the set of eleven animals for the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) with the words "the work is to be done," the text shows the surplus of one when [the number] is divided; therein, one is left over—it does not become one [of the days]. How so? There are eleven animals and twelve days; by stating that there is a surplus of one, it implies that these are twelve days.
It causes [the sacrifice] to proceed. Furthermore, if there were thirteen days, there would be an absence of two [components], not of one;
therefore, for this reason as well, it is an auxiliary part of the day, not a separate ritual action.
Sūtra 43: [The case of] the designation of praise is prohibited by way of its connection with a limb, like the observance of a vow.
(Śrauta Sūtra 1.1)

In this Sūtra, the refutation of two [objections] regarding the *sruca* ladles is stated. As for what was said—that there is a difference because of the distinct designation of the mental day (*mānasa-ahar*) as something separate, and because it is praised together with that mental [day], and that one does not praise oneself by means of oneself—here it is replied: this is not so.

This is not contradictory; for it is observed that the praise of a whole may be expressed through a part, as in the case of the *saṃvatsara-sattra* by means of the ritual of the *mahāvrata*: "These [people] indeed depart from the pair when they undertake the *saṃvatsara*;

two couples copulate within the altar; by that very pair, they do not depart. Having thus stated the defect of the whole, one favors the whole by means of the ritual of its constituent part, the *mahāvrata*.

He shows that praise is expressed by means of its constituent parts; for even in common worldly usage, a whole is indeed indicated by its parts, as in the expression, "Devadatta is handsome because of his long hair. Therefore, there is no fault here in the fact that the twelve-day sacrifice (*dvādaśāha*) is praised in this manner.

The reading is thus throughout. Here, "sutiyapadeśam" (the designation as a son) should be considered as referring to the living being (*jīva*). It is more appropriate for the reading to be "na vipratiṣiddham" (it is not contradictory).

"Because of the statement [of the scripture], it is not ending with that.
(Bhāṣya-nirṇaya 2). Bhāṣya: As for what was stated—that this is a different statement—thus, in the case of the Dvādaśāha, the sequence ends with the Mānasa."

One [should perform] the entire sacrifice as the archetype. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 45 ||
In this context, the *sacrifices* (satras), beginning with the Dvādaśāha, serve as the examples. Regarding these, there is a doubt: should one person perform the sacrifice, or many?

What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? "One. Why? Because "as in the archetype" (*prakṛtivat*); in the Jyotiṣṭoma, which is the archetype, there is a single performer; therefore, by extension of that rule (*codaka*), for the sake of following the injunction, one alone should perform it. But surely, many are heard [to be mentioned] in the scripture?
"Only those who know thus sit together; only those who know thus enter into the *sacā*.
It is replied: the *sacā* is enjoined for those who possess desire, and they are indeed mutually independent;
even if they perform it individually, nevertheless, with reference to the performance of the *sacā*, many [are required].

The plural number will be used because they act in this way. Just as in the world, the plural is seen even for those acting individually—such as, "If the god should rain, many would practice agriculture"—it will be appropriate. The reading in the Ka0 saṃ0 pu0 is "tadaṅgatvena."
The tenth quarter-verse.
"Many Brāhmaṇas would cook those five animals"—thus it is said. Likewise, there is the observation of usage even in the Veda:
"Having moved away from the Sadas, they should sacrifice with the Pṛṣṭha-prasthāna. So it is here as well.
The plural forms "āsīran" and "upeyuḥ" will occur.
But on account of the scriptural statement, it should belong to many. (Siddhānta) || 46 ||

Commentary: This is not the case—that only one should sacrifice, not many. What then? Many should sacrifice. Why? Because of the scriptural statement; for there is this scriptural statement: "They should sit," "They should approach."
Thus, an application connected with plurality is enjoined; by virtue of this direct statement, it would set aside the single *kalā* obtained through the general rule (*codaka*).
If it be argued that there would be a designation [of the sacrifice] by means of the word [‘bhū’]. (Sūtra 47) (0)

As for what was said— that, having observed a connection with a general action, the use of the plural number will occur as in common worldly usage, just as in the expression "they should perform agriculture," and that such a plural form is seen even in the Veda, as in "they should sacrifice with the Pṛṣṭhaja-manīya [rite]"— that must be refuted.
Bhāṣya:
Not so, because of the designation as a single entity. (Sūtra 48; Ārambhaṇa-nirṇaya)

This [view] that it has a single agent does not hold true. Why? Because of "the designation as one. How so? It says thus: "He who accepts the Soma-offering (sattra) indeed eats a corpse; let only one sacrifice. By setting aside the *sattra* and prescribing the status of a single agent for another [rite], it implies that its [the *sattra*'s] nature is to have multiple agents. As for the argument "as in common worldly usage," that is not tenable; for in the world, a word being uttered merely restates a matter already established by other means, referring to a general action as "oneness" (*ekatā*). *ekakartṛkam*: having a single agent. *sacamapodya*: having set aside the *sattra*. *sāmānyakriyā*: general action. *kākākṣī*: [referring to the term *ekatā*]. *pū0*: [abbreviation for *pūrva-pakṣa*, the prima facie view].
[Page 648] It is understood that it is uttered after having considered its connection with the Mīmāṃsā system. As for the argument that it is "like the Udavasānīya,"...

That too is appropriate in the case of the *udavasānīya* sacrifice; for there, having observed various separate *udavasāna*s (concluding acts), only the action itself is enjoined. And it has already been stated that its multiplicity is merely restated because it is already established by virtue of having a common agent. Here, however, the commencement of the action is preceded by the word;

the word connects the performance with the plurality [of agents]. Therefore, since they are being adopted on the basis of the authority of the word (*śabdaprāmāṇya*), [the plurality is indeed intended].
Since plurality is intended to be expressed regarding the action, many would employ [the word].
And it shows the removal [of the original]. (01) || 48 ||
Commentary: For this reason as well, many indeed should sacrifice. Why? Because of the observation of the collective preparation (*sannivāpa*).

It speaks of the collective preparation of many fires: "Those intending to sacrifice with five animals should perform the collective preparation; those about to offer the *sāvitra* oblations should perform the collective preparation. If [they act] collectively...

In this way, the simultaneous offering (sannivāpa) of many fires becomes possible; for if one were to perform it individually, the observation of a simultaneous offering would not be possible. Therefore, from this also, it is understood that a sattra belongs to many.
Furthermore, the specific mention of "of many" with respect to a single [entity] would be redundant.
Commentary:

From this we see that there is a collective performance. Why? Because it is stated thus: "He who is indeed the householder among many sacrificers is the one who undertakes the *sattra*; for he brings about the greatest prosperity. This refers to many sacrificers having a single householder.

By stating a specific result in this active context, [the text] demonstrates the simultaneous performance of many [priests]; otherwise, since there would be a single agent and a single result when there is only one sacrificer, the relationship between general and specific would be untenable, and the mention of a specific result would be redundant. Yet, such a mention of a specific result does exist; therefore, for this reason as well [it must be so].
It is understood that many indeed should go. (10.6.14 Śrauta Sūtra)

In the case of the vessels, there is indeed an entitlement for the sacrificers themselves as officiating priests.
The other priests shall be as in the archetype sacrifice. 51. (0)
In this case, the example is indeed the Sattra sacrifice; it has been stated that there are many performers in those [sacrifices].
Now, a doubt arises: are those very sacrificers (satrin) the officiating priests (rtvijas), or should others be appointed?
What is the prima facie position? Others should be appointed as the officiating priests.

Why? Because in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, other performers are indeed enjoined as required elements; therefore, here too, when the Sattra is being performed according to the archetype (prakṛti), "others" alone must be enjoined for the sake of favoring the extended injunction (codaka). In this way, it will be performed in accordance with the archetype.
Or rather, they should be the sacrificers, because of the connection with the designation [of the priests]; thus, the status of being a sacrificer should belong to them. (Siddhānta) || 52 ||
Bhāṣya: This is not so—that the priests are others; rather, the priests are "the sacrificers themselves.
Why? Because of the connection with the designation of the priests in the act of saluting the sacrificer.

For the meaning of the term *dīkṣā* (consecration), being enjoined as something well-known through its connection with designations such as *adhvaryu* and so forth—which are based on the performance of ritual acts—indicates that those sacrificers possess the status of *adhvaryu* and the rest. How so? If they perform those ritual acts, then they are connected with those designations based on those causes, and not otherwise; therefore, it is understood that there is a relationship between them and those ritual acts. What is that statement? "The *adhvaryu* [consecrates] the *gṛhapati*... and so forth.
Having initiated the Brahman, he initiates the Hotṛ, and then the Udgātṛ;

beginning thus, all the officiating priests (ṛtvij) are introduced in connection with initiation. Therefore, it is understood that the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests when the ritual is well-conducted.
[Page 650] If it is argued that there is a consecration of the agent because of the scriptural statement, as in the case of the *ādhātṛ* priest. (Sūtra 53, Purvapakṣa)
If you think that the sacrificers themselves are the officiating priests (*ṛtvij*), that is not correct;

This is not the case—that there is a division of the sacrificial fee (dakṣiṇā); rather, the sacrificial fee should be given as a whole. Why?
Because "there is no division in the purchase" (parikraya). That is to say, those sacrificial fees would be used for the purpose of purchasing [the services].

For indeed, sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are prescribed with reference to the ritual action (*kratu*). How so? Because that much belongs to the person’s purpose; for that which possesses a fruit is what the person intends to perform, and for one performing that while taking assistants, this specific act is called "hiring" (*parikraya*). And the individual part does not possess the fruit, since the production of the fruit results from the whole; and hiring being performed with reference to the whole, [it applies to the whole].
Since the purchase has been completed for the sake of producing the whole, it is not performed again in the interim.

Furthermore, since a specific purchase is being enjoined in connection with the word *pauṇḍarīka*, it is understood that it applies only to that which is denoted by that word; for the word *pauṇḍarīka* denotes the whole.

The parts [of the sacrifice] are not [the objects of the injunction], for they are indicated by the term denoting the whole, and that very fact constitutes the fault. Indeed, figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) is resorted to only when there is no other possibility (*asambhava*), and here there is no such impossibility. Therefore, having accepted the whole, the priests should perform their duties only once. Consequently, the purchase (*parikraya*) is performed once; and in this single performance, there is compliance with the injunction regarding the ritual procedure (*prayogavacana*), and because the commencement of the performance is singular, it possesses a broad scope (*mahāviṣayatā*).
Regarding the word "of the treatise" (śāstrasya), for this reason as well, this alone is the logical conclusion.

Because of the predominance of the *śrā* (the primary ritual) and because the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) are subordinate to it, all these [fees] pertain as a remainder to all the days; and whatever refinement (*saṃskāra*) pertains to that which has become a remainder is performed by each respective *śrā*.
Therefore, "on each day" there is "the complete refinement."
If it is argued that [the two are] not [identical] because they have the same meaning, [we reply: no. (Sūtra 68) (Pūrvapakṣa 26)

And even in a single instance...

"I am already conditioned by that [initial] refinement; since the purpose of the refinement has been accomplished while they were being given, there is no further need for refinement. Therefore, they should be refined only once."

"Because of the difference in time at the point of origin. At the point of origin, the sacrificial fees (dakṣiṇās) are heard to be connected with a specific time: "Therefore, in the world of the Triṣṭubh, the sacrificial fees are given at the midday pressing (mādhyandina-savana)."

All the *śrajas* (sacrificial offerings) are subsidiary elements (*śeṣabhūta*) to all [the pressings]; and since the midday pressings (*mādhyandināni savanāni*) of those [offerings] are distinct, and because no specific distinction is perceived therein, the loss of the consecration (*saṃskāralopa*) would belong only to that [pressing] at which they are not performed, due to the difference in the performance (*prayogabheda*); nor [does it apply] to either one [of the two pressings].
When they are being consecrated, they become something else once consecrated; therefore, they should be consecrated separately.

"It will come to be. To this it is replied: It is true that in all cases the status of being a subsidiary (*śeṣabhāva*) is based on scriptural injunction;

Thus, when this distinction is stated, only as many [mantras] as have been presented are excluded because their purpose has been served by that distinction; other mantras possessing those same indicative marks (*liṅga*) do not follow as a consequence. Therefore, there is the inclusion of only those specific ones that possess the indicative mark, and not all of them. Furthermore, it is not proper for the principal element to be repeated merely out of deference to a subordinate quality (*guṇa*), simply because such qualities exist. In this way, there will be both brevity and facility in performance. Moreover, on this view, the indicative mark itself remains fully effective.

How so? For the indicative mark (*liṅga*) is stated as the defining characteristic of the *sāmidhenī* verses; and although not all verses possessing that mark are employed, those that are used remain indeed characterized by that mark and do not possess any other mark. Why? Because of the scriptural statement; for there is this statement: "He measures on a cloth, and he brings it down with a cloth. By the force of this statement, it must be so regulated. (10.6.20)

"The skin"—why? Because "the whole is enjoined. It is the entire animal dedicated to Agni-Soma that is prescribed, not the status of being dedicated to Agni-Soma for the individual limbs separately.
Therefore, having cut portions from the substance in the form of the animal, they are to be offered to Agni and Soma.

In the case of the *śrahiṣṭha* and *paśubandha* sacrifices, there would be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*); therefore, the entire sacrificial post (*paraśu*) constitutes a single oblation (*havis*).

And this it demonstrates: "Now, the Kāpeyas of the Salāṅga lineage should take the front part of the right foot; that becomes the portion of the whole animal. And likewise: "The Gopāyanas of the Sthamba lineage should take the front part of the right foot; that becomes the portion of the whole animal. Thus, [it refers to] the whole.
It shows the cutting-off (avadāna) of the sacrificial animal; therefore, for that reason as well, the entire sacrificial animal is a single oblation (havis).
Or rather, it applies to each individual limb, because the limbs are conceived separately, as in the case of the cups (grahas).
The word "vā" (or) sets aside the alternative view: it is not the case that for us there is only one sacrificial offering (*havis*) for the animal sacrifice.

[The opponent says: "It is for the sake of the *mīmāṃsā*-grass. But what then? It is a distinct sacrificial portion (*havirbheda*) for each limb. Why? Because of the "separate preparation" (*pṛthak-prakalpanatvāt*): the limbs are prepared separately—"He cuts a portion from the heart first, he cuts a portion from the tongue, he cuts a portion from the breast, he cuts a portion from the two forelegs, he cuts a portion from the two flanks, he cuts a portion from the rectum. This cutting of portions is heard [in the scripture] as being performed upon the heart and so forth; this would not be possible if it were not a distinct portion.

Therefore, the supreme [sacrificial substance] must be manifested through the form of the animal and so forth; for when that [supreme substance] is being manifested, there is no subsequent deficiency of the animal and so on.

Consequently, this follows: if the sacrifice were performed with the mere external form of the animal, it would cause a deficiency; and having internalized that deficiency of the animal and so on, one is unable to directly define the sacrificial material.

Therefore, that generic form (ākṛti) ought to assist by means of questioning; subsequently, whatever substances such as the heart and so forth belong to the animal victim, from those one should cut off portions and offer them—
as in the case of "the cup" (graha)— just as in the Soma sacrifice, where one "takes the Aindravāyava cup" and "takes the Maitrāvaruṇa cup."
Because of the separate conceptualization in the statement, "He takes the draught for the Aśvins," the sacrificial oblation (*havis*) is the Soma juice, not the Soma plant;

this should be understood in the same way here as well. Furthermore, the injunction as a whole remains entirely consistent even when the oblation consists of the constituent parts. Moreover, the observation cited there is all the more appropriate if there are multiple oblations.
How so? It shows that the gift of the entire Panorakhada cannot be performed by another through a desire for favor, as it is handed over to the Pārava. (10/7/10)
By means of these specific limbs, such as the heart and so forth, this is the locus for the realization of the *yāmās* and *uḍās*.
Because of the difference in the sacrificial oblation, there is a repetition of the rite; therefore, the portioning (avadāna) should be made from each of them. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 3 ||

It has been established that there is a distinct oblation for each individual mark (*pratyaṅka*). This is now being deliberated upon: the word "iti" appears as if it were dropped [in the text]. Should the sacrifice be accomplished with any one part of the offering material, or should portions be cut from all of them, or should it be done by means of a selection—that is, by some [specific] part? What is the prima facie view? That portions should be cut from all of them, and thus the act of cutting (avadāna) should be repeated. Why? Because of the diversity of the offering materials (havirbheda).

The sacrificial oblations (*havīṃṣi*) are divided; those which are mentioned in the section on portions (*avadāna*), such as the heart and so forth, and the remaining parts which are demarcated by the form of the animal (*paśvākṛti*), from all of these [parts] the portion must be cut off. For it is by the form of the animal that certain specific features are demarcated; therefore, if the portion were cut from only a single limb, all the specific features demarcated by the form of the animal would not be included.

If they were to be taken together, then the status of being a subsidiary (*aṅgabhāva*) would not be established by means of the animal's form (*paśvākṛti*). For it is only when the "meat-night" (*māṃsarātri*) is delimited by various specific qualifiers that it is brought to the state of being a subsidiary; otherwise, it is not. Indeed, when there is a single oblation (*ekahaviṣṭva*), the portions of the limbs delimited by the animal's form flow forth exactly as prescribed through the mere repetition of all the cuttings-off (*avadāna*). If the limbs were prepared separately, one who cuts from a single limb would omit certain specific features; however, by repeating the cuttings-off, [all features are preserved].
[The opponent says: "It encompasses all specific individuals; therefore, the animal must be offered from among all [of them].

[Objection: "The entire post is pierced by one [stake], because it is mentioned as a whole.

(Pūrva-pakṣa) Bhāṣya: In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the animal dedicated to Agni-Soma, according to the text: "When the initiated one immolates the animal for Agni-Soma. In this regard, a doubt arises: is the entire post [pierced] by one [stake]?

Is it the oblation (*havis*) itself, or is it a distinct oblation for each individual limb? What is the prima facie view? That the oblation is one. Why? Because it is enjoined as a whole; for the state of being dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīyatā*) is enjoined with respect to the entire *parvan*, not separately for the limbs.
Therefore, having cut off portions from that substance consisting of fifty animals, they should be offered to Agni and Soma.

If the word "animal" (*paśu*) were not used in the sense of a sacrificial oblation (*havis*), there would have to be a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). Therefore, the entire animal constitutes a single oblation.
And this [text] shows it: "Now, the Kāpeyas said: 'If one were to cut off a portion from the front part, that would be a portion of the whole animal. Furthermore, the Gopāyanas say:

"One should cut from the eastern part of the right fore-foot; thus one cuts from the entire animal"—this shows that the cutting of the animal is performed from the whole. Therefore, for this reason also, the entire animal constitutes a single oblation.
Or rather, it pertains to each individual limb, because the limbs are conceived separately, just like the planets. || 2 ||
The word "or" (vā) in the commentary sets aside the previous position: it is not the case that the six animals constitute a single oblation.
What then? There is a distinction of oblations for each limb. Why? Because they are separately prepared.
The various limbs are designated separately:

"He cuts from the heart, he cuts from the tongue, he cuts from the breast, he cuts from the two forelegs, he cuts from the two sides, he cuts from the rectum. It follows; thus it occurs: if the sacrifice were performed with the form of the animal, it would be defective; and by concealing that animal-form, it is not possible to directly define the sacrificial substance.

The heart and other organs which are mentioned are the sacrificial oblations (havīṃṣi); having cut portions from them, they are to be offered.

This is "like the cups" (grahavat)—just as in the Soma sacrifice, where one says, "He takes the cup for Indra-Vāyu," "He takes the cup for Mitra-Varuṇa," "He takes the cup for the Aśvins"; because of this separate preparation, the Soma juice is the oblation, not the Soma creeper itself.

In this way, it should also be understood here. For even in the case of that which is not a sacrificial oblation (*ahaviṣya*), the entire injunction (*codanā*) is indeed applicable through the act of offering (*praṇāyya*). Now, as for the observation mentioned there, it is all the more appropriate when there are multiple oblations.
How so? Because the cutting off of the entire animal (*paśu*) by another [person] while smelling it does not [constitute a fault].
It is explained thus: he shows [this]. (10.7.10)

Is the sacrifice to be accomplished by means of any one part whatsoever, or must the portion be cut from all [the parts], or rather, by way of exclusion, from some [specific] part? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? That the portion must be cut from all [parts], and thus the act of cutting (avadāna) must be repeated. Why? Because "of the difference in the sacrificial materials" (haviḥ-bheda);
for the sacrificial materials—the heart and so forth—which are mentioned in the context of the cutting, are distinct.

And the remaining [limbs] are delimited by the animal-form (*paśvākṛti*); from all of those, the portion must be cut off. For certain specific features are delimited by the animal-form; if the portion were cut from only a single limb, then all the specific features delimited by the animal-form would not be included, and thus the status of being a constituent part (*aṅgabhāva*) would not be established through the animal-form. Indeed, it is by delimiting the mass of flesh as qualified by multiple specific features that it is brought to the status of being a constituent part.

It cannot be otherwise; for when there is a single oblation (*ekahaviṣṭra*), since the collection of limbs is delimited by the form of the animal, the cutting (*śravattam*) occurs exactly as prescribed simply by not repeating the cutting of all the portions. However, if the limbs were prepared separately, one who cuts from only a single limb would omit certain specific parts; but by repeating the cuttings, one includes all the specific parts. Therefore, it is said: "One must cut from all [the limbs]."

He says: "But surely, since the specific individuals (viśeṣa) delimited by the form of the animal are for the purpose of the sacrifice, the sacrifice would be accomplished by any one of them. It is replied: It would indeed be accomplished, if the connection of the specific individuals with the sacrifice were directly stated in scripture; however, it is the form of the animal (paśvākṛti) that is heard [in scripture]. Therefore, when the specific individuals are being grasped...

Since the status of being an auxiliary (aṅgabhāva) is thus established, for that purpose, no specific distinction is understood through the injunction of performance (prayogavacana); it is not discerned which specific [auxiliary] is included and which is not. Therefore, all are taken in order to favor the injunction of performance, even in the absence of that specific [distinction] which was not grasped.

If one were to assume that it is exactly as it was heard [in the text], then by performing the slaughter of the animal and the surrounding of the altar, no additional purpose whatsoever would have been accomplished; thus, disregard for that [purpose] would be entailed. Therefore, one should cut portions from all [parts], both from the heart and others, and from what remains.
There should be a restriction (parisaṅkhyā) because of the specific instruction similar to that of the *ājyabhāga* offerings. || 4 ||

The portion to be cut off (avadāna) is to be taken from the heart and other specified parts, not from what remains. Why? Because of their specific mention; for the heart and the others are specifically mentioned in the statement: "These eleven are the portions to be cut from the animal.

It is not a mere restatement; rather, because there is a further hearing of [the Self] as devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), this serves to exclude those other [qualities] that were not heard. In the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice, there is the Agniṣomīya animal sacrifice, [established by the rule]: "The initiated one who should immolate the Agniṣomīya animal. Therein, the Sviṣṭakṛt offering is obtained through the force of the general rule (codaka);

What is established? That [the offering] is from the remnants of the sacrifice (ijyāśeṣa). Why? "Which are the three components? Even in the case of the compound *saptapada*, how is this so? It is said: this is a collective compound (*samāhāra-samāsa*), those whose collective aggregation has been stated, or which possess a connection through a single action or quality, are [the components].

Nor does one abandon the archetypal (prakṛta) subsidiaries merely because other subsidiaries are mentioned; for when some subsidiary is mentioned in a modification (vikṛti), it does not take on the status of a single syntactical unit with those archetypal subsidiaries.
Why? Because its expectancy is: "In what manner should one perform [the rite]?"

"What indeed should one do?"—in this regard, the mode known as "possession of subsidiaries" (aṅgavattā) is already established in the archetype (prakṛti), and it is required by the injunction of performance (prayogavacana). However, in the ectype (vikṛti), possession of subsidiaries is not already established; it must first be inferred and then becomes required. Nor can one abandon what is already established to establish a connection with something that must be inferred.

This is logical; therefore, even in that case, the subsidiary elements (aṅgas) are brought in by the extended application (codaka). And once the archetypal (prākṛta) elements have been grasped, the injunction of the modified (vaikṛta) elements would otherwise be purposeless;
thus, having postulated those elements, they are indeed included by the performance-injunction (prayoga-vacana) which encompasses all subsidiaries.

Where the fivefold oblation is heard, it is precisely there that it sets aside the fourfold oblation, and not elsewhere; just as it does not set it aside in another ritual sequence (*krama*), so too the *āpūrvya* oblation is capable of setting aside the fivefold oblation.

"One sacrifices the animal" (paśumālabhate). Thus it is said. To this it is replied: even so, the fivefold cutting (pañcāvatta) would be established for the primary sacrifice (apūrva). How?

For that injunction is one and the same regarding the limb-sacrifice (aṅgayāga) of the omentum (vapā); if the fivefold cutting is connected with that, then it ought to apply to the limbs as well. Because there is no word that would cause [the procedure] to cease. Therefore, in the case of the subsidiaries, it is not "fourfold.

Furthermore, regarding such subsidiaries, once the "fivefold" has arisen, another injunction is heard: "He cuts them up," which refers to the cutting of the omentum for the purpose of preparing the sacrificial offering. Therefore, even regarding the limbs, there are exactly five prostrations.
Thus ends the seventh quarter of the tenth chapter in the Mīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Śrī Bhaṭṭa Nārāyaṇa Svāmin.

The phrase "he makes [the cake] a vessel" is used for the sake of its figurative significance (arthavāda). What, then, is the meaning here? It is for the purpose of praise:

that even though the two *ājyabhāga* offerings are not actually performed in the case of Soma, they are nonetheless present. "How could they not be performed?"—this is the praise for that purpose. (10.8.20)

In the first section (*adhikaraṇa*), the word *na* has the sense of exclusion (*paryudāsa*); in the second, however, it has the sense of a commendatory statement (*arthavāda*). Now, what is the definition of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*)? The definition is stated: "But a prohibition would be that which is characterized by *jyotiṣṭoma*," as for example: "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra*."

In that case, it is not possible to interpret this as a mere exclusion (*paryudāsa*), for then there would be no connection at all—namely, that "one takes up the *ṣoḍaśin* [cup] in the *atirātra* sacrifice, excluding the *śratirātra*. Nor is it possible through the force of an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*). Therefore, the connection is with the statement "he does not take it up. Now, one might object: "An injunction and a prohibition, being mutually contradictory, cannot coexist. It is replied: by virtue of the authority of the scriptural word (*vacana-prāmāṇyāt*), the prohibition will prevail by setting aside the injunction; and the injunction likewise...

If one maintains that there is no other way than negation, then a false cognition will be postulated; for when it is an affirmation, it is not a negation, and when it is a negation, it is not an affirmation.

Now, [it may be argued that] an affirmation would always result in the negation [of its opposite]. To this it is replied: this has already been stated—that due to the authority of the scriptural word and because of contradiction, a false cognition arises regarding the single application of the injunction.

"Having taken [one], one does not take even a second"; therefore, it is established by either alternative. Now, an objection is raised: "In the absence of another alternative, there would be a deficiency (vaiguṇya). To this it is replied: True, there is a deficiency; yet even in the face of that deficiency, the accomplishment of the rite itself is understood from the authority of the scriptural statement. Therefore, there is no fault. However, where there exists another mode of expression for the sentence, there no option (vikalpa) arises, as for example:
"One should perform the *ye yajāmahe* formula at the *manu-yājas*. (10.8.350)
The section concerning the status as an explanatory passage (*arthavāda*) of the prohibition beginning with "One should not [eat] wild sesamum seeds" (*na añjati jarttilān*).

If one does not postulate another [result], then [the statement] would be a mere explanatory eulogy (arthavāda), because of its lack of purpose and because of the capacity of the other [element]. || 7 ||
In the Agnihotra, it is stated: "One should offer either *jarbharī* and *vāvadī* or one should offer *gavedhuka* and *vāmśā*;
[in doing so] one does not harm domestic animals nor wild ones."
Thus it is said: "Now, one should offer the Agnihotra with wild sesame (*jartila*) and *gavedhuka* seeds mixed with milk.
Regarding this, there is a doubt: should one offer [the oblation] with wild sesame seeds...?

Is the injunction "He offers with *jartila* seeds or with *gavedhuka* seeds," while "Not as an oblation are *jartila* seeds and *gavedhuka* seeds" is the prohibition; or rather, both of these are for the purpose of an explanatory statement (*arthavāda*), while "He performs the *agnihotra* with milk" is the injunction? What is the prima facie view? That "*jartila* seeds or *yava* seeds" is the injunction, because the word of injunction is directly perceived, and so too is "not as an oblation."

The prohibition is perceptible; the injunction "one offers the Agnihotra with milk" is a subsequent injunction, precisely because it is perceptible. This being the case, there is an option: one may offer either with *jartila* (wild sesame) gruel or with *gavedhuka* (coix) gruel, or else one should not offer with those two, but rather with milk. And not...

An exclusion by way of affirmation (*paryudāsa*) is appropriate here; for the word "not" (*na*) has no semantic capacity [to negate] either *jartila* grains or *yava* grains, nor even *gavedhuka* or *yava* grains, because it forms a compound with the word "oblation" (*āhuti*). Or, if such a capacity were assumed, there would be no syntactic connection at all—[the meaning would be] "an oblation consisting of non-*jartila-yava-grains," rather than "an oblation of *jartila-yava-grains*."

Regarding the injunction "he offers," if it were a prohibition (*paryudāsa*), the injunction would be purposeless because the entire [set of materials] would be excluded; furthermore, if it were an injunction for *cīra* grass, the prohibition would be redundant since *jartila*, *sāka*, and *vedhuka* grains are not otherwise obtained [as alternatives].
Therefore, it is an option (*vikalpa*).

This being the case, we reply: there would be a prohibition of the meaning [of the injunction] if one were to postulate another injunction; for if the injunction "One offers the Agnihotra with milk" were already established, then the statement regarding the *gavedhukā* offering—even though it is a statement of prohibition—would serve as an explanatory praise (*arthavāda*), because it would otherwise be purposeless.
For a prohibition becomes purposeless when one is indeed offering with milk; it is only by virtue of that fact [that the prohibition has its purpose].

The *jartila* seeds and *gavedhukā* grass constitute the *śrānāti*. Now, how can this be an oblation (*āhuti*) and yet be employed in the sacrifice? It is "by virtue of the capacity of another" (*parasāmarthyāt*);

that is, the capacity of the injunction regarding *jartila* and *gavedhukā* and of the prohibition [of other grains] is established by the subsequent injunction: "One offers the *agnihotra* with pathyā [grain]."

It exists; therefore, everything is a single sentence. How so? "One should offer oblations of wild sesame gruel or wild rice gruel"—this is connected directly with the statement of censure itself: "This is indeed not a sacrificial oblation (anājati)."
And as for the disparagement of *jartila* (wild sesame) and *gavedhukā* (coix grass), that is for the purpose of praising the injunction regarding milk.

How so? The oblation of *jartila* and *gavedhukā* possesses certain qualities, yet in it there are neither domestic animals nor wild ones. Even so, with respect to the milk-oblation, it is indeed not a substitute (*anājatireva*). Thus...

"The milk-oblation is more excellent" means that the statement "one should offer a gruel of wild sesamum seeds" is not intended as a prescription for what ought to be done, but rather for the purpose of prohibition. For if it were an instruction on what should be performed, something would have to be inferred; however, in connection with a prohibition, there is praise of the other alternative through direct censure, which is consistent with the immediate sequence [of the texts], just as in the case of [the warning against] poison.

"It should never be cultivated"—this is stated for the purpose of connecting with the prohibition of the duty regarding the *viṣabhataṇa* grass, not for the sake of its performance; it should be understood in the same way here as well. (90|8|40)

Bhāṣya: Regarding the offerings to Tryambaka in the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, they recite: "It is to be sprinkled with clarified butter."
They deliberate: "Should one sprinkle it with clarified butter? If one were to sprinkle it, one would place the animals in the mouth of Rudra;

if one were not to sprinkle it, one would not place the animals in the mouth of Rudra. However, they say: 'It must indeed be sprinkled, for there is no oblation that is not sprinkled. Likewise: "The Agnihotra is to be offered."

The exponents of the Veda deliberate thus: "It should not be offered as an oblation; for if one were to offer it, one would be offering it just like the previous offerings; but if one does not offer it, the fire would fly away. Therefore, it should be offered silently;
thus, one offers it just like the previous offerings, and the fire does not fly away. This is the meaning here.
Regarding the matter of uncertainty: "Should the cakes for Tryambaka be sprinkled with clarified butter, or should they not be sprinkled?
and "Should the Agnihotra be offered, or should it not be offered?"—these two constitute injunction and prohibition here:
"In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, the cakes for Tryambaka, made of barley and prepared on a single potsherd, [are offered] with the Tryambaka mantra."
Mādhava says: "They have been examined.
[Page 746] Is this mention of these two for the purpose of an explanatory eulogy (arthavāda)? What, then, is the prima facie view?

We say it is both injunction (*vidhi*) and prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), because that is their nature; for the form of injunction and prohibition is perceived through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*). Furthermore, by hearing [the words], their purpose as an injunction and their purpose as a prohibition are understood from the sentence (*vākya*), while their purpose as a mere explanatory praise (*arthavāda*) is also understood; yet direct statement (*śruti*) is more authoritative than a sentence. Moreover, a partial exclusion (*paryudāsa*) is not possible here. Therefore, regarding the Agnihotra, whether it should be offered or should not be offered—when it is to be offered...

At that time, the *cyammaka* offerings should either be sprinkled with clarified butter or not sprinkled; however, when they are indeed to be sprinkled, the statement regarding the sprinkling is for the purpose of clarifying the meaning, as it is stated again to prevent the doubt that the prohibition might imply their total absence.

This being the case, we reply: these examples are similar in timing to those cited in the preceding section. What is this similarity in timing? It is that after first stating an injunction and a prohibition, their connection is subsequently established; thus, this is identical to the previous section. Those injunctions and prohibitions which are heard are not for the purpose of being performed or avoided [independently].

Rather, it is for the sake of inquiry that he spoke thus: "One should perform the oblation, one should not perform the oblation"—thus do the exponents of Brahman inquire; likewise, they inquire, "The Agnihotra should be offered, or it should not be offered. And this inquiry is for the purpose of praising other injunctions, as is directly evident.

The relationship between the word and its meaning requires nothing to be postulated; for it is only in the case of injunctions and prohibitions that something might need to be postulated— such as, "If one were to sprinkle [the butter], one would place it in the mouth of Rudra"—
on the grounds that this sprinkling is more meritorious because even such a fault is not taken into account.

Thus, one should offer oblations in such a way that they are offered as before; for it is said that "if one were not to offer them, the fire would fly away"—in this manner, the offering with thirst (*tṛṣṇā-homa*) is praised, because when it is performed, both defects are avoided. (10850)

Sūtra 12: Since there is no specific qualification, the prohibition of giving, offering oblations, and cooking for one who has been initiated (*dīkṣita*) would apply to all giving, offering oblations, and cooking.

(First Pūrvapakṣa) Bhāṣya: In the Jyotiṣṭoma it is heard: "The initiated one does not give, does not offer oblations, and does not cook. Regarding this, the following point is subject to doubt: Is this a prohibition of all giving, offering oblations, and cooking?

Is it a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*) of those not joined with the seasonal sacrifices (*ṛtu-yajña*), or even of those joined with the seasonal sacrifices that are obtained through the force of the water-rite (*codaka-prāpta*), or is it an exclusion (*paryudāsa*)? What is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? It is a prohibition of all offerings involving cooking. Why? Because of "non-distinction"—there is no word expressing a specific distinction.
Therefore, there is a prohibition for all [of them]. Sūtra: Or rather, it should be the duty of those not connected with a sacrifice, because the sacrifice is directly enjoined. (2nd Pūrvapakṣa)
Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position; it is not a prohibition of all [prohibitions]. Of which ones, then? It says:
"It would be a duty for those connected with the sacrifice. Why? "Because the sacrifice is directly enjoined."

For there is indeed a direct scriptural injunction regarding giving and the other [virtues]; therefore, the prohibition would apply only by excluding what is directly enjoined.
Sūtra: "Or rather, it belongs to that [other case] as well, because there is no distinction. (Sūtra 14, Pūrvapakṣa 3)

Alternatively, that which is "inferential"—namely, what is obtained through the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) for that sacrifice—is prohibited, for that is inferential and not directly perceived (*pratyakṣa*); the prohibition applies to what is directly heard in the scripture.
However, because it serves as a supplementary part of the sentence (*vākyaśeṣatvāt*), there should be an exclusion (*paryudāsa*) of the other.
In the case of a prohibition, there would be an option. (Siddhānta) || 15 ||
The word "but" (tu) is for the purpose of emphasis. It would be a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) serving as a prohibition;

that is, it is a supplementary statement prohibiting—by way of exclusion (paryudāsa)—the previously mentioned acts such as giving and so forth, which were stated without distinction, specifically in relation to the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice.

[The word "na"] would be the remainder of the statement "one should give every day," just as [the word "na"] is [the remainder] of the statements regarding the oblation and cooking; thus it is for both. Since there is no exclusion (*paryudāsa*), there would be an option (*vikalpa*) in the case of a prohibition (*pratiṣedha*), and that has been stated to be improper; therefore, it is an exclusion (*paryudāsa*). This they recite in the Jyotiṣṭoma sacrifice: "He offers on the path.

In the *Rājasūya*, it is stated: "Having taken up the mound of an anthill, one should sacrifice. This is also heard: "That which one sacrifices in the Āhavanīya fire, by that his desired deity becomes pleased. In this regard, the following point is subject to doubt: should the offering be made on the path in the Jyotiṣṭoma, or in the Rājasūya?

Regarding the ant-hill mound (*valmīkavapā*)—is there an option (*vikalpa*) between these two [the path and the ant-hill] with respect to the *āhavanīya* fire? What is the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*)? Since the path and the ant-hill mound serve the purpose of the oblation (*homa*), their combination (*samuccaya*) is not established; for the oblation is accomplished by either one of them, since the purpose of the oblation would be fulfilled by either.
If it were claimed that both of these serve the purpose of the oblation...

Why? Because when an accomplished entity and that which is to be accomplished are mentioned together, the accomplished entity exists for the sake of that which is to be accomplished; and there is no absolute sublation regarding the subject matter of the path.
[In the case of the mantra] "The Āhavanīya fire is the slayer of enemies," it is accepted in one alternative (pakṣa) of the option.
This being the position reached, we reply: "That scriptural injunction which is without distinction is set aside by a specific injunction from afar."
It might be that what is taught specifically would be distant from this—in other words, unrelated.

For that [specific teaching] would then be "doubtful. How so? If the general rule is for the purpose of defining the specific, then it applies even to the specific; but if it is not for the purpose of defining it, then it does not apply. Thus, it is doubtful.

Alternatively, it is doubtful whether the general rule is contradicted by the specific rule. Or rather, it is doubtful whether the general rule applies to that specific case or to another; thus, that general injunction would not apply to the specific injunction. What is the reason? Because "an option is improper. How is an option improper? It is said: if the status of being the locus for the *varhiṣ* and other materials is heard [prescribed] for these oblations, yet it does not exist in the alternative case, then one who resorts to an option [commits an error].

It must be considered as lacking authoritative basis (*pramāṇāpetā*). If the status of these [fires] as the locus for the path and so forth is not heard [in scripture], then that [status] occurs only optionally; thus, it is indeed devoid of authority. Furthermore, the mention of "the path" (*vartma*) being heard [in the text] would be unintended (*avivakṣita*).

Now, if it were argued: "Its existence in the alternative case follows from the sense (*artha*), and that sense is the accomplishment of the oblation (*homa*) by means of the *āhavanīya* fire," then, if only the accomplishment of the oblation were to be performed, [the rule would follow].

It might also be pierced by means of the *āhavanīya* fire for that purpose; however, in this case, the status of being the locus for the armor and so forth is also enjoined, and that would not be included if the *āhavanīya* were employed [as the sole locus]. If it were not included, the injunction regarding the performance (*prayoga-vacana*) would be contradicted.

To this it is replied: although the status of being the locus for the path and so forth is also enjoined, since [the vessel] serves as a subordinate factor (guṇabhūta) in the oblation, it makes the oblation proper; thus, even if it is not included in that [specific context], it is not a defect, for it will become proper through another locus.
Therefore, there is indeed an option (vikalpa).

It is said: "No. Here, the connection with the *varma* and other oblations is enjoined, and that [connection] is the primary element, not the oblation itself; for if that were not included, it would not be performed according to what was heard in the text.
To this it is replied: "Even when the connection is being enjoined, this is what is enjoined: there is one thing to be accomplished."
The means of accomplishment (*sādhana*) is one, and that which is to be accomplished (*sādhya*) is the primary element, and that is the *homa*. Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*).

Even when a connection is heard [in the text], the *homa* must necessarily be performed, for it is stated: "One should perform the *homa*; thus the *āhavanīya* fire is indeed obtained. This is because, in that context, the *āhavanīya* is not a subordinate member (*aṅga*). How so?

Why is it not an auxiliary (*anaṅgatva*)? Because it does not apply to the specific cases (*viśeṣeṣu*). How is there no application? Because when the path (*vartman*) is already established as the locus (*adhikaraṇatā*), it is impossible for it to be both the cognition and the instrument (*karaṇa*) for the locus of the *āhavanīya* fire; for that which is known to have the path and so forth as its locus cannot be intended as having the *āhavanīya* fire as its locus.

[Whether] to know or to perform [it]. Śrā [says]: "It must be performed in such a way as is possible"—this will refer to the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha) in the future tense; therefore, having set aside the *am̐sa* [portion], the *āhavanīya* fire will be used. It is replied: This would indeed be so, if the instruction regarding the *āhavanīya* were not possible without setting aside the path (*vartma*) and so forth.

For there are two ways to manifest [the meaning]: either by sublation (*bādha*) or by exclusion (*paricaya*). In the case of sublation, the cognition "on the path" (*vartmani*) would have to be discarded; therefore, exclusion is preferable.
[The opponent] says: "Even in the case of exclusion, the cognition that 'it exists in the Āhavanīya fire' would be set aside."

[Page 752] We maintain that the cognition of the Āhavanīya fire depends upon the person; is it not also possible that this [cognition] cannot be produced, or that it will not be produced? He says: "This which is called the general cognition..."

He expects the performance in all specific cases; thus, since the Āhavanīya fire has been prescribed for these and other [offerings] as well, the notion of the Āhavanīya fire regarding the *varma* and other offerings cannot be set aside. Therefore, setting aside the *varma* and other offerings, it would remain [applicable].

It is said: thus, a word denoting a universal does not express particulars; for if it did express them, it would not be applicable to a cow born this very day, because there has been no prior perception [of that individual]. However, it is applicable to the universal, because the universal has been perceived previously. Therefore, a word denoting a universal does not express particulars; and for that reason...
In the case of the *madahoma*, there is the cognition of the *āhavanīya* fire. One does not address [the fire] by its primary function;
how then? By way of indication (*lakṣaṇā*). And indication would be sublated by direct statement (*śruti*).
Therefore, when "path" and so forth are obtained through direct statement in relation to the paths and so on, this *āhavanīya* is to be understood [as the object].
And as for the phrase "to perform":

he says, "But might this not also be the reverse—that since the Āhavanīya fire has already been reached, the understanding of it as the *vartma* (path) and so forth would be impossible"? This could indeed be the case;

however, the understanding of it as the *vartma* and so forth is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), whereas the understanding of it as the Āhavanīya is based on indirect indication (*lakṣaṇā*); and the understanding based on direct scriptural statement is more powerful.

Thus it has been stated. [Objection: "But surely the cognition of the *āhavanīya* fire is also scripturally enjoined (*śrauta*) even with respect to the general category [of oblations]. [Reply: It is said: the cognition of the *karma* (the act of offering) and so forth is also scripturally enjoined with respect to the general category; for that [fire] is prescribed as qualified by the *homa* (oblation), and it does not qualify this [act] when it is not a *homa*. Therefore, excluding the *amādi-homa*, the *āhavanīya* fire shall be employed in other *homas*. (10.7.80)

But when a scriptural injunction, though heard in a specific context, is not modified and occurs outside of that context, it serves to prohibit the archetypal [elements], like the *ājyabhāga* offerings. (Pūrvapakṣa 17)
Commentary:
Without reference to any specific context, it is stated: "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

This [injunction], having been set aside by the specific prescription of fifteen [verses] in the archetype (*prakṛti*), applies to all modified forms (*vikṛti*). However, in certain modified forms, it is heard again: "In the *vaiṣṭadha* and *adhvarakalpā* [sacrifices]..."
"In the Cāturmāsya sacrifices, at the Micavindā and the Vaidhātavyā, there is the *śrāyayapeṣṭā*.
It is now considered for what purpose this [text] is heard in those modified rites (*vikṛti*): what is the conclusion?

Regarding the scriptural injunction (*śāstra*) that is taught outside of a specific context (*aprakaraṇa*), which is then heard again in a particular modified rite without being part of its original modification—what is the result?

Therefore, in order to exclude the set of archetypal (prakṛta) subsidiaries, [the text states] regarding the Vaimṛdha and other sacrifices: "One should recite seventeen Sāmidhenī verses," meaning that one should not perform any other archetypal [element]. Nor is it understood that the number seventeen applies only to the Vaimṛdha and others, and not to other modified (vikṛti) sacrifices; for since that [number] is heard directly by an explicit statement (śruti) in those [sacrifices], it cannot be set aside.
But in the case of a modification, it should be for that purpose. (Yukti 18)

Bhāṣya: If, however, some modification of the *sāmidhenī* verses were heard [in the text], then it would be understood that they are enjoined for the sake of that modification; but no such modification is heard. Therefore, it is solely for the purpose of setting aside the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rule. Sūtra: Or rather, it is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*), because of its connection with the season (*ṛtu*), as it is an injunction not made in connection with a specific context (*anārabhyavidhāna*). (19) (Conclusion)
The word "or" (vā) in Bhāṣya 2.2.2 excludes the [previous] position; this remainder of the discussion concerns the three types of Vedic injunctions (*vidhi*). "Anā—" [etc.]...

Regarding the beautiful arrangement: "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses"; this applies to these specific modifications (*vikṛti*). Therefore, it would not apply to other modifications. [Objection: But surely that which is directly heard in the scripture applies to other modifications as well?

It should not be set aside. It is said: it is true that the *sāmidhenī* verses are directly heard [in the Veda], yet they are not taken up for the sacrifice because there is no connection with the sacrifice;

even the injunction of performance does not take them up when there exists a sentence establishing a connection with the *vaimṛdha* and other rites. As for this *sāptadaśya* (the number seventeen) which is mentioned as unattached (*anārabhya*), that—
The statement that "the *vaiśvadeva* and other [offerings] are subsidiary parts" is a direct scriptural text (*pratyakṣa-vākya*); therefore, no other injunctions take hold of them.
Furthermore, if they were not included within a ritual context (*akratu-grahaṇa*), the sevenfold nature of the *sāmidhenī* verses would be rendered fruitless and thus would not be performed.

Consequently, the supplementary portion of the sentence applies to the *vaiśvadeva* and others by virtue of an injunction that does not require a separate commencement (*anārambha-vidhi*). An objection is raised: "But surely this results in a split of the sentence (*vākya-bheda*)?"
It is as follows: "There are seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; they are [used] in the *vaiṣṭadhā* and other rites. It is said in reply: these are two sentences;
the latter sentence prescribes a specific detail of that very matter which was proposed by the former sentence; thus it is called a "remainder of the sentence" (*vākyaśeṣa*). (1017/8 a0)

Regarding the *darvī-homa*, it is heard in scripture: "Svāhā to the Earth! Svāhā to the Atmosphere! Svāhā to Vāyu! And there is also a general statement not connected to a specific context (*anārabhya-vacana*):
"Food is offered to the gods either with the *vaṣaṭ*-call or with the *svāhā*-call. In this regard, there is a doubt: does this [apply] to that [general case]?

The supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa) is as follows: "By means of the utterance of *svāhā*, food is offered to the gods"—this being the case in this *darvihoma* sacrifice with the formulas "To Earth, *svāhā*!
and "To the Intermediate Space, *svāhā*!"—is this indeed a supplementary statement, or is it not?

Regarding those offerings for which the *svāhākāra* has not been prescribed, should there be a *svāhākāra* in them as well? What [is the conclusion]?

This being the position reached, we reply: In the case of mantras, there can be no status as a syntactical supplement. For there is no single-sentence unity (*ekavākyatva*) between two sentences, one injunctive and the other non-injunctive; the Brāhmaṇa is injunctive, while the mantra is non-injunctive. Furthermore, in the immediately preceding section there was no connection with a ritual act (*kratu*), but here—
The connection is understood thus: "Food is offered to the gods by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call or the *svāhā*-call";

for here, the offering (*pradāna*) is the primary element. Moreover, there is an instruction regarding the subordinate element (*guṇa*): when that [offering] is performed, the utterance is "Svāhā to the Earth" (*pṛthivyai svāhā*), and not "Svāhā, to the Earth" (*svāhā pṛthivyai*).
Thus; therefore, the utterance of *svāhā* exists even in other *darvihoma* offerings as well.
Sūtra: And those [fires] are without mothers, because they are seen [to be so]. (21) (01)
Mādhava: Even though the *svāhākāra* is not explicitly prescribed for the *darvihoma*, it is nevertheless seen in certain instances, as in:
"With ghee, do you two, Heaven and Earth, fill yourselves; he offers into the two forks of the *audumbara* wood;
he causes the sound to be heard from the wind; when it reaches the ground, he utters *svāhā*"—thus it is established.
He indicates the utterance of "svāhā"; and because of the prohibition [of it]. (22) (02)

In some cases, however, there is a prohibition: "He does not utter the word 'svāhā', nor does he recite the mantra. Since a prohibition must be preceded by a prior possibility of occurrence, it functions as a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to that possibility.
It is determined. (10.7.10 Śrauta-sūtra)

The *agnyatigrāhya* cup should not be employed in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), because it is taught [only] in connection with the archetype (*prakṛti*). (Pūrvapakṣa 23)
This is stated: "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar," and likewise, "The *atyagrāhya* libations are indeed the support of the sacrifice. In this regard, there is a doubt:

does the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) extend the *atyagrāhya* to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), or not? What is the prima facie view? That the *atyagrāhya* does not apply to the modified sacrifice, because of the scriptural statement regarding the piling of the fire-altar.
The *śramyati-graha* does not apply to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*). Why? Because it is taught in the context of the modified sacrifice;
for it is indeed taught in the modified sacrifice: "Now, therefore, one sacrifices to Agni with the *agniṣṭoma*;
him with the *uktha*, him with the *atirātra*, him with the *caturrātra*, him with the *pañcarātra*, him with the *ṣaḍrātra*... [and so forth].

"By means of a seven-night [rite], by that an eight-night, by that a nine-night, by that a ten-night"; likewise, "If one were to take it with the *pṛṣṭhya*, they would touch the *pṛṣṭhas* while the sacrifice is facing forward;
if one were to take it with the *uktha*,"—the general rule (*codaka*) does not extend the application to what is directly perceived in any particular instance.
And it is enjoined in the modification.
"And the *grahaṇa* (seizing) occurs every month, as before.
(Yukti) Bhāṣya: And this is heard [in scripture]: "Every month, the *śratigrāhya* cups are drawn.
If the extended application (*codaka*) were to bring them [forward], then there would be no such instruction as "they are not seized every month. Therefore, they are indeed seized every month.
Or rather, there is a taking [of the mantra] in the heart, because of their equality. (Siddhānta) || 25 ||

Or rather, the *agni* and *atigrāhya* are taken up by the extended application (*codaka*); for there is no distinction between this [sacrifice] and its other constituent parts such that one could say, "it takes up other constituent parts" while "this one does not take them up"— this is not tenable.
Sūtra:
And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (26) (Yukti)

Furthermore, a sign is indeed seen: "One who desires, 'May I be born with a beautiful head in this world,' should pile up the *kacita* fire-altar; he should pile up the *śīrṣacita* fire-altar. Likewise, "Five..."

"One takes the *śatigrāhya* cups dedicated to Indra. This indicates that the specific features of the *atigrāhya* cup—namely, its shape like a heron (*kaṅka*) and its dedication to Indra—are obtained in the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*).
Hṛdayabhāṣya: The inclusion [of the term] should be of equal application. (Sūtra 27; 10th section).
Now, as for the objection that "it is taught in the modified sacrifice" (*vikṛti*), that must be refuted.

It is replied: the injunction is the same in whichever modified sacrifice it is taught and in its archetype (*prakṛti*); in the remaining modified sacrifices, the general rule (*codaka*) brings it forth.
The mention of "in the month" is for the purpose of prohibiting repeated practice.
