Now, as for the mention of "monthly" (*māsi*): how is this to be understood? It is for the purpose of prohibiting repeated performance; that is, they are not offered day after day, but rather at the end of each month. (10.7.110) [This concludes] the section concerning the four-fold cutting of portions in the context of preparatory rites and malevolent magic.

Sūtra: Because it exists for the sake of the production [of the offering], the fourfold [ladle] belongs to the primary act due to its connection with the oblation; the additional clarified butter (ājya) is not equal [to the other materials] because, like in common worldly practice, its production is subordinate [to the purpose]. Bhāṣya: [The fourfold ladle is used] because it is intended for the production of the offering. Since it is connected with the primary act of the oblation, the additional clarified butter is distinct; it is not on the same footing as the other materials, because—just as in the world—the production of that [butter] is subordinate to its intended use.
|| 28 || (Pūrvapakṣa) ||
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is stated: "One offers the fourfold portion.

Regarding this, the following point is subject to deliberation: does the fourfold portion consist of the two [acts of] spreading the base (upastaraṇa) and pouring over (abhighāraṇa) together with [the main oblation], or...?

Should the fourfold cutting be performed from the principal substance itself, and the spreading and sprinkling be done with an additional portion? What is the prima facie view? The fourfold cutting should be performed from the principal substance itself. Why? Because "the purpose is established by its origin"—the production of the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) serves the purpose of the oblation, as stated in the text: "That which belongs to Agni, prepared on eight potsherds, is not omitted at the new moon and full moon sacrifices. That which one offers...

The fourfold cutting (caturavatta) must be performed; and for the sake of the oblation, there is the spreading of the base (upastaraṇa) and the pouring over (abhighāraṇa) of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa).

Therefore, the fourfold portion of the sacrificial cake is to be given. There would be "excessive clarified butter" (adhikam ājyam), for that is not equal to the sacrificial cake; in the case of the sacrificial cake, that [butter] becomes a heavy burden for the purpose of the oblation.

Regarding the clarified butter (*ājya*): although there is a *ṣaḍavatta* (sixfold portioning) together with that clarified butter, nevertheless, in the act of offering (*homa*), it is treated as being only a *caturavatta* (fourfold portioning), just as in common worldly usage one says, "Devadatta is a heavy eater" (*prasthabhuk*), even though his consumption may actually exceed a *prastha* due to things like roots and tubers; nevertheless, he is designated as a "heavy eater."
The condiments are for the sake of the boiled rice.
And because of the scriptural statement regarding the refinement of that [sacrifice]. (30) (Yukti)

Furthermore, the under-spreading (upastaraṇa) and the sprinkling over (abhighāraṇa) are heard of as being for the purpose of consecrating the principal portion (pradhānāvadāna), according to the text: "In that he under-spreads and sprinkles over, he makes it indeed a form of nectar (amṛta).
Therefore, it is understood that the principal substance, together with the four portions, must be offered in conjunction with the under-spreading and the sprinkling over.
Or, together with those two, he should perform the single act of the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering and sprinkle [the oblation] twice.
Because of the statement regarding the attainment of that [result]. (Siddhānta 31)
"Or rather, one should perform the fourfold cutting after having cut twice from each of those two portions of the oblation.
Why? Because the statement regarding its attainment says that the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering is performed by means of a double repetition of the entire [oblation].
[Page 759]
10th Adhyāya, 8th Pāda: "He spreads [the butter] once, he cuts [the portion] once, he pours [butter] over it twice, for the sake of the fourfold cutting."
By means of the mention of "four-fold," he indicates the full [oblation] as having four portions; otherwise, it would have six portions, and by that, it would be prior.
He says: "This is merely a description; let the attainment [of the rule] be stated. It is said in reply:

Regarding the four-fold oblation, it is heard in scripture: "He offers the four-fold [oblation]," but not regarding the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) or the curd-mixture (sānnāyya) intended for the oblation.

Or rather, it is not heard [in the scripture] that "one should make the substance intended for the oblation fourfold"; for if the "fourfold" were heard without being connected to the oblation, it would be meaningless.
Now, if it is argued that "it will be meaningful because it is included within the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*)," that is not so, because [the connection] is direct.

When there is a statement directly connected to the *homa* (oblation), such as "He offers the fourfold-cut portion" (*caturavattaṃ juhoti*), no other assumption of a general injunction for performance (*prayogavacana*) is appropriate. And since this is an explicit statement, no distinction is heard in the text as to whether [the substance] is "for that purpose" (*tadartha*) or "not for that purpose" (*atadartha*). Whether for that purpose or not for that purpose, the substance joined with the fourfold cutting must be offered;
in this way, the direct Vedic word (*śruti*) is upheld. In the alternative view, however, the syntactical connection (*vākya*) would have to be upheld.

And there would be an option [regarding the phrase] "he takes out the oblation," if the oblation were offered as four spoonfuls; likewise, this other scriptural statement would either be a restatement of what is already established or it would have to be an option for the fourfold portion.
However, since the latter case does not exist, such an option would not be logical; therefore—
The fourfold portion is formed by means of the great under-spreading and the sprinkling over.
And because, after denoting them as equal, there is a sequential enumeration of devotion toward all of them. (Sūtra 32, Yukti)

"These four offerings are indeed the four portions: that which he approaches is for the invocation; that which is the first portion cut off is for the *yājyā* verse; that which is the subsequent portion is for the deity; and that which he sprinkles with clarified butter is for the *vaṣaṭkāra*. Thus, there are four portions in the fourfold offering (*caturavatta*).

In the Rājasūya sacrifice, it is stated, "One should offer the sacrificial fat (vapā) from an anthill. This is also heard: "By that which they offer in the Āhavanīya fire, his desired deity becomes pleased."

In this regard, there is a doubt concerning the following point: should the path in the Jyotiṣṭoma and the ant-hill mound in the Rājasūya be abandoned, or is there an option between these two and the Āhavanīya fire? What is the prima facie view? Since the path and the ant-hill mound serve the purpose of the oblation, their simultaneous combination (samuccaya) is not possible.

Because the completion of the oblation (homa) has been accomplished by one or the other, if it were claimed that both are for the purpose of the oblation, why so? Because when an existing thing (bhūta) and a thing to be accomplished (bhavya) are mentioned together, the existing thing serves the purpose of the thing to be accomplished; and there is no absolute contradiction regarding the scope of the path. Thus, the oblation in the Āhavanīya fire is established, and in the case of an option, one alternative is indeed favored.

This being the case, we reply: that scriptural injunction which is given without specification would be set aside by that which is taught with specification; that which is taught specifically would be distant from it—meaning it would be unconnected.
For that [general rule] is indeed doubtful. How so? If the general [rule] is for the purpose of indicating the specific, then...
It would apply even to the specific case; yet, if it is not for the purpose of indicating a characteristic (*lakṣaṇārtha*), then it does not apply—thus it is doubtful.

Alternatively, it is doubtful because the general rule (*sāmānya*) is contradicted by the specific rule (*viśeṣa*). Or else, it is doubtful because the general rule might apply both to that specific case and to another—thus it is doubtful. Therefore, that general injunction would not apply to the specific injunction. What is the reason? Because it would be improper (*anyāyyatvāt*).
[Regarding] the option: how is the option improper? It is replied:

if the locus such as the "path" (*vartman*) and so forth is heard of in these oblations, then for one who resorts to an option—thinking that it does not exist in this case—a construction contrary to the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) must be imagined; or, if the locus such as the "path" and so forth is not heard of in these [oblations], [then there is no option].
Therefore, the claim that "it exists when there is cooking" is entirely devoid of valid authority; furthermore, the mention of the "path" (*vartman*) heard in the text would be rendered meaningless.

Now, if it should be argued: "By implication, its existence occurs when there is cooking, and that purpose is the accomplishment of the oblation (*homa*) by means of the *āhavanīya* fire," then, if only the accomplishment of the oblation were to be performed—[as follows on page 761].
In the tenth chapter, [sixth] section:
It might be established by implication through the Āhavanīya fire; however, in this case, the status of being the locus for the *varma* and so forth is also enjoined.
If that [offering] were not brought together when the Āhavanīya fire is being taken up, the injunction regarding the performance would be contradicted in the absence of such a bringing together.
To this it is replied: "Even though the status of the *varman* and so forth as the locus is also enjoined, in the case of the *homa*..."

"Because it possesses qualities, it makes the oblation correct; therefore, even if there is no synthesis [of the details], that is not a defect, for it will become correct through another section [of the ritual]. Thus, there is indeed an option.
To this, it is said: "No; here the connection with the *varma* and other oblations is enjoined, and that is the primary element, not..."

[Regarding] the *homa*: if that were not included, it would not be performed exactly as heard [in the scripture]. To this it is replied: "Even when there is a connection, two things are enjoined—one is the goal (*sādhya*) and one is the means (*sādhana*). That which is the goal is the primary element, and that is the *homa*. Therefore, there is an option (*vikalpa*)."

And even when the connection is heard, the *homa* must be performed using the *āhavanīya* fire; for at the time of the *homa*, the *āhavanīya* necessarily applies. That is not so, because the *āhavanīya* is not an auxiliary (*aṅga*) [to the specific action]. How is it not an auxiliary? Because it does not apply to the particulars. How is there no application? In the case of its being the locus (*adhikaraṇa*) of the path-rite (*vartmīya*).

Since, while the status of the *āhavanīya* fire as the locus [of the sacrifice] exists, it is impossible for that which is known to have the path (*vartman*) and so forth as its locus to be either known or made into something having the *āhavanīya* fire as its locus.

[The opponent] says: "It should be done in such a way as is possible; thus, [the injunction] will apply to the meaning of the verbal suffix (ākhyātārtha). Therefore, setting aside the path and so forth, the Āhavanīya fire shall be used. [The author] replies: This would indeed be so, if the instruction regarding the Āhavanīya could not be established without setting aside the path and so forth. For there are two ways to act: either by setting aside the path and so forth, or by excluding them. In this case, there must be setting aside (bādha).
"In the case of the path," the cognition would have to be set aside; therefore, the refutation is superior.
He says: "Even in the case of the refutation, the cognition that 'it is the Āhavanīya fire' would be sublated.

We rely on the cognition of the *āhavanīya* fire; is it not also possible that this [cognition] cannot be produced?
Or rather, will it not be produced? He says: "This is called a general cognition (*sāmānyapratyaya*);
it must function with respect to all particulars (*viśeṣa*). If this is so, then [it applies] here in these cases and elsewhere as well."

"Therefore, the Āhavanīya fire is prescribed; in that case, the notion of it being the Āhavanīya when the *varmī* and other [fires] are absent cannot be set aside. Consequently, setting aside the *varmī* and other oblations, the [Āhavanīya] should remain established. To this it is replied: "This is not so; for a word denoting a general category does not denote specific instances."
And if it were to denote [the individual], one could not apply the term to a cow born today, because there has been no prior perception of it;

whereas it is possible [to apply it] to the universal, because that has been perceived previously. Therefore, the universal does not denote the individuals, and for that reason, there is no cognition of the *āhavanīya* fire in the *vīdi-homa*. Or, if it were to denote [the individual], it would not do so in its primary sense.
How then should one address [the fire]? By means of indication (lakṣaṇā); for indication would be sublated by direct statement (śruti).
Therefore, when the ladle (darvī) and so forth have been established in the ladle and so forth by direct statement, it is impossible to understand or to employ the Āhavanīya fire [in their place].

He says: "But might this not also be the reverse—that when the *āhavanīya* fire is obtained, the cognition of the *vatma* (the calf) and so forth cannot take place? This would indeed be so; however, the cognition of the *vatma* and so forth is based on direct scriptural statement (*śruta*), whereas the cognition of the *āhavanīya* is based on figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*). In that case, it has been stated that the cognition based on direct scriptural statement is stronger. [Objection: "But even regarding the general category, the cognition of the *āhavanīya* is based on direct scriptural statement. [Reply: It is said: the cognition of the *vatma* and so forth is also based on direct scriptural statement with respect to the general category, for it is prescribed in relation to the specific act of offering (*homa*), and not...
"This [text] specifies this: therefore, excluding the *āmikṣā* sacrifice, in other *ahīna* sacrifices, the *āhavanīya* fire shall be employed. (10.7.80)

But when a scriptural injunction is heard in a specific context outside of the general section, it remains unmodified like the *ājyabhāga* offerings, for the purpose of excluding the archetypal (*prākṛta*) rule. (Pūrvapakṣa 17)
Without reference to any specific context, it is enjoined: "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses.

This [injunction], being set aside in the archetype (*prakṛti*) by the specific prescription of fifteen verses, applies generally to all sacrifices; however, it is heard again in certain modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*), namely: in the *vaimṛdha*, the *adhvarakalpa*, the *cāturmāsya*s, the *maitrāvaruṇī*, the *traidhātavī*, and the *āgrayaṇeṣṭi*.
Regarding those modifications (*vikṛti*), it is considered for what purpose the hearing [of the text] occurs: what is the prima facie view?

It is argued that when a scriptural injunction is heard outside of the context (*aprakaraṇe*) and is then heard again in a specific modification (*vikṛtiviśeṣe*) without being modified, its purpose is to prohibit the set of archetypal (*prākṛta*) subsidiaries—for example, in the case of the *Vaimṛdha* and other sacrifices, where it says, "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses," meaning one should not perform any other archetypal [number]. Nor is it understood thus: that the number seventeen applies only to the *Vaimṛdha* and others, and not to other sacrifices; for in those [other sacrifices], that [archetypal rule] is directly perceived (*pratyakṣeṇa*).
What has been heard through the oral tradition cannot be subverted.
But in the case of a modification, it would be for that purpose. (Sūtra 18) (Pūrvapakṣa)

Bhāṣya: If, however, some modification of the *sāmidhenī* verses were heard [in the text], then it would be understood that they are enjoined for the purpose of that modification; but no such modification is heard. Therefore, it is solely for the purpose of setting aside the original (*prakṛta*) rule. Sūtra 19: Or rather, it should be a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) because of its inclusion within the sacrifice (*kratu*), since the injunction is not made in connection with a specific context (*anārabhya-vihita*). (Conclusion)

The word "vā" (or) excludes the alternative. This is a supplementary statement regarding the injunction for the three [priests] beginning with the *adhvaryu*: "One should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses; one should place the *vidhati* within these. Therefore...

It would not apply to other modifications (*vikṛti*). [Objection: "But surely that which is heard directly in the scripture should not be set aside in other rites. [Reply: It is said: True, it is heard directly regarding the *sāmidhenī* verses, but it is not grasped by the sacrifice (*kratu*), because there is no connection with the sacrifice; even the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*) does not grasp it.

When there exists a direct statement (*vākya*) establishing a connection with the *vaiṣṇava* and other [deities], that which is the seventeenfold nature (*sāptadaśya*) mentioned as unattached (*anārabhyavāda*) is an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of the *vaiṣṇava* and others; this is a direct statement (*pratyakṣa-vākya*). Therefore, other modified sacrifices (*vikṛti*) do not adopt it.
Furthermore, if it were not adopted within a sacrifice (*kratu*), the seventeenfold nature of the *sāmidhenī* verses would be rendered fruitless and thus would not be performed.

Therefore, the supplementary statement regarding the *vaiṣṭhadha* and other rites belongs to the injunction that was not previously commenced. An objection is raised: "But surely there is a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*), [involving the statements] 'The *sāmidhenī* verses are seventeen' and 'These [are used] in the *vaiṣṭhadha* and other rites. It is replied:
These are two distinct sentences; the latter expresses a specific qualification of the very same matter that was stated by the former sentence.
That which is enjoined by means of a sentence is called a "sentence-remainder" (vākyaśeṣa). (1.1.7–8, Commentary)

In the section concerning the *darvihoma*, it is heard in scripture: "To the earth, svāhā! To the intermediate space, svāhā! To Vāyu, svāhā! And there is a general statement not tied to a specific context: "Food is offered to the gods either with the *vaṣaṭ* call or with the *svāhā* call. In this regard, there is a doubt: is this [the case] for that [general rule]?

Is this a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa)—namely, that "the oblation is offered to the gods with the utterance of Svāhā"—in this case of the *davihoma*, as in the formula "To the Earth, to the Mid-region, Svāhā"? Or is this not a supplementary statement?

"In which offerings is the utterance of *svāhā* not prescribed, and in which is it prescribed? What is the prima facie view? That, according to the immediately preceding section, it is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*).

This being the position, we reply: "In the mantras, there should be no status as a supplementary statement," for there can be no syntactic unity between a prescriptive sentence and a non-prescriptive sentence; the Brāhmaṇa is prescriptive, while [the mantra] is non-prescriptive.

This is a mantra. Furthermore, in the immediately preceding section there was no connection with a sacrifice, whereas here a connection is understood—namely, "food is offered to the gods by means of the *vaṣaṭ*-call or the *svāhā*-call"—for here the act of offering (*pradāna*) is the primary element. Moreover, there is an instruction regarding a subordinate quality (*guṇa*) in that [context].
In the case of the ladle-oblation (darvihoma), the utterance is "Svāhā to the Earth," and not "To the Earth, Svāhā";
therefore, the syllable *svāhā* exists in other ladle-oblations as well.
Sūtra: And those [fires] are not [to be established] from the mother, because they are seen [in the texts]. (21) (01)
Commentary: Even in that case where the *darvihoma* is not explicitly enjoined, the utterance of *svāhā* is nevertheless observed there; for it is said:

"With ghee, O Heaven and Earth, do you two fill yourselves"—here one offers at the forked branch of the *udumbara* tree, pours out [the ghee] from what has been recited, and upon its reaching the ground, he utters *svāhā*. This is the established rule.
He shows the utterance of *svāhā*; and because of the prohibition. (22) (02)
In some cases, however, there is a prohibition: "He does not utter the words 'svāhā' nor perform the mantra."
And [the opponent] says, "It is not so"; since a negation must be preceded by a prior apprehension, it is determined that this is a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*). (Sūtra 10.17.10a0)

The Agnyatigrāhya [offering] should not be performed in the modified sacrifice (vikṛti), because it is taught specifically for that [modified sacrifice]. (Pūrvapakṣa 23)

This is stated: "He who, knowing thus, piles the fire-altar," and likewise, "The *atigrahya* cups are indeed the support of the sacrifice. In this regard, there is a doubt: does the *codaka* (the rule of transfer) extend the *atigrahya* cups to the modified sacrifice (*vikṛti*), or not? What is the prima facie view? That "there is no application of the *atigrahya* in the modified sacrifice"—meaning, the *atigrahya* which belongs to the fire-altar piled with bricks does not apply to that which is known [to be without bricks]. Why? Because of the specific instruction regarding that which is known [to be without bricks].

For that is taught as a modification: "Now, therefore, one sacrifices to Agni with the Agniṣṭoma; him [one sacrifices] with the Ukthya, him with the Atirātra, him with the Caturrātra, him with the Pañcarātra, him with the Ṣaḍrātra, him with the Saptarātra, him with the Aṣṭarātra, him with the Navarātra, him with the Daśarātra. Likewise, "That which..."

If one were to take [the *pṛṣṭha*] with "pṛṣṭhya," they would be grasping the *pṛṣṭhas* of the *prāśana* sacrifice; if one were to take it with "uktha," surely the general rule (*codaka*) does not extend it to the *atirātra*s, since it is enjoined directly for a specific modification (*vikṛti*).
And likewise, there is the seizing [of the fire] in the month of Māgha. (Yukta) || 24 ||
And this is also heard in scripture: "The Śrutigrāhyas are offered month after month.

If the extended application (codaka) were to establish them, there would be no need for the direct instruction (upadeśa), "Month after month, they are not offered. Therefore, [the Śrutigrāhyas] are established by direct injunction.
Or rather, there is no grasping [of the rule], because of their equality. (Siddhānta) || 25 ||

Or rather, the *āmikṣā-graha* is indeed included by the extended application (*codaka*), for there is no distinction between this and the others; it is not tenable to say that while other subsidiary parts (*aṅga*) are taken up, this one is not.

And because of the observation of an indicative mark. (26) (Yukti)

In the Bhāṣya, an indicative mark (liṅga) is also seen: "One who desires, 'May I be well-headed when I am born in this world,' should pile the Kaṅkacit fire-altar; one should pile the Śīrṣacit fire-altar. Likewise: "He takes five Atigrāhya cups for Indra. [This indicates] the specific features of the shape of a heron (kaṅka) and the dedication to Indra (aindratā).
He shows the attainment of the modification of what is to be grasped by the mind.

The mention [of the term] should be a common injunction. (10th Adhikaraṇa)

Now, as for what was stated—that "it is taught in the modified sacrifice" (vikṛti)—that must be refuted. It is replied: the same injunction applies to that modified sacrifice in which it is taught, as well as to its archetype (prakṛti); in the remaining modified sacrifices, the extended application (codaka) brings it forth.
The mention of "every month" (nūnamāsi) is for the purpose of prohibiting [the practice] repeatedly.
(2 Śrauta Sūtra, 9th Adhyāya, 1st Khaṇḍa)
Commentary: Now, as for the mention of "monthly"—how is this? It is for the purpose of prohibiting repetition;
[the cups] are not drawn day after day, but rather they are drawn month after month. (10.7.110) Commentary.
The section concerning the four-fold cutting, together with the under-spreading and the over-pouring.

• [Sutra 28: Because it exists for the sake of the production [of the offering], the fourfold [ladle] belongs to the principal [offering] due to its connection with the oblation; the clarified butter is additional because of its inequality, as in common worldly practice, since it is produced as a subordinate element. (Purvapaksha)
In the context of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, it is recited in the scripture: "He offers with four portions. And that [page 768].

This matter is subject to doubt: is the fourfold portion (caturavatta) formed together with the under-spreading (upastaraṇa) and the over-sprinkling (abhighāraṇa), or should the fourfold portion be taken from the principal substance alone, while the under-spreading and over-sprinkling are additional? What is the prima facie view? The fourfold portion should be taken from the principal substance alone. Why? Because of the purposefulness of its origin—the origin of the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is for the sake of the oblation, as in the text: "That which belongs to Agni is on eight potsherds."

"On the new moon day and on the full moon day, one becomes unswerving. Whatever one offers as an oblation, that should be performed with four cuttings; and since the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) is for the purpose of the offering, along with the under-spreading and over-sprinkling of clarified butter, therefore four cuttings must be made from the sacrificial cake. There would be "an excess of clarified butter."
For that [clarified butter] is not equal to the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*); in the context of the cake, the clarified butter is subordinate (*guṇabhūta*) to the purpose of the oblation.

Therefore, although there is a sixfold portion (*ṣaḍavatta*) together with the clarified butter, nevertheless, in the act of offering (*homa*), it is considered a fourfold portion (*caturavatta*) just as in common worldly usage, where one says, "Devadatta is a bread-eater," even though...
Although the measure becomes greater due to the addition of husks and so forth, it is nevertheless designated as a *prastha*; likewise, condiments are for the sake of the cooked rice.
And because of the scriptural mention of its refinement. (30) (Yukti)

Furthermore, the spreading of the base (upastaraṇa) and the pouring over (abhighāraṇa) are heard of as being for the purpose of consecrating the principal portion (pradhānāvadāna), according to the text: "In that he spreads the base and pours over it, he makes this very [portion] an offering of nectar (amṛta).
Therefore, it is understood that the fourfold oblation (caturavatta) consisting of the principal substance must be offered together with the spreading of the base and the pouring over.

Or rather, one should pour the clarified butter over the Sviṣṭakṛt offering together with those two [portions] once; for there is a scriptural statement regarding that attainment. (Siddhānta) || 31 ||
Commentary:

"Or together with those two. Having cut twice from the oblation, one should perform the fourfold cutting. Why? Because the statement regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering—"by cutting twice for the sake of the single cutting"—is an injunction that supersedes that [previous rule].
And because of the repetition of the word "foot.

"By saying, 'He sprinkles twice and pours out twice for the sake of the fourfold portion,' it shows that the fourfold portion is completed by means of the double pouring; otherwise, it would be completed by a sixfold portion.
[The opponent] says: "This is merely a scriptural observation (darśana); let the basis for its application (prāpti) be stated. To this it is replied: It is established by the fourfold portion.
It is heard in the scripture: "He offers with four mouthfuls. This does not refer to the sacrificial cake (puroḍāśa) or the clarified butter (ājya) intended for the oblation;

for it is not heard in this way: "One should make that substance which is for the purpose of the oblation four-mouthful-sized. If the "four-mouthful-sized" were heard [as a rule] without being connected to the oblation, it would be meaningless.
Now it is argued: "It will be meaningful because of the inclusion of the *prayogavacana* (the statement of performance). This is not so;

since there is a direct statement regarding the connection with the *homa* (offering) in the injunction, "He offers the fourfold-portioned [oblation]," no other *prayogavacana* need be postulated. And in this direct statement, no distinction is heard as to whether it is "for that purpose" (*tadarthāt*) or "not for that purpose" (*atadarthāt*); rather, it is simply a substance joined with the fourfold cutting, whether for that purpose or not.

In this way, the Śruti is upheld; in the other case, the sentence would be upheld, and there would be an option regarding the statement "he cuts off the portions," should the oblation be given as fourfold. Likewise, this other scriptural hearing would become a redundant restatement of what is already established, or [it would refer to] the fourfold portion.
If one were to conceptualize it as being non-existent, then such conceptualization would not be logical;
therefore, the fourfold portion is formed by means of the great under-spreading and the sprinkling of clarified butter.
And because, after denoting them as equal, there is a sequential enumeration of devotion toward all of them. || 32 ||

(19) There are indeed these four divine portions of the oblation which he cuts off: that which is the first portion is for the introductory formula (*anu-vākyā*); that which is the subsequent one is for the offering verse (*yājyā*); and that which is the last is for the deity.
"He holds it up for the sake of non-sixfoldness"—thus there are four portions for the fourfold offering (*caturavatta*);
"one should cut off four or three portions," so reads the Kāṇva recension.

By reciting [the mantras] such as the *anuvākyās* with expressions of devotion, he indicates the acts of spreading the base (*upastaraṇa*) and so forth while proclaiming them part by part; therefore, [the formula] "fourfold" is used together with the spreading of the base and the pouring over (*abhighāraṇa*).

The word *dadh* signifies a share (*bhāgadheya*), just as in the expressions "a share for Kaṭaka" or "a share for Mārṣita"; thus, "shares for the gods" (*devadadhāni*) means the portions belonging to the gods. (10.7.1250)
The section concerning the fourfold cutting [of the omentum] even in the case of the Upāṃśu sacrifice.
It should be restricted, as in the case of the number seventeen; thus [the opponent argues]. (Pūrvapakṣa) || 33 ||
In the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there is the Upāṃśuyāja, regarding which it is stated: "He offers with four cuttings.

In this regard, a doubt arises: should the four cuttings be performed in the Upāṃśuyāja, or not? What is the prima facie view? It should be restricted [to the Upāṃśuyāja], just as the number seventeen (sāptadaśya), though taught independently (anāramyādhīta), when heard again in relation to specific enumerated modified sacrifices (vikṛtis), applies only to those for which it is a supplementary statement (vākyaśeṣa).

It is thus restricted; likewise, this [quality of being whispered] also, because it depends upon the spreading of the base (upastaraṇa) and the pouring over (abhighāraṇa), would be restricted to those two cases—the vegetable oblation (auṣadha) and the milk offering (sānnāyya)—and would not apply to the Upāṃśuyāja.
Or rather, because the oblation is subordinate, there would be an intention to express it as such.
|| 34 || (Siddhānta) ||

Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position. This is not the case—that it is not the rule that there must be four cuttings at the *upāṃśuyāja*. Rather, the quality of "four cuttings" (*caturavatta*) is prescribed for the act of offering (*homa*), and that would apply even to the *upāṃśuyāja* offering; therefore, here too, four cuttings must be made. Now, as for what was said—that the four cuttings apply only to the vegetable oblation (*auṣadha*) and the milk oblation (*ānnāyya*) because they serve as the substratum for the under-spreading (*upastaraṇa*) and the over-pouring (*abhighāraṇa*)—that is not so. The mention of under-spreading and over-pouring is not a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the rule regarding the four cuttings, just as [the number] seventeen is not a supplement to the rule "one should recite seventeen *sāmidhenī* verses."
Thus, in the cases of the *micavinda* and others, there are seventeen [verses] in sequence; it is not so here, for if there were four [verses], how [could this be]? Chapter 10, Section 10.
"One should take four portions (*caturavatta*) and pour clarified butter over them (*abhighārayet*). How then?

One should offer the *dra* (clarified butter) conjoined with the four-fold portion, and one should spread a base (*upastṛṇīyāt*) and pour clarified butter over the sacrificial oblation (*havis*). Wherein the offering of the oblation—both while being spread with a base and while being poured over—is characterized by the four-fold portion, there the four-fold portion is not to be taken from the primary substance; whereas in cases where [the portion] is otherwise than a four-fold cutting from the primary substance...

It is fourfold; and that [fourfold portion] must be offered from the principal substance. What is intended to be expressed is that once it has become fourfold, it is to be offered, not that it should be made fourfold by taking portions here and there. Therefore, even when there is only one [offering], the fourfold division must be performed. (10.7.13–50)
The section concerning the mention of the Āgneya and Aindrāgna sacrifices within the context of the New Moon and Full Moon rites.

The instruction regarding the two *puroḍāśa* cakes applies to those [sacrifices] under discussion, because that is what is heard in the scripture, just as in the case of the *vaiśyastoma*. (Sūtra 35, Pūrvapakṣa 1)

Regarding the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, this is recited: "One should cause a non-Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with these two very *puroḍāśa* cakes—namely, the one dedicated to Agni and the one dedicated to Indra-Agni. Concerning this, there is a doubt: (1) Is this a supplementary statement (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the injunction of qualification, "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," specifying that the non-Soma-sacrificer [should use] these two *puroḍāśas*; or (2) is it the originative injunction (*utpatti*) of two distinct rites, meaning that one should sacrifice with two other such *puroḍāśas*?
Alternatively, it is an instruction regarding the performer of the subsidiary acts: "The officiating priest should cause [the sacrificer] to sacrifice with these two sacrificial cakes" (3);

or else, it is an instruction regarding the time: "One should sacrifice with these two at the time of the Soma sacrifice" (4); or again, it is an injunction for the offering to Indra-Agni and a restatement of the offering to Agni (5); or finally, it is a restatement of both (6)—these are the possible positions.
What, then, is established? — That it is a remainder of the context (adhikāra-śeṣa); namely, this [statement] "one who desires heaven" in the Mīmāṃsā system. [Page 772]

"One should sacrifice"—this is the injunction. From these two "sacrificial cakes" (*puroḍāśau*), one desiring heaven who has not sacrificed with *Soma* should sacrifice. Why? Because of the scriptural statement (*śruti*). For the two sacrificial cakes are referred to by the word [in the text] as possessing that scriptural statement; therefore, they are not additional. And the activity of the agent is that of one who has not sacrificed with *Soma*.

These two are connected by direct scriptural statement (*śruti*), not by time; for time would have to be inferred, and direct scriptural statement is more authoritative than inference. In that regard, either the two cakes belong to one who has performed the Soma sacrifice, or they do not belong to one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice.
If, with reference to the two cakes, one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice is enjoined, then...
The non-performer of the Soma sacrifice is not entitled to the *sānnāyya*; thus, the restrictive particle *eva* (only) becomes meaningful:

"The non-Soma-sacrificer [is entitled] to the two *puroḍāśas* alone, and not to the *sānnāyya*. If, on the other hand, the two *puroḍāśas* were prescribed with reference to the non-Soma-sacrificer, then there would be no *puroḍāśas* for the Soma-sacrificer; and that is not the case.

The word *eva* occurs [in the sense of restriction], as in: "One should offer the two *puroḍāśa* cakes only for one who does not sacrifice with *soma*"; or as in: "Whomever you know to be vigilant, wise, and endowed with *brahmacarya*, he would not be angry at you for anything whatsoever."
"O Brahmin, tell this to him, the guardian of the treasure."
Just as one should say "know this very [thing]" instead of "know this pure [thing]," so it is here as well.

Since the remainder of the sentence concerning the injunction of qualification (*adhikāra-śruti*) applies to both modes of expression, this prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) holds in both ways; just as in the case of the Vaiśyastoma sacrifice, where the remainder of the injunction of qualification is "A Vaiśya should sacrifice with the Vaiśyastoma," so too here it is indeed the remainder of the injunction of qualification.

• But there is no connection with the obligatory [act] in the case of a rule within the context of the non-obligatory; therefore, it is not a subordinate element (*aṅga*). (Sūtra 36) (Second Purvapakṣa)
In the *Hṛdayabhāṣya*, however, the word "tu" (but) sets aside the [previous] position: "This is not so; [it is established by] the context and the remainder of the passage."

Thus, the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are indeed obligatory, as it is said: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa throughout one's life. These two sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśa) are auxiliaries toward the result; it is illogical that they are prescribed for one who is not a Soma-sacrificer. How so?
For the two cakes will exist as part of the obligatory Darśapūrṇamāsa, and thus they will be of benefit even to one who is not a Soma-sacrificer.
It would not be tenable [to claim] that the injunction regarding the *puroḍāśa* cakes has a "connection" with the "eternal" aggregate of the New and Full Moon sacrifices;

therefore, the scriptural sentence regarding the non-performer of the *Soma* sacrifice is not a supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) [of that injunction]. Rather, it is the originative injunction (*utpatti*) of two additional distinct rites. This connection is not made in such a way: that these two *puroḍāśa* cakes...
If it were the case that these two [offerings] prescribed for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices are being enjoined with respect to the *asomayājī*, how then is it?

Rather, for one who desires heaven but is not a performer of the *soma* sacrifice (*asomayājī*), it is these two acts—the offering to Agni (*āgneya*) and the offering to Indra-Agni (*aindrāgna*)—that are enjoined.
And if they are enjoined, they are distinct acts from the previous ones. In that regard, "these two which... [is said].

Thus, this reiterative statement will be dependent upon the dharma, just as in the case of: "Having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman for this very [sacrifice] on the Revatī verses. And in this way, the word *punar* (again) will have the sense of "furthermore," as in: "Having eaten with rice, Devadatta should eat with rice again."

Just as it is understood that "having eaten, Devadatta should eat again," so too here, although the *puroḍāśa* cakes are already prescribed for one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice by the injunction for the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), they are prescribed once more for the non-Soma-sacrificer; thus it is understood that "one should cause the non-Soma-sacrificer to sacrifice with the two *puroḍāśa* cakes alone," meaning with those possessing their specific ritual properties (*taddharmaka*).
And even if [the agent] exists [in the body], it is not [present] in only one part, because the agent is the primary entity. || 37 ||
Commentary (by Yu).

And since there remains a portion of the *adhikāra* (the governing context), the connection of the two *puroḍāśa* cakes with the agent who does not perform the *soma* sacrifice is not tenable; for in the remainder of the *adhikāra*, the agent is indicated as the primary element, and that [agent] does not exist [in the case of the non-soma sacrificer].
[Page 774]

The status of being primary applies to the fruit [of the sacrifice], and the two sacrificial cakes (*puroḍāśa*), which are merely constituent parts of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*), cannot be the means for accomplishing that fruit. Nor can the fruit be inferred on the basis of the authority of a scriptural statement, because there exists another mode of interpreting the statement. Furthermore, even that [inference] does not constitute a subordinate element of the qualification (*adhikāra*).
But because of the smallness [of the number], it is so with respect to the *stoma*. (0ni0) || 38 ||
As for what was described— namely, "like the Vaiśyastoma"— that is appropriate in the case of the Vaiśyastoma, because it is performed in its entirety.

The Vaiśyastoma is not a part of anything else; in that case, a result is possible, whereas here no result is possible, nor is there any single permanent element here connected with the impermanent. Therefore, it is dissimilar to the Vaiśyastoma.
If it be argued that [the result] would belong to the agent. (Sūtra 38) (Third Purvapakṣa)

If you think that it is not possible for this to be a supplementary statement to the scriptural injunction regarding qualification (*adhikāra-śruti-śeṣa*), then it is said in reply: the origination (*utpatti*) of two separate rites is not possible, because of the correlative expression "these two which... (*yāvetau*).

It may be understood through secondary indication (lakṣaṇā). How so? It is an instruction regarding the agent of the subordinate act—not the agent of the principal act. The expression "one should cause to sacrifice" (*yājayet*) is a direct statement concerning the causal agent itself, [whereas] the agent of the root *yaj* [in *yajeta*] would be [indicated] only through secondary indication. Furthermore, there will be no acceptance of a contradictory relationship between the permanent and the non-permanent.
Nor shall a fruit be postulated for a single part, as in the case of the one who has not performed the *Agniṣomīya* sacrifice [being enjoined] with respect to the two *puroḍāśa* cakes.
The instruction for the officiating priest, "he should cause [the sacrifice] to be performed," will lead to prosperity.

As for that which was stated—"Or rather, it may be merely a time [for the sacrifice], because no specific [result] is seen" (4.4.20)—the same principle applies here as well: at the time of the Soma sacrifice, these two *puroḍāśa* cakes of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) are present. What will happen in this case? The fault of having to postulate a result [for the cakes] will not occur.

It will come to pass that when [the sacrifice] operates upon the aggregate, then the fruit will belong to all the combined elements. Furthermore, it is possible to determine the time by means of the specific indicative mark (*viśeṣaliṅga*) of the Soma-sacrifice:
"At that time, one should sacrifice with the two *puroḍāśa* cakes alone, not with the *sānnāyya*."
Sūtra: But if there is Sānnāyya for one who has performed the Soma sacrifice, there is no conjunction with those two [offerings], because their times are distinct.
(4th Pūrvapakṣa Siddhānta)
Commentary (bhāṣya) 1:
The word "tu" (but/however) sets aside the [previous] leaf. "If" "this" [is the case], it applies to one who performs the Soma sacrifice.
• "The fruit is produced for the community" (samudāyasya phalaniṣpattiḥ) is the reading in the manuscript.

Hearing [the injunction] cannot be for the sake of [indicating] time. Furthermore, the *sānnāyya* offering belongs only to one who performs the *Soma* sacrifice; thus, when that [qualification] is not suspected, it is a statement made while suspecting it, just as in the verse: "If the scriptures were authoritative, they would have attained the supreme goal. For it is heard in scripture: "One who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice should not offer the *sānnāyya*. This being the case, it is not [time].

The hearing [of the text] is for the purpose of indicating time. How so? Because no "connection" (samavāya) with those two *puroḍāśa* cakes has been established for the *sānnāyya*; because they are separated by time: the two *puroḍāśas* are obtained prior to the Soma sacrifice, while the *sānnāyya* is obtained after it; therefore, one need not strive for its sake. Consequently, it is not for the purpose of indicating time.
The hearing [of the text] is for the purpose of distinguishing the time, and it is indeed an injunction for a separate ritual act.

Or rather, because it has already been prescribed, when there is doubt regarding a repeated mention for the sake of a subordinate quality, the scriptural statement would be for the purpose of two deities; just as [the Agniṣomīya] is not intended [to be a single deity], so too the Āgneya is [intended] as having a single deity because of the observation [of the singular number]. (Sūtra 43, Fifth Pūrvapakṣa)
The word "or" (api vā) serves to exclude the alternative view. This is not an injunction for a separate ritual action;
rather, it is a restatement (anuvāda) concerning the Āgneya offering, because it has already been prescribed. For that [offering] is indeed prescribed in both cases by the text:
"When the cake on eight potsherds dedicated to Agni is offered at the new moon and the full moon, it becomes imperishable."

The rule for the Aindrāgna [offering] applies because it is prescribed in both places; since it does not otherwise obtain there, this scriptural statement is intended to enjoin the Aindrāgna at the full moon sacrifice (paurṇamāsī). Just as the Āgneya is recited even though it is not intended [for that specific time], so too is there an injunction for both, and its manifestation is seen in the text: "He divides the Āgneya into four parts."
Thus it is said; likewise, in the *Sākaṃprasthāpya* sacrifice, after having performed the rites with the two *ājyabhāga* offerings, [one proceeds] with the cake (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to Agni.
But Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] that it is an injunction. (Sūtra 44; Fifth Pūrva-pakṣa, Conclusion)

The word "but" (tu) in the commentary sets aside this view as well: it is not the case that in the Āgneya there is a restatement (anuvāda) and in the Aindrāgna there is an injunction (vidhi); rather, there would be an injunction regarding the time for both.
Why? Because the teacher Bādarāyaṇa held the view that the injunction for the *sānnāyya* (the offering of milk) applies even prior to the Soma sacrifice;

for the *sānnāyya* is prescribed even for one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice, as it is heard in the scripture: "Therefore, he should bring it together. Likewise, here the Sākapūṇis [hold] that there is indeed *sānnāyya* even for one who does not perform the Soma sacrifice.
Therefore, the meaning of the word *kākhā* is "conjunction."
Or rather, [the conclusion follows] from the cognition of what has been prohibited. (Siddhānta) || 45 ||
Commentary: The word "or" (vā) sets aside the previous position. It is not the case that this is an injunction of time;
rather, it is the originative injunction of two rites performed at midday, nor is it a restatement (anuvāda) of the Āgneya or the Aindrāgna.

It is not an injunction; rather, it is a restatement (*anuvāda*) of both. How so? This sentence is for the purpose of enjoining the *sānnāyya* offering for one who has performed the *Soma* sacrifice; therefore, it is not an injunction for the *aindrāgna* offering either, for in that case the sentence would be split. The connection is made thus: "These two *puroḍāśas* are obtained for one who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice, and for one who has performed the *Soma* sacrifice, there is also the other, the *sānnāyya*. One should cause him who has not performed the *Soma* sacrifice to sacrifice with the two *puroḍāśas* alone—namely, these two, the *śrāyasa* and the *aindrāgna*—and [one should cause him to sacrifice] with the *sānnāyya*.
By the statement "one who has performed the Soma sacrifice," the status of being an Ācārya is prescribed for the Soma-sacrificer by one sentence,
and by another sentence, it is prescribed for one who has not performed the Soma sacrifice; therefore, this is a restatement (anuvāda) of both cases.
And likewise, there is the observation of another purpose [in the case of the *bhāṣya* on the *taṅ* suffix], [Sūtra 46] (Yukti).
And this point is shown even with reference to another matter, namely that it does not apply to other ritual acts. How so?
The reading in the Kāṇva-Kauthuma manuscripts is: "tadu sameva jayet"; the reading in the Ādarśa-Pulaka manuscripts is: "tadubhayameva jayet" [Page 778].
Listening cannot be for the sake of [merely] passing time. Furthermore, the status of being a teacher belongs only to one who has performed the Soma sacrifice;
to speak of such a possibility when it is not even suspected is like saying:
"If the scriptures were authoritative, they would have attained the supreme goal."

For it is heard thus: "One who has not performed the Soma sacrifice should not offer the Sānnāyya. This being the case, the scriptural statement is not for the purpose of [specifying] time. How so? Because no "connection" (samavāya) between those two cakes and the Sānnāyya has been established, since the two cakes exist prior to the Soma sacrifice, as they belong to a different time.

Vigor and honor are already attained; one need not strive for them. Therefore, the scriptural mention [of the time] is not for the purpose of specifying a time, nor does it enjoin a separate ritual action.

Or rather, because it has already been enjoined, when there is doubt regarding a repeated mention for the sake of a quality, the scriptural statement should be for the purpose of two deities; just as [the Agneya] is not intended [to be so], the Agneya [offering] has only one deity, as seen from the text. The word "or rather" (api vā) serves to set aside the previous position. This is not an injunction for a separate ritual action;

"That which is the cake on eight potsherds for Agni is constant at the new moon and the full moon."

The rule for the Aindrāgna [offering] applies because it is prescribed in both places; where it does not otherwise obtain, this scriptural statement is for the purpose of prescribing the Aindrāgna at the Full Moon sacrifice. But Bādarāyaṇa [maintains] that it is an injunction. (Sūtra 44; Fifth Pūrva-pakṣa, Conclusion)

It is said in reply: The *upāṃśuyāja* is heard in scripture as having the "interval" (*antarāla*) as its qualifying attribute. For the status of having the interval as its attribute is not enjoined specifically for that particular full-moon sacrifice where an interval exists; rather, it applies without distinction to the sacrifice with two cakes (*dvipuroḍāśā*).

And that injunction applies to the sacrifice with a single cake; therefore, since there is no purpose for it in the case of a single cake, it shall not be performed. [Objection: This being so, because of the absence of the *upāṃśuyāja*, the single-cake sacrifice should not be performed at all. The interval is not heard as a subordinate element (*guṇa*), but rather for the purpose of defining the time.
"There are two *puroḍāśa* cakes; [the *upāṃśuyāja*] is between them. How so? For it is prescribed that those two *puroḍāśas* are "blind" (i.e., separated), as it is said:
