For that very time which is understood as being between two cities or two fortnights is precisely what is designated as "the latter" relative to the former.

If this is so, then even though there are not two *puroḍāśas* in a single *puroḍāśa*-offering, nevertheless that former [offering] belongs to Agni; therefore, the subsequent one has that very same time which is interposed between them.

It is just as when it is said, "One should come at the time of the serpent," "One should come at the time of the conch," or "One should come at the time of the drum"—even in a village where there are no serpents, no conchs, and no drums.

That very time is the occasion, for it is there that the arrival [of the offering] takes place; it should be understood in the same way here as well. Therefore, the *upāṃśuyāja* must be performed in the case of a single sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*).
The absence of tautology is for the purpose of praise. (0ni0) || 70 ||

Now, as for what was stated—namely, "because it serves the purpose of preventing *ajāmitva* (redundancy)"—that must be refuted. To this, it is replied: This is a praise (*praśaṃsā*) of the *upāṃśuyāja* by way of its diversity;
however, it is not this very thing, namely *ajāmitva*, that is enjoined here as the fruit. Why? Because the purpose of that which has already been enjoined is what is enjoined [as a result].
And if this were the case, the *upāṃśuyāja* would not have been previously enjoined; for [otherwise] there would be no injunction [of it].
Furthermore, the prescription of a purpose would be a defect; nor is "making it non-marrowy" (ājāmi-karaṇa) some desired result.

Therefore, this is a mere praise, just as in the case of the spreading [of the base] and the pouring [of butter], which have no literal utility: "Ghee is indeed immortality; the oblation is mortal. When he spreads [the base] and pours [the butter], he makes that very oblation immortal."
Thus, therefore, the upāṃśuyāja must indeed be performed even in the case of an offering consisting of a single puroḍāśa cake.
Thus ends the eighth quarter of the tenth chapter in the venerable Mīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by Śabarasvāmin. || 0 ||
[Page 791] Regarding the calculation of the results of the groups (*varga*) for the planets beginning with the Sun when they are conjoined in an astrological treatise (*tantra*):
because of the connection with their respective purposes, there would then be a single state (*ekabhāva*) for those that are otherwise separate.
It is an action, because of its connection with a single word.

In the tenth chapter, the characteristics of *vādha* (annulment) and *abhyuccaya* (addition) have been treated; now, in the eleventh, we shall establish the characteristics of *tantra* (the common performance) and *āvāpa* (the insertion). Among these, that which, being performed once, benefits many is called *tantra*, such as a lamp lit in the midst of many Brahmins.

That which assists by way of repetition is *śrāvāpa*. For example, the anointing of those very same Brahmins. Regarding this, they cite the worldly maxim: "That which is common [to many] is not a motivator for the sake of another;
even so would it be in the case of *prasaṅga*, when its own rule already exists. Thus.

The meaning of the statement "the tantra would be common" has been explained. Regarding the principle "but that which is not a motivator for another," when something has arisen for the sake of another and, being performed for that very purpose, benefits a third party, that third party is not its motivator; for example, the immolation of an animal (paśvālambha), though produced for the sake of the sacrifice and performed for that purpose alone, also benefits the red, speckled, and black [animal]. "In this very way there would be prasanga (incidental application)," yet there is this distinction: "when one's own injunction is present. Even if another injunction exists for this [act], [it is still considered incidental].

However, because the purpose is already accomplished through the procedure for another, it is not performed again; just as the *prayāja* offerings, though extended by the *codaka* rule to both the animal sacrifice and the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*), benefit the animal-cake through the very same performance for the animal sacrifice, and thus are not performed again for the sake of that cake.
[Page 792]

Now the subject at hand is being discussed. Among those matters, the definition of *āvāpa* (the insertion of subsidiaries) was promised; that is now stated. In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the principal acts such as the *Āghāra* libations are mentioned, and for them, heaven is heard as the fruit:

"One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the *Darśapūrṇamāsa*. Does that [fruit] accrue to them collectively (*tatreṇa*) or individually (*bhedena*)? This same principle should be observed regarding the *Cāturmāsya* and other sacrifices as well.

"But surely heaven is not heard of here as the fruit—since by the word *svargakāma* (desiring heaven) a person is denoted, and by the word *yajeta* (he should sacrifice) the performance of the sacrifice [is denoted], and their connection is through the sentence;
by what, then, is the fruit now stated? He says: "By this very word *svargakāma*. [Objection: "But [this denotes] a person..."
"This is the speaker. Indeed, there is no such person as one "desiring heaven" (*svargakāma*). [Objection:
But surely he for whom there is a desire for heaven is one "desiring heaven. [Reply: We do not even know what it is that constitutes the desire for heaven;
for he who is desiring heaven at one moment becomes one who does not desire heaven at another.

Thus [it is said]: "In that case, this is an instruction regarding time—namely, 'when one desires heaven, then one should sacrifice. Even here, there is no specific time at which one would necessarily desire heaven; for all desires arise without restriction at all times.

And no specific point of time can be designated by this [injunction]. "In that case, then, this is neither an instruction regarding the person nor an instruction regarding time; rather, the desire for the fruit is the occasion:
when a desire for heaven has arisen, one should sacrifice, just as it is said, 'one should sacrifice when the potsherd is lost.'"

The refutation of this position has already been stated by means of the *sruva* ladle itself: "If it is argued that those desiring a fruit are the occasion (*nimitta*), [we reply] 'no, because of their obligatory nature' (6.2.10). Ritual acts such as the *agnihotra* are obligatory; if they were prescribed only as being contingent upon an occasion, their obligatory nature would be destroyed. Furthermore, the injunctions for their obligatory performance—such as "for as long as one lives"—would be contradicted, as would the indicative marks (*liṅga*).
"It is accumulated" (upacayate) is the reading found in the Kaśmīra manuscript, the Saṃskṛta manuscript, and the Bu-ston manuscript.
[Page 793]

And [there are such texts as]: "Verily, he who, being a performer of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, should let the full moon or the new moon day pass by, falls away from the heavenly world. By process of elimination, this is indeed a connection with a result. But how can a result be established by this?

To explain that, it is said: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice. Does this mean that one who desires heaven is enjoined to perform the sacrifice—as in the case of "those with red turbans"—or does it mean that the sacrifice is enjoined for the sake of one who desires heaven—as in "one who is oily should bathe" or "one who is hungry should eat"? And in that regard, if [it is the former]... one who desires heaven...

[If it were for the sake of the ritual act itself,] it would be taught for the sake of the action; yet even when taught, one would not engage in it—for who would undertake exertion for the sake of another? Thus, the injunction regarding the action would indeed be purposeless. However, if the sacrifice is for the sake of one who desires heaven, then it benefits that person, and the person performs it for his own sake; thus, the injunction regarding the action becomes meaningful. Furthermore, in the injunction of the sacrifice, the direct meaning of the Vedic word (*śruti*) is upheld.

In the injunction for one desiring heaven (*svargakāma*), this shall be the meaning of the sentence: therefore, the sacrifice is a means of assistance to one who desires heaven. If that [sacrifice], which brings about the acquisition of many sons, cattle, villages, food, and so forth for one desiring heaven, were to produce any one of those—such as sons, food, and the like—then the word "desiring heaven" would have its literal sense abandoned and would merely denote a person in general; and in that case, it would be utterly redundant, for even without that expression, a mere person is understood from the verb alone. Therefore, heaven arises from the sacrifice.

In this regard, when multiple [rites] are combined in such cases as the Darśapūrṇamāsa and others, a doubt arises: is their fruit one, or is it distinct? What is the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣa)? It is that they are distinct. What is the reason? These primary rites, such as the Āgneya and others, are produced as separate entities by injunctions that do not depend on one another, and thus they require a fruit separately.
When a fruit such as heaven is heard of in proximity to them, because they require it separately, it is connected with each one individually.
Therefore, the conclusion reached is that there is a difference in the result for each principal act.
This being the position reached, the following is commenced: "Because of the connection with a specific purpose, there is a separate nature [of the acts] from that.
[Page 794]

"There may be a single action because of the connection with a single word. Even though these [rites], such as the Āgneya and others, are distinct, there "may be a single action" for them. Why? Because of the "connection with a purpose"—that is, because of the connection (saṃyoga) of these combined rites toward a single purpose, which is the fruit (phala). Regarding the term "single action" (*ekakarmyam*): here the word *karman* denotes the fruit, in the sense that it is "done" (*kriyate*). Those things which have one [fruit] are "single-actions" (*ekakarmāṇi*); their state is "singleness-of-action" (*aikakarmyam*), meaning "having a single fruit. How so?
Furthermore, it is understood that there is a connection with the fruit for the Āgneya and other rites taken collectively? Because of their association with a single word;

for there is one word that denotes these [rites] when they are combined, and by means of that, having denoted them, the connection with the fruit is established in the statement: "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa."
Therefore, the fruit is understood to result from those who have come together, not individually; just as when it is said,

"A well is to be dug by the village," or "A tank is to be dug by the village," the well being enjoined in connection with the word "village"— which denotes a collective— is dug as one by the people acting together, and there is no separate well for each individual.
So it is here as well.
The purpose [of the remainder] would be divided according to each ritual action, as in the case of the *śeṣa* (remnant) rule. || 2 ||
(Ācārya) ||

This is not an absolute rule—that whatever is expressed by joining it with a collective term must belong only to the collection as a whole; for something may also belong to the individuals separately. For example, in the expressions "food for the group" (*gaṇāya annam*) and "ointment for the group" (*gaṇāya anulepanam*), although the remainder of the ointment and so forth is expressed by joining it with the word "group," which denotes a collection, it does not relate to the collection itself. With what, then? It relates to the members of the collection; for the bathing and other services are repeated for each individual. Therefore, [the principle applies] "like the remainder" (*śeṣavat*).

It would be split, and the system would become like a well; thus, this reason—the conjunction with a collective term—is not specific to the Vaiśeṣika school. Therefore, another reason must be stated, namely, "the distinction lies precisely here.
That very point is now being stated:
[Page 795]
But in the case of those not so prescribed, it would not be thus. (Siddhānta) || 3 ||
In the Bhāṣya (6.1.1),

it is not the case that the fruit is enjoined with reference to the sacrifice— namely, "one should perform the sacrifice for the sake of heaven"— but rather, the sacrifice is enjoined with reference to the fruit— namely, "one should bring about heaven by means of the sacrifice."

Thus [it is asked]: what is the reason? The injunctive suffix in "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) enjoins the sacrifice by means of direct statement (*śruti*), whereas it would enjoin the fruit by means of syntactical connection (*vākya*). And when the meaning of a direct statement is possible, the meaning of a syntactical connection should not be accepted, because the meaning of a direct statement is primary. What, then, would happen if the fruit were [enjoined]?

Is it enjoined? If the result were being enjoined, the meaning of the root *yajati* (to sacrifice) would have to be restated as an *anuvāda* (a reference to something already known), for there can be no syntactical connection between two things that are both being enjoined. Furthermore, such an *anuvāda* would apply to the *Āgneya* and other sacrifices which are proximate;

and since these have arisen as mutually independent and distinct entities, the result is connected with them precisely through their individual distinctions. On the other hand, if the meaning of the root *yajati* itself is being enjoined...

The sacrifices beginning with the Āgneya are enjoined by the word expressing the collective whole as things to be undertaken for the accomplishment of the result; since they are thus enjoined, their state of being combined is understood as a quality due to their specific proximity, and this [quality] is intended to be significant, because there is no reason for it not to be so intended.
"If sacrifices were being enjoined, they could not be qualified by the term *darśapūrṇamāsa*;
for that which is being enjoined cannot have a qualifier, because a qualifier itself cannot be unenjoined, nor can there be a mutual relationship between two things that are both being enjoined.
What, then, is to be done here by way of qualification? Since the *āgneya* and other sacrifices possess their own forms...

In proximity to the term *dīkṣā*, the word "yajeta" (he should sacrifice) in the injunction "one should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" denotes the collective whole. For what purpose, then, is the word "Darśapūrṇamāsa" used? It is purposeless and is merely a restatement of what is already established (*nityānuvāda*), just as in the cases: "seen by the god Indra," or "the *iḍā* ends the *tithi*."
"It concludes," and "he does not perform the after-offerings. Alternatively, it is logical that the sentence-meaning itself is enjoined here;
for if the meaning of the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) were being enjoined, the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* would be meaningless.

Thus it becomes necessary [to accept this]; for in the sense of the sentence as a whole, the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* is meaningful as a qualifier. Although the root *yajati* (sacrifices) is also obtained for the purpose of enjoining the efficient force (*bhāvanā*), it is heard again; and its repetition is justified because the word *darśapūrṇamāsa* denotes a sacrifice. Therefore, nothing is meaningless. Consequently, this [interpretation] is superior.
For since the remaining [substances] are prescribed for the sake of another, there would be a separate application for each principal [offering]. (Sūtra 4, Ārtika-nirṇaya)

Commentary: As for the term "residual" (*śeṣavat*): the application of the "residue," such as ointment and so forth, is prescribed for the sake of another [the ritual] by way of being a refinement of the person (*puruṣa-saṃskāraka*). In this way, it serves a visible purpose; otherwise, an invisible purpose would have to be postulated. In that case, the group [of substances] serves the purpose of characterizing the person. And because of the connection, it is capable of characterizing the persons. Whether one should postulate an invisible result or resort to figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*)—[this is the question].
Since a secondary indication (lakṣaṇā) has been observed, it is proper to assume it; therefore, the group [of verses] serves as a characteristic mark for the person.

Furthermore, the characteristic mark is not connected with the ritual action, but rather with that which is indicated by it. For example, in the command "Bring the white cloth," when two white cloths serve as a characteristic mark for the person.
Just as [the two acts] being mentioned are not connected with the act of bringing at that time, so here too the group (*gaṇa*) is not connected with the ritual action;
rather, it is the individuals themselves who are connected with the action. Therefore, the anointing and other such acts differ for each primary object (*pradhāna*).
(11.1.10) The performance of the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) is simultaneous when they serve a single purpose.
Now, a doubt arises regarding the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*): do they perform their function collectively or individually? To this, it is said:
"But because of the difference in the words denoting the auxiliaries, there should be a difference in the results, as in the case of the sacrifices. (Pūrvapakṣa 5)
[Page 797] Chapter 19, Section 1.

Just as there is a single fruit for the principal rites when they are performed together, it is not so with the subsidiaries (*aṅga*); that is, there is no separate purpose for each subsidiary, nor is there a separate fruit for each individual subsidiary. What is the reason? "Because of the difference in verbal expression" (*śabdabheda*), which means "because of the difference in injunctions" (*codanābheda*). By such mutually independent injunctions as "He sacrifices with the *samidh*" and "He sacrifices to *tanūnapāt*," the subsidiaries are enjoined individually. These...
Each [action] desires its own purpose separately, not collectively, because collectivity is not prescribed.

Therefore, their connection with the purpose is understood to be separate, "like the sacrifices" (*kratu-vat*); just as in the case of sacrifices, when they are enjoined separately, their connection with the fruit occurs separately.
"But there is no difference in meaning; since they have the same purpose, they constitute a single action. (Siddhānta Sūtra 6)
Commentary:
It is appropriate that there is a difference in the fruits of the sacrifices; for in those cases, distinct fruits have been declared by the verbal testimony:
"One desiring spiritual luster (brahmavarcasa) should offer a caru-oblation to Sūrya," and "An eleven-potherd cake to Indra-Agni."

"One desiring offspring should offer [the sacrifice]," it is said. Here, there is a single purpose (*aikārthya*): all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) have one purpose, which is to assist the primary rites (*pradhāna*). For the auxiliaries are prescribed with a view toward providing assistance;
thus, they all serve a single purpose. But if this is so, then because they serve a single purpose, there would be an option (*vikalpa*) among them.

[An objection] is raised: "Does [the subordinate element] not attain [the status of being a primary action]? The refutation of that will be stated in the sūtra, “But because the injunction has a single tone” (JS 2.1.46), wherein it is shown how there is no optionality. Therefore, because they serve a single purpose, the subordinates have a single function.
[Sūtra 7: "If it is argued that [the Veda is not eternal] because of the difference in words. (Ā)

Commentary: "Now, as for the objection that—because of their non-difference from the whole—the difference in purpose among the constituent parts is logical, that must be refuted. It has been refuted by [the fact of] having a single purpose. "It is not refuted, for all [parts] would assist the primary [act], yet they would perform distinct functions, just like the various factors of action (*kāraka*)."

All things beginning with the *kalā* assist the ritual action; nevertheless, there is a distinction in the effects for each individual agent. This, then, is what is being refuted: if the subsidiaries were [connected] by means of sentences such as "with the *samidh*" and so forth...
The application is stated as follows: "The *samidh* sacrifice is to be performed; the *tanūnapāt* sacrifice is to be performed.

From that, there would arise an expectancy for a purpose (*prayojana*). And if such an expectancy were present, it would occur through differentiation. However, in this case, the application is not being stated; rather, only the form is being described—namely, that a sacrifice characterized in this way exists here.

It is so. For what reason? Because there is no expectancy for an application-statement (*prayogavacana*), and because the application is already established by another means. But where has their application been stated? We shall show it in the subsequent sūtra. If there is no expectancy for a purpose here, then from where could a purpose arise, and from where a distinction?
No; because it has the purpose of the ritual action, the designation should apply to the performance, since that is its purpose. (Sūtra 8, Śrautaprayoga-nirṇaya)
Commentary:
When the "performance" (*prayoga*) of the primary rites is being stated, there would be the same designation for the subsidiaries as well—
that is, by that very word which expresses the performance of the primary rites, the performance of the subsidiaries is also expressed.

It is said: "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa [sacrifices]. Why? Because they are for the sake of action; that is to say, because they have the purpose of ritual performance. The Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices are heard of as being for the sake of the fruit, in the injunction: "One should bring about heaven by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices. Regarding this, a further inquiry arises: "How? This [inquiry] is resolved by the injunctions concerning the *samit* and other [subsidiary offerings], such as: "He offers the *samit*," "He offers to *Tanūnapāt*," and so forth. For what reason is that?

"Because they have that as their purpose"—these injunctions regarding the *samid* and other offerings have that [the sacrifice] as their purpose, because they are required by it, because they lack fruit themselves, and because they are in proximity to that which possesses a fruit. This very [set of offerings] constitutes the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) for the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices in accomplishing their fruit; and indeed, there can be no injunction of a ritual action without a procedure.
It becomes meaningful; therefore, the performance of the ritual action is enjoined together with its procedure (*itikartavyatā*).
And thus it is established that by the very word which is the injunction for the performance of the primary act (*pradhāna*), the performance of the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) is enjoined.
This being the case, the subsidiaries are indeed enjoined by a single word. And as for that—
[Page 799] "Because the principal acts are connected with a single word, there is a unity of result; the same applies to the subsidiary acts.
To this, he says: "This is not tenable. Why?"
Sūtra: Because the injunction regarding the agent has multiple purposes, it applies to both subordinate and principal elements. (0)

Furthermore, regarding the agent, there is an injunction for the primary [action], such as "One should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa," and an injunction for the subsidiaries, such as "With the [sacrifices] together with their subsidiaries. These two have different purposes: the injunction for the primary is for the sake of the fruit, while the injunction for the subsidiary is for the sake of the primary. In that regard, the primary actions are to be enjoined with respect to the fruit.
The subsidiaries are to be restated, and it is not possible for an injunction and a restatement to occur simultaneously.
Therefore, it is not possible to enjoin both the primary acts and their procedure by means of a single sentence.
Consequently, the subsidiaries are not included within the original injunction of the primary acts.
Regarding this, he says: "This is not improper; this is proper. Why?
Because the commencement [of ritual action] is preceded by speech. (Śābarabhāṣya, Adhikaraṇa 10)

Commentary: Commencement (*prārambha*), activity (*vyāpāra*), and action (*kriyā*) are synonymous. Here, the action of heaven by means of sacrifice is expressed as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*); that is, one should bring about heaven through sacrifice—one should engage in activity for the sake of heaven.

This is the meaning. However, this is not known: what is that operation? And since the placing of fuel (anvādhāna) and so forth are heard of in its proximity; because they are required by it and because of their proximity, this follows: "this is the operation by which the sacrifice produces heaven."
When that [injunction] is being formulated, there is no split in the sentence (*vākyabheda*).

Alternatively, the injunction is not contradictory with respect to the primary acts toward the result, and the subsidiary acts toward the primary acts. How so? Because through the New and Full Moon sacrifices, the transcendental potency (*apūrva*) which is the means to heaven [is produced].

It is said: a statement specifying that [difference] is employed; for example, "Desiring cattle, one should sacrifice having made the Vāravantīya the Agniṣṭoma-sāman upon these very Revatī verses. Therefore, [Page 800]...
The performance of the subsidiaries is enjoined by the very injunction that prescribes the performance of the principal act. (11.1.2)
The section concerning the withdrawal of all [subsidiary] elements in optional rites such as the Dama and Pūrṇamāsa sacrifices.

This is now considered: Is there an application of the *agnihotra* and other rites even when they are joined with only a portion of their constituent parts (*aṅga*), or rather only by including all the constituent parts? Now, what occurred in that regard? "The undertaking should be for one capable of everything" (3.3.10). In that context, a consideration was made regarding the regular commencement: "As long as one lives, [one should perform] the *darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices..."

Regarding this injunction, "One should sacrifice as long as one lives," which prescribes a lifelong restriction on performance, is there a requirement to include all auxiliary elements (*sarvāṅgopasaṃhāra*), or not? Here now, the consideration concerns the performance for the sake of a result, according to the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa."

Regarding this undertaking for the sake of heaven prompted by the injunction (*codanā*), is the performance to be carried out exactly as in the obligatory (*naiyamika*) rite, or is there a requirement to include all the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*)? What, then, is the prima facie view (*pūrva-pakṣa*)? It should be completed even with a single part, because the purpose is fulfilled; it would be like other sacrifices when they have been commenced, where the subsequent [parts] follow. (11) (Pūrvapakṣa)
Commentary:
Even by means of a single part of the auxiliary rites, [the rite] "would be completed," meaning it would be performed.

Why? Because [the requirement] is fulfilled. When it is stated, "One should exert oneself for the sake of heaven by means of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices," there arises an expectancy as to how one should exert oneself; that expectancy is satisfied even by a single subsidiary (aṅga), such as "He offers with the *samidh*. Thus, one should exert oneself in this manner, whether by two subsidiaries, three subsidiaries, or more. Whosoever performs as many subsidiaries as he can, he obtains a corresponding amount of assistance (*upakāra*).
He shall cast it; as, for example, in the case of the offerings to Sūrya, Yama, Prajāpati, Nirṛti, and others within the *akrāntara* sacrifices,
as stated in the eleventh chapter, ninth section.

679. He experiences the fruit corresponding to as many actions as he performs; however, because there is no difference in their proximity [to the agent], it is not the case that all auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) are obtained simultaneously. And when they are obtained, it should be like the subsequent [milkings]. For example, regarding the rule: "Having milked three cows while restraining his speech, having released his speech and without touching [the others], he milks the subsequent ones silently," the word "subsequent" (*uttara*) fulfills its purpose with respect to as many cows as one possesses; even so, here too, for whomever there are as many [actions]...
To whatever extent he is capable, he will perform that many limbs.
If it is argued that [the secondary act] does not [apply] because there is an absence of a result, [we reply: no. (12) (0)

If you, sir, should think that there is the performance of indeterminate particles (kaṇas) joined with only a portion of the constituent parts, that is not so. Why? Because "there would be an absence of the fruit. For as much as is heard—that this must be performed by one desiring heaven—there would be an absence of the fruit for one who does not perform it in its entirety. Indeed, the entire Veda has declared: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice," and [this applies] to the whole.
Because the entire collection of ritual acts, beginning with the kindling of the fires (*śrauta-anvādhāna*), has not been studied.
No, because of the connection with ritual action, the purpose would not be a defect of the word.
|| 13 || (Śrauta-nirṇaya) ||

Commentary: This is not so; there is no absence of fruit when there is a deficiency in the subsidiaries (*aṅga*). Why? Because of the connection with the primary action (*pradhāna-karman*); for the fruit is connected with the primary action—as in, "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices"—but not with the subsidiaries. The subsidiaries, however, are employed through the requirement (*ākāṅkṣā*) of that [primary action]. That...

And it has been stated that one’s purpose is fulfilled even by a single [element]. If this is so, then if "purpose" (prayojana) means the assistance rendered by the subsidiaries and the "fruit" (phala) is heaven and so forth, there would be no verbal defect; for if the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices have fruit as their purpose, the scriptural statement "One desiring heaven [should sacrifice] with the Darśapūrṇamāsa" would not be faulty.

Furthermore, those injunctions regarding the subsidiaries, such as the *samid* offerings, which exist in its proximity, would not be defective insofar as they contribute to its benefit. Therefore, there is no absence of the fruit due to the absence of the subsidiaries.
If it is argued that [the rite is one] because of the single word [denoting it]. (Sūtra 14)

If it is argued, "O observer, that fruit [arises] from the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and not from the *samit* and other [subsidiary acts]," this is not correct. What is the reason? "Because of the unity of the word (*ekaśabdyāt*). There is a single word that prescribes the performance of both the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices and the *samit* and others: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa. By that [single word], the connection with the fruit is established; so how can it be said that the fruit comes from the Darśapūrṇamāsa and not from the others?
Sūtra: It is not a quality because it is not distinct from the object and because of its equality [with it]. 15.
(Śrauta Sūtra, Adhyāya 12, Khaṇḍa 1)
Commentary: Not all [subsidiary acts] are connected with the fruit; rather, it is only the New and Full Moon sacrifices (darśapūrṇamāsa).

How is this known? Because it is heard that "one should effect heaven by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices," thus the status of being the instrument (*karaṇatva*) toward heaven belongs specifically to the New and Full Moon sacrifices, and not to the *samit* and other subsidiaries; for it is through expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*) that they [the subsidiaries] [are connected].

There is the apprehension [of the action], and that expectancy regarding its mode of being—namely, "how should one perform it?"—belongs to the act, not to the instrument, because the latter has already been specified by the words "by means of the New and Full Moon sacrifices" (*darśapūrṇamāsābhyām*). Therefore, there is no connection of the *samit* and other subsidiaries with the fruit. And if they were so connected, they would be equal in status to the *āgneya* and other primary rites.

And because of their equality, they lack specific qualities; therefore, as for what was stated—that there is a performance even of those [mantras] possessing only a partial constituent—that is simply not the case.

If you consider that those who recite the sūtra "aikakarmyāt" (due to the unity of the action) intend this meaning— that just as the subsidiaries are performed for the sake of the primary acts, so too the primary acts are performed [in relation to the subsidiaries]— therefore, let there be a single performance;
let only one subsidiary be employed, for even by means of one, the primary act becomes as if accompanied by all the subsidiaries.
[Page 807] Chapter 8, Section on Existence (bhāva).
There is no deficiency [of the means] because the object is not distinct [from it], due to their equality. || 15 ||
(Ācārya-nirṇaya)

This is not so. Why? Because of the distinctness of purpose (*arthapṛthaktvāt*). There is a distinctness of purpose, which is a distinctness of benefit (*upakārapṛthaktvam*): when there is utility through one constituent part, the benefit is small; when through many, it is great. How is this known? Because of equality, there would be a lack of quality (*aguṇatvam*); for if [the result] were the same whether by one or by many, there would be no excellence.

If there were a single benefit, then only one [of the many] would possess the status of being an auxiliary (*aṅga*), while for the others there would be "non-qualification," meaning they would lack the status of being auxiliaries;
and that would render the undertaking of so many [auxiliaries] purposeless. Nor can there be an option (*vikalpa*) among them, as stated in the sūtra:
"But because the injunction has a single form of expression. Therefore, when there is a multiplicity of auxiliaries, there is a multiplicity of results.

Because there is a single scriptural statement regarding the specific [act], because it is prescribed as not being optional, because of the connection with that which is heard as eternal, and because the meaning is obtained simultaneously, the meaning of its own word should be as it is obtained, like the *nivīta*; thus, its application should occur in every performance. (Siddhānta 16)
Bhāṣya:

Let it not be thus—that the performance of the subsidiaries (aṅga) is by way of a single part—but rather, how is it? It is by means of the inclusion of all the subsidiary parts. Why? Because of the "single-hearing" (ekaśrutitva) of the injunction; that is, because the subsidiaries are [spoken of] by a single word.

The performance is enjoined by the statement, "One should sacrifice with the Darśa and Pūrṇamāsa," as has been stated regarding the requirement for everything. However, that requirement—whether it pertains to the entire ritual procedure, such as the placing of the fire (agnyādheya) and so forth, or to a single part thereof—is not intended here. Why? Because in the injunction of the unseen potency (apūrva), [the requirement is] restricted.
* "We shall examine the alternative view that there is a distinction [between the subsidiaries]," such is the reading of the Tāndaka Vārttika.
[Page 808] The subsidiaries are not enjoined simultaneously; rather, sometimes one performs the *samidh* sacrifice, and so on.

[If it is argued that] sometimes [the rule applies] as "tanūnapātam," how then [is it to be understood]? It is "as if eternal" (*nityavat*); and just as they are heard [in the texts], so are they connected according to their respective requirements. Now, if it should be said: "Even though they are heard as if eternal, only a portion of them will be required"—this is not tenable. Why? Because of the simultaneous attainment through the purpose (*arthena*). By the purpose—that is, by the assistance rendered to the primary act—the subsidiaries (*aṅga*) converge simultaneously, like young pigeons on a threshing floor; and in that regard, no distinction is perceived such that "this is obtained" and "this is not. Therefore, all are obtained. And [the principle is] "according to what is obtained" (*yathāprāptam*).

"In the case of its own word's meaning, it is like the *nivīta* [rule]. Just as in the injunction "The priests proceed wearing the sacred thread around the neck (*nivīta*)," because there is no specification of particular priests and all are present, all the priests become *nivīta*; so too here, there would be application in every performance.
Likewise, there would be an instruction regarding ritual action. (17) (0)
And by doing so, the number of oblations mentioned in the passage, "Fourteen oblations are offered on the full moon day, thirteen on the new moon day," will not be merely nominal.
The repetition [of the mantra] occurs during other sacrifices. (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti-nirṇaya 1)
Commentary:

Regarding that which was stated—"just as in other sacrifices"—this is appropriate, since there is distinctness "in other sacrifices. Having stated, "One desiring spiritual luster should offer a *saurya* oblation," it is further stated, "the *aindrāgna*..."

"One desiring offspring should offer an oblation on eleven potsherds. What follows from this? From this it is understood that their purpose is achieved by each independently of the others, not by acting together; for when the preceding injunction has been completed, the subsequent one is enjoined separately. Now, in this case, "because the injunction is heard as a single [unitary] statement..."
By this reasoning, it is logical that the constituent parts perform their function collectively; therefore, there is no inequality with respect to the sacrifices.
[Page 809] Bhāṣya 75

Because there is no scriptural statement regarding the northern [altar] for specific details, and because the purpose has been fulfilled, one should be understood as acting according to one's desire at the time of the self-sacrifice. (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti-nirṇaya 2)

As for what was said—that it should be performed when the Uttarās have arrived—that is correct; however, regarding the statement that "in the Uttarās, until the milking," this is not because of a direct scriptural injunction (*aśrutitvāt*). The milking of the Uttarās is not being enjoined (*vidhīyate*), but rather it is restated (*anūdyate*). What is the reason? Because there is an injunction of specific acts such as the releasing of speech (*vāgvisarjana*) and so forth.
That statement, having its purpose already fulfilled, is not capable of enjoining the milking of the subsequent [cows];
for if it were so enjoined, there would be a syntactical split (*vākyabheda*). Furthermore, an explanatory restatement (*anuvāda*) occurs only regarding a matter already established.
And by implication, the milking of all [the cows] is already established; for by implication, they are not to be milked individually. Rather, all of them [are to be milked].

How are they to be milked? We shall explain this later, in the passage: "Likewise, there is a prohibition of milk for children" (11.1.48). Therefore, one should understand that "it is according to one's desire"—that is, he milks as many cows as he possesses. (11.1.3)
The section concerning the further practice of the Kāmyaka vow.

Regarding optional rites (*kāmya*), there arises this consideration: should each optional rite be performed separately, or should it be repeated more frequently by one desiring a greater abundance of the fruit? What is the prima facie view? Sūtra: Because the result is to be produced through the undertaking of the action, as in the case of agriculture, the fruits should accrue with each new undertaking. (20) (Conclusion)

Commentary: In the case of optional rites (*kāmya-karman*), there is a difference in the fruit with each performance, because the fruit is to be realized through the performance. How is this known? First, prior to the rite, the fruit is as [stated] in the Ka0 Saṃ0 Pu0 reading: "as when [the materials] have been obtained."
"The *Nyāyamālā* states: 'The author of the *Vārttika*, considering the section (*adhikaraṇa*) to be purposeless, has explained the name [of the section] within this very section.
[Page 810]
According to the Mīmāṃsā,

it does not exist; for if it were to exist, it would have to exist at the time of the purpose (the fruit), yet from scripture it is understood that it exists at the time subsequent to the action, and prior to the action, it does not exist, nor does it exist at the time of the action.
That which exists is cultivated by that [means]; "cultivated" (*kṛṣitvat*) means just as grain is produced through plowing.
If it is not cultivated, then even though it may exist again and again, it will remain like this [unproductive], just like grain [that has not been sown].
• And the qualification of all [persons] is established because [the rite] is something to be performed; there is no distinction.
And having established this, there will be an application (*adhikāra*) for all the *karṣū*s being performed again and again; therein these scriptural indications (*darśana*) will be appropriate:
"For those who would die first, there is the Gaurītirātra; for those [who die] second, there is the Āyuḥ"; "first..."
"One should sacrifice," "one should sacrifice repeatedly"—this indicates repetition; therefore, there should be repetition as much as one desires.
Sūtra: It should be flour, because its purpose has been fulfilled, like a subordinate element. (Pūrvapakṣa)

Bhāṣya: However, only a "great" (mahat) optional rite (*kāmya-karma*) should be performed. Why? Because its purpose has been fulfilled; the purpose of the injunction (*codanārtha*) is accomplished by performing it once, and once it is done, there is nothing further to be performed. What, then, is the purpose of the injunction? It is the fruit for the performer of the sacrifice (*yāga*), and the fruit for the performer of the oblation (*homa*). How so?

How so? It is said: here, in such expressions as "one should sacrifice" (*yajeta*) or "one should offer oblations" (*juhuyāt*), the verbal root denotes the action (*kriyā*), while the suffix denotes the agent (*kartṛ*). Of these two, the agent is the primary element and the action is the subordinate element;

the base and the suffix express their meaning together, with the suffix's meaning being predominant. This principle of the predominance of the suffix's meaning applies specifically to the case of *anuprayoga* (the subsequent use of a verb).

[In expressions such as] "Devadatta exists" or "Devadatta cooks," the fruit [of the action] is said to belong to the one who offers the oblation and the one who sacrifices. By virtue of being co-existent with that which is intended by the speaker, he becomes both the offerer and the sacrificer; thus, a second usage [of the term] would be purposeless, because its purpose has already been fulfilled, just like a subordinate part (aṅga). For example, [it is like] the omission of a subordinate part belonging to the principal [act].
The eighth quarter of the *Sādhyā*.
Since the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*) are to be performed for each [principal rite], and since that has been established as being accomplished by performing them once, they are not repeated.
Therefore.
And so too, in common worldly usage, is the relationship between word and meaning. (23) (0)
Commentary: "In common worldly usage as well," the meaning of the word is exactly the same; when told, "Bring the wood," one brings it once, and not again and again.

Or rather, in the case of their association, one should understand that there is freedom of choice, because there is no scriptural injunction; thus, these would be mere statements within the ritual rules. (Pūrvapakṣa Siddhānta 24)

Bhāṣya: Or rather, it should not be thus—that when there is contact with the object desired by the seeker, he remains engaged solely in the performance of the ritual act. How then? "According to his desire."

It may be understood as occurring either always or many times; one who desires the ground of the fruit [should perform it] many times, while one who is contented [may do so] immediately. Why? Because there is no scriptural statement (*aśruteḥ*); for here, no fruit is heard to be the cause of the sacrifice. As for that which...

The base and the suffix express the meaning of the suffix together; thus, in nominal words based on action, such as *pācaka* (cook) or *lāvaka* (reaper), [the agent is expressed]. But in a verb, neither the agent nor the action is primary.

Rather, "a verb has the state of being (*bhāva*) as its primary meaning," for it expresses the efficient force (*bhāvanā*) directed toward something, and that which is connected to this efficient force.

Because the collection of means (*sādhanagrāma*) is required—namely, "one should sacrifice," [but] by what? for what purpose? how?—if the agent were primary, there would be no requirement for means due to the absence of an object to be accomplished; for it does not happen that one asks of a "cook," "by what? for what purpose? how? Furthermore, *bhāvanā* (productive activity) is predicated of the fruit, not of the action, because of its designation with the instrumental case—as in "one should sacrifice with the *udbhid*" and "one should sacrifice with the *balabhid*."

Thus, if it were something to be brought into being (*bhāvya*), it would have been indicated by the accusative case; for heaven is desired because of its connection with desire, as expressed in the phrase "one who desires heaven" (*svargakāmaḥ*). Consequently, this results in the following: that one who desires heaven [should attain it] by means of sacrifice—[Mīmāṃsā, page 812].

"One should cultivate heaven"—in this regard, that which is cultivated is non-existent at the time of its manifestation; for the manifestation of what already exists is not possible. If it is argued that through action something is cultivated, then it will be cultivated again and again, just like a farmer. Therefore, one who desires the fruit should practice the optional rite (kāmya-karma) as much as desired.

And if it were necessarily the case that [the sacrifice] must be performed by all together, then in the injunctions regarding the cows and so forth— such as "those who should sacrifice for the first time"— these words would have to be supplied, namely,
"they should sacrifice for the second time"; and thus the sentences would be split, [as in the case of] "and those who..."
"They should perform the second [sacrifice]; for them, the Gaura-atirātra [is the concluding rite]. [Sūtra 25:
"Because of the single word, it is thus with regard to the auxiliary rites. (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti-nirṇaya 1)
As for the statement "like the subsidiaries" (*aṅgavat*), it is logical that the subsidiaries are performed once,
because of the "single word"— that is, there is a single word there which is the instructor of both the subsidiaries and the primary rites, and that [word]...
It has been stated that [the agent] grasps the constituent parts (aṅga) by means of dependence (apekṣā).

And that dependence, regarding the constituent parts which are co-existent (sahabhū), exists as a real entity (bhūtārtha). Therefore, in that case, there is no need for repeated performance due to a cause;
however, in this case, the action (karman) is the producer of the fruit, and for each application (prayoga), it produces a different [result].
The reason has been stated thus: "origination is not contradictory"; therefore, it is most excellent.
The characteristic of the *kheāka* [chant] is that it is performed by the *kamaryā*s. (Pūrvapakṣa-yukti-nirṇaya 2) || 26 ||

Regarding the phrase "and as in the world": in the world, a person is primarily intent on the purpose; because of the necessity of the task, he may utter a word repeatedly, even though it has already been spoken. For example, when told "Bring it," he might not bring it immediately. However, here, in the science of grammar (*śabda-śāstra*), activity proceeds according to the literal meaning of the words. Therefore, [the objection] "as in the world" does not apply.
There is no corroborative instance. (11.1.4 Śrauta-sūtra)
Chapter 11, Section 1:
The Section on Repetition Concerning the Threshing and Other Rites Until the Completion of the Result.
Since ritual actions have their purpose fulfilled by wealth, liberation would therefore result from the direct perception of that [wealth] and its destruction.
(Bhāṣya)

In cases such as "They carry the rice-grains" and "He grinds the rice-grains," which have defective purposes, there would be a performance [of the action] from the time the rice-grains are produced until the flour is produced. Why? Because in the performance of these actions, a specific purpose is accomplished—namely, the rice-grains and the flour—and there is a need for them here because the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) is to be prepared.
Therefore, it is understood that the performance of these actions is solely for that purpose. This would be so even if the pestle were used only once.

If, upon raising [the pestle] and bringing it down, one should kill [the grain], or if, while drawing [the millstone] forward or backward with a stone, that very purpose for which they were employed should be accomplished, then there would be completion through the accomplishment of that purpose; thus, there would be repetition until the rice-grains are produced, or until the flour is produced. (11.1.5)

[Objection: There is no restriction regarding the performance of acts whose fruits are not seen, such as the *avadāna* (cutting off) and so forth. [Reply: But since [such results] are not observed in the mere dharma itself, there would be no cessation [of the cycle of rebirth] through the literal meaning of the Vedic injunctions.

But when a visible purpose is not accomplished—as in the case [of the injunction]: "Having filled the *udumbara* mortar with all medicinal herbs, one threshes; therein he places a brick"—there is no purpose served by the production of rice-grains (*taṇḍula*), because the effect of rice-grains, such as the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) and so forth, has not been enjoined there.
Therefore, since the meaning of the word is accomplished by that single performance, there should be no repetition.
[The reading in the Kaśmīra manuscript (ka0 saṃ0 pu0) is *saṣkulān piṭhām pinaraḥ*.
The reading *pāca piḍhanineḥ* appears in the Kaśmīra manuscript.]

But for those who are at the gateway of Mīmāṃsā, there is indeed the threshing of the grain of their own views, which consists of the labor of casting down the well-plastered foundations of their positions.

The position is that [the term] "it proceeds" applies; for them, repetition must occur only until the extraction of that [grain] juice, and not when the extraction is merely slight. For even without a cause for that juice, usage is observed, as in: "They thresh the *kaṣāya*," and "They thresh the *kiṇva*. And this is not a mere figurative expression (*gauṇa*).

The application [of the term] is [to the act of threshing], because there is no distinction [in its meaning]. Furthermore, through the well-known meaning of its constituent parts, it is understood as referring specifically to the act of threshing (*avaghāta*). Nor is the whole [term] established in any other sense. Since the operation upon rice-grains (*taṇḍula*) is generally mentioned, there is a preponderance of usage for that [meaning], which is why this confusion has arisen. (11.1.630)
The section concerning the performance of the *prayāja* and other subsidiaries only once.
Taking the *prayāja*s and others as examples, it is considered: is there indeed only a single performance?

Furthermore, should there also be practice (*abhyāsa*) of what has been heard? In this regard, since the rule "But because [the result] is not seen in the case of mere heating, there would be no completion [of the purpose] when the meaning of the word is [merely] verbal" suggests that the performance should occur only once, the following is stated: Sūtra 28: Or rather, like a sacrifice, by means of inference, there should be an abundance of results in the case of repeated practice.
(Pūrvapakṣa)
[The Bhāṣya: Practice must be performed. Why? Because in practice there will be an abundance of fruit.

How is this known? By inference. What is that inference? That which was previously lacking in assistance to the primary rite before the performance of the auxiliary rites, from that [practice] it subsequently arises; by that [inference].
It is understood that "surely it is performed by a limb"; and if it is performed, then one will perform it again and again.
"Like a sacrifice"—just as in ritual acts such as the Saurya and others, the fruit is produced by the action, so that through the repetition of the act there is an abundance of fruit, even so here.
Chapter 9, Section 9.
Because the cause is one. (Siddhānta) || 30 ||

Bhāṣya: An auxiliary (*aṅga*) should be employed once, not repeatedly. Why? Because it is a causal factor (*kāraka*). The single causal function of the auxiliaries is to provide assistance to the primary rites (*pradhāna*). What, then, is this [assistance]? It is that by which the primary rites yield their fruit; and this is accomplished by the performance of the auxiliary once. Since the primary rites have already come into being through that [single performance], [repetition is unnecessary].
Furthermore, the application of the auxiliary parts is for the sake of producing a result; if it is not [already] present, then there is certainly no application.
Since it was not assisted by that great [cause], how could it be assisted when being performed again? What is the point?
"If there were no restriction regarding the measure, it would not be so.
(Yukti) Commentary: And if there were no restriction—namely, that the performance could be with or without [the prescribed number]—then [the rule of] "fourteen... would not hold.

Regarding the restatement of the number of oblations as if they were permanent—namely, "there are two oblations on the full moon day" and "thirteen on the new moon day"—this would not be possible [if there were repetition]; for if it were so, it would have to be understood as an optional alternative (pākṣika), and thus its established form (rūpa) would be contradicted. Therefore, there is no repetition.
Because the fruit is accomplished through its commencement, there would be a difference in the fruits in the case of sacrifices.
|| 32 || (Pūrvapakṣayukti-nirṇaya) ||

"May they assist you," [says] Durgā. There is practice regarding the wives [of the gods]: "Because of the commencement and completion of the fruit. Through the commencement of the action, the fruit is accomplished therein; by another commencement, another is brought to completion.
As for the subsidiary (aṅga), however, its stated measure of fruit is the accomplishment of the fruitfulness of the primary rites (pradhāna).
If that is accomplished by what has been performed once, there is no further performance. Thus is the reason stated. Therefore, [it is] *anu*...
The preacher.
3c It is proper to maintain one's own territory.
[Page 816]

"But there would be no repetition because of the unity [of the purpose]; it would be as meaningless as eating [the same food] once, since the purpose is not limited in quantity. Furthermore, since the primary act is for the sake of the action, there would be no fixed rule. (Ābhāsya 33)

Bhāṣya: [The opponent says,] "Since the purpose is accomplished by the constituent part (aṅga) being performed once, repetition is purposeless. To this we reply: "But repetition is meaningful for the collection of constituents; repetition is not purposeless. How so? "Repetition would be purposeless because of oneness"—if a single constituent, even when repeated, were to accomplish the same purpose, its repetition would be purposeless, just as [repeating] eating [is].
It is not the case that a single ritual act (*phala*) being practiced at one time produces satisfaction, and thus it is not repeated;
for here, the "immeasurability of the purpose" (*aparimāṇatvam arthasya*) is such that it is not known [in advance] that a subsidiary act (*aṅga*) will produce a specific amount of assistance.
[Objection: But surely it performs as much as is necessary so that the principal act (*pradhāna*) becomes fruitful?

"It is understood. True, this is so; however, "with respect to the primary [act], there would be no fixed rule because it is for the sake of the purpose of the action. Since the primary act is for the sake of the fruit-producing action, and the fruit of the primary act is immeasurable, that [fruit] will be greater when the assistance from the subsidiary acts is greater, and smaller when it is less. Furthermore, in the case of repetition, there would be an unlimited amount of assistance, because that [assistance] is something to be produced (*kārya*). Therefore, there would be no fixed rule [regarding the number of repetitions]. Always.
"Application" means practice or repetition.
• Size would result from the cognition of separateness and so forth. (Sūtra 34) Śrautasūtra.

As for the objection that "the number of oblations is contradicted," [we reply: because the assistance is distinct, and since the principle of the unseen potency (*apūrva*) applies here, this mention of the number of oblations would be a restatement (*anuvāda*). It would be "by way of injunction" with respect to the injunctions of the oblations themselves—namely, "there are fourteen injunctions of oblations on the full moon day and thirteen on the new moon day. Thus, the number [of acts] is not inconsistent; rather, it is the number of injunctions regarding the oblations that is expressed through figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*).
It is established.

[Page 817] Or rather, there would be no repetition, because the injunction for performance is a single unit, because the entire scripture applies simultaneously, and because ritual action would otherwise be fruitless; for it exists solely for the purpose of being performed.
|| 35 || (Caryā-niścaya) ||

Commentary: "Or rather, there is no repetition of the subsidiaries. Why? "Because of the unity of the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*). There is a single injunction of performance for both the subsidiaries and the primary rites; because of its unity, there is an instruction for "everything simultaneously," namely: "One should sacrifice with this rite together with its subsidiaries. Since the purpose is accomplished by the subsidiaries being performed once, there is no reason for their repeated performance. [Objection: "But will there not be a greater degree of assistance (*upakāra*)?"
If the auxiliary parts (*aṅga*) were to produce an unseen benefit (*adṛṣṭa-upakāra*), then it might be inferred that through their repetition there would be an increase in that benefit;

however, the auxiliaries produce only a seen purpose for the primary rite, namely its possession of auxiliaries (*aṅgavattā*). And even upon repetition, that possession of auxiliaries remains exactly the same. Furthermore, this [possession] is connected to the fruit [of the sacrifice], as expressed in "one should sacrifice with [the rite] possessing its auxiliaries" (*sāṅgena yajeta*); thus, it is not the auxiliaries themselves [that are connected to the fruit].

The auxiliary parts (aṅgas) become purposeful through their accomplishment of that [main sacrifice]. However, this seems improper: for when the fore-sacrifices (prayājas) exist, then neither the main sacrifice nor the transcendental result (apūrva) exists; and when the main sacrifice or the apūrva exists, then the fore-sacrifices do not exist. Thus, in the absence of the unseen (adṛṣṭa)...

When there is merely the fuel-stick (*samid*) and so forth, they do not even exist as constituent parts (*aṅga*); how, then, could there be any assistance? Furthermore, if there were no *apūrva* (transcendental result) in the subsidiaries other than the mere act of sacrifice (*yajati*), then there would be no extended application (*codaka*) at all for the *iṣṭi* sacrifices that are subsidiaries of the Soma sacrifice. In the absence of the *apūrva*, there is no expectancy for the procedure (*itikartavyatā*). Since the procedure for the root *yaj* (to sacrifice) is already known, the extended application would not transmit a procedure.

Furthermore, these scriptural observations would not be tenable: "He offers one hundred and one *prayāja* and *anuyāja* offerings; he offers nine *samiṣṭayajus* offerings; having cast away the enclosing sticks (*paridhi*), he offers the *hāriyojana*.

Therefore, this is another interpretation: there is no repetition of the subsidiaries because the injunction for performance is one; since there is a single injunction for performance for both the subsidiaries and the primary rites, [the result applies] to all of them.
[Page 818] There is the simultaneous instruction for the principal acts, and there is no repetition of the principals. Why?
Because the purpose is accomplished by the principals performed once, as in the injunction: "One desiring heaven should sacrifice with the Darśapūrṇamāsa."

When the meaning of the Vedic injunction has been thus accomplished, the fruit ordained by that scripture is obtained; therefore, there is no further reason for the performance of the action. Likewise, regarding the auxiliary rites (*aṅga*), once they have been performed once, the purpose of the scripture that enjoined those auxiliaries has been fulfilled. When that [purpose] has been achieved, it should be understood that the fruit of the auxiliaries as apprehended by the scripture is now obtained. This being the case, repetition would be useless. Furthermore, [this is so because] the fruit is perishable.

"It will come to be. Therefore, whatever fruit belongs to the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices is employed as an auxiliary benefit within the *bhāvanā*, not as the production of a new fruit. If a new fruit were produced by the auxiliaries, that would be merely the fruit of the auxiliaries themselves; however, auxiliaries do not possess fruits. While the primary rites accomplish their own functions, an unseen (*adṛṣṭa*) benefit is produced by them, and once that has been performed, it does not need to be repeated; therefore, there is no repetition of the auxiliaries.
There is an abundance of fruit.
• Or rather, there is repetition [of the action] in the cases of cutting, cleansing, and trimming, because of the scriptural statement regarding the singular number. (0) Bhāṣya.
"Or rather, there is repetition of the subsidiaries. Why? Because it is heard in the Piṇḍapitṛyajña:
"The sacrificial grass (barhis) is cut once," likewise in the Anuyāja: "He wipes the enclosing sticks (paridhi) once," and in the Sviṣṭakṛt: "He cuts off [the portion] from the northern half once."
Therefore, if there is the application of the suffixes for the non-existent (*asat*), then these statements are logically consistent;
hence, there is repetition (*abhyāsa*).
"But there is no non-repetition, because it is expressly stated.

(Śrauta-ni0) Commentary: And there is no non-repetition of the subsidiaries according to the principle of the word "anu". For instance, in the case of cutting the sacrificial post (*yūpa*) and so forth, because of the explicit statement, the repetition of all the subsidiary acts is understood to be required.

It is heard in scripture: "For the sake of Spring, one should sacrifice kapiñjala birds. Regarding this, it is deliberated:

should three, four, or five be sacrificed as alternatives, or should exactly three be sacrificed? What is the prima facie view? Sūtra: Because all [numbers] are obtained through the plural number, there should be an option. (Pūrvapakṣa)
They cannot coexist with the option. Why? Because "all are obtained":

all these specific [mantras] are obtained by means of the plural number; they are all his utterances, and because they are employed in every case, they cannot coexist through combination due to the absence of desire [for such]; therefore, there is an "option" (vikalpa).

The statement "Devadatta is strong" does not occur in relation to an elephant or a lion, but rather in relation to men of his own kind; likewise, a grammatical formation (*saṃsthā*) is also [considered] impure only in relation to a grammatical formation itself. Thus ends the first section (pāda) of the second chapter of the Siddhāntakaumudī, verse 28.

It ought to be inferred. First of all, that [number] does not depend on unity, because the plural number is never seen in the case of two, whereas it is observed in all cases starting from three; therefore, it is understood that it depends on duality, and that—

The plural number is understood [to denote more than two]. Why? Because it exists when that [plurality] is present, and it is absent when that is absent; it occurs when there is a plurality, such as three or more, and it does not occur when there are two or one.
Thus, the designation "plural" (*bahuvacana*) is etymologically meaningful. And there is the statement of those who are learned [in grammar]:

Regarding the rule "The plural is used for many" (Pāṇini 1.4.21), if plurality were the sole meaning of the plural number, he would have simply said "the plural is used for three" (*triṣu bahuvacanam*), because that would have been more concise and free from ambiguity. Therefore, "many" refers to those exceeding duality; thus, it is established that the plural applies to three and above. And so...

It is not the case that a single word cannot have multiple meanings; furthermore, since all [numbers] are plural in form, there is no usage whatsoever by way of metaphorical indication (*lakṣaṇā*). If it is argued that "it is used without a prefix (*nirupapada*) for three, but with a prefix (*sopapada*) for four and so on—as in 'four Brāhmaṇas' (*catvāro brāhmaṇāḥ')"—that is false, for even in the case of three, it is used with a prefix.

For example, [the words] "those who are in the world" and "the three Vedas. Furthermore, if the state of being a bird (*jitva*) were to convey its meaning without a qualifying prefix, then when it is said, "Kapiñjala birds for the spring," this very inquiry would not even arise: namely, whether or not the Kapiñjala birds are to be sacrificed. Just as in this case no such inquiry is made—whether the Kapiñjala birds are to be slaughtered—[so it would be here].

Or are they peacocks or pigeons? For what reason? Because peacocks or pigeons are not the denoted meanings of the word *kapiñjala*. Likewise here, if plurality alone were the denoted meaning of the plural number and not the other numbers, then this very inquiry would not arise, as it did previously.
If it is argued that its application has been observed [in other cases], [we reply: No. (38) (0)
Now, it might be argued: "The use of the plural number is observed in cases such as four and so forth, as in the expression 'four Brāhmaṇas'; therefore, there is deliberation [on this matter]."
The vision of the village of Gīgā is likewise here. (Caryāmelāpakapradīpa) [Page 822]
The Bhāṣya says: Furthermore, the usage of the word *kapi* is observed for both the pigeon and the peacock—
for instance, a large pigeon is called "this is a *kapiñjala*, not a pigeon," and likewise a peacock is called "this is a *kapiñjala*, not a peacock."
If it is argued that [the term] "mostly" (*prāyas*) means "with devotion" (*bhaktyā*), [we reply: no. || 41 || (Ā) ||
Bhāmaha says: "The word *kapiśca-manda* is employed out of devotion (*bhaktyā*), and in the usage of *bhā*, there is no [literal] meaning of the word."
Sūtra-bhāṣya: Likewise in the other case. (Conclusion) || 42 ||

It has been stated that even in the other case, the term "four Brāhmaṇas" is used by way of figurative indication (lakṣaṇā); however, when there is the employment of figurative indication, the primary meaning of the word is abandoned. Furthermore, the number that belongs to the meaning of the nominal stem (prātipadika) is expressed by the verbal suffix (vacana), as in "Brāhmaṇas," where the meaning of the nominal stem [is four].

Or rather, just as in the case of "two" (*dvi*) or "one" (*eka*), the meaning of the nominal stem (*prātipadika*) is not its number; therefore, the plural form "four" (*catvāraḥ*) would not be applicable.
If it were argued that there exists a plurality (*citva*) inherent in the four as constituent parts, and that the grammatical expression is based upon that, [we reply:]...
Duality also exists there, as does unity; indeed, by this very [principle], the dual number and the singular number would arise.
Therefore, the use of the plural number for four and so on is not due to a connection with consciousness (*cit*), but rather the plural number applies to them by force alone.
Consequently, all numbers from two up to the highest possible limit (*parārdha*) are the referents of the plural number. All.

"Is it not the case that the abundance of the fruit will be the cause? This is not so. Regarding those many ritual procedures (*kalpa*) that are heard of, some are light and some are heavy; in that regard, from the performance of a heavy procedure, the abundance of the fruit is inferred due to the capacity of the performer's exertion (*āyāsa*). For example, as in: "One [cow] is to be given, six are to be given, twelve are to be given, twenty-four are to be given. But here, there is only one procedure.

The *bhāvanā* (productive operation) is identical in its threefold nature and so forth [to that of other rites]; therefore, if one were to set aside what is light (*laghu*) and perform what is heavy (*guru-kalpa*) therein, it would not result in an abundance of fruit (*phala-bhūyastva*), because there is no difference in the meaning of the scriptural injunction (*śruti*).
For example, when the scripture says, "One should sacrifice the *parama*," if one were to sacrifice a large or very costly animal, [the result would not differ].

There is no greater fruit for him who would transgress the instruction of the learned regarding meat-eating. If there were indeed sin in acts of violence such as those performed at sacrifices (*haidikīṣu hiṃsāsu*), then he would incur that sin;
but even if there were no sin, he would still incur the reproach of the learned, being censured thus: "Having destroyed the meaning of the Veda, he slaughters animals for the sake of meat."
Therefore, the brown monkeys should be sacrificed.

The section concerning the performance of subsidiaries such as the *āghāra* oblation by way of a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), despite the difference between the principal rites such as the *Āgneya* sacrifice.
In the *Darśapūrṇamāsa* sacrifices, the principal rites are the *Āgneya* and others; their subsidiaries are the *āghāra* and others.
Regarding these, it is considered: is there a separate performance of the subsidiaries for each respective principal rite?

Or rather, [is it] by way of a collective application (*tatra*) for all? Now, what occurred there?—"As in the case of the sacrifice, through inference, there would be an abundance of fruit in the repetition" (11.1.28). There, the discussion proceeded concerning the entire Darśapūrṇamāsa; here, however, it concerns each respective primary act.

This is considered: what is the prima facie view? Sūtra: Because the subsidiaries are for the sake of the principal action, there would be a difference in the performance due to the difference in those [subsidiaries]. (Pūrvapakṣa) 53.

Commentary: In the performance of the "limbs" (subsidiaries), there would be a "division of action," meaning a division of the ritual act; that is, the performance of the subsidiaries would occur separately for each primary rite. Why? Because they are "for the sake of the primary acts"—the meaning is "because they exist for the sake of the primary. Indeed, the subsidiaries are taught for the purpose of the primary, [and thus] they possess those subsidiaries.

"How could they be primary rites (*pradhāna*)? And since there is a connection with the subsidiaries (*aṅga*), the primary rites do not possess simultaneity; nor indeed [is it the case that] "not for the gods," as is the reading in the Ka0 Saṃ0 Pu0 manuscript.
[Page 827]

It is intended [to be expressed], for in that case the principal acts are not being enjoined, but rather the subsidiaries; and a quality of a matter that is not being enjoined is not intended to be significant, as in the case of the singularity in "He cleanses the post" (*yūpam sammārṣṭi*). If this is so, then a connection with the subsidiary must be made for each individual principal act; those...

If they were performed only once, they would be connected without distinction, as in the case of the *ekādaśinī* sacrifice with the *prāyaṇīya* and *udavasānīya* offerings; and it has been stated in the sūtra "Because the injunction is heard as a single unit" (11.1.1.60) that the connection must be made with all [the subsidiaries] together. Therefore, there is a division of subsidiaries according to each primary.
• And there would be a violation of the sequence if simultaneity were the case. (The prima facie argument. || 54 ||
The primary acts are sequential, and they must be performed with their respective subsidiaries in that same order.
In this regard, if the subsidiaries were common (tantra), then one could perform the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice without having first completed the Āgneya sacrifice along with its subsidiaries.

If it were commenced [as one], then there would be a "disruption of the sequence" (*kramakopa*) among the principal rites. However, if there is a distinction, then having concluded the Āgneya rite along with its subsidiaries, the Agnīṣomīya rite is commenced along with its subsidiaries; thus, there is no disruption of the sequence.

Another says: if the subsidiaries were to constitute a single ritual procedure (*tantra*), then as long as the *tanūnapāt* offering assists the Agni sacrifice, so long must the *samit* offering assist the Agnīṣomīya sacrifice; such is this [position].

Furthermore, the sequence of assistance is difficult to maintain; moreover, the primary factors such as the removal of embers differ with respect to each concurrent action, and through these differences, there will be no lack of distinction among the substrates and so forth.
Sūtra: But for those that are equal, there should be simultaneity, because they are taught by a single word and no distinction is perceived. (Siddhānta) || 55 ||
*saṃsparśādīni iti ka0 saṃ0 pu0 pāṭhaḥ | [Page 828] Bhāṣya.
The word "tu" (but) is used to adopt an alternative view. It is not the case that one view is superior to the other, namely, that there is a distinction [between the subsidiaries];

rather, there is simultaneity—that is, a single performance. The subsidiaries, being employed all at once, are connected simultaneously with all the primary rites, because they are "equal" (*tulyānām*) in terms of being expressed by a single word, and because they are subsequently [performed] together.
Regarding this meaning, because no distinction is perceived: these [elements] have the same location, time, and agent.
For instance, in the case of the Darśapūrṇamāsa sacrifices, there are four officiating priests (ṛtvij) for both the Full Moon and New Moon sacrifices, as stated in:

Because there is a desire to perform everything, and because no distinction is perceived among the various items being prepared— such as the *śrādhāra* and others, or the *tūṣṇīkaca* and others— as to whether they belong to the *Āgneya* or the *Āgnīṣomīya*, they are suitable for all of them; therefore, they serve all purposes,

The performance of the constituent parts (aṅgas) occurs through repetition; in that case, the number of oblations (āhuti) as fourteen or thirteen would not be possible, for there are indeed fourteen and thirteen injunctions regarding the oblations. —Thus [it is argued]. This is not an injunction of number, because the number is already obtained through accumulation alone;

rather, this is a restatement (anuvāda), and it is appropriate as a restatement because it refers to what is already known. This number is known in relation to the oblations (*āhuti*), not to the individual acts; therefore, it is a statement concerning them.
Vādarāyaṇa [maintains that] the application [of the rites] occurs according to rule, even when there is no division of the context.

The various types [of rites] are to be understood; therefore, the performance is according to the *śruti* and the *tantra*. The mention of Bādarāyaṇa is for the sake of honor, not for the purpose of adopting his specific opinion.
