A modification is non-permanent; it occurs either when a desire arises or when a specific occasion (*nimitta*) presents itself. The intention to perform the occasional rite does not override the intention to perform the permanent rite.

It establishes [the rule], for that [modification] occurs only when the original is present; therefore, it arises without subverting it. If it did not subvert it, the Vedic injunction would be rendered purposeless.

"There is an eight-night *ahīna* sacrifice; it consists of the *viśvajit* and *abhijit* as *agniṣṭoma*s on both sides, with a six-day period (*ṣaḍaha*) in the middle that possesses light (*jyotis*) on both sides. Since those two undergarments serve the same purpose, an option would seem to apply; however, it is stated that there should be the "vatsatvak" (calf-skin) and no option, because the calf-skin is obtained by its specific name, whereas the unhemmed garment is obtained through the general rule (codaka). It has been stated that the word denoting a name is more powerful, according to the rule: "Or rather, [the name] is not [a mere] designation because it is additional" (7.4.15). If there were no acquisition [of the details] through the name, then by virtue of its abundance, the *jyotiṣṭoma* would remain unestablished as the archetype (*prakṛti*). But such is the case;

Although these names exist as designations for the Dharma, nevertheless, power resides only in that which is primary and unconquered.

Or rather, there is no distinction; for the upper garment is indeed made of calf-skin. || 2 ||
Commentary: There is no restriction that it must be calf-skin alone; rather, there is a combination.

In the case of combination, the injunction regarding the performance, which requires the inclusion of all constituent parts, is upheld. [Objection: "But surely the calf-skin is set aside because the name [of the garment] is stronger. [Response: It would be set aside only if there were a contradiction; however, there is no contradiction between the two. How so? Calf-skin will serve for the purpose of the upper garment (*uparivāsas*), while the bark-cloth (*dhāva*) will serve for the lower garment (*udarya*).

[The upper garment] is obtained through the conduct of the person; [therefore] the rule "one wears the upper garment over [the lower]" does not apply. This is not so; it also applies to woolen upper garments (*uparivāsas*), as in "one wears a blanket" (*kambalaṃ paridhatte*) or "one wears a deer-skin" (*rauravaṃ paridhatte*). Therefore, there is a combination (*samuccaya*) [of both garments]. (12.3.10)
Section 1:
The determination that among the various sacrificial cakes (puroḍāśas), the mantra belongs specifically to the puroḍāśa alone.
In the case of those [rites] that are not to be performed separately, there should generally be a rule of common application (tantra).
|| 3 || (Pūrva-pakṣa) ||

In the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa it is heard: "After the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) of the Agniṣomīya sacrifice, he offers the oblations to the Devasravas. Regarding the Anubandhyā sacrifice as well, there are the Devikā oblations. In that case, the ritual procedure (tantra) should be determined by the majority; because of the multiplicity of the subsequent offerings (anu-nirvāpya), that procedure belongs to the animal-cake.

It is established. Furthermore, a statement containing the word *sviṣṭakṛt* is observed regarding the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering: "He makes an oblation from the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) and the offerings to the Devas and Devikās for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt.

This is appropriate in that context when there is a subsequent offering (*anunirvāpyā*). But when it refers to the animal-cake [of the animal sacrifice], then it would contain the word *tatra*. Therefore, it is not restricted.
In the Mīmāṃsā system:
because of its adventitious nature, it is its own property; or rather, because of its specific scriptural authority, it belongs to the other.
And because of its primacy. (Siddhānta) Commentary:
The subsequent offerings (*anunirvāpyas*) are adventitious, because of a specific scriptural statement; for thus it is heard in scripture:
"He offers the animal-cake (*paśupuroḍāśa*) subsequently. Since this is so stated in scripture, the animal-cake comes first.

Since those [offerings] are to be performed subsequently, they are secondary, while the other is primary. Therefore, because of their adventitious nature and because of the primacy of the other, the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) should be its own portion (svadhākī).
• And because it is its own proper place. (Yukti) || 5 ||

Furthermore, the place of the animal-cake (paśupuroḍāśa) is after the offering of the omentum (vapā-pravāraṇa); it must also have its subsidiaries in that very same place, because they share the location of the principal rite. If there were a common procedure (tantra) for the cooked portions (pacyamuni-vāyā), then its subsidiaries—the subsidiaries of the animal-cake—should be performed in that place.
Since those [other rites] would be without their own proper place, the ritual procedure (*tantra*) of the *puroḍāśa* must be performed for the sake of providing them with their proper place.
If it is argued that [the rule does not apply] because of the mention of the *sviṣṭakṛt* [offering], [we reply: No. (Ābhāsa)
Regarding what was stated [in the previous sūtra], that is now refuted: "The modification is like the Pavamāna," [said by someone]. (Prāyaścitta-nirṇaya)

Commentary: And thus, when the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering of the *paśupuroḍāśa* is reached through the principle of extension (*tantra*), there shall be no modification because of the specific scriptural statement: "He offers to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. A statement containing the word *sviṣṭakṛt* must be performed—just as, for example, because of the statement "He prepares [the oblation] for Agni Pavamāna," the preparation is performed with the word *pavamāna*, so it is here as well.
Or rather, it is unchanging, because it exists in its own nature even with respect to the injunction. //8//
(Śrauta-nirṇaya)
Commentary:
"Without modification" means that the statement should be made with the three *triṣṭubh* meters, "just as in the archetype."

Because of the extension [of the rule]. As for the argument that "it is because of a direct statement," here no modification (*vikāra*) is being enjoined; rather, what is enjoined is the *samavadāna* (the taking of portions together) of the *devikā* oblations, as in: "He takes the portion together for Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. If another modification were being enjoined there, the sentence would suffer from split-utterance (*vākyabheda*). [Question: "How then is the mention of *Sviṣṭakṛt* to be understood? [Answer: "Because of its existence with respect to the injunction"—the injunction for the *Sviṣṭakṛt* in the context of the New and Full Moon sacrifices (*darśapūrṇamāsa*) is that which bears the word *Sviṣṭakṛt*; this statement refers to that, and it is for the purpose of indicating it. Therefore, that which belongs to Agni...

The phrase "the remaining portion" (śeṣabhāga) means as much as may be said up to that point; thus, for the *sviṣṭakṛt* offering to Agni, it is said: "to Agni Sviṣṭakṛt. Just as in the cases "the sacrificial grass (*barhis*) consists of *śara* grass" and "the clarified butter (*ājya*) is fresh butter (*navanīta*)," where the original function is expressed by a word denoting a substance through a modification of the archetype (*prakṛti*), so too here, by the word *viṣṭalaccha*, the archetypal [function] is [indicated].
The deity [is] characterized by the sky. (12.3.20)

Section on the Aggregation of Qualities that Assist through Different Means of Operation. Commentary: This section concerns the aggregation of qualities that assist [the action] by means of different doors of operation.
Since the subordinate elements are prescribed in connection with a single primary action, they should belong to all such actions.
When many subsidiaries are enjoined for a single ritual act, the performance of all of them should take place;

this is "conjunction" (samuccaya). In this way, the disposal (prāsana) of all will become purposeful, and the injunction regarding the performance, which encompasses all auxiliary parts, is upheld—just as in the case of the Āghāra offering: "He pours the Āghāra straight, he pours it continuously, he pours it eastward. (12.3.30)

But if they have a single purpose, they may be treated as alternatives; for if there were a combination, there would be a repetition of the principal act. (Siddhānta) || 10 ||

But those which have a single object— that is, a single purpose— are inseparable, as for example:

In the Mīmāṃsā system, rice and barley [are to be used together]; likewise, incense substances such as *svādira* and others, as well as the *hadrathantara* chant, should not be treated as optional alternatives. Why? Because "in the case of combination, there would be the repeated performance of the primary act."
If a second [auxiliary] is undertaken when one has already been performed, there would be a repetition of the principal act, and that is improper.

Why? Because the principal act is performed either for the sake of the fruit or for the sake of the removal of obstacles, not for the sake of the auxiliary; and once the great [principal] has been performed, what need is there for it?
Exertion is fruitless.
"If it be argued that one should practice [the mantra] because it possesses meaning" (Sūtra 11). (Cārvāka objection)
If you think that repetition is useless, it is not useless;
for it is purposeful as it serves to remove other qualities. Therefore, one should practice.
Not so, because it is not heard [in the scripture]. (Sūtra 12) (Purvapakṣa 1)
Commentary: This is not tenable. Why? Because "it is not based on scriptural statement" (*aśrutilāt*). Repetition is not heard [in the scripture];
there is no authority for it, so by what means would one perform it? He will state that its purposefulness consists in the manifestation of another quality, saying:
"Its purposefulness would exist at a different time" (Sūtra 1.2.50).
And because, when [the former] exists, it is a scripture concerning practice. (Yukti 1) || 13 ||
Commentary:
There exists a scriptural rule regarding repetition: "In the *saṃsava* sacrifice, one should perform both;
in the *gosava*, one should perform both"; and it is also heard in the *ekāha* sacrifice called *apaciti*: "One should perform both the *bṛhat* and the *rathantara*."
Thus, if there were a combination [of both], it would not be possible; therefore, for this reason as well, there is an option.
And it shows [the object] as being accompanied by conceptual construction. (Yukti 2) || 14 ||
The perception appears as if variegated: "Whether they be of *bilva*, *khadira*, or *pālāśa* wood.

"11.2: The sacrificial posts (*yūpa*) for other sacrificial rites (*yajñakratu*) are [made of various woods], but in this case, it should be made of *khadira* wood alone.
By thus prescribing the *khadira* wood for the Vājapeya sacrifice, he restates an alternative option; therefore, for this reason as well—
Conceptual construction.
• There may be purposefulness at a later time. (Candrananda’s Commentary) || 15 ||
And as for the argument that the teaching of another quality would be purposeless—it is not purposeless; it will have its purposefulness in another time, that is, in another performance.
Since that [performance] possesses purposefulness, there is no need for repetition.

[This is] the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). [Objection: "But surely there is no authoritative means of knowledge even for an alternative (*vikalpa*). [Reply: No; in the case of an alternative, nothing is done that was not already heard [in scripture]. It is heard: "One should sacrifice with rice" (*vrīhibhir yajeta*), and one sacrifices with those; and also "one should sacrifice with barley" (*yavair yajeta*), and one sacrifices with those as well, in terms of the substance itself. Because the purpose is accomplished in a single performance, it is not intended that both be used together. [Objection: "Then why are they not mixed? [Reply: This is not right, because the capacity of each to be an independent means of accomplishment is heard [in scripture]; that would be contradicted if they were mixed. Therefore, there is an alternative.
The section on conceptual construction concerning those who have attained mastery over the concentrations of turning away from objects.
And because in the expiations there is a connection with the completed [offering] by means of a single [verse], therefore there is the removal of the whole. || 16 ||

Commentary: Those [rites] enjoined by specific purposes are of two kinds: some are for the purpose of remedying defects that have arisen through negligence or error, and some are subsidiary members (aṅga) of the ritual occasion. Among these, those for the purpose of remediation are as follows: "If the sacrifice should be interrupted during the season, one should offer an oblation in the Gārhapatya fire with the mantra 'bhūḥ svāhā'."

Now, if it is from the Yajus, he says "Bhuvaḥ svāhā" in the Dakṣiṇāgni; if from the left, "Svaḥ svāhā" in the Āhavanīya; if they are not known, then "Bhūr bhuvaḥ svaḥ svāhā" in the Āhavanīya itself—thus [it is said].
[Page 1016]

In the Mīmāṃsā system, the phrase "he would go to ruin" (śrārtim iyāt) means that he would meet with destruction. [Question: "But what is the destruction of the sacrifice? [Answer: It is its failure to produce the result.

[It consists of] non-performance [of what is enjoined] and the practice of what is prohibited. But how can there be an expiation (*prāyaścitta*) for the purpose of restoring what has already been destroyed? Because of the connection with the scriptural statement: "One should perform this for one who has fallen into distress";
for if it remains destroyed even when that [expiation] is performed, what is the purpose of performing it?
If it is argued that "the subsidiary (aṅga) is for the sake of the cause [of the primary]," it must be said:
that which makes the primary fruitful is called a subsidiary;
and since the primary has become fruitless due to its destruction, if that [subsidiary] is made fruitful by this [act], then this [is the case].

My dear friend, if that fruit were to follow [the action], then by this [fruit] the action would be made fruitful; well then, it is understood for the sake of compensating for what has perished. But if it is not made [fruitful], then that which was said—that the cause is a subsidiary part of the action—is simply non-existent. Moreover, in various places...
In the supplementary portion of the text, it is heard that the loss of concentration itself is addressed: "Agni, indeed, is the purifier among the gods; they should worship him with his own share;

he alone leads him along the path for one who undertakes this vow. Therefore, these [rites] are for the purpose of removing defects. There should be an option (*vikalpa*) among them. Why? Because they serve a single purpose (*aikārthyāt*). How is there a single purpose? Because these [defects], such as the "unripe" (*niṣpakṣena*) and others, are defects.

There is a "combination" of each of those [expiations] individually—[as stated]: "If that sacrifice should meet with failure, one should offer with the mantra 'bhūḥ svāhā'"; thus, there is the "removal" of every defect by means of each one.
If the defect is not removed by one, then the second and subsequent ones become distinct applications.
Therefore, it is a conceptual construction (*vikalpa*). The same should be understood regarding memories as well. (12.3.540)
The section concerning the combination of occasional expiatory rites.
The conjunction (samuccaya), however, [is used] in the sense of destroying faults. || 17 ||
But as for those [rites] which are not for the purpose of destroying defects, in those there is "combination" (samuccaya). Which are they?
[Page 1017]
Patha 19, Sandhyā 2, Pāda.

Again, what are those? Those which [are prescribed] for one who has not performed what was heard [in scripture], and not for the practice of what is prohibited, it is said: "If the sun should rise upon this man while his Agnihotra remains unoffered, he should offer a cooked oblation (caru) to Sūrya."

"One should offer a cake on one potsherd to Sūrya; and when the Agnihotra has been prepared and the sun rises while it is still burning, the husband and wife, having restrained their speech, should remain sitting together until the fire has been extinguished. In this case, O dull-witted one, there is no fault, because since there is an absence of fault, there is no need for expiation (*nirghāta*). [This applies] when the sunrise occurs while the fire is still burning.

An action is prescribed on account of a specific occasion; that [action] is occasional (*naimittika*). Since it arises within the context of a ritual action, it is understood to be an auxiliary (*aṅga*) of that action. And as many as are those [auxiliaries] that arise, they are all concluded by the injunction of performance (*prayogavacana*); their combination constitutes the whole. (12.2.3–60)
Commentary:
During the rainy season, at midday, the meaning of the mantra is the primary authority.
The application of mantras should be according to their own specific function because of their connection with ritual acts, since that [function] is the cause for their use. (Pūrvapakṣa 18)

When the *kaṇi*-suffixes are not employed, there should be the application of the "mantras" according to their own specific rules (*svadharma*). These rules for them at the time of learning are such as: "One should not study during a festival (*parvan*)," "One should not study when there is wind," "One should not study when there is thunder," and so forth. Why? Because "the rule has that as its cause" (*dharmasya tannimittatvāt*). This rule is caused by the employment of the mantra, and this [employment] is also a mantra-employment. Therefore, in this case as well—
It must be so.
Because there is an injunction regarding the knowledge [of the mantra], its application should occur at all times, since the application is for the sake of the ritual act. (Siddhānta 18)
Commentary:

"The application [of the mantra] should occur at all times," even during periods when study is prohibited (*anadhyāya*). Why? Because this prescription of rules (*dharma*) pertains to that application which is for the purpose of learning; it is a rule specifically for the act of acquisition (*grahaṇa*).

Mīmāṃsā—In the tenth [book], it is stated that therefore one performs the drawing [of the cup] with a quality. [Question: "But what is this quality? [Answer: By means of the *aviśeṣa* (non-distinction).

[The opponent says: "It is without a basis. But how is it known that this *dharmaka* suffix has the sense of grasping (*grahaṇa*)? [The answer is: It occurs at the time of grasping, not at the time of the act itself. [The opponent objects: 'Let it not be so; it will have the sense of drawing forth (*karṣa*). And being in the sense of drawing forth, it would apply wherever there is a mantra. [The author] replies: No, it does not apply to the *dharmas*."
It is prescribed; however, there is no such thought as "this is the vessel" or "the grasping is being brought about in this way.
Therefore, it is for the purpose of grasping. Furthermore, the application of the action is not for the sake of grasping, but rather for the sake of the ritual act (*karman*);
therefore, there is no non-attainment of the *dharma*. Moreover, [this applies] to both *pacati* and *pacyate*.
There is a prohibition against study; if the ritual action is performed during a time of confusion, there is the futility of the injunction;

if it is performed on a non-parvan day, the same fault remains. Application [of the rite] follows from the direct Vedic statement (śruti), while non-application follows from the truth [of the prohibition]; since the Vedic statement is authoritative, [the rite] is not [performed]. Therefore, it is not [to be done].
The rule regarding the application [of grammatical operations] is to be respected. (12.3.70)
The section on the recitation of mantras according to the essence of the ancient teachings by Kavi.

Some mantras are taught in the Brāhmaṇa with the colloquial accent (*bhāṣika-svara*), such as the one [taught] by the Ācārya in the Aśvamedha sacrifice: "imām agṛbhṇan raśanām ṛtasya" (RV 1.162.18). What, then, is the colloquial accent? It is said:—
"The followers of the Chandogas, the Bahvṛcas, and likewise the Vājasaneyins—
[the one] who knows the higher and lower [accentuation] is indeed called a Bhāṣika.
The term "Bhāṣikas are the most wise" is the restrictive rule (bādhaka).
[Page 1019] 11. Two feet were fashioned.

In those *maka* verses, there would be no prohibition of the *prāvacana* accent; it would be unrestricted. Why? Because of the instruction regarding a different accent, just as in the case of "airavat. Just as the word *girā* is excluded at the time of the ritual performance due to the instruction regarding the word *irā*, how then is it known that this is an instruction concerning the accent and not the mantra itself? The mantra need not be instructed, for it is obtained from its very form; however, the accent, being untaught, would not be obtained. Therefore, it is the instruction of that [accent].

• Or rather, there is no instruction regarding the mantra for the reciter, because the scriptural statement [regarding the mantra] is intended to cause fear due to the likelihood of a transgression. (Siddhānta) || 21 ||

[The opponent says: "Or rather, this [accentuation] belongs to the instruction of the mantra, not to the colloquial (bhāṣika) accent. How is this known? Because the word for the object has a form similar to the instruction of the mantra. What is that similarity? He says: 'Thus, in the taking up of the horse's tethering-post. And this [tethering-post] is taken up by means of the mantra, not by means of the colloquial accent; for the mantra brings about the act of taking up, whereas the other does not. [The proponent asks: "Why is this stated? [The opponent replies: "Because the colloquial usage is set aside; the colloquial accent prevails in the Brāhmaṇa, and within that [Brāhmaṇa], [the mantra is included]."

The section concerning the optionality of sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*) of various numbers at the establishment of the sacred fires (*ādhāna*):
"But there should be an option regarding the numbers, because of the contradiction in the scriptural injunctions. (Sūtra 7)

In the context of the *Ādhāna* (fire-consecration), there are injunctions regarding the sacrificial fees (*dakṣiṇā*), such as: "One cow for the gods," "Six cows for the gods," "Two cows for the gods," and so forth. Regarding these, the inquiry is whether they are to be combined (*samuccaya*) or whether there is an option (*vikalpa*).
Since the performance-injunction (*prayoga-vacana*), which encompasses all constituent parts, establishes their combination, it is replied: "But there is an option with respect to the number."

[It might be argued: "Why? Because of a contradiction in the Vedic texts (*śrutivipratiṣedhāt*). For [the text] 'one deity' (*ekā devā*) enjoins a substance delimited by oneness as the means for the purchase (*parikrayasādhana*); likewise, '[six] deities' (*ṣaḍ devāḥ*) enjoins [a substance] delimited by sixness. If both 'one' and 'six' were to be combined, there would arise a conflict: the purchase would be performed with a substance delimited by both, and that would constitute a contradiction between the scriptural injunctions of oneness and sixness."

[Objection: "But surely, no purchase (*parikraya*) is heard of here; rather, there is a gift (*dāna*), as it is said: 'One gives, one gives'. [Reply: To this it is said: A gift consists in the transfer of one's own property to another; and that is for the purpose of making the other one's own master (*svāmī*). For [the giver] himself is indeed the owner of what he has given away.

He performs it, and thereby the purpose of the giver is fulfilled; thus the purpose is accomplished in a visible manner. If, on the other hand, the gift itself were assumed to be the means, then an unseen result (*adṛṣṭa*) would have to be postulated. Furthermore, the scriptural mention of "one" and so forth occurs specifically in the context of hiring (*parikraya*):
he who hires with seven [coins] does not thereby become one who has hired with one or with six.

For they do not say "one" or "six," but rather "seven"; thus, there is this contradiction with the Vedic revelation (*śrutivipratiṣedha*), and therefore there is an option (*vikalpa*) regarding the numbers. (12.41–50) | 27.6 [Page 1038]

612: The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by virtue of his great compassionate power, beholds and delivers those who suffer. At that time, the Bhagavān was staying in Rājagṛha on Vulture Peak Mountain together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. Then the venerable Śāriputra rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “O Bhagavān, why is the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara called ‘Avalokiteśvara’? What is the reason for this? The Buddha told Śāriputra: “If there are many hundreds of thousands of myriads of koṭis of beings who hear the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara and single-mindedly call upon him, then all their afflictions will immediately be extinguished; therefore he is called ‘Avalokiteśvara. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to offer worship to the Buddhas of the ten directions, they should wholeheartedly take refuge in the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great compassionate power, and can bestow fearlessness upon those who are afraid. Śāriputra, if there are sons or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should rely upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara as their teacher.

Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is able to skillfully expound the profound prajñāpāramitā. Then the venerable Śāriputra said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, how should a son or daughter of good family who wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā rely upon the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara as their teacher? The Buddha told Śāriputra: “If a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should observe that within form there is no self, nor what belongs to a self; within feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness, there is no self, nor what belongs to a self. Śāriputra, because form is empty, it is neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are likewise empty; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharmas; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a bodhisattva relies upon prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the heart of non-attachment, free from all obstacles.

Because there are no obstacles, he has attained ultimate nirvana. All the Buddhas of the three times, relying upon prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the unequaled mantra, which is able to remove all suffering and is true and not false. Thus the mantra is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. When the Buddha had spoken these verses, the venerable Śāriputra and the entire great assembly, along with the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, having heard what the Buddha said, rejoiced and practiced accordingly. 613: Chapter on the Practice of Avalokiteśvara Bodhisattva, the Sixth. At that time, the venerable Subhūti rose from his seat, bared one shoulder, placed his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed the Buddha, saying: “O Bhagavān, if a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell in the perfection of giving? The Buddha told Subhūti: “If a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should give away all internal and external things without attachment, and even give away their own bodies without attachment. Why is this? Because when giving, they do not perceive a giver, a recipient, or a gift. This is called practicing the perfection of giving in the profound prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell in the perfection of morality? The Buddha told Subhūti: “If a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should dwell in the precepts of restraint, the precepts of gathering wholesome dharmas, and the precepts of benefiting sentient beings. Why is this? Because they do not perceive a transgression, nor do they perceive one who transgresses. This is called practicing the perfection of morality in the profound prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell in the perfection of patience? The Buddha told Subhūti: “If a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should dwell in patience toward all dharmas. Why is this? Because all dharmas are ultimately empty and cannot be grasped. This is called practicing the perfection of patience in the profound prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell in the perfection of vigor? The Buddha told Subhūti: “If a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should dwell in vigor without being weary of the three realms. Why is this? Because the three realms are ultimately empty and cannot be grasped. This is called practicing the perfection of vigor in the profound prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell in the perfection of meditation? The Buddha told Subhūti: “If a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should dwell in the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless absorptions, and the nine successive stages of cessation. Why is this? Because they do not perceive the characteristics of meditative concentration. This is called practicing the perfection of meditation in the profound prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell in the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha told Subhūti: “If a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should contemplate all dharmas as empty in nature, signless, wishless, unconditioned, and unarisen. Why is this? Because they do not perceive the characteristics of wisdom. This is called practicing the perfection of wisdom in the profound prajñāpāramitā. Subhūti said to the Buddha: “O Bhagavān, if a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell in the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment? The Buddha told Subhūti: “If a son or daughter of good family wishes to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should dwell in the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who dwells in suffering and seeks suffering; the person who dwells in suffering and seeks happiness; the person who dwells in happiness and seeks suffering; and the person who dwells in happiness and seeks happiness. And how, monks, does one dwell in suffering and seek suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a low family—a family of outcastes, hunters, bamboo-workers, cartwrights, or scavengers—poor, with little food and drink, where sustenance is obtained with difficulty, and where clothing, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick are meager. He is also ugly, unsightly, and deformed, with limbs that are incomplete; he is weak, with little strength, and small in stature. Furthermore, he is afflicted by many diseases: his head aches, his ears ache, his nose aches, his teeth ache, his eyes ache, his chest aches, his back aches, his sides ache, his belly aches, his limbs ache, or he suffers from fever, chills, or a combination of both. Thus, being afflicted by many diseases, he dwells in suffering. And how does he seek suffering? He engages in unwholesome bodily conduct, unwholesome verbal conduct, and unwholesome mental conduct. Having engaged in such unwholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell. Thus, having dwelt in suffering, he seeks suffering. This, monks, is called the person who dwells in suffering and seeks suffering. And how, monks, does one dwell in suffering and seek happiness? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a low family... [as above] ...he is afflicted by many diseases. Thus, being afflicted by many diseases, he dwells in suffering. And how does he seek happiness? He engages in wholesome bodily conduct, wholesome verbal conduct, and wholesome mental conduct. Having engaged in such wholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, having dwelt in suffering, he seeks happiness. This, monks, is called the person who dwells in suffering and seeks happiness. And how, monks, does one dwell in happiness and seek suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a high family—a family of Khattiyas, Brahmins, or householders—wealthy, with abundant food and drink, where sustenance is easily obtained, and where clothing, food, bedding, seats, and medicines for the sick are plentiful. He is handsome, attractive, and fair to behold, with complete limbs; he is strong, powerful, and large in stature. Furthermore, he is free from many diseases:

his head does not ache, his ears do not ache, his nose does not ache, his teeth do not ache, his eyes do not ache, his chest does not ache, his back does not ache, his sides do not ache, his belly does not ache, his limbs do not ache, nor does he suffer from fever, chills, or a combination of both. Thus, being free from many diseases, he dwells in happiness. And how does he seek suffering? He engages in unwholesome bodily conduct, unwholesome verbal conduct, and unwholesome mental conduct. Having engaged in such unwholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, a lower realm, or in hell. Thus, having dwelt in happiness, he seeks suffering. This, monks, is called the person who dwells in happiness and seeks suffering. And how, monks, does one dwell in happiness and seek happiness? Here, monks, a certain person is born into a high family... [as above] ...he is free from many diseases. Thus, being free from many diseases, he dwells in happiness. And how does he seek happiness? He engages in wholesome bodily conduct, wholesome verbal conduct, and wholesome mental conduct. Having engaged in such wholesome conduct, at the breaking up of the body, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, a heavenly world. Thus, having dwelt in happiness, he seeks happiness. This, monks, is called the person who dwells in happiness and seeks happiness. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

3.6 12. The Twelve Links of Dependent Origination (dvādaśāṅgapratītyasamutpāda) in Reverse Order. 1. Aging and death (jarāmaraṇa). 2. Birth (jāti). 3. Existence (bhava). 4. Grasping (upādāna). 5. Craving (tṛṣṇā). 6. Feeling (vedanā). 7. Contact (sparśa). 8. The six sense bases (ṣaḍāyatana). 9. Name-and-form (nāmarūpa). 10. Consciousness (vijñāna). 11. Formations (saṃskāra). 12. Ignorance (avidyā). Thus, from aging and death down to ignorance, these twelve factors are called the "twelve links of dependent origination. Furthermore, regarding these twelve links, there are three types of time periods: past, future, and present. Among them, ignorance and formations belong to the past; birth and aging-and-death belong to the future; and the remaining eight links belong to the present. Moreover, within these three time periods, there are two types of suffering: the suffering of birth and the suffering of aging-and-death. Within the past time period, there are two causes: ignorance and formations. Within the future time period, there are two results: birth and aging-and-death. Within the present time period, there are two causes: craving, grasping, and existence; and two results: consciousness through feeling. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are four types of conditions: the condition of cause, the condition of object, the condition of immediate antecedent, and the condition of predominance. Among them, ignorance is the condition for formations by way of the condition of cause. Formations are the condition for consciousness by way of the condition of cause. Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form by way of the condition of object. Name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases by way of the condition of object. The six sense bases are the condition for contact by way of the condition of object. Contact is the condition for feeling by way of the condition of object. Feeling is the condition for craving by way of the condition of immediate antecedent. Craving is the condition for grasping by way of the condition of predominance. Grasping is the condition for existence by way of the condition of cause. Existence is the condition for birth by way of the condition of cause. Birth is the condition for aging-and-death by way of the condition of object. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of characteristics: the characteristic of affliction, the characteristic of action, and the characteristic of basis. Among them, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the characteristic of affliction. Formations and existence are the characteristic of action. The remaining seven links are the characteristic of basis. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of categories: the category of the agent, the category of the instrument, and the category of the result. Among them, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the category of the agent. Formations and existence are the category of the instrument. The remaining seven links are the category of the result. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of aspects: the aspect of the field, the aspect of the seed, and the aspect of the harvest. Among them, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, and feeling are the aspect of the field. Consciousness is the aspect of the seed. The remaining seven links are the aspect of the harvest. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of continuities: the continuity of affliction, the continuity of action, and the continuity of basis. Among them, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the continuity of affliction. Formations and existence are the continuity of action. The remaining seven links are the continuity of basis. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of connections: the connection of affliction, the connection of action, and the connection of basis. Among them, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the connection of affliction. Formations and existence are the connection of action. The remaining seven links are the connection of basis. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of accumulations: the accumulation of affliction, the accumulation of action, and the accumulation of basis. Among them, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the accumulation of affliction. Formations and existence are the accumulation of action. The remaining seven links are the accumulation of basis. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of sufferings: the suffering of birth, the suffering of aging-and-death, and the suffering of the intermediate state. Among them, birth and aging-and-death are the suffering of birth and the suffering of aging-and-death. The remaining ten links are the suffering of the intermediate state. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of conditions: the condition of cause, the condition of object, and the condition of immediate antecedent. Among them, ignorance is the condition for formations by way of the condition of cause. Formations are the condition for consciousness by way of the condition of cause. Consciousness is the condition for name-and-form by way of the condition of object. Name-and-form is the condition for the six sense bases by way of the condition of object. The six sense bases are the condition for contact by way of the condition of object. Contact is the condition for feeling by way of the condition of object. Feeling is the condition for craving by way of the condition of immediate antecedent. Craving is the condition for grasping by way of the condition of predominance. Grasping is the condition for existence by way of the condition of cause. Existence is the condition for birth by way of the condition of cause. Birth is the condition for aging-and-death by way of the condition of object. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of functions: the function of production, the function of maintenance, and the function of manifestation. Among them, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the function of production. Formations and existence are the function of maintenance. The remaining seven links are the function of manifestation. Furthermore, among these twelve links, there are three types of gates: the gate of affliction, the gate of action, and the gate of basis. Among them, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the gate of affliction. Formations and existence are the gate of action. The remaining seven links are the gate of basis. Among them, ignorance, craving, and grasping are the seed of affliction. Formations and existence are the seed of action. The remaining seven links are the seed of basis. 10. ... [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are these four? They are: first, the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva); second, the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva); third, the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva); and fourth, the self-nature of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-svabhāva). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names and signs (nāmanimitta) based on the objects of the five sense faculties, which are themselves non-existent; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the imagined self-nature. What, Mahāmati, is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of the various appearances of objects arising from the habit-energy (vāsanā) of false discrimination; it is like a dream, a mirage, a city of the Gandharvas, or the reflection of the moon in water. This is called the dependent self-nature. What, Mahāmati, is the perfected self-nature? It is the state of the dependent self-nature being eternally free from the imagined self-nature; it is the realization of the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena, which is the realm of the Tathāgatas. This is called the perfected self-nature. What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature of the ultimate truth? It is the cessation of all mental activity (cittamanomanovijñāna), the non-arising of all dharmas, and the realization that all things are originally quiescent and unborn. This is called the self-nature of the ultimate truth. [The Blessed One continued: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of emptiness (śūnyatā). What are these four? They are: first, the emptiness of characteristics (lakṣaṇa-śūnyatā); second, the emptiness of non-existence (abhāva-śūnyatā); third, the emptiness of non-existence of own-being (abhāvasvabhāva-śūnyatā); and fourth, the emptiness of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-śūnyatā). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the emptiness of characteristics? It is the fact that the five aggregates are devoid of the characteristics of permanence and eternity, and are like a dream or a phantom. This is called the emptiness of characteristics. What, Mahāmati, is the emptiness of non-existence? It is the absence of the nature of a self and what belongs to a self within the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. This is called the emptiness of non-existence. What, Mahāmati, is the emptiness of non-existence of own-being? It is the fact that all dharmas have no intrinsic nature of their own, as they arise dependently through causes and conditions. This is called the emptiness of non-existence of own-being. What, Mahāmati, is the emptiness of the ultimate truth? It is the state where the dependent self-nature is realized as being eternally free from the imagined self-nature, and where the perfected self-nature is fully understood. This is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth. [The Blessed One further said: "Mahāmati, you should understand that these four kinds of emptiness are the gateway to the realization of all dharmas. By means of this understanding, one transcends the duality of existence and non-existence and enters into the stage of the Tathāgata. [The Blessed One continued: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvana. What are these four? They are: first, the nirvana of the extinction of individuality (pudgalanairātmya); second, the nirvana of the extinction of both individuality and phenomena (dharmanairātmya); third, the nirvana of the extinction of the habit-energy of false discrimination; and fourth, the nirvana of the ultimate cessation of all mental activity. These, Mahāmati, are the four kinds of nirvana. [The Blessed One concluded: "Therefore, Mahāmati, you should cultivate the wisdom of non-discrimination and abandon the views of existence and non-existence. In this way, you shall quickly attain the supreme enlightenment of a Buddha.

388 ... [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are the four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of the ultimate truth (paramārtha-svabhāva). [Mahāmati asked: "What, Blessed One, is the imagined self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the attachment to names and signs (nāmanimitta) as being real entities, based on the false discrimination of the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields. [Mahāmati asked: "What, Blessed One, is the dependent self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the manifestation of objects through the power of false discrimination, like seeing a rope as a snake or water in a mirage. [Mahāmati asked: "What, Blessed One, is the perfected self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the non-dual nature that is free from the imagined and the dependent, which is the realm of the Tathāgatas and the noble ones, realized through the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti). [Mahāmati asked: "What, Blessed One, is the self-nature of the ultimate truth? [The Blessed One replied: "It is the suchness (tathatā) of all dharmas, which is unchanging, undifferentiated, and the object of the wisdom of the noble ones. [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, what is the distinction between the dependent self-nature and the perfected self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: "The dependent self-nature is characterized by causal conditions and is subject to change; the perfected self-nature is eternally free from those conditions and is the very essence of the dependent. [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, how many kinds of false discrimination (vikalpa) are there? [The Blessed One replied: "There are seven kinds: namely, the false discrimination of words (abhilāpa), the false discrimination of objects (artha), the false discrimination of self-nature, the false discrimination of differences, the false discrimination of attachment to characteristics, the false discrimination of attachment to the characteristics of difference, and the false discrimination of attachment to the characteristics of both. [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, how many kinds of consciousnesses (vijñāna) are there? [The Blessed One replied: "There are eight kinds of consciousness: the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), the ego-consciousness (manovijñāna), and the six sense-consciousnesses (ṣadvijñāna). [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, what is the characteristic of the storehouse consciousness? [The Blessed One replied: "It has the seeds of all dharmas as its characteristic, and it manifests as the body, the dwelling place, and the enjoyment of objects. It is like a great ocean, where the waves of the six sense-consciousnesses arise and cease according to conditions, while the storehouse itself remains undisturbed. [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, why does the storehouse consciousness not perceive its own seeds? [The Blessed One replied: "Because it is subtle and its activity is internal, it does not perceive its own seeds, just as a flame does not burn itself. [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, how is the transformation of the basis (āśrayaparāvṛtti) attained? [The Blessed One replied: "When the habit-energies (vāsanā) of false discrimination are extinguished through the realization of the non-existence of external objects and the mastery of the three self-natures, the storehouse consciousness undergoes a revolution, and this is called the transformation of the basis. [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, what is the meaning of 'emptiness' (śūnyatā)? [The Blessed One replied: "It means that all dharmas are devoid of the imagined self-nature, yet they are not empty of the dependent and perfected self-natures. It is like a painted image: though it appears as a person, it is empty of a person, yet it is not empty of color and form. Thus, emptiness is the non-existence of duality within existence, and the existence of non-duality within non-existence. [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, what is the meaning of 'non-self' (anātman)? [The Blessed One replied: "It means that all dharmas are devoid of a self-substance (ātman) and what belongs to a self (ātmīya), and that they are merely manifestations of false discrimination. Just as a magician creates illusions, so do the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields appear; they have no self or anything belonging to a self. [Mahāmati asked: "Blessed One, what is the meaning of 'nirvana'? [The Blessed One replied: "It means the cessation of the habit-energies of false discrimination, the exhaustion of the continuity of birth and death, and the attainment of the bliss of the noble ones. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, perceives that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivers beings from their suffering.

Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness. They are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells free from perversion, until finally attaining Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, know this, Śāriputra: the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, the peerless mantra, which relieves all suffering and is truly real, for it is not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, it is as if a great banyan tree were to grow near a village or a town. Its roots would extend for half a krośa, its trunk for half a krośa, and its branches and foliage would spread for half a krośa. Then, a man with good eyesight standing on the bank of the Ganges River, looking toward the west, might say: ‘That great banyan tree has not yet reached the western ocean; it will reach the western ocean when its roots, trunk, and branches have grown. Ānanda, do you think that person’s statement would be correct? “No, Blessed One. “Ānanda, in the same way, if a bhikkhu dwells with his mind well-restrained by mindfulness regarding the six bases of contact, he is one who has reached the goal, attained the ultimate security from bondage, lived the holy life, done what was to be done, and laid down the burden. He is one who has reached the supreme goal, transcended all suffering, and is no longer subject to future birth. Ānanda, suppose there were a young man or woman, sixteen years of age, endowed with the full vigor of youth, and they were to look at their own reflection in a clear mirror or in a vessel of oil. What do you think, Ānanda? Would that young man or woman be able to point out the signs of aging—such as wrinkles, gray hair, or teeth falling out—within themselves? “No, Blessed One. “In the same way, Ānanda, if a bhikkhu dwells with his mind well-restrained by mindfulness regarding the six bases of contact, he is one who has reached the goal... and is no longer subject to future birth. Ānanda, suppose a bhikkhu were to dwell with his mind well-restrained by mindfulness regarding the six bases of contact. If others were to strike him with clods of earth, sticks, or weapons, he would feel neither anger nor resentment. What do you think, Ānanda? Would such a bhikkhu be one who has reached the goal, attained the ultimate security from bondage, lived the holy life, done what was to be done, and laid down the burden—one who has reached the supreme goal, transcended all suffering, and is no longer subject to future birth? “Yes, Blessed One. “Ānanda, it is because of this that a bhikkhu who dwells with his mind well-restrained by mindfulness regarding the six bases of contact is one who has reached the goal... and is no longer subject to future birth.”

The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who dwells in suffering and does not transcend suffering; the person who dwells in suffering but transcends suffering; the person who dwells in happiness and does not transcend suffering; and the person who dwells in happiness and transcends suffering. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells in suffering and does not transcend suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is of little faith, of little virtue, of little learning, and of little wisdom.

This, monks, is called a person who dwells in suffering and does not transcend suffering. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells in suffering but transcends suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is of little faith, of little virtue, of little learning, and of little wisdom. However, he has developed the mind of loving-kindness even for a single session. By this, monks, he transcends the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, and the states of woe. This, monks, is called a person who dwells in suffering but transcends suffering. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells in happiness and does not transcend suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is of great faith, of great virtue, of great learning, and of great wisdom. However, he has not developed the mind of loving-kindness even for a single session. By this, monks, he does not transcend the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, and the states of woe. This, monks, is called a person who dwells in happiness and does not transcend suffering. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells in happiness and transcends suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is of great faith, of great virtue, of great learning, and of great wisdom. Furthermore, he has developed the mind of loving-kindness even for a single session. By this, monks, he transcends the plane of misery, the bad destination, the lower world, and the states of woe. This, monks, is called a person who dwells in happiness and transcends suffering. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world."* *This passage is an excerpt from the *Cattāro puggalā Sutta* (AN 4.95).*

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses four qualities, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through perfect knowledge.

What are these four? Here, Ānanda, a noble disciple possesses confirmed confidence in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly enlightened, accomplished in true knowledge and conduct, fortunate, knower of the world, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. He possesses confirmed confidence in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals—this Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. And he possesses the virtues dear to the noble ones—untorn, unbroken, unspotted, unsplattered, liberating, praised by the wise, untarnished, leading to concentration. [The Blessed One continued:

“Ānanda, when a noble disciple possesses these four qualities, he is one who has reached the goal, done what was to be done, laid down the burden, attained the true goal, destroyed the fetters of existence, and is liberated through perfect knowledge.”

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a lotus flower; the person who is like a blue lotus flower; the person who is like a white lotus flower; and the person who is like a red lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction, pervading it, suffusing it, filling it, and extending it throughout the entire world—above, below, across, everywhere, and in every way. Having done so, he dwells with a mind full of compassion, sympathetic joy, and equanimity toward one direction, pervading it, suffusing it, filling it, and extending it throughout the entire world—above, below, across, everywhere, and in every way. Just as a lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and remains unsullied by the water; even so, monks, that person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness... compassion... sympathetic joy... and equanimity toward one direction... and in every way. This, monks, is called a person like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... and in every way. He does not, however, dwell having attained the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsrava-kṣaya-jñāna) in this very life. But when his body breaks up, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, among the devas of the Brahmā realm. Just as a blue lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, remains submerged in the water; even so, monks, that person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness... and in every way, yet does not attain the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints in this very life, but is reborn among the devas of the Brahmā realm. This, monks, is called a person like a blue lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... and in every way.

He does not, however, dwell having attained the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints in this very life. But when his body breaks up, after death, he is reborn in a happy destination, in a heavenly world, among the devas of the Ābhāsvara realm. Just as a white lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, remains at the surface of the water; even so, monks, that person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness... and in every way, yet does not attain the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints in this very life, but is reborn among the Ābhāsvara devas. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus flower. And how, monks, is one a person like a red lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness toward one direction... and in every way. He does, however, dwell having attained the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints in this very life. Just as a red lotus flower, though born in the water and grown in the water, rises up above the water and remains unsullied by the water; even so, monks, that person dwells with a mind full of loving-kindness... and in every way, and attains the higher knowledge of the destruction of the taints in this very life. This, monks, is called a person like a red lotus flower. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, monks, one person dwells having made a vow for the present life; another dwells having made a vow for the future life; another dwells having made a vow for both the present and future lives; and another dwells having made no vow at all. “And how, monks, does a person dwell having made a vow for the present life? Here, monks, a certain person is virtuous, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha, perfect in conduct and resort, and seeing fear in even the slightest faults, he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. He acquires gain, honor, and praise through his virtue. Having acquired gain, honor, and praise through his virtue, he becomes intoxicated with that gain, honor, and praise, grows negligent, falls into negligence, and through that negligence, he falls away from that very virtue. This, monks, is called a person who dwells having made a vow for the present life. “And how, monks, does a person dwell having made a vow for the future life? Here, monks, a certain person is immoral, of bad character, unvirtuous, of corrupt conduct, and not seeing fear in unwholesome deeds, he commits various evil actions. He acquires gain, honor, and praise through his immorality. Having acquired gain, honor, and praise through his immorality, he becomes intoxicated with that gain, honor, and praise, grows negligent, falls into negligence, and through that negligence, he falls away from that very immorality. This, monks, is called a person who dwells having made a vow for the future life. “And how, monks, does a person dwell having made a vow for both the present and future lives? Here, monks, a certain person is virtuous, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha... [as above] ...he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. He acquires gain, honor, and praise through his virtue. Having acquired gain, honor, and praise through his virtue, he becomes intoxicated with that gain, honor, and praise, grows negligent, falls into negligence, and through that negligence, he falls away from that very virtue.

This, monks, is called a person who dwells having made a vow for both the present and future lives. “And how, monks, does a person dwell having made no vow at all? Here, monks, a certain person is virtuous, restrained by the restraint of the Pātimokkha... [as above] ...he trains himself by undertaking the training rules. He does not acquire gain, honor, or praise through his virtue. He does not become intoxicated with that lack of gain, honor, and praise; he does not grow negligent, nor fall into negligence, and through that lack of negligence, he does not fall away from that very virtue. This, monks, is called a person who dwells having made no vow at all. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : :

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, monks, one person dwells having abandoned both the pursuit of sensual pleasures and the pursuit of unwholesome states, and he does not experience the noble joy and happiness that transcend the world. This is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Then, monks, another person dwells having abandoned both the pursuit of sensual pleasures and the pursuit of unwholesome states, and he experiences the noble joy and happiness that transcend the world. This is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Then, monks, another person dwells having abandoned the pursuit of sensual pleasures, yet he has not abandoned the pursuit of unwholesome states; he does not experience the noble joy and happiness that transcend the world. This is called the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Then, monks, another person dwells having abandoned the pursuit of sensual pleasures, yet he has not abandoned the pursuit of unwholesome states; he does not experience the noble joy and happiness that transcend the world. This is called the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. When this was said, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “Blessed One, as for the person who dwells having abandoned both the pursuit of sensual pleasures and the pursuit of unwholesome states, and who does not experience the noble joy and happiness that transcend the world—this person, Blessed One, is still far from the destruction of the taints. “But, Blessed One, as for the person who dwells having abandoned both the pursuit of sensual pleasures and the pursuit of unwholesome states, and who experiences the noble joy and happiness that transcend the world—this person, Blessed One, is close to the destruction of the taints. “Blessed One, it is just as if there were a mountain stream flowing toward the east, and a man were to come along carrying a basket of seeds. • *The Great Treatise on the Stages of the Path to Enlightenment* (Byang chub lam rim chen mo) by Je Tsongkhapa. **Chapter One: The Preliminaries** **1. The Importance of Renunciation** In order to achieve liberation from cyclic existence, one must first cultivate the mind of renunciation. This is because even if one attains the meditative concentrations and superknowledges of the worldly realms, these are not sufficient to bring about the permanent cessation of suffering. As long as one does not turn away from the cycle of birth, aging, sickness, and death, one remains subject to the various forms of misery within the three realms of existence. Therefore, it is essential to develop a firm resolve to escape from samsara. **2. The Nature of Suffering** To generate this renunciation, one must understand the pervasive nature of suffering. All conditioned phenomena are characterized by the three types of suffering: the suffering of suffering (*duḥkha-duḥkhatā*), the suffering of change (*vipariṇāma-duḥkhatā*), and the suffering of conditioning (*saṃskāra-duḥkhatā*). Within the three realms of existence, beings experience the intense physical and mental pain of the hells; the constant anxiety and deprivation of the hungry ghosts; the toil and fear of the animals; the restlessness and competition of the asuras; and the inevitable fall from their high status experienced by gods and humans alike. Thus, the entire expanse of cyclic existence is nothing but a vast ocean of suffering. **3.

The Rarity of the Opportunity** Having understood the nature of suffering, one must recognize the extreme rarity of the opportunity to practice the Dharma. The attainment of a human rebirth endowed with the freedoms and advantages is as difficult to find as a blind turtle encountering a single yoke floating on the vast ocean. Furthermore, the appearance of a Buddha in the world and the preservation of his teachings are exceedingly rare. Having obtained such a precious vessel, it would be utterly tragic to waste it on worldly distractions rather than seeking liberation. **4. The Impermanence of Life** Since the time of death is uncertain and life is as fleeting as a dewdrop at sunrise or a bubble on water, one must not procrastinate in one's spiritual practice. Death can strike at any moment—whether from illness, injury, or natural causes—and when it occurs, nothing but one's virtuous roots can accompany one to the next life. Therefore, one should focus exclusively on accumulating merit and purifying obscurations while there is still time. **5. The Definitive Refuge** Finally, to protect oneself from the terrors of cyclic existence, one must take refuge in the Three Jewels: the Buddha, the Dharma, and the Sangha. The Buddha is the teacher who has realized the truth; the Dharma is the path that leads to liberation; and the Sangha consists of those who have successfully traversed that path. By relying upon them with unwavering faith, one establishes the foundation for all further spiritual progress. *Thus concludes the first chapter on the preliminaries.*

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a heap of filth; the person who is like a jewel casket; the person who is like a blue lotus; and the person who is like a white lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a heap of filth? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind obsessed by sensual desire, accompanied by much lust, much fever, much attachment, much thirst, much craving, much passion, much bondage, much infatuation, much clinging, and much grasping. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, perceives that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivers beings from their suffering. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness;

they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, no ear, no nose, no tongue, no body, and no mind; no form, no sound, no smell, no taste, no touchable object, and no mental phenomenon; no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; there is no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Having transcended all inverted views, he ultimately reaches *nirvāṇa*. In this way, Śāriputra, all Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra. It removes all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of the *prajñāpāramitā* should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With these words, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, as well as the world with its gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, rejoiced and praised what the Buddha had taught.

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be, and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food, gross or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. Thus spoke the Blessed One. These changes help form the correct grammatical forms of words. Visarga Sandhi Visarga sandhi involves the changes that occur when the visarga (: is followed by certain sounds. The visarga can be replaced by other sounds, such as sibilants or vowels, depending on the following letter. Vowel Sandhi Vowel sandhi deals with the changes that occur when two vowels come together. Depending on the specific vowels involved, they may combine to form a single long vowel or undergo other transformations. Consonant Sandhi Consonant sandhi involves the changes that occur when consonants meet. This includes rules for doubling consonants, changing their form, or adding nasalization. Samprasāraṇa Sandhi Samprasāraṇa sandhi is a specific type of vowel sandhi where certain vowels are replaced by their corresponding semivowels (e.g., i → y, u → v). This process is often seen in the formation of certain verb forms and nominal derivatives. Pragṛhya Sandhi Pragṛhya sandhi refers to situations where certain vowels remain unchanged despite being followed by another vowel. These vowels are considered "protected" (pragṛhya) and do not undergo the usual vowel sandhi changes. Avagra
