The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, monks, some person dwells having abandoned both internal and external clinging; he has cut off craving, severed the fetters, and by means of right knowledge, he has made an end of suffering.

This is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, some person dwells having abandoned internal clinging, but not external clinging; he has cut off craving, severed the fetters, and by means of right knowledge, he has made an end of suffering. This is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, some person dwells having abandoned external clinging, but not internal clinging; he has cut off craving, severed the fetters, and by means of right knowledge, he has made an end of suffering. This is called the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, some person dwells having abandoned neither internal nor external clinging; he has cut off craving, severed the fetters, and by means of right knowledge, he has made an end of suffering. This is called the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : : [The Buddha then spoke in verse: “Some person here, having abandoned both internal and external clinging, Has cut off craving and severed the bonds; through right knowledge, he has made an end of suffering. Another person here, having abandoned internal clinging but not external, Has cut off craving and severed the bonds; through right knowledge, he has made an end of suffering. Another person here, having abandoned external clinging but not internal, Has cut off craving and severed the bonds; through right knowledge, he has made an end of suffering. And another person here, having abandoned neither internal nor external clinging, Has cut off craving and severed the bonds; through right knowledge, he has made an end of suffering. These are the four persons who have reached the ultimate goal, Who have transcended all attachments and crossed over the flood. Having seen the Dhamma with their own eyes, they have attained Nibbāna; They are the ones who have truly conquered Māra and his army. : : :

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, monks, a certain person is one who has already crossed over and gone beyond, having abandoned both the near shore and the far shore, a brahmin who has reached the further shore, a tamer of the self, a perfectly awakened one. This, monks, is the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, a certain person is one who has crossed over and gone beyond, having abandoned the near shore but not yet the far shore, a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. This, monks, is the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, a certain person is one who has crossed over and gone beyond, having abandoned the near shore but not yet the far shore, a once-returner who, after returning to this world only one more time, will make an end of suffering. This, monks, is the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, a certain person is one who has crossed over and gone beyond, having abandoned the near shore but not yet the far shore, a non-returner who, having attained parinirvāṇa right here in this very life, will not return from that world.

This, monks, is the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : : Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One; it is marvelous, Blessed One! How well this has been spoken by the Blessed One: ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “If, Blessed One, a noble disciple were to possess even a mere fraction of these four qualities, he would still be reckoned as a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. That is to say: “He would have faith in the Buddha thus: ‘The Blessed One is an arahant, perfectly awakened, perfect in knowledge and conduct, sublime, knower of worlds, unsurpassed leader of persons to be tamed, teacher of devas and humans, the Buddha, the Blessed One. “He would have faith in the Dhamma thus: ‘The Dhamma is well-expounded by the Blessed One, directly visible, immediate, inviting one to come and see, applicable, to be personally realized by the wise. “He would have faith in the Saṅgha thus: ‘The Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is practicing the good way, practicing the straight way, practicing the true way, practicing the proper way; that is, the four pairs of persons, the eight types of individuals. This Saṅgha of the Blessed One’s disciples is worthy of gifts, worthy of hospitality, worthy of offerings, worthy of reverential salutation, the unsurpassed field of merit for the world. “If, Blessed One, a noble disciple were to possess even a mere fraction of these four qualities, he would still be reckoned as a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, with enlightenment as his destination. “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, monks, one person dwells having made himself the object of his own attention; another dwells having made others the object of their attention; another dwells having made both himself and others the object of their attention; and another dwells having made neither himself nor others the object of their attention. “And how, monks, does a person dwell having made himself the object of his own attention? Here, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. It is in this way, monks, that a person dwells having made himself the object of his own attention. “And how, monks, does a person dwell having made others the object of their attention? Here, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. It is in this way, monks, that a person dwells having made others the object of their attention. “And how, monks, does a person dwell having made both himself and others the object of their attention? Here, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. It is in this way, monks, that a person dwells having made both himself and others the object of their attention. “And how, monks, does a person dwell having made neither himself nor others the object of their attention? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with a mind imbued with loving-kindness toward one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth; so above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with loving-kindness—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will. He dwells with a mind imbued with compassion... with a mind imbued with sympathetic joy... with a mind imbued with equanimity toward one quarter, likewise the second, likewise the third, likewise the fourth;

so above, below, across, and everywhere, to all as to himself, he dwells pervading the entire world with a mind imbued with equanimity—vast, exalted, measureless, free from enmity, and free from ill will. It is in this way, monks, that a person dwells having made neither himself nor others the object of their attention. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : :

: : : The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, perceives that all five aggregates are empty, and thus delivers all beings from their suffering. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all dharmas are marked with emptiness;

they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor replete. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; because there is no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; because there is no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; because there is no realm of sight up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; because there is no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; because there is no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; because there is no wisdom and no attainment—therefore, O Śāriputra, in this emptiness there is nothing to attain. Because there is nothing to attain, the Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* as his refuge and dwells free from fear, having forever transcended all inverted dreams and nightmares, until he reaches *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, the peerless mantra, which relieves all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of the *prajñāpāramitā* should be proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Thus spoke the Blessed One. With joy, the Venerable Śāriputra and the entire assembly, along with the world of gods, humans, asuras, and gandharvas, praised what the Buddha had taught. : : :

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Vehicle. It is also called ‘The Sūtra on the Ten Stages,’ and it is also called ‘The Sūtra on the Ten Grounds. You should learn it thus. Then the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Vehicle’? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, because it is great in its basis, great in its objective, great in its practice, great in its skillful means, great in its wisdom, great in its liberation, great in its knowledge and vision of liberation, great in its power, great in its fearlessness, great in its unique qualities, and great in its unsurpassed state—therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Vehicle. “Furthermore, Ānanda, because it carries all beings across the great river of saṃsāra; because it leads all bodhisattvas to the city of omniscience; because it is the mother of all Tathāgatas; because it is the source of all dharmas of the Buddhas; because it is the foundation of all the qualities of a Buddha; because it is the treasury of all the jewels of the Dharma; because it is the light that dispels the darkness of ignorance; because it is the medicine that cures the disease of afflictions; because it is the rain that nourishes the crops of the roots of virtue; and because it is the path that leads to the city of Nirvāṇa—therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Vehicle. “Moreover, Ānanda, because it is vast and immeasurable like space; because it is profound and difficult to fathom like the ocean; because it is stable and unshakable like Mount Sumeru; because it is pure and stainless like the sky; because it is luminous and radiant like the sun and moon; because it is cool and refreshing like the great lake Anavatapta; because it is powerful and majestic like Indra’s thunderbolt;

because it is gentle and compassionate like a father toward his children; because it is impartial and equal toward all beings; and because it is the ultimate refuge for all who seek protection—therefore, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Vehicle. “Ānanda, those who hear this Dharma-discourse, believe in it, understand it, and practice according to it, shall all attain the stage of non-retrogression and, in the end, reach the city of omniscience. Therefore, you should receive, uphold, read, recite, explain, and practice this Dharma-discourse with diligence. Why is this? Because it is the supreme treasure of the Buddhas of the three times. At that time, the Venerable Ānanda, having heard these words of the Blessed One, was filled with joy and faith. He prostrated at the feet of the Blessed One, circumambulated him three times, and departed. The assembly of monks and the great multitude of bodhisattvas, having heard the Buddha’s teaching, were overjoyed and faithfully practiced it. Thus ends the first chapter, titled “The Introduction,” from the Mahāyāna sūtra *The Sūtra on the Ten Stages*, translated by the Tripitaka Master Xuanzang of the Great Tang.

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a shallow pond; the person who is like a deep pond; the person who is like a lotus flower; and the person who is like a great lotus flower. And how, monks, is a person like a shallow pond? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith, yet he does not dwell much in that faith;

he is endowed with virtue, yet he does not dwell much in that virtue; he is endowed with learning, yet he does not dwell much in that learning; he is endowed with generosity, yet he does not dwell much in that generosity; and he is endowed with wisdom, yet he does not dwell much in that wisdom.

This, monks, is called a person who is like a shallow pond. And how, monks, is a person like a deep pond? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith and dwells much in that faith; he is endowed with virtue and dwells much in that virtue; he is endowed with learning and dwells much in that learning; he is endowed with generosity and dwells much in that generosity; and he is endowed with wisdom and dwells much in that wisdom. This, monks, is called a person who is like a deep pond. And how, monks, is a person like a lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith, yet he does not dwell much in that faith... [and so on for the other qualities] ...he is endowed with wisdom, yet he does not dwell much in that wisdom; however, he is one who delights in solitude, delights in seclusion, delights in detachment, delights in renunciation, and delights in the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who is like a lotus flower. And how, monks, is a person like a great lotus flower? Here, monks, a certain person is endowed with faith and dwells much in that faith... [and so on for the other qualities] ...he is endowed with wisdom and dwells much in that wisdom; he delights in solitude, delights in seclusion, delights in detachment, delights in renunciation, and delights in the destruction of the taints; and furthermore, he attains even in this very life the deliverance of mind and deliverance by wisdom that are taintless, having been made to become through the destruction of the taints. This, monks, is called a person who is like a great lotus flower. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world.”

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. What are the four? They are: physical food, coarse or subtle; contact as the second; mental volition as the third; and consciousness as the fourth. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One, the Teacher, further spoke these verses: “Physical food is the sustenance for beings here, Contact is said to be the sustenance for the senses; Mental volition is the sustenance for those in the realm of desire, And consciousness is the sustenance for those in the realm of form. If one does not understand the origin and the cessation Of these four nutriments along with their causal conditions, One cannot transcend birth, old age, and death, Nor can one find peace from suffering. But if one understands the origin and the cessation Of these four nutriments along with their causal conditions, Having abandoned birth, old age, and death, One attains peace from all suffering. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, those monks rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. : : : At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage at his feet, and sat down to one side. As he was seated, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well-taught by the Blessed One are these four nutriments for the maintenance of beings who have already come to be and for the support of those seeking a new existence. ... [as above] ... One attains peace from all suffering. “It is so, Ānanda! It is so, Ānanda! It is wonderful, Ānanda, that you have understood this matter through such a brief teaching. For, Ānanda, if one were to teach the Dhamma thus: ‘Friends, whatever is felt, that is included within suffering’—this would be sufficient for a noble disciple to dwell with a mind detached from the world of sense-desires, detached from the world of form, and detached from the formless world, having attained final Nibbāna in this very life. This is what the Blessed One said. Having said this, the Fortunate One rose from his seat and entered his dwelling. Then the Venerable Ānanda, thinking, “The Teacher has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling,” rose from his seat, approached the Venerable Sāriputta, paid homage at his feet, and sat down to one side.

As he was seated, the Venerable Ānanda said to the Venerable Sāriputta: “Friend Sāriputta, the Blessed One has risen from his seat and entered his dwelling after speaking on this very matter of the four nutriments... Then the first man would say: ‘Friend, I did not point out the moon’s disk to you; I pointed out the moon itself. And the other would say: ‘Friend, I do not deny what you have said; I am dull-witted and do not see the moon. But since I see the moon’s disk, which is like a copper-colored pot, let that suffice for me. In the same way, friend Ānanda, when the Blessed One taught the Dhamma thus: ‘Whatever is felt, that is included within suffering’—this would be sufficient for a noble disciple to dwell with a mind detached from the world of sense-desires, detached from the world of form, and detached from the formless world, having attained final Nibbāna in this very life. “Friend Sāriputta, it is as if a man were to say: ‘I shall show you the moon,’ and pointing out the moon’s disk, were to say: ‘That is the moon. The Blessed One said this: “Ānanda, if a bhikkhu were to dwell with his mind well-established in these four establishments of mindfulness for even seven days, one of two fruits could be expected for him: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. This is what the Blessed One said. Elated, the venerable Ānanda delighted in the Blessed One’s words. Then the venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “Venerable sir, it would be good if the Blessed One would teach me the Dhamma in brief, so that, having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. “Ānanda, if you were to dwell with your mind well-established in these four establishments of mindfulness for even seven days, one of two fruits could be expected for you: either final knowledge in this very life, or, if there is a residue remaining, the state of non-returning. “But, venerable sir, how does a bhikkhu dwell with his mind well-established in these four establishments of mindfulness? “Here, Ānanda, a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure in regard to the world. 110 13: [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are the four? They are: the imagined self-nature (parikalpita-svabhāva), the dependent self-nature (paratantra-svabhāva), the perfected self-nature (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature as the basis of false discrimination (mithyā-vikalpa-adhiṣṭhāna-svabhāva). Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is that which is grasped by ordinary people through names and signs (nāma-nimitta) regarding objects that have no intrinsic nature; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the imagined self-nature. What is the dependent self-nature? It is that which arises depending on causes and conditions, being devoid of the characteristics of the imagined self-nature, yet serving as the basis for the manifestation of the imagined self-nature. This is called the dependent self-nature. What is the perfected self-nature? It is the state in which the dependent self-nature is completely free from the characteristics of the imagined self-nature, and is realized as the suchness (tathatā) of all phenomena. This is called the perfected self-nature. What is the self-nature as the basis of false discrimination? It is the storehouse consciousness (ālayavijñāna), which is the support for the arising of all false discriminations. Because it is the foundation upon which all deluded thoughts depend, it is called the self-nature as the basis of false discrimination. [The Blessed One continued: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, based on these four kinds of self-nature, there are three kinds of non-self (anātman): the non-self of persons (pudgala-nairātmya) and the non-self of phenomena (dharma-nairātmya). By realizing these two kinds of non-self, one enters the stage of the Bodhisattva and attains the transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti). Mahāmati, what is the emptiness of characteristics? It is that all phenomena are devoid of the characteristics of permanence and impermanence, and are thus empty of their own defining marks. It is that when one perceives a thing and finds that its specific characteristic does not exist, one says it is empty. For example, when one looks for a rabbit’s horns and they are not found, one says they are empty. This is called the emptiness of non-existence. What is the emptiness of existence? It is that all phenomena are empty because they lack an intrinsic nature of their own, even though they appear as existing due to the continuity of causes and conditions. This is called the emptiness of existence. What is the emptiness of mutual non-existence? It is that when one thing is absent in another, one says it is empty. For example, a cow is not a horse, and a horse is not a cow. This is called the emptiness of mutual non-existence. At that time, the venerable Mahāmati rose from his seat, bared his right shoulder, knelt with his right knee on the ground, joined his palms toward the Buddha, and addressed him, saying: "World-Honored One, please explain to me the characteristics of the Tathāgata-garbha, which is the essence of the Dharma-realm, the womb of the Tathāgatas, and the support of all phenomena. How many kinds of Tathāgata-garbha are there? [The Blessed One replied: "Mahāmati, the Tathāgata-garbha has two aspects: it is both identical to and different from the Ālayavijñāna. Why is this? Because the Tathāgata-garbha is the support for the arising of the seven evolving consciousnesses, it is identical to the Ālayavijñāna. However, because it is the ultimate reality (dharmadhātu) that is free from the outflows and is the source of the noble wisdom, it is different from the Ālayavijñāna. Furthermore, Mahāmati, the Tathāgata-garbha is the support for the arising of all phenomena, just as the ocean is the support for the waves. It is neither born nor destroyed, and it is eternal, constant, cool, and unchanging. It is the self-nature of all Buddhas, and it is the refuge for all sentient beings. If there were no Tathāgata-garbha, there would be no desire for liberation, nor would there be any attainment of nirvana. [The Blessed One continued: "Moreover, Mahāmati, there are five kinds of Nirvana. What are the five? They are: the Nirvana of the extinction of the aggregates (skandha-nirodha-nirvāṇa), the Nirvana of the exhaustion of the outflows (āsrava-kṣaya-nirvāṇa), the Nirvana of the realization of the self-nature of phenomena (dharma-svabhāva-abhisamaya-nirvāṇa), the Nirvana of the non-arising of phenomena (anutpāda-dharma-nirvāṇa), and the Nirvana of the Tathāgata-garbha (tathāgata-garbha-nirvāṇa). Mahāmati, the first three are the Nirvanas of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas, who are attached to the characteristics of the aggregates and the outflows. The fourth is the Nirvana of the Bodhisattvas, who realize the non-arising of all phenomena. The fifth is the true Nirvana of the Tathāgatas, which is the realization of the Tathāgata-garbha as the ultimate reality. [The Blessed One further said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of transformation of the basis (āśraya-parāvṛtti). What are the four? They are: the transformation of the basis of the body, the transformation of the basis of the senses, the transformation of the basis of the mind, and the transformation of the basis of the wisdom of the Dharma-realm.

By the transformation of the basis of the body, one attains a body that is free from birth and death. By the transformation of the basis of the senses, one attains the divine powers and the mastery over all sense organs. By the transformation of the basis of the mind, one attains the wisdom that is free from the dualistic grasping of subject and object. By the transformation of the basis of the wisdom of the Dharma-realm, one realizes the equality of all phenomena and attains the supreme enlightenment of the Tathāgata. [The Blessed One concluded: "Mahāmati, you should know that these four kinds of transformation of the basis are the fruits of the practice of the Bodhisattva path. By relying on the Tathāgata-garbha, one can transcend the realm of the Śrāvakas and Pratyekabuddhas and enter the stage of the Tathāgata. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should always cultivate the contemplation of the Tathāgata-garbha. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the venerable Mahāmati and the great assembly of Bodhisattvas rejoiced and upheld the words of the Buddha. 110 13: End

260. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound Prajñāpāramitā, perceives that all five aggregates are empty, and thereby delivers all beings from suffering and distress. Thus has the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara practiced the profound Prajñāpāramitā. At that time, the Bhagavat was at Rājagṛha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of bhikṣus and a great assembly of bodhisattvas. At that time, the Bhagavat addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should observe that all dharmas are marked with emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no sensation, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; no realm of the eye up to and including no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and because there is nothing to attain, a bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the mind-free state of non-attachment, free from all hindrances. Because there are no hindrances, there is no fear; transcending all inverted dreams, he reaches ultimate nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment.

Therefore, know that the Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra; it can remove all suffering and is true and not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā should be spoken: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra and the bodhisattva mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, having heard from the Buddha’s mouth this profound Prajñāpāramitā, rejoiced and faithfully accepted it. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, perceives that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivers all suffering beings from peril.

Śāriputra, if there were any sentient beings who, having heard this teaching on the *prajñāpāramitā*, were to believe, accept, and uphold it, one should know that such persons have, in former lives, already practiced the *prajñāpāramitā*. Why is this? Because those who hear this *prajñāpāramitā* and do not feel fear or trepidation are indeed rare. Furthermore, Śāriputra, if a good man or a good woman were to take as many worlds as there are grains of sand in the Ganges River and fill them with the seven precious jewels, and offer them as a gift to all the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas; and if another person were to hear even a single verse of this *prajñāpāramitā* and, having heard it, believe and accept it—then the latter would generate a far greater accumulation of merit than the former. Why is this? Because the *prajñāpāramitā* is the mother of the Buddhas, the progenitor of the Buddhas, and the guide of the Buddhas. All the Buddhas, Tathāgatas, Arhats, and Samyaksaṃbuddhas of the past, present, and future, by relying upon this *prajñāpāramitā*, have attained Anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi. Therefore, Śāriputra, one should know that this *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spell, the spell of great knowledge, the unsurpassed spell, the peerless spell, which pacifies all suffering. It is true and not false. Thus should the *prajñāpāramitā* mantra be recited: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, beheld that all five aggregates were empty and thereby delivered all beings from suffering and distress. Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. It is the same for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no field of the eye up to and including no field of mental consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, origin, cessation, or path; no wisdom and no attainment, and even no non-attainment. Therefore, Śāriputra, because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on the *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells free from perverted views, ultimately attaining *anuttara-samyak-saṃbodhi*. Therefore, know that the *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, and the peerless mantra, which relieves all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of the *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Chapter 1: The Proclamation of the Mantra. 183. At that time, the Venerable Śāriputra addressed the Buddha, saying: "O World-Honored One, what was the original cause and condition for the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara to plant roots of goodness? The Buddha told Śāriputra: "In the past, countless, immeasurable, inconceivable, and unspeakable numbers of kalpas ago, there was a Buddha named Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddho Bhagavān. That prince Sarvasattvapriyadarśana, seeing the Buddha Lokeśvararāja Tathāgata, Arhat, Samyaksambuddha, Vidyācaraṇasaṃpanna, Sugata, Lokavid, Anuttara, Puruṣadamyasārathi, Śāstā devamanuṣyāṇām, Buddho Bhagavān, together with a great assembly of monks, was filled with joy and faith. 11. The Chapter on the Noble Ones (Āryavarga) At one time, the Blessed One was dwelling at Śrāvastī in the Jeta Grove, the monastery of Anāthapiṇḍada. At that time, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada approached the Blessed One, paid homage with his head at his feet, and sat down to one side. Sitting there, the householder Anāthapiṇḍada addressed the Blessed One: “Venerable Sir, it would be well if the Blessed One would teach me the Dharma in brief, so that having heard it, I might dwell alone, withdrawn, diligent, ardent, and resolute. The Blessed One replied: “Householder, if you were to practice according to my teaching, then for you it would be well. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said: “Venerable Sir, how should I practice according to the Blessed One’s teaching? The Blessed One said: “Householder, if you were to abandon the five hindrances—those defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom—and dwell with your mind established in the four foundations of mindfulness, then for you it would be well. What are these four? Householder, here you should dwell contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. You should dwell contemplating feelings in feelings, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. You should dwell contemplating the mind in the mind, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. You should dwell contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and dejection regarding the world. Householder, if you were to practice according to my teaching in this way, then for you it would be well. The householder Anāthapiṇḍada said: “Venerable Sir, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! Just as one might set upright what had been overturned, or reveal what was hidden, or show the way to one who was lost, or bring an oil lamp into the darkness so that those with eyes might see forms, even so has the Blessed One taught the Dharma in various ways. Venerable Sir, I go for refuge to the Blessed One, to the Dharma, and to the Saṅgha of bhikṣus. May the Blessed One accept me as a lay follower who has gone for refuge from this day forth for as long as life lasts. Then the householder Anāthapiṇḍada, having delighted and rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One, rose from his seat, paid homage with his head at the Blessed One’s feet, and departed keeping him on his right. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; form is not other than emptiness, and emptiness is not other than form. The same is true for feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all dharmas are marked with emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death and no extinction of old age and death; no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the mind free from hindrance. Because there is no hindrance, there is no fear; transcending all inverted dreams, he reaches ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the unsurpassed mantra, the unequalled mantra, which relieves all suffering and is truly real, not false. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, if one were to speak of the qualities of the Tathāgata, they would not be exhausted even in a hundred thousand eons; yet, Ānanda, I shall now briefly describe for you the qualities of the Tathāgata. His conduct is pure, his speech is truthful, and his mind is liberated. He is endowed with the six supernormal knowledges and the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha. He is the refuge for those without refuge, the protector for those without protection, and the island for those without an island.

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? 20. The Chapter on the Refutation of the Self (Ātman) and the Refutation of the Person (Pudgala). I. The Refutation of the Self. Section One: Refuting the Self through Scriptural Authority. Verse 1: The self is not the aggregates, nor is it distinct from them; it does not possess the aggregates, nor do the aggregates belong to it; the self is not within the aggregates, nor are the aggregates within it. Thus, the self is not found in any way whatsoever. Commentary: Herein, the Vaibhāṣikas assert that the self is substantially existent, while the Sautrāntikas maintain that it is nominally existent. To refute both views, this chapter is composed. Now, first, the refutation of the self through scriptural authority is presented. The verse states: "The self is not the aggregates... and so forth. This means that the self is neither identical to the aggregates, nor is it something other than them. It does not possess the aggregates, nor do the aggregates belong to it. Furthermore, the self is not located within the aggregates, nor are the aggregates located within the self. Consequently, the self cannot be established in any manner whatsoever. Why is this? Because the self is not perceived as a substantial entity apart from the aggregates. If it were distinct from the aggregates, it would be perceived like a jar or a cloth; however, no such perception occurs. Therefore, the self is not distinct from the aggregates. Nor is the self identical to the aggregates, for if they were identical, the self would be subject to arising and ceasing, just like the aggregates. Furthermore, since the aggregates are multiple and impermanent, the self would likewise become multiple and impermanent. Moreover, the self is not the possessor of the aggregates, because there is no separate substance that could act as a possessor. Nor do the aggregates belong to the self, because there is no owner to whom they belong. Finally, the self is not contained within the aggregates, nor are the aggregates contained within the self, because neither can be apprehended as having a spatial location relative to the other. Thus, the self is not found in any way whatsoever. Section Two: Refuting the Self through Reasoning. Verse 2: If the self were the aggregates, then upon the destruction of the aggregates, the self would also be destroyed. If the self were distinct from the aggregates, then it would be permanent. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self through reasoning is presented. The verse states: "If the self were the aggregates... and so forth. This means that if one were to claim the self is identical to the aggregates, then when the aggregates are destroyed at death, the self would also be destroyed. However, the proponents of the self maintain that the self is eternal. Therefore, the self cannot be identical to the aggregates. Conversely, if one were to claim the self is distinct from the aggregates, then it would follow that the self is permanent and independent of the aggregates. Yet, no such permanent entity is ever perceived. Therefore, the self cannot be distinct from the aggregates either. Section Three: Refuting the Self by Examining its Characteristics. Verse 3: If the self were permanent, it would not experience pleasure or pain; it would not perform actions, nor would it undergo transmigration. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self by examining its characteristics is presented. The verse states: "If the self were permanent... and so forth. This means that if the self were truly permanent, it would be incapable of experiencing the sensations of pleasure and pain, as these are by nature impermanent. Furthermore, a permanent entity could not perform virtuous or non-virtuous actions, as action requires change and effort. Finally, a permanent self could not undergo the process of transmigration from one life to another, as it would be eternally fixed in one state. Therefore, the self cannot be permanent. Section Four: Refuting the Self by Examining its Causes. Verse 4: If the self were the cause of the aggregates, then the aggregates would arise without a cause; if the aggregates were the cause of the self, then the self would be impermanent. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self by examining its causes is presented. The verse states: "If the self were the cause of the aggregates... and so forth. This means that if the self were the primary cause of the aggregates, then the aggregates would arise independently of other conditions, which contradicts the principle of dependent origination. Conversely, if the aggregates were the cause of the self, then the self would be subject to arising and ceasing, and thus impermanent. Therefore, the self cannot be established as either the cause or the effect of the aggregates. Section Five: Refuting the Self by Examining its Relationship to the Body. Verse 5: If the self were the body, then the self would be material; if the self were distinct from the body, then it would be perceived elsewhere. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self by examining its relationship to the body is presented. The verse states: "If the self were the body... and so forth. This means that if the self were identical to the physical body, then the self would be composed of matter and subject to decay. If, on the other hand, the self were distinct from the body, it should be perceptible in a location separate from the body; however, no such entity is ever observed. Therefore, the self cannot be established as either identical to or distinct from the body. Section Six: Refuting the Self by Examining its Relationship to the Faculties. Verse 6: If the self were the faculties, then the self would be multiple; if the self were distinct from the faculties, then it would be perceived without them. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self by examining its relationship to the sense faculties is presented. The verse states: "If the self were the faculties... and so forth. This means that if the self were identical to the six sense faculties, then the self would be multiple, as there are six distinct faculties. If the self were distinct from the faculties, it should be perceivable even in the absence of the faculties, such as in a corpse; however, no such self is perceived. Therefore, the self cannot be established as either identical to or distinct from the faculties. Section Seven: Refuting the Self by Examining its Relationship to Consciousness. Verse 7: If the self were consciousness, then the self would be impermanent; if the self were distinct from consciousness, then it would be perceived without it. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self by examining its relationship to consciousness is presented. The verse states: "If the self were consciousness... and so forth. This means that if the self were identical to consciousness, then the self would be impermanent, as consciousness arises and ceases moment by moment. If the self were distinct from consciousness, it should be perceivable even in the absence of conscious thought; however, no such entity is ever perceived. Therefore, the self cannot be established as either identical to or distinct from consciousness. Section Eight: Refuting the Self by Examining its Relationship to the Mind. Verse 8: If the self were the mind, then the self would be impermanent; if the self were distinct from the mind, then it would be perceived without it. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self by examining its relationship to the mind is presented. The verse states: "If the self were the mind... and so forth. This means that if the self were identical to the mind, then the self would be impermanent, as the mind undergoes constant transformation. If the self were distinct from the mind, it should be perceivable even in the absence of mental activity; however, no such entity is ever perceived. Therefore, the self cannot be established as either identical to or distinct from the mind. Section Nine: Refuting the Self by Examining its Relationship to Mental Factors. Verse 9: If the self were associated with mental factors, then the self would be multiple; if the self were dissociated from mental factors, then it would be perceived without them. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self by examining its relationship to mental factors is presented. The verse states: "If the self were associated with mental factors... and so forth. This means that if the self were associated with the various mental factors such as feeling, perception, and volition, then the self would be multiple, as there are many distinct mental factors. If the self were dissociated from these factors, it should be perceivable even in their absence; however, no such entity is ever perceived. Therefore, the self cannot be established as either associated with or dissociated from mental factors. Section Ten: Refuting the Self by Examining its Relationship to the Body and Mind. Verse 10: If the self were both body and mind, then the self would be multiple; if the self were distinct from both, then it would be perceived without them. Commentary: Herein, the refutation of the self by examining its relationship to both the body and the mind is presented. The verse states: "If the self were both body and mind... and so forth. This means that if the self were identical to both the physical body and the mental continuum, then the self would be multiple, as there are two distinct entities. If the self were distinct from both, it should be perceivable even in the absence of both body and mind; however, no such entity is ever perceived. Therefore, the self cannot be established as either identical to or distinct from both the body and the mind. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, while practicing the profound *prajñāpāramitā*, perceives that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivers all suffering.

Thus, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; emptiness is not other than form, and form is not other than emptiness. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all phenomena are marked by emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither deficient nor complete. Within this emptiness, there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or mental object; no field of visual consciousness up to and including no field of mental consciousness; no ignorance and no extinction of ignorance, up to and including no aging and death and no extinction of aging and death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, the Bodhisattva relies on *prajñāpāramitā* and dwells with a mind free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, there is no fear, and having transcended all inverted dreams, he attains *nirvāṇa*. All Buddhas of the three times, relying on *prajñāpāramitā*, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Therefore, know that *prajñāpāramitā* is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra. It removes all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of *prajñāpāramitā* is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā.

30. 1. The Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint. Thus have I heard. At one time the Blessed One was dwelling at Sāvatthī in Jeta’s Grove, Anāthapiṇḍika’s Park. There the Blessed One addressed the bhikkhus: “Bhikkhus! “Venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Bhikkhus, just as whatever there is of footprints in the world, the elephant’s footprint is declared the foremost among them; for it, having encompassed them all, surpasses them in size—so too, bhikkhus, among all wholesome qualities, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost; for it, having encompassed them all, surpasses them. And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Eightfold Path? It is right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the Noble Eightfold Path. Now, bhikkhus, I shall teach you the simile of the elephant’s footprint. Listen to that and attend closely; I shall speak. “Yes, venerable sir,” those bhikkhus replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said this: “Suppose, bhikkhus, a wise man, desiring to know the extent of an elephant’s footprint, were to see the tracks of an elephant in the forest. Having seen them, he would infer: ‘The elephant that made these tracks must be either a young elephant, or a full-grown elephant, or a tusker. Why is that? Because the tracks are such as belong to an elephant. Then, bhikkhus, he might see the footprint of an elephant’s foot, the footprint of its trunk, the footprint of its ear, the footprint of its shoulder, the footprint of its belly, the footprint of its hindquarters, the footprint of its tail, and the footprint of its tail-hair. Having seen these, he would infer: ‘The elephant that made these tracks must be either a young elephant, or a full-grown elephant, or a tusker. Why is that? Because these tracks are such as belong to an elephant. But, bhikkhus, when he sees the elephant itself, he knows directly: ‘This is indeed an elephant. So too, bhikkhus, when one sees the Noble Eightfold Path, one knows directly: ‘The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is well-expounded, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. And what, bhikkhus, is the Noble Eightfold Path? It is right view... [as above] ...right concentration. This, bhikkhus, is called the Noble Eightfold Path. Just as, bhikkhus, the elephant’s footprint is declared the foremost among all footprints in the world, so too, bhikkhus, among all wholesome qualities, the Noble Eightfold Path is declared the foremost; for it, having encompassed them all, surpasses them. Therefore, bhikkhus, you should train yourselves thus: ‘We shall develop the Noble Eightfold Path, make it our vehicle, make it our basis, establish it, and fulfill it. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Elated, those bhikkhus rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One. Thus ends the Discourse on the Simile of the Elephant’s Footprint, the thirtieth in the Chapter on Similes. Having entered from the south gate, he would emerge from the north gate. Having entered from the west gate, he would emerge from the east gate. The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four ways of entering the womb. What four? Here, monks, one enters the womb with full awareness, dwells therein with full awareness, and departs from it with full awareness. This, monks, is the second way of entering the womb. “Again, monks, one enters the womb without full awareness, dwells therein with full awareness, and departs from it with full awareness. This, monks, is the third way of entering the womb. “Again, monks, one enters the womb without full awareness, dwells therein without full awareness, and departs from it without full awareness. This, monks, is the fourth way of entering the womb. “These, monks, are the four ways of entering the womb. : : : At that time, the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir; it is marvelous, venerable sir! 828. The Buddha said to the bhikṣus: “In the past, there was a king named Mahādeva who ruled over Jambudvīpa. At that time, there was a brahmin who had studied the Vedas and possessed great learning; he was well-versed in the five branches of knowledge and could recite the four Vedas. He had a son named Śroṇakoṭiviṃśa, who was intelligent and wise, capable of distinguishing right from wrong. When he reached the age of seven, he went with his father to the palace gate. There he saw a man whose hands, feet, ears, and nose were all severed, lying on the ground in great pain. Seeing this, he asked his father, ‘Father, what kind of person is this? His father replied, ‘Son, this is a thief who has been punished by the king for his crimes. The boy then asked, ‘Father, what is the meaning of “thief”? His father answered, ‘Son, this man stole the property of others; because he committed such evil deeds, he now suffers this punishment. The boy then asked, ‘Father, if one steals the property of others, will one suffer such a fate? His father replied, ‘Son, if one commits such evil deeds, one will surely suffer such a fate. The boy then said, ‘Father, I must never steal the property of others. Having spoken thus, he returned home. From that time forward, he never again took anything that did not belong to him. Because of this, when he grew up, he became a wealthy householder. Later, he encountered a śramaṇa who taught him the path of liberation. Having heard the Dharma, he developed a heart of renunciation and left the household life to become a monk. He practiced the holy life under the guidance of the Tathāgata and, through diligent effort, attained arhatship. The Buddha told the bhikṣus: “At that time, the son of the brahmin was none other than me. Because I cultivated the roots of goodness in that former life, I have now attained supreme perfect enlightenment. The Buddha further told the bhikṣus: “If a person gives even a small gift with a pure mind, the merit they obtain is vast and immeasurable. Therefore, you should always practice giving with a sincere heart. Thus the Buddha spoke, and the bhikṣus, having heard the Buddha’s words, rejoiced and put them into practice. 828. (21.16) ... [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfected accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of reality as it is (*tathatā-svabhāva*). Among these, Mahāmati, the self-nature of false discrimination consists in the attachment to names and characteristics (*nāma-lakṣaṇa-abhiniveśa*) regarding objects that do not exist. The self-nature of dependent origination consists in the manifestation of the various appearances of objects due to the habit-energy (*vāsanā*) of false discrimination.
The self-nature of perfected accomplishment consists in the non-existence of the former within the latter.
The self-nature of reality as it is consists in the non-arising of all dharmas. [End of section 21.16]

For this reason, they are called 'Buddhadharmas. Subhūti asked, "World-Honored One, for what reason are they called 'Buddhadharmas'? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, because they are neither dharmas nor non-dharmas, they are called 'Buddhadharmas. Furthermore, Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva were to fill world-systems as numerous as the sands of the Ganges with the seven treasures and give them as a gift, and if another person were to hear this Dharma-discourse and, having heard it, produce a mind of faith, the latter would generate a far greater accumulation of merit than the former. Why is this? Subhūti, all those world-systems are empty of a self, empty of a being, empty of a soul, and empty of a person. Subhūti, it is for this reason that this Dharma-discourse is called the 'Perfection of Wisdom. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should practice without apprehending form, without apprehending feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He should practice without apprehending the eye, without apprehending the ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind. He should practice without apprehending form, sound, odor, taste, touch, or phenomena. He should practice without apprehending the eye-consciousness element, up to and including the mind-consciousness element. He should practice without apprehending the element of ignorance, up to and including the element of old age and death. He should practice without apprehending the four foundations of mindfulness, the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, or the noble eightfold path. He should practice without apprehending emptiness, signlessness, or wishlessness. He should practice without apprehending the fruit of a Stream-enterer, the fruit of a Once-returner, the fruit of a Non-returner, or Arhatship. He should practice without apprehending Pratyekabuddhahood or All-Knowledge. He should practice without apprehending the level of a Śrāvaka, the level of a Pratyekabuddha, or the level of a Buddha. Why is this? Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he should practice without apprehending anything at all. Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom in this manner, Māra and his host will be unable to find an opportunity to harm him. Subhūti asked, "World-Honored One, how does a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practice the perfection of wisdom? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva should practice the perfection of wisdom by way of non-apprehension. Why is this? Subhūti, when a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a Bodhisattva, nor does he perceive a perfection of wisdom, nor does he perceive one who practices. Subhūti, it is for this reason that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom should practice without apprehending anything at all. Subhūti asked, "World-Honored One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without apprehending anything at all, how does he fulfill the six perfections? How does he enter the stages? How does he enter the concentrations, liberations, meditative absorptions, and attainments? How does he enter the doors of liberation such as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? How does he enter the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion? How does he purify the Buddha-fields? How does he mature sentient beings? How does he go forth toward the knowledge of all modes? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without apprehending anything at all, he fulfills the six perfections. He enters the stages. He enters the concentrations, liberations, meditative absorptions, and attainments. He enters the doors of liberation such as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness. He enters the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion. He purifies the Buddha-fields. He matures sentient beings. He goes forth toward the knowledge of all modes. Why is this? Subhūti, because all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended. Subhūti, it is for this reason that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practicing the perfection of wisdom without apprehending anything at all fulfills the six perfections, enters the stages, enters the concentrations, liberations, meditative absorptions, and attainments, enters the doors of liberation such as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness, enters the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion, purifies the Buddha-fields, matures sentient beings, and goes forth toward the knowledge of all modes. Subhūti asked, "World-Honored One, if all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended, how can a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, relying on the perfection of wisdom, enter the womb of a Tathāgata? How can he be born into the family of the Tathāgatas? How can he manifest the marks and signs of a Great Man? How can he display the various miraculous transformations? How can he turn the wheel of the Dharma? How can he demonstrate the entry into Nirvana? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, although all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended, yet a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, relying on the perfection of wisdom, enters the womb of a Tathāgata, is born into the family of the Tathāgatas, manifests the marks and signs of a Great Man, displays the various miraculous transformations, turns the wheel of the Dharma, and demonstrates the entry into Nirvana. Why is this? Subhūti, because the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas is not different from the perfection of wisdom, and the perfection of wisdom is not different from the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. The emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas is itself the perfection of wisdom, and the perfection of wisdom is itself the emptiness of intrinsic nature of all dharmas. Subhūti, it is for this reason that although all these dharmas are empty of intrinsic nature and cannot be apprehended, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, relying on the perfection of wisdom, performs these deeds. Subhūti asked, "World-Honored One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva relies on the perfection of wisdom and performs these deeds, is it not the case that he perceives a self, a being, a soul, or a person? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, it is not so. A Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a self, a being, a soul, or a person. Why is this? Subhūti, because a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom without apprehending a self, a being, a soul, or a person. Subhūti, it is for this reason that a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, though performing these deeds, does not perceive a self, a being, a soul, or a person. Subhūti asked, "World-Honored One, if a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva does not perceive a self, a being, a soul, or a person, how does he generate the thought of enlightenment? How does he practice the six perfections? How does he enter the stages? How does he enter the concentrations, liberations, meditative absorptions, and attainments? How does he enter the doors of liberation such as emptiness, signlessness, and wishlessness? How does he enter the ten powers, the four fearlessnesses, the four analytical knowledges, the eighteen unique qualities of a Buddha, and great compassion? How does he purify the Buddha-fields? How does he mature sentient beings? How does he go forth toward the knowledge of all modes? The Buddha said, "Subhūti, a Bodhisattva Mahāsattva generates the thought of enlightenment by way of non-apprehension. He practices the six perfections by way of non-apprehension.

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. He dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. This, monks, is called the first kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he also dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. But he does not attain internal tranquility of mind, nor does he attain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena as they truly are. This, monks, is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he also dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. And he attains internal tranquility of mind, but he does not attain the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena as they truly are. This, monks, is called the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Again, monks, a certain person dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world; he also dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. And he attains internal tranquility of mind, and he also attains the higher wisdom of insight into phenomena as they truly are. This, monks, is called the fourth kind of person found existing in the world. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : : Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir! How well spoken by the Blessed One were these words: ‘There are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “Venerable sir, how should one understand in detail the meaning of what was stated in brief by the Blessed One? “Ānanda, when a bhikkhu dwells contemplating the body in the body, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, his mind inclines toward seclusion, his mind inclines toward dispassion, his mind inclines toward cessation, and his mind inclines toward relinquishment. “When he dwells contemplating feelings in feelings... mind in the mind... phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world, his mind inclines toward seclusion, his mind inclines toward dispassion, his mind inclines toward cessation, and his mind inclines toward relinquishment.

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a blue lotus; the person who is like a red lotus; the person who is like a white lotus;

and the person who is like a fragrant lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sensual desire, with his mind obsessed by sensual desire; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sensual desire. This person, monks, is called ‘one like a blue lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a red lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by ill will, with his mind obsessed by ill will; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen ill will. This person, monks, is called ‘one like a red lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a white lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by sloth and torpor, with his mind obsessed by sloth and torpor; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen sloth and torpor. This person, monks, is called ‘one like a white lotus. And how, monks, is one a person like a fragrant lotus? Here, monks, a certain person dwells with his mind overcome by restlessness and remorse, with his mind obsessed by restlessness and remorse; he does not understand as it really is the escape from the arisen restlessness and remorse. This person, monks, is called ‘one like a fragrant lotus. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : :

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who dwells in suffering and seeks after suffering; the person who dwells in suffering and seeks after happiness; the person who dwells in happiness and seeks after suffering; and the person who dwells in happiness and seeks after happiness. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells in suffering and seeks after suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is unvirtuous, of bad character, impure in conduct, secretive in his actions, not seeing danger in even the slightest faults; he dwells with much anger and much resentment. He is often angry, bears ill will, harbors malice, and is full of hatred. He is envious, stingy, deceitful, and fraudulent. He is stubborn, has evil desires, and holds wrong views. He acts in accordance with those wrong views and causes others to act accordingly. This, monks, is called a person who dwells in suffering and seeks after suffering. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells in suffering and seeks after happiness? Here, monks, a certain person is unvirtuous... [as above] ...he holds wrong views. However, he does not act in accordance with those wrong views, nor does he cause others to act accordingly. This, monks, is called a person who dwells in suffering and seeks after happiness. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells in happiness and seeks after suffering? Here, monks, a certain person is virtuous, of good character, pure in conduct, not secretive in his actions, seeing danger in even the slightest faults; he dwells with little anger and little resentment. He is seldom angry, does not bear ill will, harbors no malice, and is free from hatred. He is not envious, not stingy, not deceitful, and not fraudulent. He is not stubborn, has no evil desires, and holds right views. He acts in accordance with those right views and causes others to act accordingly. This, monks, is called a person who dwells in happiness and seeks after suffering. And how, monks, is one a person who dwells in happiness and seeks after happiness? Here, monks, a certain person is virtuous, of good character, pure in conduct, not secretive in his actions, seeing danger in even the slightest faults;

he dwells with little anger and little resentment. He is seldom angry, does not bear ill will, harbors no malice, and is free from hatred. He is not envious, not stingy, not deceitful, and not fraudulent. He is not stubborn, has no evil desires, and holds right views. He acts in accordance with those right views and causes others to act accordingly. This, monks, is called a person who dwells in happiness and seeks after happiness. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : :

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? “Here, monks, a certain person is one who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. Another person is one who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. Another person is one who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. And another person is one who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. “And how, monks, is a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom; and he does not encourage others to abandon them. This, monks, is called a person intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others. “And how, monks, is a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare? Here, monks, a certain person encourages others to abandon the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom; but he himself does not dwell having abandoned them. This, monks, is called a person intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare. “And how, monks, is a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person neither dwells having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom, nor does he encourage others to abandon them. This, monks, is called a person intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others. “And how, monks, is a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others? Here, monks, a certain person dwells having abandoned the five hindrances, defilements of the mind that weaken wisdom; and he encourages others to abandon them. This, monks, is called a person intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. “These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : : Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said:

“It is wonderful, venerable sir, it is marvelous, venerable sir! How well this has been stated by the Blessed One: ‘These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. “It is so, Ānanda, it is so! These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. : : : Then the Venerable Ānanda rose from his seat, paid homage to the Blessed One, circumambulated him keeping the right side toward him, and departed. Then the Blessed One, soon after the Venerable Ānanda had left, addressed the monks: “Monks, suppose a man were to go to a friend’s house as a guest and, while staying there, were to eat as much as he liked of the finest food. But when he had eaten his fill and risen from his seat, the host would give him a small amount of sour gruel. What do you think, monks? Would that man, because of that, feel resentment or dissatisfaction toward his host? “No, venerable sir. Why is that? Because that man knows that the host has plenty of other fine foods and drinks, and he thinks: ‘My host has given me this small amount of sour gruel because he wishes to save it for those who have already eaten their fill. “In the same way, Ānanda, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. And what are the four? “Here, Ānanda, a certain person is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others... [as above] ...intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others. “Now, Ānanda, the person who is intent on his own welfare but not on the welfare of others is like the man who eats as much as he likes of the finest food and then receives the small amount of sour gruel. He does not feel resentment or dissatisfaction toward his host. “The person who is intent on the welfare of others but not on his own welfare is like the man who, having eaten his fill, gives the small amount of sour gruel to someone else who has already eaten their fill. He does not feel resentment or dissatisfaction toward his host. “The person who is intent neither on his own welfare nor on the welfare of others is like the man who, having eaten his fill, gives the small amount of sour gruel to someone else who has already eaten their fill, and then feels resentment or dissatisfaction toward his host. “But the person who is intent both on his own welfare and on the welfare of others is like the man who, having eaten his fill, gives the small amount of sour gruel to someone else who has already eaten their fill, and feels no resentment or dissatisfaction toward his host. “Thus, Ānanda, these four kinds of persons are found existing in the world. : : : Then the Venerable Ānanda approached the Blessed One, paid homage to him, sat down to one side, and said: “Venerable sir, how many kinds of persons are there who, when they pass away, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, or in hell? “There are, Ānanda, four kinds of persons who, when they pass away, are reborn in a state of deprivation, a bad destination, the lower world, or in hell.
