220. The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, by means of his profound Prajñāpāramitā, beholds that all the five aggregates are empty and thereby delivers all suffering. Now, Śāriputra, form is emptiness, and emptiness is form; form is not different from emptiness, and emptiness is not different from form; what is form is emptiness, and what is emptiness is form. The same applies to feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness. Śāriputra, all dharmas are marked with emptiness; they are neither produced nor destroyed, neither defiled nor pure, neither increasing nor decreasing. Therefore, Śāriputra, in emptiness there is no form, no feeling, no perception, no mental formations, and no consciousness; no eye, ear, nose, tongue, body, or mind; no form, sound, smell, taste, touch, or dharma; no sight-faculty up to no mind-faculty; no realm of sight up to no realm of mind-consciousness; and no ignorance, nor the extinction of ignorance, up to no old age and death, nor the extinction of old age and death. There is no suffering, no origin, no cessation, and no path; no wisdom and no attainment. Because there is nothing to attain, a Bodhisattva relies on Prajñāpāramitā and dwells in the heart of non-attachment, free from hindrance. Since there is no hindrance, he has no fear; transcending all inverted dreams, he reaches ultimate Nirvāṇa. All Buddhas of the three periods, relying on the Prajñāpāramitā, have fully awakened to unsurpassed, complete, and perfect enlightenment. Therefore, know that Prajñāpāramitā is the great spiritual mantra, the great bright mantra, the supreme mantra, and the peerless mantra, which relieves all suffering and is true, not false. Thus, the mantra of Prajñāpāramitā is proclaimed: Gate gate pāragate pārasaṃgate bodhi svāhā. Chapter Twenty-Five: The Chapter on the Dhāraṇī of Avalokiteśvara. 221. 4. The Four Noble Truths (Catvāri Āryasatyāni) The Blessed One said: “Monks, these four noble truths are to be realized by direct knowledge. What four? The noble truth of suffering; the noble truth of the origin of suffering; the noble truth of the cessation of suffering; and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. And what, monks, is the noble truth of suffering? Birth is suffering; aging is suffering; sickness is suffering; death is suffering; association with the unpleasant is suffering; separation from the beloved is suffering; not to obtain what one desires is suffering—in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, monks, is called the noble truth of suffering. And what, monks, is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is this craving which leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there; namely, craving for sensual pleasure, craving for existence, and craving for non-existence. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. And what, monks, is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that same craving—giving it up, relinquishing it, releasing it, letting go of it, and not adhering to it. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. And what, monks, is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is this Noble Eightfold Path; namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, monks, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering.”

This is his training in the perfection of ethical discipline. When he practices the perfection of patience, he does not perceive an object of anger, nor does he perceive one who is patient, nor does he perceive patience itself. 4: The Chapter on the Four Noble Truths At that time, the Venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One, saying: “Blessed One, it would be well if the Blessed One would teach the Dharma discourse on the Four Noble Truths. The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, listen well and attend closely; I shall speak. “Very well, Blessed One,” the Venerable Ānanda replied to the Blessed One. The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, what are the four noble truths? They are: the noble truth of suffering, the noble truth of the origin of suffering, the noble truth of the cessation of suffering, and the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. “Ānanda, what is the noble truth of suffering? It is birth, which is suffering; aging, which is suffering; sickness, which is suffering; death, which is suffering; encountering what is unpleasant, which is suffering; being separated from what is pleasant, which is suffering; not obtaining what one desires, which is suffering—in short, the five aggregates of clinging are suffering. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of suffering. “Ānanda, what is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is this craving that leads to renewed existence, accompanied by delight and lust, finding delight here and there—that is, the craving for sensual pleasure, the craving for existence, and the craving for non-existence. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the origin of suffering. “Ānanda, what is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is the complete fading away and cessation of that very craving—giving it up, relinquishing it, releasing it, and detaching from it. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the cessation of suffering. “Ānanda, what is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is the Noble Eightfold Path, namely: right view, right intention, right speech, right action, right livelihood, right effort, right mindfulness, and right concentration. This, Ānanda, is called the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering. “Ānanda, these are the four noble truths. “Ānanda, what is the noble truth of suffering? It is that which has been known by me as it truly is with wisdom. What is the noble truth of the origin of suffering? It is that which has been abandoned by me through the cultivation of the path. What is the noble truth of the cessation of suffering? It is that which has been realized by me through the cultivation of the path. What is the noble truth of the path leading to the cessation of suffering? It is that which has been cultivated by me through the cultivation of the path. “Ānanda, for a noble disciple who has thus seen these four noble truths as they truly are with wisdom, there are three further turnings and twelve modes of comprehension. “What are the three turnings and twelve modes of comprehension? ‘This is suffering’—this is the first turning, the first mode of comprehension. ‘This is the origin of suffering’—this is the second turning, the second mode of comprehension. ‘This is the cessation of suffering’—this is the third turning, the third mode of comprehension. ‘This is the path leading to the cessation of suffering’—this is the fourth turning, the fourth mode of comprehension. “‘Suffering must be fully understood’—this is the fifth turning, the fifth mode of comprehension. ‘The origin of suffering must be abandoned’—this is the sixth turning, the sixth mode of comprehension. ‘The cessation of suffering must be realized’—this is the seventh turning, the seventh mode of comprehension. ‘The path leading to the cessation of suffering must be cultivated’—this is the eighth turning, the eighth mode of comprehension. “‘Suffering has been fully understood’—this is the ninth turning, the ninth mode of comprehension. ‘The origin of suffering has been abandoned’—this is the tenth turning, the tenth mode of comprehension. ‘The cessation of suffering has been realized’—this is the eleventh turning, the eleventh mode of comprehension. ‘The path leading to the cessation of suffering has been cultivated’—this is the twelfth turning, the twelfth mode of comprehension. “Ānanda, when a noble disciple has thus completed these three turnings and twelve modes of comprehension regarding the four noble truths as they truly are with wisdom, he is then called a noble disciple who is a stream-enterer, no longer subject to rebirth in the lower realms, fixed in destiny, and assured of full enlightenment.”

He dwells contemplating phenomena in phenomena, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, having removed covetousness and displeasure regarding the world. [Page 1154] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the ultimate reality (*dharmatā-svabhāva*). Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of false discrimination? It is the attachment to the characteristics of objects through the manifestation of names and forms, just as a child clings to a phantom elephant created by a magician. This is called the self-nature of false discrimination. What is the self-nature of dependent origination? It is the arising of all phenomena based on causes and conditions, devoid of the characteristics of grasped and grasper. This is called the self-nature of dependent origination. What is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It is the realization that the self-nature of dependent origination is free from the characteristics of false discrimination; it is the non-dual realm of suchness. This is called the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. What is the self-nature of the ultimate reality? It is the Tathāgata-garbha, which is the realm of the noble ones, free from the habit-energies of false discrimination, and characterized by the purity of the threefold liberation. This is called the self-nature of the ultimate reality. Therefore, Mahāmati, you should train yourself to abandon the self-nature of false discrimination and to realize the self-natures of dependent origination, perfect accomplishment, and the ultimate reality. Thus, you shall quickly attain the stage of a Buddha.

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The person who is like a young jasmine flower; the person who is like a blue lotus; the person who is like a white lotus; and the person who is like a fragrant sandalwood tree. And how, monks, is a person like a young jasmine flower? Here, monks, a certain person is of noble birth, of high lineage, and of great wealth. He is handsome, attractive, and pleasing to behold, possessing supreme beauty of complexion. Yet he is unlearned, ignorant, and lacks wisdom. He does not know what is beneficial or what is harmful. He does not know what is right or what is wrong. He does not know what is blameworthy or what is blameless. He does not know what is base or what is sublime. He does not know what is dark or what is bright. He does not know the Dhamma as it really is. Just as a young jasmine flower might be of noble birth, of high lineage, and of great fragrance, yet be unopened and not yet fully blossomed—so too, monks, is this person like a young jasmine flower. This, monks, is called a person like a young jasmine flower. And how, monks, is a person like a blue lotus? Here, monks, a certain person is of noble birth, of high lineage, and of great wealth. He is handsome, attractive, and pleasing to behold, possessing supreme beauty of complexion. He is learned, wise, and possesses insight. He knows what is beneficial and what is harmful. He knows what is right and what is wrong. He knows what is blameworthy and what is blameless. He knows what is base and what is sublime. He knows what is dark and what is bright. He knows the Dhamma as it really is. Just as a blue lotus might be of noble birth, of high lineage, and of great fragrance, yet remain closed and not yet fully opened—so too, monks, is this person like a blue lotus. This, monks, is called a person like a white lotus. And how, monks, is a person like a fragrant sandalwood tree? Here, monks, a certain person is of noble birth, of high lineage, and of great wealth. (30) ... [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are the four? They are: the imagined self-nature (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the dependent self-nature (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the perfected self-nature (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of words (*nirūḍha-vyavahāra-svabhāva*). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the imagined self-nature? It is the grasping of names, signs, and characteristics based on the aggregates, elements, and sense-fields, which are themselves devoid of intrinsic nature; it is like seeing a rope in the dark and imagining it to be a snake. This is called the imagined self-nature. What, Mahāmati, is the dependent self-nature? It is the manifestation of the various forms of consciousness arising from the causal conditions of the storehouse consciousness (*ālaya-vijñāna*) and the evolving consciousnesses (*pravṛtti-vijñāna*); it is like a dream, a mirage, a city of Gandharvas, or a reflection. This is called the dependent self-nature. What, Mahāmati, is the perfected self-nature? It is the state of the non-existence of the imagined self-nature within the dependent self-nature; it is the realization of suchness (*tathatā*), the limit of reality (*bhūtakoṭi*), and the dharma-realm (*dharmadhātu*). This is called the perfected self-nature. What, Mahāmati, is the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of words? It is the conventional expression of names, signs, and characteristics regarding all phenomena, which is established by the power of beginningless habit-energy.
This is called the self-nature as the basis for the manifestation of words. Mahāmati, these are the four kinds of self-nature. [End of Section 30]

The Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, beholding those suffering beings, by means of his profound wisdom, perceived that all five aggregates are empty and thereby delivered them from all suffering. If there be sentient beings who, having heard the name of this Bodhisattva Mahāsattva, invoke him with single-minded devotion, how does the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara provide them with protection and deliverance? The Buddha told Śāriputra: “If there be any good man or good woman who, during a hundred million eons, were to give alms to Buddhas as numerous as the sands of the Ganges River; and if another person, having heard the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, were to invoke him with single-minded devotion—then the merit of the latter would exceed that of the former. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara possesses great spiritual power and great compassionate power. If there be any sentient beings who suffer from various afflictions, and they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, he will immediately cause them all to be delivered from their suffering. “Furthermore, Śāriputra, if there be any sentient beings who fall into a great fire, and they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, the fire will not be able to burn them. If there be any sentient beings adrift upon the great ocean, encountering waves and wind, and they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, they will immediately reach a safe shore. If there be any robbers or bandits who intend to harm them, and they invoke the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, the robbers will immediately abandon their evil intentions. “Śāriputra, if a man possessed by a yakṣa or a rākṣasa invokes the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, the yakṣa or rākṣasa will immediately depart. If a woman desires a son or a daughter, and she invokes the name of the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara with single-minded devotion, she will immediately give birth to a child who is handsome, virtuous, and endowed with wisdom. Such a child will never again fall into the three evil realms for hundreds of thousands of millions of eons. “Śāriputra, if there be any good man or good woman who wishes to practice the profound Prajñāpāramitā, they should rely on the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara as their teacher. Why is this? Because the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara is a great compassionate one who provides great protection and deliverance. Śāriputra, if you wish to see the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara, you should contemplate the Bodhisattva Mahāsattva Avalokiteśvara as being like Mount Sumeru. The Blessed One said this: "Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? What, monks, is the person like a well that has been dug but not yet filled with water? Here, monks, a certain person has heard thus: 'The Dhamma taught by the Blessed One is well-expounded, visible here and now, timeless, inviting one to come and see, leading onward, to be realized by the wise, each for themselves. Having heard this, he goes to the Blessed One and asks about the meaning of the Dhamma. The Blessed One teaches him the Dhamma in brief and in detail. Having heard the Dhamma from the Blessed One, he gains faith in the Tathāgata. With faith as his foundation, he applies himself to the practice of virtue. He does not, however, attain the destruction of the taints in this very life, nor does he attain final knowledge. But when he passes away, he is reborn in a good destination, in a heavenly world. There, having attained the destruction of the taints, he realizes final Nibbāna.

This, monks, is called the person like a well that has been dug but not yet filled with water. And what, monks, is the person like a well that has been dug and filled with water, but whose rope and bucket are broken? Here, monks, a certain person has heard thus... 11–12. [The Blessed One said: “Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature. What are the four? [Mahāmati asked: “What, Blessed One, is the self-nature of attachment to words? [Mahāmati asked: “What, Blessed One, is the self-nature of attachment to multiplicity of objects? [The Blessed One replied: “It is the manifestation of external objects as having various distinct forms, such as color, shape, and so forth; this is called the self-nature of attachment to multiplicity of objects. [Mahāmati asked: “What, Blessed One, is the self-nature of attachment to false discrimination? [The Blessed One replied: “It is the grasping of subject and object through false discrimination, like seeing a rope as a snake; this is called the self-nature of attachment to false discrimination. [Mahāmati asked: “What, Blessed One, is the perfectly accomplished self-nature? [The Blessed One replied: “It is the realization of the non-existence of subject and object, which is the realm of the Tathāgatas, free from the habit-energy of false discrimination; this is called the perfectly accomplished self-nature. [Mahāmati asked: “What, Blessed One, is the emptiness of mutual non-existence? [The Blessed One replied: “It is the non-perception of the ultimate truth within the five aggregates, because it is devoid of the characteristics of birth and destruction; this is called the emptiness of the ultimate truth. [Mahāmati asked: “What, Blessed One, is the emptiness of the highest reality? [The Blessed One replied: “It is the non-perception of the highest reality within the five aggregates, because it transcends the duality of being and non-being; this is called the emptiness of the highest reality. [Mahāmati asked: “What, Blessed One, is the emptiness of non-apprehension? [The Blessed One replied: “It is the non-perception of the past, future, and present within the five aggregates, because they cannot be apprehended as existing entities; this is called the emptiness of non-apprehension. [Mahāmati asked: “What, Blessed One, is the emptiness of non-existence? [The Blessed One replied: “It is the non-perception of the five aggregates as having the nature of a self or what belongs to a self; this is called the emptiness of non-existence. (Chapter Seventy-six) The Buddha was staying at Rājagṛha on Mount Gṛdhrakūṭa, together with a great assembly of twelve thousand bhikṣus. Among them were the venerable Śāriputra, the venerable Mahāmaudgalyāyana, the venerable Mahākāśyapa, the venerable Subhūti, the venerable Mahākapphiṇa, the venerable Mahākauṣṭhila, the venerable Mahācunda, the venerable Revata, the venerable Ānanda, and so forth, along with many other great śrāvakas. There were also bodhisattvas mahāsattvas such as the bodhisattva mahāsattva Akṣayamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Vajramati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Ratnamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Anantamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Amitamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Viśeṣamati, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Samantabhadra, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Mañjuśrī, the bodhisattva mahāsattva Maitreya, and so forth, along with many other great bodhisattvas mahāsattvas. At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the venerable Śāriputra: “Śāriputra, if there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, how should they dwell in it? The venerable Śāriputra said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, how should those sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā dwell in it? The Buddha told Śāriputra: “If there are sons of good family or daughters of good family who wish to practice the profound prajñāpāramitā, they should thus contemplate: ‘Form is empty; emptiness is form. Emptiness is not other than form; form is not other than emptiness. Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are also like this. Śāriputra, all dharmas are marked by emptiness; they have no characteristics, no birth, no cessation, no defilement, no purity, no decrease, and no increase. Śāriputra, because form is empty, there is no form; because feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness are empty, there is no consciousness. Śāriputra, because the four foundations of mindfulness are empty, there are no four foundations of mindfulness; because the four right efforts, the four bases of psychic power, the five faculties, the five powers, the seven factors of enlightenment, and the eightfold noble path are empty, there are no eightfold noble paths. Śāriputra, because the four dhyānas, the four immeasurables, the four formless attainments, the eighteen special dharmas of a buddha, and the ten powers of a tathāgata are empty, there are no ten powers of a tathāgata. Śāriputra, because the four fearlessnesses, the four kinds of analytical knowledge, the eighteen unshared dharmas of a buddha, and great compassion are empty, there is no great compassion. Śāriputra, because all dharmas are empty, there is no attainment and no non-attainment. At that time, the venerable Śāriputra said to the Buddha: “World-Honored One, if all dharmas are empty and without characteristics, then what dharma does the Tathāgata fully awaken to and realize as supreme perfect enlightenment? (80) : : The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. What four? The one who goes from darkness to darkness; the one who goes from darkness to light; the one who goes from light to darkness; and the one who goes from light to light. These, monks, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Then the Venerable Ānanda said this to the Blessed One: “It is wonderful, Blessed One! It is marvelous, Blessed One! How well has the Blessed One explained the meaning of this: ‘The one who goes from darkness to darkness; the one who goes from darkness to light; the one who goes from light to darkness; and the one who goes from light to light. “Ānanda, how does a person go from darkness to darkness? Here, Ānanda, someone is of low birth, of low lineage, poor, destitute, and lacking in means. He is ugly, unsightly, and ill-favored. He is dull-witted, slow in understanding, and lacks wisdom. He performs unwholesome deeds with his body, speech, and mind. Having performed such deeds, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, or in hell. This, Ānanda, is called a person who goes from darkness to darkness. And how, Ānanda, does a person go from darkness to light? Here, Ānanda, someone is of low birth... [as above] ...and lacks wisdom. Yet he performs wholesome deeds with his body, speech, and mind. Having performed such deeds, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This, Ānanda, is called a person who goes from darkness to light. And how, Ānanda, does a person go from light to darkness? Here, Ānanda, someone is of high birth, of noble lineage, wealthy, affluent, and possessing great means.

He is handsome, beautiful, and well-favored. He is wise, intelligent, and possesses discernment. Yet he performs unwholesome deeds with his body, speech, and mind. Having performed such deeds, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a state of misery, a bad destination, the lower world, or in hell. This, Ānanda, is called a person who goes from light to darkness. And how, Ānanda, does a person go from light to light? Here, Ānanda, someone is of high birth... [as above] ...and possesses discernment. He performs wholesome deeds with his body, speech, and mind. Having performed such deeds, at the breaking up of the body after death, he is reborn in a good destination, a heavenly world. This, Ānanda, is called a person who goes from light to light. These, Ānanda, are the four kinds of persons found existing in the world. Thus spoke the Blessed One. Delighted, the Venerable Ānanda rejoiced in what the Blessed One had said. (80) : :

The Blessed One said this: “Monks, there are these four kinds of persons found existing in the world. This is called the second kind of person found existing in the world. “Then again, monks, some person dwells pursuing the practice of sensual pleasure, devoted to the practice of sensual pleasure; he regards the pursuit of the practice of sensual pleasure as the essence. This is called the third kind of person found existing in the world. “Then again, monks, some person dwells having transcended both the pursuit of the practice of bodily torment and the pursuit of the practice of sensual pleasure, and having reached the state beyond both, he dwells in the attainment of the fourth jhāna, which is neither-painful-nor-pleasant and possesses purity of mindfulness through equanimity;
he regards the attainment of the fourth jhāna as the essence. This is called the fourth kind of person found existing in the world.

“Of these four kinds of persons found existing in the world, monks, it is this last one who is the foremost, the best, the most excellent, the most sublime, the highest, the supreme, the unequalled, the peerless, the incomparable, the matchless, the unrivaled, the unsurpassed, the unexcelled, the preeminent, the chief, the leader, the guide, the charioteer, the one who has gone to the further shore, the one who has crossed over, the one who has attained Nibbāna, the one who has reached the goal, the one who has completed the journey, the one who has laid down the burden, the one who has lived the holy life, the one who has accomplished his task, the one who has cast off the fetters of existence, the one who is liberated through perfect knowledge, the one who is cooled, the one who has become an Arhat.”

[The Blessed One said: "Subhūti, it is thus: when a bodhisattva mahāsattva practices the perfection of wisdom, he does not perceive a self, nor does he perceive a sentient being, a soul, or a person. He does not perceive form, nor does he perceive feeling, perception, mental formations, or consciousness. He does not perceive the eye, nor does he perceive forms, nor does he perceive eye-consciousness. He does not perceive the ear, nor does he perceive sounds, nor does he perceive ear-consciousness. He does not perceive the nose, nor does he perceive odors, nor does he perceive nose-consciousness. He does not perceive the tongue, nor does he perceive tastes, nor does he perceive tongue-consciousness. He does not perceive the body, nor does he perceive tangibles, nor does he perceive body-consciousness. He does not perceive the mind, nor does he perceive mental phenomena, nor does he perceive mind-consciousness.

He does not perceive the element of earth, nor does he perceive the elements of water, fire, wind, space, or consciousness. He does not perceive the realm of desire, nor does he perceive the realm of form, nor does he perceive the formless realm. He does not perceive ignorance, nor does he perceive volitional formations, nor does he perceive consciousness, name-and-form, the six sense bases, contact, feeling, craving, grasping, becoming, birth, or old age and death. He does not perceive suffering, its origin, its cessation, or the path. He does not perceive the fruit of stream-entry, nor the fruit of once-returning, nor the fruit of non-returning, nor arhatship, nor pratyekabuddhahood, nor even unsurpassed, perfect, and complete enlightenment. Subhūti, because a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma whatsoever, he is called a 'bodhisattva'. [Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva does not perceive any dharma, how does he train in the perfection of giving? [Subhūti asked: "Blessed One, if all dharmas are empty, how does a bodhisattva mahāsattva generate the thought of awakening? How does he practice the six perfections? At that time, the World-Honored One addressed the great assembly of bodhisattvas, saying: “Good sons, suppose there were a man who, having traveled through many countries, arrived at a certain place where he encountered a great fire. He was surrounded on all sides by flames, with no way to escape. Frightened and terrified, he cried out for help. At that moment, his father came from afar, seeing him in such distress, and thought to himself: ‘This child of mine has fallen into a great danger; I must use skillful means to save him. Thinking thus, he employed various expedients to call out to his son, saying: ‘Come here, my son! Come here, my son! But the son did not hear his father’s voice. Why is this? Because he was too far away. Then the father further used skillful means, speaking to his son and saying: ‘I have prepared for you various toys—ox-carts, goat-carts, and deer-carts. Come quickly, my son, and take them! Hearing this, the son was filled with joy and immediately ran toward his father. Why is this? Because he desired those playthings. At that time, the father, seeing his son had come near, spoke to him again, saying: ‘These ox-carts, goat-carts, and deer-carts are all for you to enjoy as you please. Good sons, what do you think? 32. ... [The Blessed One said: "Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (svabhāva). What are the four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (parikalpita-svabhāva), the self-nature of dependent origination (paratantra-svabhāva), the self-nature of perfect accomplishment (pariniṣpanna-svabhāva), and the self-nature of reality as it is (yathābhūta-svabhāva). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of false discrimination? It is the attachment to the characteristics of objects through the manifestation of names and forms (nāmarūpa) based on the unreal imagination (abhūtaparikalpa). This is called the self-nature of false discrimination. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of dependent origination? It is the manifestation of the various appearances of objects arising from the seeds of the habit-energies (vāsanā-bīja) of unreal imagination; this is called the self-nature of dependent origination. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of perfect accomplishment? It is the non-existence of the self-nature of false discrimination within the self-nature of dependent origination; this is called the self-nature of perfect accomplishment. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the self-nature of reality as it is? It is the realization of the non-existence of the two self-natures—namely, the self-nature of false discrimination and the self-nature of dependent origination—and the attainment of the stage of Tathāgatahood by means of the wisdom of the noble ones (āryajñāna); this is called the self-nature of reality as it is. Thus spoke the Blessed One. At that time, the World-Honored One further addressed Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of nirvana. What are the four? They are: the nirvana of the extinction of the characteristics of the aggregates (skandha-lakṣaṇa-kṣaya-nirvāṇa), the nirvana of the extinction of the continuity of the causal chain (prabandha-hetu-kṣaya-nirvāṇa), the nirvana of the non-duality of existence and non-existence (bhāvābhāva-advaya-nirvāṇa), and the nirvana of the exhaustion of the characteristics of the knowable (jñeya-lakṣaṇa-kṣaya-nirvāṇa). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the nirvana of the extinction of the characteristics of the aggregates? It is when those who hold views of eternalism and nihilism, having perceived the characteristics of the five aggregates, realize that they are like illusions, dreams, and reflections, and thus attain liberation; this is called the nirvana of the extinction of the characteristics of the aggregates. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the nirvana of the extinction of the continuity of the causal chain? It is when those who hold views of eternalism and nihilism, having perceived the characteristics of the five aggregates, realize that they are like illusions, dreams, and reflections, and thus attain liberation; this is called the nirvana of the extinction of the continuity of the causal chain. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the nirvana of the non-duality of existence and non-existence? It is when those who hold views of eternalism and nihilism, having perceived the characteristics of the five aggregates, realize that they are like illusions, dreams, and reflections, and thus attain liberation; this is called the nirvana of the non-duality of existence and non-existence. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the nirvana of the exhaustion of the characteristics of the knowable? It is the realization of the non-existence of the two self-natures—namely, the self-nature of false discrimination and the self-nature of dependent origination—within the self-nature of perfect accomplishment, and the attainment of the stage of Tathāgatahood by means of the wisdom of the noble ones; this is called the nirvana of the exhaustion of the characteristics of the knowable. Thus spoke the Blessed One. At that time, the World-Honored One further addressed Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of mind-only (cittamātra). What are the four? They are: the mind-only of the realm of phenomena (dharmadhātu-cittamātra), the mind-only of the stage of practice (bhūmi-pratipatti-cittamātra), the mind-only of the stage of fruition (phala-cittamātra), and the mind-only of the ultimate limit (koṭi-cittamātra). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the mind-only of the realm of phenomena? It is the manifestation of all phenomena as being like illusions, dreams, and reflections, and the realization that all phenomena are devoid of the characteristics of duality; this is called the mind-only of the realm of phenomena. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the mind-only of the stage of practice? It is the cultivation of the stages of the bodhisattvas, beginning with the first stage up to the tenth stage, by means of the wisdom of the noble ones; this is called the mind-only of the stage of practice. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the mind-only of the stage of fruition? It is the attainment of the stage of Tathāgatahood by means of the wisdom of the noble ones, having transcended the stages of the bodhisattvas; this is called the mind-only of the stage of fruition. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the mind-only of the ultimate limit? It is the realization that all phenomena are beyond the reach of words and letters, and the attainment of the state of the Tathāgata which is free from the characteristics of all dharmas; this is called the mind-only of the ultimate limit. Thus spoke the Blessed One. At that time, the World-Honored One further addressed Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of the perfection of wisdom (prajñāpāramitā). What are the four? They are: the perfection of wisdom of the non-arising of all dharmas (anutpāda-prajñāpāramitā), the perfection of wisdom of the non-extinction of all dharmas (anirodha-prajñāpāramitā), the perfection of wisdom of the non-duality of existence and non-existence (bhāvābhāva-advaya-prajñāpāramitā), and the perfection of wisdom of the exhaustion of the characteristics of the knowable (jñeya-lakṣaṇa-kṣaya-prajñāpāramitā). Among these, Mahāmati, what is the perfection of wisdom of the non-arising of all dharmas? It is the realization that all dharmas are originally unborn because they lack the characteristics of self and other; this is called the perfection of wisdom of the non-arising of all dharmas. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the perfection of wisdom of the non-extinction of all dharmas? It is the realization that all dharmas are originally unextinguished because they lack the characteristics of birth and death; this is called the perfection of wisdom of the non-extinction of all dharmas. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the perfection of wisdom of the non-duality of existence and non-existence? It is the realization that all dharmas are neither existent nor non-existent because they are like illusions, dreams, and reflections; this is called the perfection of wisdom of the non-duality of existence and non-existence. Furthermore, Mahāmati, what is the perfection of wisdom of the exhaustion of the characteristics of the knowable? It is the realization of the non-existence of the two self-natures—namely, the self-nature of false discrimination and the self-nature of dependent origination—within the self-nature of perfect accomplishment, and the attainment of the stage of Tathāgatahood by means of the wisdom of the noble ones; this is called the perfection of wisdom of the exhaustion of the characteristics of the knowable. Thus spoke the Blessed One. At that time, the World-Honored One further addressed Mahāmati the Bodhisattva-Mahāsattva, saying: "Mahāmati, there are four kinds of the path of practice (pratipad). It is the cultivation of the thirty-seven factors of enlightenment (bodhipākṣika-dharma) and the realization of the emptiness of persons (pudgala-śūnyatā); this is called the path of practice of the śrāvakas. [Page 1180] Furthermore, Mahāmati, there are four kinds of self-nature (*svabhāva*). What are these four? They are: the self-nature of false discrimination (*parikalpita-svabhāva*), the self-nature of dependent origination (*paratantra-svabhāva*), the self-nature of perfected reality (*pariniṣpanna-svabhāva*), and the self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha. Therein, Mahāmati, the self-nature of false discrimination consists of the attachment to names and forms (*nāmarūpa*) as being real, based on the manifestations of one's own mind. The self-nature of dependent origination consists of the arising of all dharmas through the power of causes and conditions, like a dream or a magical illusion. The self-nature of perfected reality consists of the non-existence of the former two self-natures within the latter, and the realization that all dharmas are devoid of the duality of grasper and grasped. The self-nature of the Tathāgata-garbha consists of the womb of the Tathāgatas, which is the storehouse of the seeds of all dharmas, endowed with the eighty-four thousand groups of teachings, and is the source from which the bodies of the Buddhas and Bodhisattvas arise. Mahāmati, these are the four kinds of self-nature. You and other Bodhisattvas should thoroughly investigate them so as not to fall into the views of the philosophers. Thus it is said: "The false discrimination, the dependent, and the perfected; The Tathāgata-garbha is likewise taught. These are the four kinds of self-nature; One should examine them well.

The Blessed One said: “Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is called ‘The Great Collection. Thus should you remember it. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, what is the cause, what is the reason, for which these bodhisattvas mahāsattvas have come from other world-systems to hear this Dharma-discourse? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, it is because they desire to hear this Dharma-discourse that these bodhisattvas mahāsattvas have come from other world-systems. Furthermore, Ānanda, there are bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who, having heard this Dharma-discourse, will attain the stage of non-retrogression. There are others who, having heard it, will attain the stage of certainty. And there are yet others who, having heard it, will quickly attain unsurpassed perfect enlightenment. At that time, the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how many bodhisattvas mahāsattvas have come from other world-systems to hear this Dharma-discourse? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, there are bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who have come from as many as ten thousand buddha-fields, twenty thousand buddha-fields, up to a hundred thousand buddha-fields, and even from as many as a hundred thousand koṭis of nayutas of buddha-fields. They have all come to hear this Dharma-discourse. Then the venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, it is wonderful, it is marvelous! To what extent does this Dharma-discourse, ‘The Great Collection,’ bring about the maturation of the roots of virtue of the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, to such an extent that it brings about their maturation. Moreover, Ānanda, if a bodhisattva mahāsattva hears this Dharma-discourse, even for a single day, or for half a day, or for a single watch of the night, or for a single watch of the day, or even for the duration of a finger-snap, then that bodhisattva mahāsattva has planted roots of virtue under many hundreds of thousands of buddhas. Why is that? Because, Ānanda, this Dharma-discourse is the source from which all the qualities of a buddha arise. The venerable Ānanda addressed the Blessed One: “Blessed One, how should one practice so as to uphold this Dharma-discourse? The Blessed One replied: “Ānanda, one should practice with reverence, with respect, and with a mind free from pride. One should not seek to find fault with it, nor should one be attached to its literal meaning. One should practice in accordance with its true intent. Furthermore, Ānanda, one should not disparage those bodhisattvas mahāsattvas who have come from other world-systems, but should instead honor them and offer them service. This is how one should practice so as to uphold this Dharma-discourse. When the Blessed One had spoken thus, the venerable Ānanda and the entire assembly, including the bodhisattvas mahāsattvas, the śrāvakas, the gods, the nāgas, the yakṣas, the gandharvas, the asuras, the garuḍas, the kiṃnaras, and the mahoragas, were filled with joy and rejoiced in what the Blessed One had taught. Thus ends the "Great Collection" Dharma-discourse, the first chapter.
